bouncing their way through a computation (Edward Fredkin and Tommaso Toffoli's, 1982), could in
principle run without dissipating at all; Bennett (2003) wrote that such ballistic machines compute
at constant velocity without dissipating any energy, and that they must be kept isolated from heat
baths and noise. Keeping one on course against noise means correcting its errors, and whether that
brings the dissipation back I don't settle here; in 2003 Bennett called the thermodynamics of error
correction a subject that appears to be in its infancy. The bead of Jun, Gavrilov and Bechhoefer
(2014) shows the other half. Put through the same moves as an erasure but with no tilt, so
nothing is squashed, its work extrapolated to the slow limit came out at $0.05 \pm 0.03\,kT$,
within two error bars of zero: no floor under it, which is what the premise says.
Keeping something costs, on top of that, either a merge, which under Landauer's premise owes a floor of
$kT\ln 2$ per bit that no slowness removes, or a state the device has never used before. Taking a
fresh state escapes the floor and does not settle the implementation's finite-time dissipation. And a finite set of states,
where every state has a next one, forces the merge.

I also built a numerical bead to see the steps, using a quartic double well.
It follows the experiment's sequence: lower the barrier for one second, ramp
the tilt, remove the tilt, then raise the barrier for one second. This is a
chosen potential and a numerical approximation, not the measured trap. The
starting positions are sampled from a numerical approximation to the thermal
distribution in that potential, with equal chances of starting in either well.

Keep three accounts as it moves. Changing the trap while holding the position
fixed does work on the bead. Moving the bead in the fixed trap transfers heat
to the bath. Whatever is left changes the bead's potential energy. These are
the steps the script actually adds up:

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[thiele]
\node[pipe,text width=5.8cm,minimum width=0pt] (a)
  {Old trap\\Bead at its old position};
\node[pipe,text width=5.8cm,minimum width=0pt,below=1.1cm of a] (b)
  {Changed trap\\Same position};
\node[pipe,text width=5.8cm,minimum width=0pt,below=1.1cm of b] (c)
  {Same changed trap\\New position};
\draw[pipearrow] (a.south) -- node[right=8pt]{work in} (b.north);
\draw[pipearrow] (b.south) -- node[right=8pt]{heat out} (c.north);
\end{tikzpicture}

\small Work in minus heat out equals the change in stored energy.
Either transfer can be negative on an individual step.
\end{center}

The work account includes removing the tilt and restoring the starting trap.
The heat account uses the potential difference during each displacement.
Those two accounts balance on every simulated path to rounding precision.
That checks the accounting; it does not show that the time steps are small
enough to reproduce continuous motion exactly.

Here is what came out, with 3,000 paths at each setting and a time step of
half a millisecond. Each setting uses a specified tilt, chosen earlier to
make roughly nine erasures in ten work. Success means ending in the right well.
The last two columns average only those successes; energies are in units of
$kT$. The time column is the tilt ramp, with the two one-second barrier ramps
in addition.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{rrrr}
\toprule
Tilt time (s) & Success rate & Heat out on success & Work in on success\\
\midrule
2  & 0.909 & 2.517 & 2.501\\
5  & 0.916 & 1.466 & 1.490\\
10 & 0.913 & 1.073 & 1.095\\
20 & 0.899 & 0.830 & 0.907\\
40 & 0.893 & 0.773 & 0.782\\
80 & 0.869 & 0.693 & 0.719\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Heat and work are close in some rows and less close in others. The difference
is measured by the simulation, not supplied as a constant correction. At the
last setting the sampling standard errors are about $0.023\,kT$ for heat and
$0.011\,kT$ for work. They do not include error from the time step or the model.

Now try to make a floor out of those six points. Fit the successful heat to a
constant plus a number divided by the tilt time: the constant is
$0.674\,kT$, with sampling error about $0.015\,kT$. Halve the time step and
repeat the six settings: it becomes $0.732\,kT$, with sampling error about
$0.016\,kT$. The second run also samples different paths, so this comparison
mixes sampling and numerical error. It is enough to stop me treating a fitted
constant near $\ln 2$ as a confirmation. The barrier ramps are still one second
long, the tilt changes between settings, and this fit does not take the whole
protocol to a slow limit.

There is a useful theoretical comparison, but it is a comparison with work.
For the continuous thermal model, beginning in equilibrium and ending with the
same symmetric trap, the detailed Jarzynski relation gives the successful
paths a mean-work bound $kT\ln(2p)$, where $p$ is the success probability.
Averaging the successful and failed paths gives the bound
$kT[\ln 2+p\ln p+(1-p)\ln(1-p)]$. At nine successes in ten these are about
$0.588\,kT$ and $0.368\,kT$. B\'erut, Petrosyan and Ciliberto's 2013 paper,
\href{https://arxiv.org/abs/1302.4417}{Detailed Jarzynski Equality applied to a Logically Irreversible Procedure},
works through the success-conditioned relation. Neither formula is a heat
bound for this simulation without also accounting for its change in stored
energy. Nor does an exact bookkeeping identity make the discrete simulation
obey every continuum fluctuation relation exactly.

The script is \texttt{scripts/bead\_erasure\_sim.py}. It reports heat, work,
stored-energy change, sampling errors and the descriptive fits, and accepts a
smaller time step for checking them. The slower settings here use less mean
work and release less mean heat. That is what this calculation demonstrates.
It does not determine a universal floor or reproduce the laboratory's fitted
constant.

\begin{longtable}{p{0.28\textwidth} p{0.64\textwidth}}
A merge, the floor & Jun, Gavrilov and Bechhoefer (2014): one bead in a feedback trap.
Squash two wells to one: $0.71 \pm 0.03\,kT$ of work, in the slow limit. Run the same
moves without the tilt, so nothing is squashed: $0.05 \pm 0.03\,kT$, also in the slow limit, within two error bars of zero. $\ln 2$ is $0.693$. Same bead, same trap. \\[3pt]

and Bokor (2016), nanomagnetic memory bits, within two standard deviations of Landauer;

$= kT\ln 2 + B/\tau$ fits with $B = 8.15\,kT\cdot\mathrm{s}$; left free, the floor of the fit
comes out at $0.72\,kT$. The floor is reached only as the time goes to infinity. \\[3pt]
The distinction itself & The same bead: the paper estimates a characteristic
Kramers escape time of about 3,000 seconds at $8\,kT$, and about ten seconds
at $2.2\,kT$. Those are statistical time scales. The barrier height controls

coherence in an isolated gas of thousands of atoms. A collective quantity of a closed system comes
back around; the full state of the gas wasn't shown to return, and couldn't be. \\[3pt]

The cited erasure experiments test specified memories and protocols, including
symmetric-memory Landauer bounds and heat versus duration. They are not an
exhaustive survey of physical computation, nor an experimental proof of the
abstract state-space dichotomy. \href{https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevD.23.287}{Bekenstein's bound}
relates entropy to energy and size under its physical assumptions; it does
not supply a finite enumeration of arbitrary device states. The finite-state
theorems here take their finite set as a mathematical hypothesis.

\subsection{Every scale pays the same way}

One more question, and it's the one that decides whether any of this is about the world or
only about my pictures. A state is a description. The dial on a lab bench is a state, and so
is each atom in it, and so is each atom together with the light it gave off. Describe the same
thing coarser or finer and you get different states. Does what keeping takes change with the zoom?

It doesn't, and the reason fits in one picture. Draw the fine states, and draw a fence around each
group of them that counts as one coarse state. Say the coarse picture merges: two coarse states
step to one coarse state. Then, when the fine states are finitely many, the fine step can't keep
them all apart either. Count them. If the fine step sent different fine states to different fine states
and none of them stepped out of the fenced set, it would be a reshuffle of the fine states, with every
fine state landed on exactly once afterwards. But some fenced group is now landed on by nothing, because the coarse step
missed a coarse state (two coarse states went to one, so on a finite set some coarse state
is stepped to by nothing), and so nothing lands on any fine state in that group. A reshuffle leaves no state out. So
something gave: the fine step merges too, or some fine state stepped out of the fenced set, or the
fenced set has no end. The three ways come back one level down, though stepping out of the fenced set isn't taking a fresh state; it's
where the coarse picture stops tracking the fine one.

\begin{theorem}[Every scale pays the same way]\label{thm:every-scale}
Let a fine machine have one rule $F$ on a set $X$ of states, let $A$ be a set of its states, and
let a coarse description be a map $\pi$ from $X$ to a set $S$ of coarse states that takes $A$
onto $S$, with a coarse rule $f$ on $S$ such that $\pi(F(x)) = f(\pi(x))$ for every $x$ in $A$.
If the coarse rule merges two coarse states, then at least one of these holds: $F$ merges two
states of $A$; $F$ takes some state of $A$ outside $A$; or some run of $F$ from a state of $A$ stays in $A$ and never comes back to a state it has visited. \end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose the fine machine avoids all three ways out. It stays inside $A$, keeps different
states apart, and every run eventually visits a state it has visited before. Follow one
run to its first repeat. The two visits have the same state, so their predecessors must
agree too: different predecessors are never allowed to land together. Walk backwards
like that until the earlier visit reaches the start. The later visit has reached the
same start. The run is a loop from the start, with no loose approach leading into it.

Now watch that loop through the coarse window. Every fine step gives the coarse step
specified by $f$. When the fine state returns to its start, its picture returns too.
Every coarse state has a fine state above it, because $\pi$ takes $A$ onto $S$.
So every coarse state also lies on a loop.

That rules out a coarse merge. Suppose two different coarse starts had the same next
state. Call the lengths of their loops $L_1$ and $L_2$. Wait $L_1L_2$ steps from the
starts: that is a whole number of circuits for both loops, so each must be back at its
own start. But after their first step they were together. The same rule cannot separate
them afterwards, so at the end of that wait they are still together. Their starts must
have been the same after all.

The coarse rule does merge, by hypothesis. The fine machine therefore cannot avoid
all three alternatives. In the last alternative, every tick visits another state of
$A$, so no finite collection can hold the run.
\end{proof}

When I say a coarse description is exact about a set of fine states, I mean what the theorem asks: it follows the fine step on the set, and every coarse state describes some state in it. Put it next to the permanent flip. On a finite coarse picture, a reading that goes up and stays
up is raised by a merge (the cell above, on three states; Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges}, two
chapters on, in general). By this theorem, at every finer
description that the coarse one is exact about, keeping that reading is again a merge, though not always where the reading rose, or a step off the described states, or a run that takes a fresh described state at every step. The dial and its
light are the example. In the dial's own picture, two blends of readings decay to one
either-or, a merge (Section~\ref{sec:pointer}). In the picture of dial and light together, the
step is one-to-one, and it's the second case: the light starts blank and leaves carrying the
copy, so the fine step leaves the set of states where the light is still blank. At the fine scale
nothing merges; the step leaves the states the coarse picture describes. And the heat floor sits where the merge
really is. Landauer's premise charges the scale whose step merges states that were really
possible; a description that merges only because it stopped looking at the light owes that
floor nowhere merely because of that projection. Leaving the set where the light is blank is not the
same as visiting a fresh full state at every later tick. To infer an endless
fresh-state run, the theorem needs its third alternative. To infer heat,
specify the physical preparation and what happens to the light or reservoir.

\subsection{What keeping takes, and where the toll comes in}

So that's the whole of what keeping takes, set out before anybody writes a price on anything. The toll, which the
next chapter states, is what keeping takes, written into a step. It's the price of something being the case: a reading that goes from no
to yes and stays is a distinction that stays, and a distinction that stays is a state the run has used and can't
give back. Anything whose state includes distinctions it can't give back pays what the toll prices:
the bead, the cell, the memory bit, a world with a past. Give one a price list that obeys the toll
and it's a Thiele machine, and when the cell could have held anything, Landauer's premise puts a
heat floor under that raise, because on a finite cell the raise is a merge. The toll keeps its
shape there, charged in heat instead of units of cost. And what keeping takes, deterministic or noisy or
quantum, comes to this: the Brownian walker has a positive dissipation rate at nonzero drift, and
the cited diffusion and jump models give finite-time distributional bounds
under their own hypotheses; keeping something
costs on top of that either a merge, with Landauer's floor when the merged states were really
possible, or a state never used before; and a finite machine, where every state has a next one, forces the merge. The step law, the
noisy steps and the unitary steps are proved, and the table above says how near the laboratory
has come to each; the heat is physics.

That's also why the rule sits on the raise and not on the merge. The toll charges for what is kept
whichever column pays for it, merge or fresh state. A price on merges charges only the merge column, so it
misses something kept by taking a state never used before: the machine that keeps every history, the first way out two chapters on, raises its reading at
zero cost under it. And it
charges merges that keep nothing, like the reset that lowers a flag. The toll doesn't ask that reset for a unit of cost, and it still merges two states, so in a real device it owes Landauer's floor whenever the
bit it lowers was really unknown; the ledger leaves that to physics, the same as the dissipation of
happening.

Next comes the smallest model that keeps that cost on its own ledger: two boxes on a sheet of
paper, a tally, and one rule.

%===========================================================================
\section{A record and a toll}
\label{sec:toll}
%===========================================================================

The last chapter found what keeping takes and kept no count of it. Now give it a ledger. Take a record with two
positions, no and yes, and build the smallest thing that could carry a charge for its change,
on paper, with a pencil. Write the charge into its rules and see what follows. Keeping it this
small is what lets you see which part of the construction does which part of the work.

The usual models charge a computation for two things: how long it runs and how much space it
uses. The bits it destroys have been counted too, as the opening said, by Li and Vitányi and by
Demaine and his coauthors. What this part charges is something else: what the computation keeps and
can't take back.
This part is about that charge, which gets paid in a merge, carrying a heat floor when the
merged states were really possible, or by taking a state never used before, and which the last chapter showed can't be talked
down to zero. The record built below is the smallest thing that can carry the charge, and the
tally next to it counts every time the record goes up. Whether a machine has to charge it as a
unit of cost, and on which premises, is the next chapter.

One thing needs saying about what a flag stands behind, because it stays out of the picture a while. What
I'm about to build prices vouching for anything at
all: a flag goes up, and the rule doesn't ask what the flag is standing behind. A sorting of a
pile into groups, the kind of structure Part~II starts from (Section~\ref{sec:structure}), is the
first kind of claim I care about. It isn't the only kind, and the book comes back to what a flag
stands behind in Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}, and on a machine in Section~\ref{sec:smallest},
where a flag stands on a checked claim. Until then nothing about the flag leans on groupings. The floor in
this section, the reason for it in the next, and the latch in Part~II all work whatever the reading is about, partition or no partition. When groupings come in,
in Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}, it's as a theorem: a reading that says a grouping has been checked
and committed sees the grouping only through its partition, and what it entitles is exactly the
groupings that refine it (Theorem~\ref{thm:partition-reading}). So the grouping gets a job,
and an exact one.

But first the word, because I've got a new one and I don't trust it either: record, receipt,
certificate, vouch. People have been making marks that other people are supposed to rely on
for a very long time, and I wanted to know what they thought they were doing, and what it
cost them, and whether any of them ever said the thing I need said. So
here's what I could reach, pushed on with you, and I'll tell you where the search ran out.

\subsection{Clay, seals, and seven witnesses}

Start a little over five thousand years ago, in the Near East, with people who counted sheep with
little clay tokens. To send a count across a distance without the courier changing it, they
put the tokens inside a hollow clay ball, pressed the shapes of the tokens onto the outside
while the clay was soft, and sealed it. The archaeologist Denise Schmandt-Besserat has
spent a career on these, and she puts the practice at around 3300 BC; the ball is called a bulla. The push is one you can do with
a cookie tin, with a paper seal glued across the lid and rim. Let it dry, then try
opening the lid without tearing or disturbing the seal. The bare lid would come
straight off; it is the seal that makes this a test. A substitute seal could fool
you, so this little trial shows a disturbance, not an unforgeable history. In the
clay ball, the outside shows the count inside and opening the ball breaks it.
That is the property the tin and seal are trying to reproduce.
The idea is a real one and it will show up again in a form you won't expect: a record is worth
something only if it can't be silently undone.

Now law, which is where people get serious about who's allowed to say what happened. The
book of Deuteronomy, chapter nineteen: nobody is convicted on the word of one witness; it
takes ``two or three.'' The Roman jurist Gaius, writing in the second century, says a will the
praetor will honour is one sealed by seven witnesses. Why seven? Gaius doesn't say. The
legal historian Henry Maine, in 1861, had an answer: the older Roman will was a mock sale, done in
front of five witnesses, a man holding the scales, and the buyer of the estate, seven people in
all, and when the ceremony fell away the seven seals kept the count. Maine's is the only account
of it I found, so treat it as his. Gaius's own text does show they kept those old formalities
around a will, and it isn't hard to see why anyone would: one person can lie, and a will moves a
fortune, and the dead man can't object. So the record isn't the paper; it's the number of independent people who have put their own
seal, their own name, their own risk, next to the claim. Try it: write ``paid five dollars,
signed A'' on a napkin and ask a friend to forge it. It takes them ten seconds. Now require two
other people to initial it at the moment of payment and each keep a copy. If the readers compare those independently kept copies and trust their
holders, changing your napkin alone will be exposed. Stolen copies, forged
initials, collusion or a reader who never compares them can defeat the test. The claim didn't change,
but what stands behind it did.

Which brings me to seals, and the medieval historian Michael Clanchy, whose book is called
\emph{From Memory to Written Record}. England between the Norman Conquest and the early 1300s
was learning to trust writing. Until then it
had trusted people who remembered. The lesson was painful: seals were forged, charters were forged, and historians today have a whole craft of
telling real charters from fake ones because the fakes are so many. A seal is only as good as
whoever holds the stamp. Keep that one too, because in 2011 a certificate authority called
DigiNotar found out, at the cost of its existence, that a mathematically perfect signature is
worth exactly what the custody of the key is worth, and intruders had taken control of the
machines that signed. It is the same failure nine
hundred years apart, and I find that oddly comforting.

And then the obvious next question: if seals could be forged, what caught the forgeries? It wasn't
the seals. The most famous forged record in European history is the Donation of Constantine,
a document in which the emperor Constantine supposedly handed rule over Rome and the western
empire to the Pope. It was most likely written in the eighth century, some four hundred years
after Constantine died, and it was leaned on for centuries. Around 1440 a scholar named
Lorenzo Valla took it apart by its Latin: the language belonged to a much later age, and it
used words, ``satraps'' among them, that no Roman of Constantine's day would have used for his
officials. (Valla wasn't even
first. Nicholas of Cusa, a German churchman and philosopher who later became a cardinal, had
already called it a forgery in 1433, in \emph{De concordantia catholica}, a long book on how
the Church and the empire ought to hang together. I know that from the reference works, and I
haven't read the book. Valla's is the version people
remember, which is a pattern that keeps turning up.) Look at what kind of check that was.
The question wasn't ``is the stamp real.'' It was ``could these words have been written when they say they
were.'' A record can pass the first and fail the second, which is a hint that what I keep
calling one thing, a record, is doing more than one job.

\subsection{Two columns and a stamp}

The one I'd never have guessed mattered is bookkeeping. Around 1300, the ledger of a
Florentine company called Farolfi, kept at its branch in Provence, shows the earliest complete example anyone
has found of a trick merchants were working out: write every transaction twice, once where the money came
from and once where it went, and the two columns have to balance. The treasurers of the city of Genoa kept their ledger for
1340 that way, and accounting historians still count it among the most famous government
account books of the Middle Ages kept in double entry. And in 1494 a friar named Luca Pacioli printed the method in a mathematics book,
and it spread. The method is double-entry bookkeeping, and it's easy to take it for just a tidy
habit.

Do it for one day. Keep two columns of every dollar that moves, and total them at night. Now
have a friend secretly change one entry in one column. The totals disagree; you catch it. Now
have them change the matching entry in both columns. The totals agree, and you've caught nothing.
Push on that and you've found what double entry actually is: a check for slips, which a
careful liar walks straight through. Did Pacioli see that? I can only get at it secondhand. The scholar Forrester, in a paper on the University of Strathclyde's accounting-history pages, reads him as reporting that in many places the
books were taken to the local consul to be authenticated before a single entry went in. The
stamp is a witness again, from outside. The two columns are the discipline; the stamp is the
claim that someone other than you will stand behind the fact that these are the books.
That works only as far as the authentication and custody distinguish this
set of books from a substitute. Keep both halves separate in your head, because one is a method and the other is a
commitment.

And then I found the place where this got turned into a motto. The Royal Society, founded
in London in 1660 and still running, picked as its motto \emph{Nullius in verba}: take nobody's
word for it. (Where did they get it? From somebody's words, naturally. It's half a line of the
Roman poet Horace, from a verse letter to his patron, saying he isn't bound to swear by the
words of any master. So the society that takes nobody's word for it took its motto from a poet
and cut the line to fit. That's not a contradiction, and it's a nice picture of the method:
borrow what's useful, say whose it was, and don't swear by it.) The historian Steven Shapin wrote a paper about what that meant in practice,
and the answer is more interesting than the slogan. Robert Boyle, pumping the air out of a
glass globe to see what happens to a candle or a bird, had three problems: the machine, the
report, and the witnesses. He solved the third by having gentlemen present who'd sign their
names, and the second by writing the report so richly that a reader who wasn't there could
picture the scene and count as a witness anyway. Shapin calls that virtual witnessing, and he
notes, dryly, that the air pump was very expensive, seventeenth-century big science. So there
\emph{was} a cost; it just wasn't a cost of declaring the fact. It was the cost of the instrument
and of getting enough people into the room. Hold on to that distinction, because the rest of the book hangs on it.

\subsection{A demon, and the step that pays}

Now comes the strangest entry, and the one that gets closest. In 1867 the physicist James Clerk
Maxwell, in a letter to his friend the Scottish physicist Peter Guthrie Tait, imagined a ``very observant and neat-fingered being'' sitting
at a tiny door between two halves of a box of gas, letting fast molecules through one way and
slow ones the other, so that one side heats up and the other cools with no work done, which
is supposed to be impossible. The being got called Maxwell's demon, and physicists have been
arguing about it for a hundred and fifty years, which should tell you something.

In 1929 Leo Szilard, a young Hungarian physicist working in Berlin, cut the demon's box down to a single molecule, and that made information part of the accounting.
The tempting move, and the one Szilard's own accounting made, is to put the whole heat floor on finding out which side the molecule is on.
Bennett separated finding out from restoring the memory for another round: measuring onto a
blank record can, in principle, be thermodynamically reversible, and resetting an unknown
record is a different operation. That does not mean a real measuring device costs nothing to build
or run. It says that learning and resetting do not carry the same unavoidable entropy
cost, and I'm about to pick a step to charge, so I need that distinction before I do.

Bennett's version of the rule, in a 2003 paper you can read, is that what must cost is ``the
erasure of a bit or the merging of two computation paths.'' That is erasing, or taking two possible
situations and making them one. And in the same paper he lists copying unknown data onto a blank
place to write among ``the most important logically reversible operations,'' the kind he says can, at least in principle, be run thermodynamically reversibly. So, in the one place in all of this where a record is priced by
physics, the unavoidable erasure charge belongs to \emph{forgetting} the unknown record. Making
a record on a blank place carries no such charge of its own. It does use up the blank place,
which is a state the machine hasn't used yet. Resetting it for reuse has a
Landauer bound when that reset removes entropy under the thermal premises. Read
that twice, because it's not what I expected either.

Making a record on a blank place is one operation. Landauer's 1961 paper names
another: set a bit to one whatever it held. If that bit is the whole state, down
goes to up, up stays up, and two possible states become one. Landauer called this
``restore to one.'' On an uncertain input it removes information, and a heat bound
then needs the thermodynamic premises.

A larger machine has more state than its flag. Two starts can both finish with the
flag up while remaining different elsewhere. The next chapter proves that, on a
finite machine whose reading is permanent, any instruction that raises it must
merge some full states. It does not say the state whose flag just rose is one of that
pair. Put one state outside the set that reads yes and two states inside it. Send the outside
state to the first inside state, and send both inside states to the second. The flag rises for the
outside state, but the two inside states are the ones that merge. These arrows describe
alternative starts, not three things happening in one run.

That is the distinction the one-bit picture hides. The instruction has a collision
somewhere, and the actual distribution of starting states determines whether that
collision removes uncertainty. A known starting state loses none under the entropy
premise, even when its flag rises (Theorem~\ref{thm:known-state}, next chapter).
A separate uncertain memory may have a reset cost, but neither its existence
nor an earlier heat payment follows from specifying a known start. The ledger can
still charge the instruction under merge pricing. A ledger charge, information
loss and a device's heat are three quantities to keep apart.

I'll put the rest of the lineage quickly, because it all points the same way. Regulators who
make brokers keep records on media that can't be rewritten (the SEC required exactly that, write
once and read many, from 1997 until 2022, when it allowed an audit trail as the other way to comply)
are pricing the hardware. The rule puts no charge on the act of writing. Haber and Stornetta in 1991, the timestamping that
Bitcoin's footnotes lead back to (Section~\ref{sec:established} follows them), chained time-stamped
records together with hashes so that changing an old entry breaks every entry after it (and
Ralph Merkle's hash tree, from his 1979 Stanford thesis on secrecy and authentication, lets one short value vouch for a great many records); try the dependency with five entries, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, adding each to the running
total: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15. Keep that sheet and make another with the second entry
changed to 3. Its totals are 1, 4, 7, 11, 16. The change travels down the chain.
Now lower the third entry to 2, and the last total is 15 again. Simple addition can be
fooled by compensating changes. A cryptographic chain needs a stronger function,
and someone must retain a trusted value to compare against. This trial shows the
dependency between entries; it supplies neither that function's security nor a
price on the record. Proof-of-work, which the
computer scientists Cynthia Dwork
and Moni Naor proposed in 1992 to make junk mail expensive and which Bitcoin later chained, is the
one framing where a record genuinely costs, and what it charges for is a search: how many
tries it took to find a lucky number. At the same difficulty, an empty and a full block face the same target for the header hash. The expected number of hash attempts agrees; the attempts on two actual blocks need not, and handling their transactions is additional work. So the
work prices the search. Proof-of-work charges nothing extra for the moment anything becomes certified. Robert Floyd
and Tony Hoare, two computer scientists asking how you'd prove a program does what it's
supposed to, attached claims to points in a program in 1967 and 1969 (``whenever you get here, this is true''), and
the claim is backed by a proof that's paid for off the machine. And the certificates of
complexity theory, which go back to Stephen Cook's 1971 work on NP, are strings designed to be cheap to check:
hand me the certificate and I can confirm the claim quickly. Whether they're also expensive
to \emph{find} is the famous open question of the field, P versus NP, and nobody knows; the definition promises polynomial-time verification. Polynomial time need not be small in practice, and it need not be less than the time to find every particular witness. This is a bound on checking, not a separate charge for setting an accepting flag. And from statistics, a ledger that runs the
other way: Dean Foster and Robert Stine's alpha-investing (2008) runs a long string of tests
against a budget of allowed false alarms, where every test spends some of the budget and each observed rejection earns budget back, even though some rejections can be false. That's the other way round from a price on vouching:
the testing rule spends and earns an error-control budget; a reward does not certify that the discovery is true.

\subsection{What they all agree on, and who they rule out}

Lay them down, and this time what shows through is not one thing. It's five different jobs
that the word ``record'' has been doing, and I'd been letting one word carry all five. Most of
them have a corpse next to them, and the corpses are different too.

Durability: the record can't be silently undone. The bulla, the write-once disk, the hash
chain and Bennett's card that has to be wiped all do this job. The corpse is the editable log, and the company
that kept its debts off the books: Enron hid its debt in side entities set up to keep it off
the balance sheet, which is how the Justice Department described the scheme in 2002, and its
auditor, Arthur Andersen, shredded the paper. Andersen was convicted for the shredding that
year, and the Supreme Court threw the conviction out in 2005 over how the jury had been
instructed; either way, the books concealed debts they should have shown. But notice that this job doesn't need a
witness at all. A copy will do: a hash chain nobody signed is still hard to change quietly, so
long as somebody else holds the latest link, because a chain with no copy anywhere can be
rewritten from end to end and recomputed, and nobody would know.

Authenticity: the record came from who it says it came from. Seals, the signature only a
key-holder can make, and the consul's stamp all do this one. The corpse is the forged charter and DigiNotar.
This job is about custody of a stamp, and it's a different job from durability; a perfectly
authentic entry can still be erased, and a perfectly durable one can still be a forgery.

Evidence: enough independent people stand behind the claim that lying is expensive. Two
witnesses, seven seals and Boyle's gentlemen do this one. It rules out anonymous assertion, and it rules out
``the universe keeps the receipt'', because information spread
into the environment is not a record anyone can read or rely on. This one is about numbers
of people and their risk. Paper has nothing to do with it.

Accounting: the record checks itself for slips. The two columns do this one. And one thing has to be kept
straight: the second column is \emph{not} an outside witness. It's you,
checking you. It catches a dropped digit. A careful liar gets past it, as you saw. It
belongs on this list as its own job, separate from the seven seals.

Cheap checking: a record whose correctness can be confirmed for much less than it cost to
make. Cook's certificates, the signature and the hash do this one. This one isn't universal,
and I thought it was. Whether checking needs to be cheaper than making depends on who you're
worried about and how much a wrong record costs you; plenty of records are checked by
redoing the whole thing, and that's fine when the thing is small.

Now for the thing none of them says. Not one of these jobs is
pricing the moment a record goes up and stays. Bennett prices merging and erasing, which that
moment might or might not be. Proof-of-work prices a search the designer chose. Bookkeeping prices
a discipline. Witnesses and seals price showing up and guarding the stamp. I looked, with
everything I had, and that's where it ran out. If there is a cost charged for that moment itself,
nobody in this lineage wrote it down, and that's either because it isn't there or because the
one person who did write it down is on a shelf I never found. The literal one-bit reset already has a thermodynamic analysis: Landauer's restore
to one. The question here is which premises force an instruction that raises a
record to merge full states, and which further premises put a price on that loss. So I'm going to have to try it myself, on the
smallest thing I can build, and let you watch. And I'll have to be honest about which of the
five jobs the small thing even attempts, because the toy has a permanent flag under its three moves, but no witnesses, authenticated identity or check of a claim.

\subsection{The smallest thing that could carry the charge}

Take a sheet of paper. Draw two boxes and label them NO and YES. The two boxes are the
reading, a single yes-or-no question asked of the state, and I'm going to be careful about what
the question is, because after five thousand years of seals and witnesses the word ``vouch'' is
carrying a lot and this toy carries almost none of it. The question is only: ``has the
designated flag been set.'' It is not ``is some claim about a grouping true,'' and it is not ``did
anyone check.'' There is no claim in this toy, no evidence, no checker, nobody standing behind
anything. There is a flag. Whether a flag can ever be made to \emph{mean} that something was
checked and can be relied on is a real question, and it's not this section's; I'll build toward
it later, and until then please read YES as ``the flag is up'' and nothing more. The state is
which box you're in, and that's the whole state, one bit. Then draw a line under the boxes for
tally marks. The marks sit outside the state. They're the running total you keep beside it as
you play, the way you'd keep score beside a board game.

Now give yourself three moves. STAY: you don't move, and you make no mark. WORK: you don't move
either (it's a stand-in for every ordinary step a machine takes), and you make no mark. VOUCH:
from NO you move to YES; from YES you stay in YES; either way you make one tally mark, because in
this toy the price belongs to the move's name, and where you were standing doesn't enter into it.
Now play. Start in NO, make any sequence of moves you like, and stop in YES. Count the marks. Then
try to reach YES with zero marks. You can't, and you can see exactly why: the only move that
crosses from NO to YES is VOUCH, and VOUCH makes a mark. Now erase the mark from VOUCH's rule and
play again. You reach YES with no marks, every time. The entire content of what I'm about to call
a rule is this, and I want you to see how little it is before I dress it up: I've decided that the
move which crosses the line makes a mark. Nothing in the toy's rules forces the mark. VOUCH does
merge, NO and YES both landing on YES, which is what the last chapter says a kept raise on two
states has to do; what nothing yet says is that a merge has to cost a mark. Here it's a choice,
what the last chapter says keeping takes, written down as a rule. The next chapter is about when a machine has no
choice.

Why tally marks, by the way? Because they're about the oldest receipt there is. The real
ones, the English treasury's notched sticks split down the middle, get their own story in
Part~II (Section~\ref{sec:counter}), fire and all. The tally on your paper is nothing like
those. Nobody holds the other half. You keep it, beside the board, and you could rub a mark out
and nobody would ever know. Hold on to that, because by the end of this section it's the reason
the toy does none of the five jobs a record does.

Here is the same toy, stated once, carefully, because this is the one place in the book where
I state it exactly and everything later points back here. \hyperref[sec:point]{The point} listed
the five parts in a sentence; here they're pinned down. The thing on your paper has five parts.

A set of states. (Here: NO and YES, and nothing else.)

A set of move names. (STAY, WORK, VOUCH.)

A step: for each state and each move name, where you land.

A cost for each move name: a whole number of tally marks, zero or more. (Zero, zero, one.)

A reading: for each state, yes or no.

Those five parts are the whole of it. Add the one rule below and I'll call it a Thiele machine.

The toy's reading has two places, no and yes. That is a choice for the toy, not for the model.
In the model the record is a place in any order you can read ``at or below'' on, and the toy's
reading is the smallest such order. Everything in this section is proved for the toy.
Section~\ref{sec:direction} proves the same for any order and gets the toy back as the two-place
case (Theorem~\ref{thm:dir-toll}).

I also want to be exact about what's not in it. There's no counter stored inside the state that's
forbidden from going down; the marks are the side tally from the board game, and the tally only
ever grows because the costs are whole numbers, zero or more. (A machine could keep the total
inside its state too; that's an extra part beyond the five, and Section~\ref{sec:counter} builds
it.) There's no window, no observer who sees only part of the state; that's a later question and
it gets its own section. And the cost depends only on the move's name; where you are when you
make it doesn't matter. That's on purpose: the charge is on the attempt, so you pay for making
the move, whatever it turns out to do. It's also a real simplification, and where a result needs
a price that depends on where you are, Section~\ref{sec:windows} says so and uses one. Last, the
step gives every state and every move exactly one place to land. A choice becomes a move name,
and a machine that has stopped steps to itself. A step that can land in several places by chance
is a different picture, and the noisy steps in Section~\ref{sec:what-a-chair-is} take it up. To apply the step law, fix the move being repeated, or include the program
and its control in the full state so that one autonomous rule chooses the
next step. Arbitrarily choosing different moves from outside is a different
case, worked through in the next chapter. Deterministic instructions alone
do not supply that fixed rule. Separately, giving every move a successor
even when the flag is already up keeps a price per
move name from charging exactly the raises: a move that raises the flag and has no next step
once it's up could cost one and never charge for anything else.

One rule, which I'll call the toll. For every state and every move: if the reading is NO
before the move and YES after it, the move's cost is at least one. That's the whole rule. It says
nothing about any other move. It says nothing about how big a mark is in anything you could
measure. One mark is one mark; what a mark is worth, why the smallest charge is one (why not two,
or a half?), and whether I had any right to decide that, come next. The middle question has a
short answer I'll give away now. What the next chapter forces, on its premises, is that a raise
that stays up, with only finitely many yes-states, merges two states, so any price on merges
lands on it. Costs here are whole numbers, which I chose so the ledger counts acts, and the
least whole number above nothing is one. The ``at least one'' comes from there.

And one theorem, which is the only thing the toy actually proves, and you've already proved
it by playing. Take any run of moves that starts in a NO state and ends in a YES state. Then
the marks it made add up to at least one. The argument in words is short enough that you can
hold the whole thing. Walk the run move by move, reading the box at each step. It read NO at the
start and YES at the end, and every move either leaves the reading alone or flips it, so at some
move it went from NO to YES. The toll says that move cost at least one. Every other move cost
zero or more. Add them up and the total is at least one. Notice what the argument did not need.
It didn't need the reading to \emph{stay} YES afterward; if a later move flipped it back to NO
and another flipped it to YES again, the toll charges twice, and the argument still goes
through. It didn't need the machine to be finite. It didn't need to know what any move does
besides what the reading says before and after. It needed the toll, and two things the five
parts already hand it: no cost is below zero, and the reading has only two values, so a move
that changes it from NO lands on YES. Give the reading a third value, a ``maybe'' between the
two, and the one-bit toll as written here charges nothing for NO to MAYBE; the toll over any order
in Section~\ref{sec:direction} charges every step that climbs, MAYBE included. That difference is
the whole reason the record is a place in an order and not a bit.

That's the whole theorem, and I'll state it once more in the exact form, because from here on
the book carries two layers side by side: what I mean, in words, and what's stated and proved,
in symbols you can hold me to. The symbols are few. $\mathbb{N}$ is the whole numbers 0, 1, 2,
and so on. $S$ and $I$ are just names for ``the set of states'' and ``the set of move names.''
Writing $\mathrm{step}: S \times I \to S$ means ``hand it a state and a move name and it hands
back a state.'' A \emph{run} is a list of move names, $t = [i_1, \ldots, i_n]$, played from a start
$s_0$, one after another. The double arrow $\Longrightarrow$ reads ``then'': the thing on its
left forces the thing on its right. For this first proof, keep your finger on the run and stop at the first YES.
The move immediately before that is the one whose charge matters.

\begin{definition}[Thiele machine]\label{def:thiele}
A \emph{Thiele machine} consists of a set $S$ of states, a set $I$ of move names, a step
function $\mathrm{step}: S \times I \to S$, a cost $\mathrm{cost}: I \to \mathbb{N}$, and a
record $\mathrm{rec}: S \to R$ into a set $R$ with an order $\le$ that is reflexive and
transitive, subject to one rule, the \emph{toll}: for every state $s$ and move $i$,
\[
\mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{step}(s,i)) \not\le \mathrm{rec}(s)
\;\Longrightarrow\; \mathrm{cost}(i) \ge 1.
\]
Nothing more is assumed of the order. In Coq this is the record \texttt{AxSys}.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Thiele machine with a two-place record]\label{def:certsys}
Take $R = \{\mathrm{no}, \mathrm{yes}\}$ with no below yes. The record is a
reading $\mathrm{cert}: S \to \{\mathrm{no}, \mathrm{yes}\}$, it leaves the down-set exactly
when it goes from no to yes, and the toll reads: for every state $s$ and move $i$,
\[
\mathrm{cert}(s) = \mathrm{no} \text{ and } \mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{step}(s,i)) = \mathrm{yes}
\;\Longrightarrow\; \mathrm{cost}(i) \ge 1.
\]
The run of $t = [i_1, \ldots, i_n]$ from $s_0$ ends at $\mathrm{run}(t, s_0)$, the result of
applying the steps in order, and its total cost is
$\mathrm{cost}(t) = \mathrm{cost}(i_1) + \cdots + \mathrm{cost}(i_n)$, with the empty run
costing 0. In Coq this is the record \texttt{CertificationSystem}, and
\texttt{two\_point\_nfi} derives its floor from the floor over any order
(Theorem~\ref{thm:dir-toll}).
\end{definition}

The toy on the paper is the second definition, and so is nearly everything in Parts~I and~II;
when a result holds for any order, the text says so. I write the yes-or-no reading as $\mathrm{cert}$. It names the flag whose rise
I am counting. What earns that flag its meaning will depend on the machine's rules.

A word on the label before the first result. I call a result an \emph{observation} when its proof
does little more than unfold the definitions, and in an axiomatic cost model that's what the
definitions are meant to do: the work is in choosing them, so the results that follow from them
in a few lines are labelled that way and the theorems with more in them stand out.

Take an ordinary computing machine and put a lamp and tally beside it.
Let computing run as before, leaving both alone. A separate mark leaves the
computing state fixed, adds one to the tally and turns the lamp on when its
named event holds. Forget the lamp and tally and the old computation is
still there, step for step. Below I build that box, compare different ways
to implement it, and ask exactly which differences its questions require.
The old machine may already have prices or a reading of its own; this
construction supplies the new lamp and its zero/one account. With effective
rules an ordinary computer can store all three parts.

\begin{observation}[The universal floor]\label{thm:universal-floor}
In any Thiele machine, every run that starts at a state reading no and ends at a
state reading yes has total cost at least 1: if $\mathrm{cert}(s_0) = \mathrm{no}$ and
$\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{run}(t, s_0)) = \mathrm{yes}$, then $\mathrm{cost}(t) \ge 1$.
\end{observation}

\begin{proof}
Read the states of the run from left to right. The first reads no and the last
reads yes, so there is a first state on this list that reads yes. It cannot be
the starting state. The state immediately before it reads no: otherwise the chosen
YES would not be the first. The move between them therefore costs at least one,
by the toll.

Now add the charges for the whole run. That one charge is already at least one,
and none of the other charges is negative. The total is at least one. The flag
may come down later and go up again; that cannot remove the charge I have found.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection*{The tabletop and the stamp}

Put two boxes on the table. Each has tiles on top, and the tiles spell the same answer.
On the side of one box the stamp is up. On the other it is down. Hang a camera directly
above them. The photographs are identical.

Now hand me the photographs and ask which box was stamped. Take a better photograph.
Enlarge it. Count every tile. None of that gets the side of the box into the picture.
The difference is there, in the boxes. It has been left out of what you handed me.

That is the window I want to name. $S$ is the set of full states of the boxes, and $B$
is the set of tabletop pictures. The map $\pi:S\to B$ takes a full state and returns
its picture. Every picture in $B$ comes from a box; that is what \emph{onto} says.
Pick one picture, $b$, and gather every full state that gives that picture. That whole
collection is the \emph{fibre} above $b$, written $\pi^{-1}(b)$.

Keep the whole collection in mind. The tiles can agree while the boxes differ in which
checks ran, which earlier pages were certified, and what was kept when those pages were
wiped. The fibre holds all the differences this camera leaves out. There can be two
states in it, a million, or infinitely many.

I started with one question: is the flag up? That gives me one yes-or-no reading of the
full state. A hundred different states can all answer yes. Reading that one flag tells
me where they stand on that one question; the other differences are still there.
Chapter~14 opens the gauge wider. It asks which checks passed and which editions were
certified, and counts how many states those answers require. Keep independently chosen
histories across arbitrarily many editions, all recoverable above the same final picture,
and the fibre has to be infinite. There is a proof of that in
Section~\ref{sec:history-capacity}.

To see exactly what the tabletop can do by itself, give these boxes two kinds of move.
The tile moves are horizontal. They cost zero, leave the stamp alone, and move the tiles
according to what is on the tabletop. The stamp never reaches into their gears. The stamp
moves are vertical. They leave the tiles alone and can raise the stamp or leave it where
it is. Once raised, it stays raised. A raise pays the toll already defined above.

These are the rules of the sliced machine. They give me a computational view that runs
on its own and a record that survives beside it.

\subsubsection*{Which question does the toll charge?}

Slide a tile one place to the right. Let that move cost nothing. Now ask a
new question: is the tile in the place it just reached? Before the slide the
answer was no. Afterward it is yes. If every question had to obey the same
toll, that slide would have to cost at least one.

Try the same trick on any free move that changes the full state. Ask whether
the machine is in its destination state. Again the answer changes from no to
yes. Charging every question would stop every free change. The reading in
the definition therefore matters: I have to say which question the toll
belongs to before I can say which moves are free.

\begin{theorem}[Charging every question stops free changes]\label{thm:all-readings-free}
Suppose equality of full states is decidable. The same instruction prices
satisfy the toll for every Boolean reading exactly when every zero-cost
instruction leaves every full state unchanged.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For a changed state, the question ``am I at that destination?'' supplies a
crossing, so the move cannot be free. In the other direction, a move that
leaves the state unchanged cannot change any reading. Every remaining
instruction already costs at least one, since prices are nonnegative whole
numbers. It therefore pays for any crossing it makes.
\end{proof}

Now keep one question and require its yes to stay yes. A free move cannot
raise that reading, because a raise pays the toll. It cannot lower it,
because the reading is permanent. It has to leave it alone.

\begin{theorem}[Free moves leave a permanent reading alone]\label{thm:free-permanent-reading}
The toll and permanence force every zero-cost instruction to preserve the
reading on every state.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Starting at no, a free move cannot reach yes by the toll. Starting at yes,
it cannot reach no by permanence. Those are the two possible starting readings.
\end{proof}

This gives two ways to state the reading part of the sliced rules. Require
horizontal moves to leave it alone and vertical moves never to lower it;
then every move keeps a yes. Or require that every move keeps a yes, keep
the toll and free horizontal prices, and recover horizontal preservation
by the two sentences above. The window rules still do their own work. A
paid move could change both the tiles and the stamp; permanence does not
make the tiles stand still.

\begin{definition}[Sliced Thiele machine]\label{def:passive-sliced-thiele}
A sliced Thiele machine is a Thiele machine with an onto view $\pi:S\to B$ and its
move names split into horizontal moves $I_H$ and vertical moves $I_V$. Write
$r(s)=\mathrm{cert}(s)$, with $\mathrm{no}<\mathrm{yes}$, and
$F_i(s)=\mathrm{step}(s,i)$. For each $i\in I_H$ there is a map $h_i:B\to B$ such that
\[
\pi(F_i(s))=h_i(\pi(s)),\qquad r(F_i(s))=r(s),\qquad \mathrm{cost}(i)=0.
\]
For each $v\in I_V$,
\[
\pi(F_v(s))=\pi(s),\qquad r(s)\le r(F_v(s)).
\]
The toll remains: $r(s)<r(F_v(s))$ implies $\mathrm{cost}(v)\ge1$.
\end{definition}

These laws hold on every state of the specified domain. In contrast, the
counter example's later live-state slice is a restricted interface: a failed
check leaves its domain. It is not a claim that all six native instruction
kinds satisfy these equations globally.

The states can be counter configurations, tape configurations, or any other states
meeting these rules. The same horizontal argument works with a whole set of claims as
the record: every horizontal move preserves the set and evolves the picture using only
that picture. The number of possible records never enters that argument.

Now give the two boxes the same horizontal moves. After one move the pictures still
agree. After two they still agree. Every next picture comes from the previous picture
and the move you named, and those agree at every step. Meanwhile one stamp stays up and
the other stays down. You can watch the tabletop for the whole run and never see the
difference you started with.

Give somebody permission to read the stamp and choose a different tile move because of
it, and they can signal through the tiles. Here both boxes receive the same moves. That
is how I keep the question fixed while asking what the window can reveal.

\begin{theorem}[What the tabletop can tell]\label{thm:passive-tabletop}
In a sliced Thiele machine, every horizontal word projects to the corresponding word of
the maps $h_i$ on $B$, and preserves $r$. Two states with the same view and different
records therefore keep the same view and different records after any common horizontal
word. No function of the view alone can recover $r$ on both states. A vertical move that
changes $r$ supplies such a pair: $s$ and $F_v(s)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Start with two states showing the same picture. Give them the first horizontal
move. Its rule chooses the next picture from the current picture alone, so the
next pictures agree too. Neither record changes. You are back in the same
situation, ready for the second move. Repeating this argument covers every move
in the word, including a word with no moves. On each side the picture follows
the corresponding $h_i$, and the original record stays put.

A proposed reader of the picture now receives the same input from both states.
It must give the same answer to that input, so it cannot return two different
records correctly. Finally, a vertical move that changes the record gives you
exactly such a pair: before and after, the picture agrees and the record differs.
Those must be different full states.
\end{proof}

The stamp remains in the full state through every one of those moves. The camera keeps
missing it for exactly the same reason it missed it in the first photograph.
 In Part~III a failed check can stop the gears. Hiding that stop
while asking the picture to predict every later free move would also hide the difference
between gears that turn and gears that cannot. Theorem~\ref{thm:native-static-shadow}
works through that obstruction; the live-state slice there keeps this boundary explicit.

\subsubsection*{The smallest price on the instruction}

Put three price cards beside a button: zero, one and two. Somewhere in the
machine there is a state with the lamp down where pressing that button
raises it. Cross out zero. It fails there. One pays the toll; two pays it
too. The toll has picked the smallest card, even though it has not forbidden
the larger one.

Now take a button that never raises the lamp, from any state. Zero works.
Go through the buttons this way. Put one beside each button that can raise
the lamp and zero beside each button that cannot. The price stays on the
button when you use it somewhere else. A button that raises the lamp once
still costs one when the lamp is already up.

\begin{theorem}[The least instruction price]\label{thm:least-instruction-toll}
Fix the transitions and reading, and supply a finite list covering the
states. The schedule just described is the unique pointwise least
nonnegative whole-number schedule satisfying the toll. It is also the least
schedule giving every trace from no to yes, from every start, total cost at
least one.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For each instruction, inspect the list for a state where it raises the
reading. If one is found, every valid schedule must charge at least one
there, and the instruction has the same price everywhere. If none is found,
the toll puts no positive demand on that instruction, so zero suffices.
Our schedule meets every demand and is no larger than any schedule meeting
them. Two least schedules must each be no larger than the other at every
instruction, so their prices agree. The trace claim follows by finding the
first crossing; conversely, a crossing by one instruction is already a trace.
\end{proof}

The list makes that search finish. With infinitely many states, searching
forever without finding a crossing does not tell me that none exists. For
the lift, there is a direct answer whenever each mark has an event witness:
put the lamp down over a base state where that mark's event holds, and press
it. It raises the lamp. Every mark therefore needs one, and computing moves
need zero because they leave the lamp alone. That proves the least zero/one
schedule even over an infinite base. A mark whose event never holds can cost
zero under the toll. Giving that mark a tally of one on every use is an
additional accounting rule. The unit in all of this is the unit of the
definition; to price a physical device in joules I still need its physics.

\subsubsection*{What the next move could tell us}

Put two boxes beside each other and read everything the task lets you read.
Suppose the answers agree. That is not yet enough to put the boxes in the
same pile. Press the same button on each. Perhaps one lamp now comes on
and the other stays dark. The difference mattered, even though the first
reading missed it.

Keep two states together only when every permitted finite continuation
gives the same required answer. Include doing nothing: the current answer
counts too. This tells us which differences the task can afford to forget.

\begin{theorem}[Keep what a later question can separate]\label{thm:future-reading-equivalence}
For a fixed deterministic machine, permitted instructions and required
observation, equality of observations after every finite continuation is
the unique coarsest equivalence that preserves the current observation and
is stable under every instruction. A deterministic implementation preserving
those steps and answers cannot identify two states separated by such a
continuation.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Agreement with oneself, reversal of an agreement, and joining two agreements
all hold one continuation at a time, so this is an equivalence. Doing nothing
checks the current observation. To check stability after a move, put that
move in front of each continuation. If two states were already grouped by
any observation-preserving, stable relation, apply its stability once for
every move in a continuation, then read the answer. Those states agree on
every continuation and belong to our equivalence. Our grouping therefore
contains every permitted grouping. Finally, if an implementation put two
separated states in one full state, the same continuation from that state
would have to produce two different answers. Determinism gives only one.
\end{proof}

Change the questions and the piles can change. A box that toggles between
two positions needs two distinguishable states if I ask its position. If
my only required answer is always ``ready'', and every later answer is also
``ready'', those positions can share one description. The task tells me
what has to survive.

\subsubsection*{The picture, the lamp and the tally}

Take an ordinary computing box. Put a lamp beside it and a tally beneath it.
A computing button moves the box by its old rule, costs zero, and leaves
the lamp and tally alone. A mark button leaves the box where it is, adds
one to the tally, and turns the lamp on if its named event holds there.
Once on, the lamp stays on. Start with the lamp down and the tally at zero.

Those instructions tell us what to do without telling us how to build the
box. One builder may keep every button press on a tape. Another may keep an
extra turn counter. I require each builder to show me the same three things:
the computing picture, the lamp and the exact tally. Its computing moves
must follow the base rule through that picture. Its marks must leave the
picture fixed and latch exactly the named event. Its prices are zero for
computing and one for marking; its reading obeys the toll and permanence;
its tally increases by exactly the charge on every move.

\begin{theorem}[Every such box has the same three-part description]\label{thm:lift-terminal}
Fix those base rules, mark events and accounting requirements. Every
implementation has exactly one map to the product of base state, Boolean
reading and natural tally that preserves the three readings. That map
preserves every instruction and every finite run. From a start with lamp
down and tally zero, it maps the reachable implementation states onto all
reachable states of the product lift with the matching base start.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Read the picture, lamp and tally, and write them down in that order. There
is no other choice for a map required to preserve those three readings.
Press a computing button. The picture follows the base rule. The lamp stays
put by the toll and permanence, and the tally stays put because the charge
is zero. Press a mark instead. The picture stays put, the lamp takes its old
value or the event's yes, and the tally rises by one. These are exactly the
two rules of the product lift. Repeat for every move in a finite run.

The clean starts agree in all three readings. Any reachable product state
has some finite list of buttons reaching it. Press that same list on the
implementation. The step argument makes its three readings the desired
product state. Every reachable product state therefore has a reachable
implementation state above it.
\end{proof}

Here are the three stages. First write a list of buttons. Then run it on
the builder's box. Then read the picture, lamp and tally. You get the same
result as running the list directly on the three-part description. Written
as arrows, after we have done it:
\[
\text{button lists}\ \longrightarrow\ \text{implementation states}
\ \longrightarrow\ \text{picture, lamp, tally}.
\]

The first arrow has only one possible meaning once the start and buttons
are fixed. The empty list gives the start; appending a button takes one
more step. This is the free history construction. The second arrow can
forget history. Its direction matters.

Turn a box halfway around with a free button. Turn it again. It is back
where it started, with the same lamp and tally. Now give another builder's
box a counter that goes up on every turn, without charging for it. After
two turns its counter is two larger. It meets all the requirements above:
the extra counter is separate from the tally of charges.

\begin{proposition}[Forgetting the turn count goes one way]\label{prop:lift-history-direction}
Even on reachable states, the three-part lift need not have a
step-preserving map into every implementation satisfying its contract.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
In this example two turns return every product state to itself. A map
preserving turns would have to send it to an implementation state that
also returns after two turns. No such state exists there: its extra
counter has increased by two. Forgetting that counter works in the other
direction and preserves both turning and marking.
\end{proof}

There is an exact way to tell when the reverse map would work. Whenever
two button lists reach the same source state, they must also reach the
same target state. Otherwise the map would have to send that one source
to two targets. Supply one access list reaching each source state, and
this condition is sufficient: run its access list on the target. Any other
list reaching that source gives the same target by the condition. The
empty list preserves the start, appending a button preserves a step, and
reachability leaves no other possible map. The turn counter fails exactly
this test: the empty list and two turns agree in the source and disagree
in the target.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[thiele]
\node[pipe,text width=2.8cm,minimum width=0pt] (a) at (0,0) {Front\\Lamp down, tally 0};
\node[pipe,text width=2.8cm,minimum width=0pt] (b) at (4.2,0) {Back\\Lamp down, tally 0};
\node[pipe,text width=2.8cm,minimum width=0pt] (c) at (8.4,0) {Front\\Lamp down, tally 0};
\node[pipe,text width=2.8cm,minimum width=0pt] (d) at (0,-3) {Front; turns 0\\Lamp down, tally 0};
\node[pipe,text width=2.8cm,minimum width=0pt] (e) at (4.2,-3) {Back; turns 1\\Lamp down, tally 0};
\node[pipe,text width=2.8cm,minimum width=0pt] (f) at (8.4,-3) {Front; turns 2\\Lamp down, tally 0};
\draw[pipearrow] (a) -- node[above=6pt]{turn} (b);
\draw[pipearrow] (b) -- node[above=6pt]{turn} (c);
\draw[pipearrow] (d) -- node[below=6pt]{turn} (e);
\draw[pipearrow] (e) -- node[below=6pt]{turn} (f);
\draw[proj] (d) -- (a);
\draw[proj] (e) -- node[right=8pt,align=left]{forget\\turn count} (b);
\draw[proj] (f) -- (c);
\end{tikzpicture}

\small The top row returns to the same full state. The bottom row does not.
Forgetting the turn count respects each turn; recovering it from the top row cannot.
\end{center}

\begin{theorem}[The smallest description that answers these questions]\label{thm:lift-reachable-minimal}
Under the preceding contract, two implementation states give the same three
readings after every common finite continuation exactly when their current
three readings agree. If every two distinct reachable implementation states
can be separated by such a continuation, projection is a bijection onto the
reachable product states. It preserves starts and steps and is the unique
start- and step-preserving map there.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If the current readings differ, read them now. If they agree, the two
product states are equal. Equal states obeying the same rule give equal
next states; repeat for every move. Projection preserves those moves, so
the implementation's readings agree throughout too.

Now require every distinct reachable pair to be separable. Two states
projecting to the same triple could never be separated, so they must be
one state. Projection is therefore one-to-one; the previous theorem makes
it onto the reachable product states. Any start- and step-preserving map
is fixed on a reachable state by a list reaching it: map the start, then
follow the list. It must agree with projection there.
\end{proof}

The same reasoning explains uniqueness more generally. Take two reachable
machines with the same answers to every button list from their starts, and
suppose each keeps no two states that all future answers fail to separate.
Supply an access list for each state of the first. Run that list on the
second. If two lists reach the same first state, append any continuation:
their answers agree on the first machine, hence on the second. Separation
in the second makes their endpoints equal. The map is well-defined and
preserves steps and outputs. Reachability makes it onto; separation in
the first makes it one-to-one. Following an access list forces uniqueness.

For our box, that smallest description keeps the tally because I asked
for the tally. Stop asking for it and repeated failed marks may become
indistinguishable. Ask for every past button and the extra tape starts to
matter. With a clean start and an event that never holds, no reachable
state has its lamp up. Counting unreachable lamp-up states would answer
a different question. ``Smallest'' here means no two retained states are
indistinguishable by the required future readings, including on an
infinite machine.

This way of grouping states is the familiar behavioral equivalence behind
minimal automata. The initial history construction and final observation
construction are treated in Rutten's \emph{The Method of Coalgebra},
Chapters 2 and 4 and Section 8.6.\footnote{Jan Rutten, \emph{The Method of
Coalgebra} (2019), \url{https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs4810/2025sp/Handouts/Rutten.pdf}.}
Here the box tells us exactly which observations and operations the lift
preserves. Choosing the event, the window and the accounting is where the
application enters. Once they are fixed, the argument above determines
which implementation differences can be forgotten.

\subsubsection*{What can choose the question?}

Take a dial with two faces and one button. Each press turns it to the other
face. For this question, supply no starting face, no lamp and no names with
an outside meaning. Draw its two arrows. Now exchange the names on the two
faces. The arrows describe exactly the same machine.

Suppose those arrows alone are meant to tell us which face deserves yes.
A rule that does not depend on our choice of names must give the exchanged
face the same reading. So both faces get the same answer. A nonconstant
reading cannot be selected that way. Give one face a role---the loaded
start, a completed job, a passed check---and we have supplied more to work
with. The role has to be stated and defended. Renaming the arrows did not
supply it.

The argument is two lines: the exchange takes the first face to the second;
respecting that exchange makes their readings equal. Those are all the
faces. It does not make every machine's reading constant. It rules out a
nonconstant reading selected from the transition structure alone on every
machine. \footnote{Checked in \texttt{coq/audit/IntrinsicBoundary.v}:
\path{toggle_symmetry_forces_constant_reading} and
\path{no_nonconstant_renaming_invariant_toggle_reading}.}

That fixes what the uniqueness claim can say. The box, lamp and tally have
a unique observable realization under the contract already proved. The
arrows by themselves do not choose that contract. Adding the word
``intrinsic'' cannot do the choosing for us.

\subsubsection*{Does the picture keep enough of the device?}

Put a lamp on a box and a hidden switch inside it. The button copies the
hidden switch to the lamp. Start with the lamp dark in both boxes, and
put the hidden switch down in one, up in the other.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
Lamp before & Hidden switch & Lamp after the button \\ \hline
Dark & down & dark \\
Dark & up & lit \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

A description that keeps only the lamp has one starting state, dark,
and is asked for two different next answers to the same button. It cannot
do it. Keep the hidden switch too and the problem disappears. This is a
reason the additional distinction is necessary for this task: the next
press can expose it. It is not a reason every task needs that switch.
\footnote{\path{hidden_bit_blocks_visible_only_dynamics},
\texttt{coq/audit/ObservationContract.v}.}

There is a complete test for this kind of description. First write down
the underlying configurations, the permitted buttons, every permitted
successor, the picture being retained, and the answers the task requires.
This is the operational model of the device. Then check two things.
Configurations with the same picture must give the same required answer
now. And the same button, from any configurations with that picture, must
leave the same next picture, for every permitted successor.

Both conditions are necessary. An answer decoder has only the picture to
read. A deterministic next-picture rule has only the picture and button.
Neither can return two different results on one input.

They are sufficient too, with explicit choices. Supply a representative
configuration for each picture and a permitted successor for each button
at each configuration. Decode a picture by reading its representative.
Compute its next picture by pressing the button on that representative
and taking the chosen successor. The two conditions ensure that every
other configuration and every other permitted successor agrees. Repeat
that argument at each step: all finite button lists preserve the required
answers. On a finite listed model this can be checked against its complete
table. For arbitrary state types the choices and their effectiveness are
separate data; the proof does not manufacture a search procedure.

This test allows several successors of an underlying configuration.\footnote{
\path{operational_adequacy_iff}, \texttt{coq/audit/ObservationContract.v}.} If two of them give different
required answers, no exact deterministic encoding of that same
configuration and button can represent both. \footnote{\path{branching_answers_exclude_exact_deterministic_encoding},\newline
\texttt{coq/audit/ObservationContract.v}.}
A probability distribution over outcomes, or a finer state including a
chosen input or seed, is a different contract and must be described as one.

The test starts with a model. Establishing that a real apparatus follows
that model still needs evidence about the apparatus: preparation, controls,
readout and the range over which the description is claimed. Passing the
mathematical test does not supply those measurements.

\subsubsection*{How long did we watch the lamp?}

Watch two boxes for three ticks. Both start dark and light on the first tick.
Both stay lit on the second and third. One stays lit forever. The other
has a counter inside that turns it off on the fourth tick.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
Tick & Enduring lamp & Delayed reset \\ \hline
0 & dark & dark \\
1 & lit & lit \\
2 & lit & lit \\
3 & lit & lit \\
4 & lit & dark \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The first three ticks do not tell the boxes apart. Pick any longer finite
watch and I can move the reset one tick beyond it. Both boxes can pay one
unit per tick and satisfy the basic toll. Only the first has permanence.
The permanent interface excludes the second by its rule, not by pretending
that the finite observation already excluded it.

The construction works for every finite horizon.\footnote{
\path{finite_observations_do_not_establish_permanence},
\texttt{coq/audit/IntrinsicBoundary.v}.} It is not a prediction that every
real record fails. It shows why a finite run alone cannot establish an
unrestricted forever claim. A proof from an adequate mechanism, or an
explicitly bounded reliability claim supported by measurements, has work
to do beyond reporting that the lamp stayed lit while we watched.

The universal floor is about every Thiele machine, a system with the toll among its conditions,
and about no system without it. One edge matters: the theorem does not assume that a YES state
exists. If no state ever reads YES, no run meets the theorem's hypothesis, so it's true of every
run and tells you nothing about any of them, which is a mathematician's way of saying it's true
and useless. The toy on your paper has a YES box, so it isn't useless there. It would be natural
to assume the system has to have at least one NO state and one YES state; the statement has no
such clause, and that's on purpose, because a theorem that applies to no run is still a theorem
and the toy is where you supply the runs.

The theorem also runs backwards, and that direction is one line. Suppose every run from a state
reading no to a state reading yes costs at least one, whichever state you start from. A single
move is a run of length one, so a move that takes no to yes costs at least one, which is the
toll. The floor from every start and the toll are the same rule, and nobody has to choose
between them. From one fixed start that reads no, the floor asks for the toll only at the
crossings you can reach without paying anything; a crossing you can only reach by paying has
already cost at least one by the time you get there.

And the bound of one is the smallest case of a count.

\begin{observation}[One unit per crossing]\label{thm:per-crossing}
In any Thiele machine, a run costs at least the number of its steps that take the reading
from no to yes, with no permanence assumed. Conversely, a system in which every run costs at least
