its number of such steps obeys the toll. And the bound is reached for every count: on the one-bit
machine with a set that costs one and a reset that costs nothing, setting and resetting $n$ times
from no crosses $n$ times and costs exactly $n$.
\end{observation}

\begin{proof}
Each crossing step costs at least one by the toll, every other step costs at least zero, and each
step is counted once, so the total is at least the number of crossings. Conversely, a single move
that crosses is a run with one crossing, so it costs at least one, which is the toll. On the one-bit
machine, each set from no is a crossing costing one and each reset costs nothing, so $n$ rounds
cost $n$ and cross $n$ times.
\end{proof}

And one more edge, because it's the first thing to bite when you ask a machine to stand behind
more than one thing. The definition has \emph{one} reading in it: one question, one flag, and
one crossing the toll charges. Once the flag is up, a second claim has nowhere to go, because
raising a flag that's already up doesn't move anything. So a second claim needs a reading of its
own, and a third claim a third: one reading per claim, each with its own crossing. Part~II builds
that properly, as a family of flags, one per threshold, with a step that raises any of them
charged at least one (Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-growing}). A step that raises three at once still
owes at least one, and nothing in the toll makes the charges add up flag by flag. Charges that
add need the composition assumptions for independent machines (Appendix~\ref{sec:parts}). The
same theorem has a count in it that is what finiteness takes. Picture the record as a row of
switches that only ever get turned on. Ten switches can change at most ten times in one run,
one switch per change, and then the row is full. (Across different runs the row can end in any
of its thousand and twenty-four settings; along any one run it climbs through at most eleven.)
A finite machine can keep only so many things up for good in its whole life. That's ``you can't
keep all of it,'' which Section~\ref{sec:established} says of a full trace, turned into a count.

\subsection{How the receipt earns its meaning}
\label{sec:does-buy}

Give the worker a whiteboard and a pen. Ask for an answer and a line underneath saying
``CHECKED = YES.'' The worker can write both. So can somebody who copied the answer and
did no check at all. The extra line has told you nothing about which happened.

Follow that problem into the machine. If an unchecked run can reach the same accepting
state as a checked run, there is nothing in that state that tells the two apart. To make
the receipt carry the difference, the machine has to close the unchecked route. The
worker can request the check; the worker cannot simply write its successful result into
the accepting record. That restriction is what gives the record its force.

Put a variable called checked beside the answer and you have another place to write.
The name does not give it authority. A program that can write yes there without doing
the check can manufacture the same display as the program that earned it.

For an earned receipt, I want the machine's rules to close that route. Every permitted
program must go through the required check before it can reach acceptance. The program
can ask for the check. It cannot give itself the successful verdict. That is the difference
between carrying words about a check and enforcing what those words stand for.

So when somebody offers a simulation, showing me where its bits go is the beginning.
Show me which instructions the simulated program can actually use, and prove that none
of their allowed sequences can forge acceptance. Preserving that boundary is part of
implementing this machine. A copy of the flag alone has not done it.

Now put the camera back over the tabletop. The same answer can sit above an accepting
record or an unearned one. The record has to survive, and the rules governing access to
it have to survive too. Those are the things I am asking the machine to keep.

\subsubsection*{Look before the concrete covers it}

The inspector arrives after the concrete is poured. The question is about the rebar
underneath. On one job it was sound. On the other it wasn't. Give both jobs exactly
the same finished appearance, and give the inspector only that appearance.

There is no amount of staring that tells those jobs apart. Searching for a sound
arrangement that could have produced this surface doesn't do it either. A sound
arrangement was possible on the bad job too. What matters is which arrangement was there.

Write $x$ for what was there, $f(x)$ for what remains to be inspected, and $P(x)$ for
the yes-or-no question about it. A good $x_+$ and a bad $x_-$ leave the same $f(x)$.
The inspector receives one identical input and is supposed to give two different answers.
Here is the whole obstruction.

\begin{theorem}[An erased distinction cannot answer its old question]\label{thm:inspection-before-loss}
Let $f:X\to Y$ and $P:X\to\{\mathrm{no},\mathrm{yes}\}$. If
$f(x_+)=f(x_-)$ but $P(x_+)=\mathrm{yes}$ and $P(x_-)=\mathrm{no}$, there is no
$d:Y\to\{\mathrm{no},\mathrm{yes}\}$ with $d(f(x))=P(x)$ for every $x$.
If $P$ is available before the loss, the enriched observation $(f(x),P(x))$ does answer
the question exactly and distinguishes these two cases above their common view.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The proposed $d$ would return both yes and no at $f(x_+)=f(x_-)$. The enriched observation
returns its second coordinate. Its two values are $(f(x_+),\mathrm{yes})$ and
$(f(x_-),\mathrm{no})$: the first coordinates agree and the second coordinates differ,
so the enriched states remain distinct.
\end{proof}

While the rebar is exposed, you can inspect it and keep the answer. Or preserve enough
evidence to inspect later. Either way, something that distinguishes the good case from
the bad one has to survive. Wiping an unrelated detail causes no trouble. Wiping the
last difference your question depends on leaves the next inspector with the same surface
and two possible pasts.

For one known question repeated along a run, the receipt can be very small. Start a bit
at yes and, at each check, replace it by the old answer AND the new answer. It says
exactly whether all checks so far passed. A later failure turns it down. The permanent
flag that says ``some certification occurred'' stays up. Put those gauges beside each
other and you can see why they answer different questions.

\subsubsection*{When the stamp merges two states}

Draw two boxes with the same tiles: Unstamped and Stamped. Pressing the stamp takes the
first to Stamped. Pressing it on the second leaves that whole box exactly where it is.
Draw both arrows. They land in the same place.

Call the press $V$. At a state $s$ where it raises the record, $s$ and $V(s)$ are different.
If another press leaves the full state fixed, then $V(V(s))=V(s)$. Those two different
states have the same successor.

Give the stamped box a hidden wheel that turns on every press. Now the picture has more
states in it. If every state reached after stamping still reads yes, and there are only
finitely many such states, a merge is forced somewhere along the continued pressing.
It can be later than the first press. Keep the entire move injective instead, and the
run has to keep finding distinct stamped states.
 Call that finite accepting region $H$ and the entering state $u$.
The move sends all of $H\cup\{u\}$ into $H$. There are $|H|+1$ distinct sources
and only $|H|$ possible targets, so two sources share a successor. The move preserves
the working picture, so both sources and their common successor lie in that same fibre.

An internal ledger belongs in that full-state picture too. If each press increments it,
two presses have different ledger values even when the stamp looks unchanged. Count
those states with the others. The toll tells me what to charge for a raise; the next
chapter gives the premises that connect charges to mergers. I want the arrows and the
bill on the same page, with the rule connecting them where you can see it.

Notice also that it asks nothing about how strong the system is, in either direction. A system
is \emph{Turing-complete} when it can imitate a Turing machine, and no stronger than one when a
Turing machine can imitate it. The theorem asks neither question. Whether the system is stronger than a Turing machine,
weaker, or exactly as strong makes no difference to the floor. Bring the five parts, charge the toll on the
crossing, and you're in scope. The floor doesn't check what you can compute, because it was
never about what you can compute; it's about what a move is allowed to do without costing anything.

That brings up the objection a theorist makes in about four seconds, so I'll make it first.
The toll is a floor, and a floor is easy to meet. Charge one unit for every move, whatever it
does, and the toll holds for any reading you like, since every crossing is a move and every
move costs one. So any computer with a step counter beside it, and any yes-or-no question at
all about its state, is a Thiele machine, and a clock passes. Nothing about that is a loophole; it's
what the definition says, and it means the definition, on its own, doesn't tie the cost to
anything kept or certified. It only says a crossing can't go unpriced. (It's also why ``a base that can
compute anything plus a flag that obeys the toll'' would be a cheap thing to call Thiele-complete,
and why the definition that gets that name, at the end of Part~II, asks for computing that costs
nothing and a record that tells starts apart, which no clock meets; Section~\ref{sec:complete}.) Three
things later in the book tie the cost down. The first is that bar: computing that costs nothing, a charge of one,
and a record that tells starts apart. The second is a ceiling: demand that a run's
total never exceed the number of times the flag went up. With a price that can depend on where
the step starts, that and the floor leave exactly one way of charging, one unit per raise and nothing else
(Sections~\ref{sec:counter} and~\ref{sec:windows}). With a price per move name, as in my definition, no system whose flag
ever rises meets both, because the raising move, played again from yes, which every move can be, raises nothing and still costs one. A clock fails the ceiling the first time it charges a step that raised
nothing. The third is order, on any certified machine, and the example of Part~III is one:
there, from a clean start, the flag can't go up
unless a passing check of a claim came first, then a commitment to that same claim, and a
clock can't fake that, because it's about which moves happened, and a clock only charges
(Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-cert-earned}).

There is also the matter of why the ledger doesn't charge for heat. A physical ledger would need the actual dynamics, distribution and protocol.
A ledger that simply charged every nontrivial move would charge by that rule, and that's the clock again:
it can't tell a run that kept something from a run that only ran. So the ledger leaves the
dissipation of happening to physics and counts one thing, the rise of a reading that stays. A zero abstract charge says nothing about physical dissipation; it just prices no crossing.

The other side of that is that nothing is in scope just for being a computation. A Turing
machine's run isn't an instance of this theorem because it's a run. It becomes one when
somebody supplies all five parts for it, says which states read yes, and proves the toll for
that cost. Until then the theorem says nothing about it, and I won't pretend it does; that limit is the
toll's scope. What keeping takes has no scope to supply, because every run of anything with one next state per state
takes a fresh state at every step, joins exactly one pair of its states into one, or goes round a
loop through its start and
keeps nothing (Theorem~\ref{thm:step-law}). The reading \emph{this isn't the state I started in}
rises at the first step and stays up exactly on the runs that never come back to their start, the
first two kinds, and those pay, in states never used before or in their one merge.

That's also where the hunch this book started from ended up, once I checked it: the night a
video about \emph{Flatland} convinced me there was another axis, a direction ordinary computing
is blind to (the Afterword, Section~\ref{sec:origin}, tells it). It isn't
a direction an ordinary computer can't reach. Hand a Turing machine a reading, charge the toll
on its crossing, and it's in scope like anything else. The possibility was always there. What
the usual rules leave out is the price.

The same goes for a system with no reading at all. If nothing in it answers ``is the flag
up,'' then nothing in it can say, from the inside, that anything is entitled to be relied on.
Whatever entitlement it ends up with gets carried in from outside, by somebody who signs
their name to it, and nothing in the system priced it. Smuggled entitlement isn't entitlement for the system, no matter whose name is on it. Be careful which way that cuts,
though. Whoever reads the signature can be perfectly entitled on their own account; that's what
an auditor has, and it's honest as long as it's called the auditor's. It isn't the system's. On
the example I build later, the reason to believe its checker says yes only when the
claim is true is exactly that kind: a proof, done outside any record the machine keeps, and
I'll say so when I get there (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}). What outside entitlement never is,
is something the system itself earned.

There's also a question I'll only start on here: bolt two Thiele machines together, and do
you get one? Run them side by side, each move being a move of one or the other, and add up
the costs. It depends on the reading you give the pair. Take a reading that can only go up
when one of the parts' readings goes up, like ``either flag is up'' or ``both are'': then any
crossing of the pair is a crossing of a part, that part's toll charged it, and the pair obeys
the toll. Take ``the first flag is up and the second is down,'' and it doesn't: that reading
turns on when the second flag falls, and nothing charges a fall. The first two readings are
proved in Appendix~\ref{sec:parts}: read through ``either flag is up'' the pair is a
Thiele machine whose floor is one. Read through ``both are,'' a run that starts with both
flags down and ends with both up costs at least two, and two is reached when each part can
raise its own flag for one.
From a start with one flag already up, one raise is enough, so two is a floor for the clean start
only. The third needs nothing beyond the one unpriced fall above. A related
composite is proved too, a host machine running a guest, read through ``the host's
own flag or its copy of the guest's'' (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-host-instance}). Whether every way of
building one machine out of others keeps the toll is a bigger question, and Appendix~\ref{sec:parts}
takes it as far as I could: some ways do, some provably don't, and it says which.

So why bother with the toy at all? It isn't because the lineage was looking for it. The bulla
was after durability, the seven seals after evidence, the consul's stamp after authenticity,
the two columns after catching slips; none of them was trying to put a price on the moment a
flag goes up, and I shouldn't pretend they were. The reason is narrower. Everywhere in that lineage where somebody \emph{did} locate a cost, but one, it sat on a step next to the flag. The flag itself
went unpriced as a flag: Szilard on the measurement, Bennett on the wiping, proof-of-work on the search, Boyle
on the instrument and the room, Foster and Stine on the test. One entry prices the crossing's own
shape, and I put it beside the toll on purpose: Landauer's restore to one, the literal two-state version of the crossing, whose
heat bound depends on the input uncertainty and the thermal premises. The flag's job never came into
it. The toy is the first thing I could build where the cost sits
on the crossing itself, and it proves that if you price that step, the floor follows
everywhere, for any machine with the five parts. That's not an answer; it's the question made
exact enough to be wrong. And of the five jobs, the toy supplies only a limited kind of retention: its three permitted moves never lower the flag. The abstract definition allows other machines with a reset. Adding that reset would change this toy, and the cost that doesn't go away is
kept by \emph{you}, the scorekeeper, beside the board. The machine keeps none of it. What the toy has is a
scorekeeper's receipt for the crossing. Whether the machine can be made to keep that receipt
itself, where a step could reach in and change it, is Section~\ref{sec:counter}'s question. Authenticity, evidence,
accounting, cheap checking: none of them is in here, and I'll say so again when it's tempting
to forget.

Let me say what I'll owe you by the end. Whether the toll is a choice or a necessity: the
next section, and I'll tell you now that the answer surprised me. What a unit of cost is worth in
anything physical: later, and only partly. What an observer who sees only a window can and
cannot recover, including whether they can even tell which step paid: its own section. And
whether the definition can be met by a machine that computes everything a Turing machine does,
with its record earned and not declared, and what it costs to vouch for
structure in one: Part~III shows that with an example, and takes most of its length on it.

For now you have a sheet of paper with two boxes, three moves, one rule that writes what the last
chapter says keeping takes into the step, and one theorem you proved yourself in about a minute. Don't let go of it.
It's the smallest version of everything that follows, and if it's wrong here, it's wrong
everywhere.

%===========================================================================
\section{Why the toll isn't arbitrary}
\label{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}
%===========================================================================

The first chapter of this part proved what keeping takes by counting states: a run of one rule that raises a flag and keeps it up either lands two of its states on one somewhere or never uses a state twice, so keeping is paid in a merge or by taking states never used before;
and a thermal implementation can incur additional dissipation under the specified dynamics. The merge-or-fresh-state part needs no premise beyond one next state for every state; the heat is physics, which I proved for Bennett's walker with Schnakenberg's formula taken as the model, and cited for devices whose states jump or drift at random in surroundings at a temperature. This chapter counts
the fresh states exactly, and asks what it takes to turn what keeping pays into a unit on a ledger. The flag I
built is one thing that stays; the result is about anything that stays.

The last chapter wrote what keeping takes into a toy as one rule, and in the toy the move that raises the
flag costs one because I said so. If that's all it is, the ledger is a long way of describing
a preference, and you should treat it the way you'd treat someone telling you their favourite
colour is a law of nature. So this chapter is me trying to find out whether a machine has to
charge it. I'll tell you the
shape of the answer up front, because I don't want you reading forty paragraphs to find out
whether there's a point. What keeping takes needs no ``if'' beyond a next state for every state: on any machine, keeping something is paid in a merge or in states never used before, and physical dissipation is a separate, model-dependent question; that's the paragraph above. Getting from what
keeping takes to my rule, one unit on the ledger for the step that raises the flag, takes three ``ifs'': there
are finitely many states that read yes, so the fresh states run out; the flag, once raised, stays up; and the
ledger charges every move that forgets. Then the move that raises the flag has to forget something,
two of the states it acts on landing on one, and pays. Forgetting is also the step Landauer's principle, my premise, puts a heat price on, when
what's forgotten wasn't already known; a known preparation alone supplies no positive entropy-loss floor. If the input is correlated with another memory, that larger physical account has to be specified too. Each of the three ``ifs'' is a way out of the theorem, and I'm
going to walk through each one, because what's on the other side of each is where the content
is. None of them is a way out of what keeping takes. Where the first fails, the machine pays by taking states it has never used. Where the
second fails, the flag comes back down, so nothing is kept and there's nothing to charge. Where the third fails,
the step still forgets, and only the ledger looks away.

One more thing before the three ways out, and it comes first on purpose.
Nothing in the argument uses the word certify. It uses a reading that can go from no to yes
and never back. A fuse that has blown is one. So is a seal that has been broken, a bit in
write-once memory, a block a chain has finalized, a measurement somebody wrote down and won't
take back. The argument below sends what keeping takes to whichever of them you point at, and the latch chapter (Section~\ref{sec:latch}) proves it
doesn't matter which one you pick. Certification is the
instance I build, for reasons I give in Section~\ref{sec:pointer} and don't claim to have
proved. So read this section as being about anything that stays. The flag is only the one I
keep on the table.

\subsection{A closed room with no spare chair}

Do this one with real objects, because the whole section rests on it and it's about ninety
seconds of work. Draw a box on the table and call it the yes room. Put three chairs
inside the box and one chair outside, by the door. Four people, one per chair; the people are
the states your machine could be in, and the three inside are the ones whose flag is already
up. One move of the machine moves everybody at once: each person stands up and goes to the
chair the rule sends them to. There are two rules. First, nobody inside the room may end up outside,
because the flag, once up, stays up. Second, the person by the door must end up inside,
because this move is the one that raises their flag.

Now try to finish the move with one person in each chair.

You can't. Three people start inside and have to stay inside, so they take the three inside
chairs between them, with nobody left out, because nobody may leave. The person from the door
has to come in, there is no fourth chair inside, so somebody has to share a chair, and two of
the machine's possible states have landed on one state. Now use the chairs as a guessing game:
secretly choose one starting chair, apply the rule, and report only the finishing chair. If two
starts are sent there, the report cannot tell your partner which start you chose. Watching the
people move would tell them, but that would be keeping information outside the finishing chair,
and the chair alone has forgotten something.

The whole argument is in that shared chair, and I want to name the piece of mathematics that
did the work, because it's old and it's not mine. If you put things into fewer boxes
than there are
things, some box gets two. People call it the pigeonhole principle; it's the one from
``The point,'' where Jean Leurechon used it in 1622 to argue that two people somewhere have
the same number of hairs, and the first name for it I could find came from Dirichlet, who used it in 1842 and later called it the drawer principle. It's the kind of fact a child accepts and a
mathematician spends a career finding new uses for. Here the use is that a step which forgets
nothing is a one-to-one shuffle, a one-to-one shuffle of a finite set of chairs lands on every
chair, so the inside chairs are all taken by insiders and none is left for the newcomer.
Finiteness, permanence and the flip are the three things that force a collision in the
instruction's map. The two starts that collide need not include the outsider: send the outsider
to one inside chair and send two insiders to another. A run from a known outside
chair can still have a uniquely identifiable start. The collision is a fact about
the instruction over possible states.

The precise statement of the argument is a theorem a few lines down, and it needs one word first.
``Injective'' is the mathematician's word for ``forgets nothing'': a step is injective when two
different starts always give two different ends. The theorem says exactly what the people and
the chairs said and takes exactly the three premises: a duplicate-free list that
names every state (finite), a reading that no step ever turns off (permanent), and one state
that reads NO before the step and YES after it (the flip). There is no price in it anywhere;
it is pure counting. I'll come back to what counts as physics, but notice that nothing so far
has been physics.

The exact words follow. For this whole section the setting is the five parts from
Section~\ref{sec:toll} without the toll: states $S$, move names $I$, a step, a reading, and (later) a cost.

\begin{definition}[Finite, permanent, injective]\label{def:fin-perm-inj}
The machine is \emph{finite} when there is a list of states with no repeats that contains every
state. The reading is \emph{permanent} when no move ever turns it from yes back to no: for all
$s$ and $i$, $\mathrm{cert}(s) = \mathrm{yes}$ implies
$\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{step}(s, i)) = \mathrm{yes}$. A move $i$ is \emph{injective} (forgets
nothing) when different starts give different ends: $\mathrm{step}(a, i) =
\mathrm{step}(b, i)$ implies $a = b$. A move that is not injective \emph{merges}.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[A permanent flip merges]\label{thm:perm-flip-merges}
On a finite machine with a permanent reading, if $\mathrm{cert}(s) = \mathrm{no}$ and
$\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{step}(s, i)) = \mathrm{yes}$, then the move $i$ merges.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $i$ were injective. Let $C$ be the list of states that read yes: go down the list of
every state and keep the ones that read yes. It has no repeats. (That is the only use of
finiteness: all the proof needs is a duplicate-free list of the yes-states.) By permanence,
used only for the move $i$, $\mathrm{step}(\cdot, i)$ sends every member of $C$ into $C$.
Being injective, it sends the members of $C$ to members of $C$ with no two landing on the
same one, so its images are as many as $C$ itself, and a list of that many distinct members
of $C$ is all of $C$. So the yes-state $\mathrm{step}(s, i)$ equals $\mathrm{step}(c, i)$ for
some $c$ in $C$, and injectivity gives $s = c$, so $s$ reads yes. It reads no, and that is the
contradiction, the same one the four people and the three inside chairs ran into.
\end{proof}

A list with no repeats, as long as the set it draws from, contains the whole set. Leave one
member of the set out and you have packed the list into one place fewer than it has members.
That can't be done: take away one occupied place and the member sitting in it, and the list is
still one too long for the places left, and it stays one too long until there are no places
left at all. This is the pigeonhole in the form Leurechon would recognise.

None of that is new. It has been sitting in two places for a long time, one in physics and one in
the theory of automata, and a physicist will recognise it on sight, so I'll start there. In 1876 Josef Loschmidt pointed out,
against Ludwig Boltzmann's account of how a gas settles down, that the laws of mechanics run
just as well backwards: reverse every molecule's velocity and the gas retraces its steps, so
mechanics alone can't make entropy only ever climb. Twenty years on, in 1896, a young
assistant of Max Planck's in Berlin pushed harder. He took Henri Poincaré's recurrence
theorem of 1890, which says that in a system preserving a finite measure of its accessible
states, almost every starting state returns arbitrarily close to itself, again and again, and used it to argue that nothing in such a system can
climb forever: give it time and it comes back down. The assistant was Ernst Zermelo, the same
Zermelo who'd put set theory on axioms twelve years later, axioms that keep out the paradox that
had sunk Frege's foundations of arithmetic (Section~\ref{sec:structure} tells that one). Boltzmann answered the same year, not
very politely, that the times you'd have to wait for a return are so enormous that nobody
would ever see one. (Jos Uffink, who wrote the Stanford Encyclopedia's entry on Boltzmann's
statistical physics, calls that reply drenched in sarcasm and bitterness, and calls Zermelo's
own paper a careful logical argument.)

Now look back at the table. A step that forgets nothing, on a finite set, is a reshuffle:
it moves everybody around in loops, and every loop comes back to where it started. A flag
that goes up and stays up is exactly a quantity that climbs and never comes back down. So a
reshuffle can't carry one, which is Zermelo's objection with the infinities taken out. On a finite set the loops are enough, and
Poincaré's theorem isn't needed. And the wait is at most as many
steps as there are states, nothing enormous. Zermelo was aiming it at the second law, and flags never came into it. A quantum recurrence result came in 1957, when P. Bocchieri and A. Loinger proved
returns arbitrarily close to the initial state under their conditions on a closed
quantum system. That is a neighbouring recurrence argument, not this finite-state proof:
even a finite-dimensional quantum system has continuously many states. Applying it to a
physical record requires saying how that record is read and how robustly it distinguishes
nearby states.

The second place stings more, because it's in computer science, and somebody got here first, again.
Picture a finite machine that reads letters, one move per letter. If every letter just reshuffles
the states one for one, automata theorists call it a permutation automaton, and the sets of inputs
such machines can pick out are called group languages. Jean-Éric Pin's 1992 paper on reversible
automata, machines whose letters act as one-to-one maps, sorts out exactly which languages those
machines recognise, and in that world this counting argument is folklore. The short version runs
like this. Start at
a state that reads no, and collect every input that ends at a yes. Because yes is permanent,
adding letters to the end of a collected input keeps it collected. A group language with that
property is either empty or everything, and everything would include the empty input, which ends
where it started, at no. So it's empty, no run of reshuffles raises the reading, and that's
Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges} with the moves as letters. Pin's paper is where I'd send you
to check the automata side. It isn't about flags or prices, and I'm not claiming it says
anything about them.

There is a broader way to look at the same obstruction. Suppose every allowed move
can be undone by another allowed sequence of moves. Start outside YES and try to enter
it. Once inside, permanence says every allowed sequence keeps you there. But the undoing
sequence must take you back outside. Those two demands cannot both hold.

On a finite set, a move that keeps all states apart is a reshuffle. Repeat that reshuffle
enough times and every state comes home; all but the last repetition therefore undo one
application. So the undoing sequence needed in that argument is available. Morgan Rogers
studies systems of composable moves in his 2019 and 2021 papers on toposes of monoid actions.
That more general language gives this fact another home. Here the chairs and the undoing
sequence already show why it holds.

Going quantum doesn't get around the automata version either. Alex Brodsky and Nicholas
Pippenger (2002) showed that a quantum finite automaton that measures only once, at the very
end, accepts with bounded error exactly the group languages, the reshuffle kind. One that's
allowed to measure after every letter, and to stop on what it sees, does better: it accepts
every piecewise testable language, and ``has seen a $b$ somewhere'' is one of those. A
measurement that can stop the machine is a record that stays, and it's the extra thing that
lets the bigger class in.

The third place is the closest, and it isn't old at all. In 2023 Thomas Ouldridge and David Wolpert
derived the thermodynamics of a finite automaton built the way real computers are:
the same physical step run again and again, each time touching only the part of the machine
that changes. They sorted languages into two kinds by the smallest automaton that recognises
each one. If that automaton has a letter that sends two states to one, every automaton for the
language has such a letter too, and on their derivation
recognising the language on a device like that produces entropy, waste no cleverer design gets back, unless the inputs are so finely arranged that only
one of the merged states ever actually turns up. If the smallest automaton only reshuffles, they find the language
can be recognised with no unavoidable entropy production at all. One of their worked examples is
the strings with no $b$ in them, which is my flag turned inside out: the runs that raise it are
exactly the strings that have seen a $b$. So the counting argument, a real price on it, and the
case when you already know which state you're in are all in their paper, three years before this
book. Their price is derived from the physics of the device, and mine is assumed.

There's a fourth neighbour, and I'd call it
a cousin, because it speaks another language. Constructor theory is David Deutsch and Chiara Marletto's programme for stating
physics as which transformations a device that runs in a cycle can and can't bring about, and
in it a task is irreversible when it's possible and its inverse isn't. Marletto's version of
thermodynamics (posted in 2016) leans on exactly that: tasks that are possible while their
transposes aren't. Marletto, the physicist Vlatko Vedral and coauthors (2022) made an irreversible task out
of the quantum homogeniser, a machine of reservoir qubits that interact by partial swaps,
and ran it with photons. Maria Violaris and Marletto (2022) then argued that the same machine, run
in a cycle, can turn a pure qubit into a mixed one
and can never turn a mixed qubit back into a pure one,
even though every interaction in it is reversible, and that this suggests erasure may cost something beyond Landauer's bound. The counting argument is a classical,
finite, exact cousin of that sentence: a set of states a step can't leave, a task that's
possible, and no way back. Theirs is quantum and approximate and aimed at physics' price;
mine is counted, and assumes its price. Deutsch and Marletto's paper on information (2015)
has a neighbour of the counting argument in its section 8.6: measuring one observable
disturbs another irreducibly, and nothing can undo the disturbance afterwards while the
outcome stays in an information variable. It's a second, theory-independent way of saying
that a record that stays makes the step irreversible.

So what I can claim here is narrower again, and I'd rather say exactly how. Even the pricing form is, in physics and on their derivation, Ouldridge and Wolpert's: a merge the language can't avoid costs entropy. A price assumed rather than derived isn't mine
either: Li and Vitányi (1996) took a unit charge for every bit irreversibly erased, with steps that
can be undone priced at zero, as axioms of a model of computation, and Demaine and his coauthors
(2016) put a price on named instructions that destroy bits, a unit for an AND or an overwrite. What
I didn't find anywhere I looked is what a price on merging moves forces on a reading that stays,
charged on a ledger whether or not anybody's physics is right (put a price on merging
and the flip has to pay it, which is the next subsection), and what I get out of that: the
toll, as a theorem about the ledger, the merge-or-revoke split for a single move, the exact match between ``forced to be priced'' and ``merges'', the squeeze bound counted in whole units
and its entropy form, a built machine walking out through each of the three ways out, and every proof on the page. Those are
the forms I didn't find stated anywhere I looked, and Appendix~\ref{sec:whats-mine} sorts them the
same way: the counting core classical and somebody else's, the pricing form only partly mine. The core
move is older than the computer, it had two homes before it got to mine, and its physical price
had a third.

\subsubsection*{Count the alternatives before putting a price on them}

Write $N$ different starting configurations on cards and spread them across the bench.
Run each through the same rule once. When several cards give the same full configuration,
put them in one pile. Run the rule again and gather the new piles. Once cards agree on
the full state, the same rule gives them the same next state too.

Count the different configurations after each tick. Call their set $Q_t$ and their
number $q_t$, with $q_0=N$ and $Q_{t+1}=F(Q_t)$. The difference $q_t-q_{t+1}$ tells you
how many alternatives disappeared on that tick. Four distinct configurations landing
at one state lose three alternatives in one landing pile. Keep those two counts beside
each other: three alternatives lost, one landing place.

\begin{theorem}[The alternatives balance exactly]\label{thm:ensemble-balance}
For a total deterministic rule $F$ and $N$ distinct starts,
\[
\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}(q_t-q_{t+1})+q_T=N.
\]
If all endpoints fit in $K<N$ full states, a transition at some $t<T$ identifies two
different members of $Q_t$. If all endpoints are one full state, the total loss is $N-1$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
An image has no more elements than its source, so every difference is nonnegative.
Add the differences: each intermediate $q_t$ cancels, leaving $q_0-q_T$.
If $q_T<N$, at least one difference is positive; at that step a map from more states
to fewer cannot be one-to-one. In particular, one final full state leaves a loss of $N-1$ alternatives.
\end{proof}

Turn the cards over before counting them together. Two runs might show the same answer
on the front and still carry different inputs on the back. Those are different full
configurations. The count follows everything the machine kept.

Now put a price rule beside the piles. Let $p_t$ be the price at tick $t$, and require
every landing pile to have at most $2^{p_t}$ distinct sources. The number arriving is
then at most $2^{p_t}$ times the number of places they land:
$q_t\le2^{p_t}q_{t+1}$. Multiply that inequality through the run and you get
\[
N\le 2^{\sum_{t<T}p_t}q_T.
\]
The rule connects the bill to how tightly the machine can pack the alternatives.

\subsection{Now charge for forgetting, and the toll falls out}

This is the step I'd been circling since the counting on states. In the last chapter I told
you Bennett's rule as he states it: what has to cost is erasing a bit or merging two paths a
computation could have taken. I didn't ask you to believe it. I'm not going to ask you now
either. I'm going to write it down as a rule you can accept or refuse, in the smallest form
that does any work: \emph{any move that forgets something costs at least one.} Any move that
is not injective has cost at least one. Notice what it does not say: nothing
about certifying, nothing about flags. It's a price on forgetting and only on
forgetting.

Put the two together. The first theorem says: on a finite machine with a permanent flag, the move
that raises the flag forgets something. The price says: a move that forgets something costs
at least one. So the move that raises the flag costs at least one. That is the toll, the rule
the toy was handed because I said so, and now a machine has to charge it. The proof is two lines: the first theorem
says the flipping move merges, the premise says merges are priced, done. I'll keep saying
``premise,'' because that's what it is, and because a section further on
(Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}) is about what happened to some very smart people who put a price where a premise goes and
then treated it as a law of nature, and about half of this one is me trying not to do that.

\begin{premise}[Merge pricing]\label{prem:merge-pricing}
Every move that merges costs at least one: for all $i$, if $i$ is not injective then
$\mathrm{cost}(i) \ge 1$.
\end{premise}

\begin{observation}[The toll from finiteness, permanence, and merge pricing]\label{thm:toll-derived}
On a finite machine with a permanent reading whose cost satisfies merge pricing, every move
that turns the reading from no to yes costs at least one. That is, the machine with that cost
is a Thiele machine in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:certsys}, and the universal floor
(Observation~\ref{thm:universal-floor}) applies to it.
\end{observation}

\begin{proof}
A move that flips the reading merges, by Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges}; merge pricing
charges it at least one.
\end{proof}

The theorem asks for more than it uses. Only the yes-states need to be finitely many: with a
permanent reading and finitely many states reading yes, the rest of the machine as large as you
like, merge pricing still gives the toll. With infinitely many it can fail: the first way out below
builds a machine that raises a permanent flag at zero cost while charging every merge. That machine
hasn't got out of paying. It pays by taking a state it has never used, and a price list that charges only merges never looks
at the fresh states it takes. And merge
pricing asks for more than the toll needs. Under those same two conditions the toll holds exactly
when every move that flips the reading somewhere and merges is priced. Merge pricing gives that, and the eight-state machine described later in this
section, with its jump repriced at zero, meets the toll without merge pricing.

That ``more'' has an exact size. On a finite machine a move merges exactly when it turns on some
reading that it never turns off. If it merges, take the reading ``this move can land here.'' The
move never turns it off, because everywhere it lands reads yes; and some state reads no, because
a move that sends two states to one lands on fewer states than the machine has, and from that
state the move turns the reading on. If it doesn't merge, it turns on no reading it never turns
off: that's Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges}, whose proof asks permanence only of the one move.
So on a finite machine a price list meets merge pricing exactly when it meets the toll for every
reading at once, each move answering only for the readings it never turns off. The charge on
forgetting isn't a second kind of price beside the toll. What the premise chooses is which
readings the toll answers to: the flag alone, or every reading a move keeps.

There is one more way to see the same thing, and I give it because it answers a rival I'd otherwise owe you. The
rival says: leave certification alone. Price \emph{erasure}, and keep an honest flag that reports
when something was erased. Fine; but a system can set its certificate at cost zero with its
erasure flag reporting nothing, exactly because the certifying move merged two states and
the flag didn't say so. Make the erasure
flag honest, so that it reports every move that forgets, and on a finite machine with a
flag that stays up the erasure law charges the same cost the toll does. The toll isn't a rival to
honest erasure accounting; it's what honest erasure accounting says about the certifying
move.

So, is the toll arbitrary? The honest answer is that the toll is a consequence of three
things: finitely many states that read yes (a finite memory is plenty), a flag that stays up,
and a charge on forgetting. If you accept all three, you don't get to refuse the toll; it's
forced. If you refuse any one of them, the toll on my ledger goes back to being my preference.
The cost stays where it was; what's gone is the proof that my ledger has to charge it. So the question ``did I have to pick it'' has turned into
three smaller questions, which is what progress usually looks like: a better set of things to argue about. Let me take the three ways out in order, and for each one
build the machine that leaves through it, because a premise you can't see the counterexample
to is a premise you're taking on faith.

\subsection{The first way out: keep everything, and pay by taking fresh states}

Take a strip of paper that never runs out of boxes. The machine's whole state is the strip.
Each move writes a 1 in the next empty box, and the flag is up as soon as any box has a 1 in
it.
Check the three premises. It is permanent: once there's a 1, there's always a 1. It flips: the empty
strip reads NO, and after one move it reads YES. It forgets nothing: every move can be undone by
erasing the last 1, so two different strips never become the same strip. So this is a machine
that raises a flag, keeps it up, and never merges anything. The theorem that a permanent flip on a finite machine merges has no grip on
it, and a price list that charges only merges doesn't charge it. But look at what each move does:
it writes in a box nobody has written in before. The raise takes a fresh box, and so does every
step after it, forever. It hasn't got out of paying. It's paying in the other column, by taking a state it has never used, and
a price list that only charges merges isn't looking at that column. (Each physical write may incur a model-dependent finite-time cost; what the strip dodges is the
floor a merge would add on top.) In the exact form its state is a row of 1s of any length, which is how you say the strip has no end.

If the endless strip feels like a cheat, it's a famous one. David Hilbert, in a lecture course in the winter of 1924--25, told a story about a hotel with infinitely many rooms, every one of them taken,
where a new guest still gets a room: everybody moves from room $n$ to room $n+1$, and room 1 is left empty. The hotel is that other column, the fresh states, told as a joke about a front desk: nobody shares, and every
guest in the building packs up and moves one room along, into a room that's occupied as he moves,
by a guest who's moving on at the same moment, so that one room at the front is left empty. The guests go one-to-one into a part of the hotel, with
a gap left over.
The part worth checking is that Hilbert never published it. The hotel became famous
because George Gamow put it in a popular book in 1947, and for a long time it wasn't clear Hilbert had told it at all. The historian of science Helge
Kragh first guessed that Gamow had made it up. Then Tilman Sauer, a historian of science who
had co-edited a volume of Hilbert's lectures on the foundations of physics, pointed him to Hilbert's lecture
notes, which had just been printed in 2013, and in 2014 Kragh took his guess back in a paper called
``The True (?) Story of Hilbert's Infinite Hotel.'' Keep the question mark. Even Kragh's own paper
puts the lecture in January 1924 in one place and January 1925 in another. Still, this time a story
everybody repeated turned out to have a real lecture behind it. I've learned not to count on that
happening. Bring it back to the table. In the closed room, the person from the door had nowhere to sit because the chairs ran out. In Hilbert's hotel they never do, so everybody shifts one
over and nobody has to share. The strip machine is that hotel. The argument stays the same.
What the hotel shows you is that the whole argument was about running out of states all along.

What walked out is the finiteness premise. Now cut the strip to eight boxes.
Keep the same rule: fill the next blank box from the left, leaving every
earlier mark alone. There are nine possible strips, including the blank one.
After eight moves the strip is full. What should the ninth move do?
If a full strip stays full, the seven-mark strip and the full strip both
go to the full strip. That is the collision. If the machine stops instead,
its next-step rule is partial. If it clears the strip, its YES reading
comes down. Each escape changes a premise.

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}cll@{}}
Marks so far & Strip & Next strip under the stay-full rule \\ \hline
0 & \texttt{00000000} & \texttt{10000000} \\
1 & \texttt{10000000} & \texttt{11000000} \\
$\vdots$ & $\vdots$ & $\vdots$ \\
7 & \texttt{11111110} & \texttt{11111111} \\
8 & \texttt{11111111} & \texttt{11111111} \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Eight unrestricted bits have 256 configurations. These nine are the ones
this particular prefix-filling rule permits. A fresh configuration need
not use a fresh physical box; changing a pattern can reach one too.
Keeping the whole history is exactly the move Bennett made in 1973, when he showed
that any computation can be done without forgetting if you let it keep a copy of everything it
did; Landauer, back in 1961, had already written that for a machine able to run a program that doesn't stop, the
space to hold every intermediate result ``cannot be there.'' Keeping the history is a real way
to pay. It costs a memory that never fills, and every machine you can buy has a memory that fills.

Bennett wasn't the first there, or the last. Yves Lecerf, in a short note to the French
Academy of Sciences in 1963, had already shown that reversible Turing machines can simulate
arbitrary ones, and the note went largely unnoticed. The computer scientist Tommaso Toffoli
(1980), and Edward Fredkin and Toffoli together (1982), both then at MIT, built reversible logic:
gates and circuits that compute any function and lose nothing, by carrying constant inputs in and
extra outputs out. Their basic gate wasn't new even then. Landauer's own 1961 paper writes down a
three-bit device that replaces $r$ by $p \cdot q$ when $r$ is 0 and by the negation of $p \cdot q$
when $r$ is 1,
calls it logically reversible and capable of an AND, and says each AND then needs its own supplied
ZERO and leaves its extra outputs behind. He doubted such a machine could be useful. What Toffoli
added was the proof that it computes everything. And the computer scientist Kenichi Morita (1996) proved that reversible
two-counter machines are universal, so even a machine as small as the one Section~\ref{sec:smallest} builds, handed its input encoded, can compute everything with every move one-to-one. Every one of them keeps what it doesn't forget somewhere:
a history, garbage outputs, a counter that codes the past. The strip is one of those: it keeps the whole history, box by box.

There are three separate claims here, and I need to keep them apart. The
strip machine is permanent and forgets nothing. It also has infinitely many states:
no finite list holds every finite strip. Neither of those involves a cost. The third does: the
strip can raise its reading at zero cost. Count the strip's length as a whole number and let each move add one at a price of zero.
Nothing merges, merge pricing holds, and the toll fails. This is what a price list that charges
merges and nothing else looks like on a machine with endlessly many states to take: the raised reading shows up at no
charge on the ledger because the column it's paid in is one the price list doesn't charge.

The same thing holds for one move instead of a run, and in that form it says exactly how many states the move needs.

\begin{proposition}[A raise with no merge takes endlessly many states]\label{prop:raise-needs-room}
Let a move never turn a reading from yes to no, let it raise the reading at some state $s$ (no
at $s$, yes where the move sends $s$), and let it send no two different states to the same
state. Then it sends the states that read yes one-to-one into a part of themselves that leaves
at least one of them out: the state the move sends $s$ to. So there are infinitely many states
that read yes. With finitely many, the raising move merges two states.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The move sends every yes-state to a yes-state, because it never turns yes to no, and it sends
different states to different states. It sends $s$ to a yes-state. If some yes-state $c$ were
also sent there, the move would send $s$ and $c$ to one state, so $s = c$; but $s$ reads no and
$c$ reads yes. So the yes-states are sent one-to-one into the yes-states with that one left out.
If there were only $n$ yes-states, that would put $n$ things one-to-one into $n - 1$ places,
which the pigeonhole forbids. So there are infinitely many.
\end{proof}

The proposition is Hilbert's front desk as a theorem, and it's also exactly how Richard Dedekind
defined an infinite collection in 1888: one that can be matched one-to-one with a part of itself
that leaves something out. So with no merge, every raise has to send the kept things one-to-one
into a part of themselves with a gap left over, and only endlessly many of them have a gap to
spare.
Taking a fresh state isn't the absence of what keeping takes but the other way of paying it, and only a machine with endlessly many states
can keep paying that way.

\emph{Which state is being counted.} Whether a move merges depends on what the state keeps. The
strip keeps its history, so nothing merges; cut it to eight boxes and the stay-full rule merges.
Section~\ref{sec:landauer} proves the general form (Theorem~\ref{thm:u24-history}): keep the
list of every earlier state alongside the current one and every fixed-instruction step is
one-to-one. (Keeping only the one state before isn't enough: two states that differ only in what
came before them still land together.) So a merge
price is a fact about a move on a stated state space. Each price derived in this book is derived
on the whole state its definition gives, and three things go with it: which state that is, what
lies outside it (nothing outside it is charged), and whether the move is one primitive instruction
or a composite run of several. Relabelling the states one-to-one changes no price, since it sends
merges to merges and one-to-one moves to one-to-one moves. Adding history to the state, or
projecting part of the state away, changes the machine being modelled, and the price can change
with it.

The first way out deserves a number, because ``a memory that never fills'' is doing all the work and
I'd rather see what keeping takes than take it on trust.

\begin{proposition}[Merge, or a fresh state every step]\label{prop:heat-or-room}
(1) Let a machine run by one rule, so that every state has exactly one next state, and let its
reading never go from yes back to no. Take any run in which the reading goes from no to yes.
Then either some step of the run merges two of its states (two different states of the run
have the same next state), or the run never visits the same state twice. So on a machine with $M$ states, a run that keeps a record
and never merges has fewer than $M$ steps. (2) Let an operation send every value to one fixed
value and leave that value alone. Take a machine with $M$ states run by one rule, a reading of
its states, and $N$ different starting states, exactly one of which already reads the fixed
value, such that from every start each of the next $T$ states reads the fixed value. If no two
different states among those the runs sit in at steps $0$ to $T-1$ have the same next state
(the operation is carried out through $T$ repetitions without merging), then
$M \ge 1 + (T+1)(N-1)$. When $N \ge 2$, a bounded memory delays the merge and does not avoid it; with only the resting start there need be no merge.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
(1) Suppose no two different states of the run share a next state, and suppose the run still
visits some state twice, once early and once later. Walk the two visits back together, one step
at a time: two equal states whose predecessors are both in the run had equal predecessors,
because nothing merged. The early visit gets back to the start first, and the later visit is
then at the start too. So the run comes back to its start after some number $p$ of
steps, and since one rule gives the next state, it comes back again after $2p$, $3p$, and so on
forever. The start reads no: a yes there would stay yes all along, and the reading does go from
no to yes. Some of those returns come after the raise, where the reading is yes and stays yes,
and each of them is the start, which reads no. So the repeat was impossible. A run that never
merges takes a state it hasn't used at every step, and with $M$ states that's at most $M - 1$
steps.
(2) Count the states along paths. Walking two equal states back together, as in (1), is allowed
at any step from $1$ to $T$, because the states one step earlier are at steps $0$ to $T-1$.
Each of the $N - 1$ starts not already in the fixed reading, followed through $T$ repetitions,
occupies $T + 1$ states, and none twice: a repeat would walk back to the start equalling a later
state of its own path, and every later state reads the fixed value while the start does not. Two
of those paths cannot share a state either: walk back to the earlier time, and either two
different starts are one state, or a start is a state that reads the fixed value. That
is $(T+1)(N-1)$ states. The start that already reads the fixed value, followed through $T$
repetitions, ends in one more: if that state were on one of the paths, walking back would again
put a start at a state that reads the fixed value. One more is all that start is owed, not
$T + 1$: every state on its own path reads the fixed value, so walking back along it finds no
contradiction, and the path may fold onto one state, as it does in the machine built below.
\end{proof}

The number is exact, not only a floor, and you can build the machine that reaches it. One
state for the start that already reads the fixed way; the operation leaves it there.
For every other start, lay out a row of states, one state longer than the number of
repetitions you want to survive. The first state in the row reads the way that start reads,
the rest read the fixed way, and the operation walks the row, sending its last state to
the common fixed state. This also works for zero requested repetitions, when a row
contains only its start. Count the states: one, plus a row for each of the other starts.
For as many repetitions as you asked for, no two distinct visited source states land on
one. If there is at least one other start, the next repetition merges its row's last state
with the fixed state: both go to the fixed state. With no other start, the one fixed state
idles forever and no finite retention horizon follows. A single fixed reading isn't
needed either. If the operation sends every state to one of a few resting states and leaves each
resting state alone, and every resting state is one of the starts, the same walking back counts the same rows
inside each resting state's own catchment, the starts that end at it. The total comes to one state per start, plus, for every
repetition, one more state for each start that isn't a resting state. With one resting state that is the
bound in the proposition, and the same rows in each catchment show it exact.
In the exact form: $N$ starts, $L$ of them resting states, $T$ repetitions, at least $N + T(N - L)$ states,
and that many are enough. In bits: a memory of $B$ bits has at most $2^B$ states, so surviving $T$
repetitions with one resting state takes $B \ge \log_2\bigl(1 + (T+1)(N-1)\bigr)$. The memory grows with the
logarithm of how long the history is kept; a fresh state at every step isn't a fresh cell at every
step.

So the strip uses fresh configurations for as long as its record stays up
without a collision. Cut its permitted state space to a finite size and
the counting bound applies. A configuration is a pattern, not a newly
allocated cell. Bennett's 1989 construction saves storage by undoing and
redoing intermediate work while retaining enough to recover it. Those
extra transitions buy a time--space tradeoff. They do not let a fixed
autonomous run under this fresh-state premise reuse a configuration.

Bennett's Brownian model supplies a separate tradeoff: reducing its bias
reduces its mean forward speed and its heat per net forward step. At zero
bias its mean drift is zero, although individual random walks still move.
Theorem~\ref{thm:time-bill} concerns that model, not every physical step.
There are two accounts: configurations in the structural argument, and
entropy production under specified thermal dynamics. The total autonomous
run just counted, after a new permanent raise, must have a collision
somewhere in its continued orbit or take endlessly fresh states. The
collision need not be on the entry arrow. Counting gives that alternative;
a physical implementation determines its resource costs.

\subsubsection*{Two levers, and whether their hidden moves commute}

Put two reset levers on the box. Pull left then right, and look at the tabletop.
Now start over and pull right then left. The picture agrees. Open the box as well:
are all its hidden parts in the same places? That is the extra demand in this example.
The order of the levers must leave the whole machine the same.

Use three tabletop values, $0,1,2$. The first lever wipes only $1$ to $0$. The second
wipes only $2$ to $0$. They commute on the tabletop. Choose one starting full state above
each value and allow every word of at most $T$ lever pulls. Call everything reached by
depth $t$ $R_t$. Through the promised horizon, each lever must give different successors
to different states in $R_{T-1}$, even if those states were reached at different times.
You know which lever was pulled, so the two levers may reuse a landing state.

\begin{proposition}[The exact room for exclusive resets]\label{prop:exclusive-room}
For $T\ge1$, the minimum finite installed carrier has $T+3$ states without a commutation
requirement, and $2T+2$ with commuting hidden levers. These are also the respective
minimum sizes of $R_T$ when larger carriers are allowed. With commuting levers that are
one-to-one on their \emph{whole} domain, the minimum $|R_T|$ is $2T+3$, attained for every
$T$ by one infinite machine. At $T=0$ the reachable minimum is three in each class.
\end{proposition}

Count the zero states first. Write $F,G$ for the hidden levers and $z,a,b$ for the starts
reading $0,1,2$. At depth $t$, let $Z_t$ contain the states reading zero. The first lever
takes every state in $Z_t$, and also $a$, into $Z_{t+1}$. Their successors must be distinct.
So $|Z_t|\ge t+1$. Add $a$ and $b$ and there are at least $T+3$ states.

A single line of zero states reaches that number. Use $z_0,\ldots,z_T$, advance the line
with either lever, and fix its last state. Put $F(a)=z_0$, $G(b)=z_0$, $G(a)=a$ and
$F(b)=b$. The final zero state stays outside $R_{T-1}$. Try the levers in opposite orders
at $a$, though, and the hidden states disagree. To make them commute, count again.

\begin{proof}[Counting when the hidden levers commute]
Start above $1$ and pull only the lever that leaves $1$ alone on the tabletop.
The hidden box can still move. Watch its first $T+1$ states,
$a,G(a),\ldots,G^T(a)$. Do the matching experiment above $2$, watching
$b,F(b),\ldots,F^T(b)$. The first list reads $1$ throughout; the second reads $2$.
If either list never repeats, its $T+1$ states, the at least $T+1$ zero states already
counted, and the other starting state give $2T+3$. There is enough room already.

So suppose both lists repeat. A deterministic run first follows an approach and then
enters a loop. Let the first approach take $r$ pulls and its loop take $p$ pulls;
let the second take $s$ and $q$. The loop lengths $p,q$ are at least one.
Call their first loop states $\alpha=G^r(a)$ and $\beta=F^s(b)$.
There are $r+p$ different states on the first approach and loop, and $s+q$ on the second.
All have been reached within the promised horizon.

At those loop states, switch levers. From $\alpha$, the first $F$ pull changes the
reading from $1$ to zero. From $\beta$, the first $G$ pull changes $2$ to zero.
There are $L=T-r$ pulls left in the first experiment and $M=T-s$ in the second.
Write the resulting two rows of zero states as
\[
A=\{F(\alpha),\ldots,F^L(\alpha)\},\qquad
C=\{G(\beta),\ldots,G^M(\beta)\}.
\]
Neither row repeats. If two entries agreed, walk their predecessors backwards together.
All those predecessors occur by depth $T-1$, where the lever keeps sources apart.
Eventually the earlier entry would reach the nonzero seed while the later one still
read zero. That is impossible. The rows therefore contain $L$ and $M$ states.

Can the rows cross? Suppose their $i$th and $j$th entries are the same state.
Pull $F$ another $q$ times. Seen from the second row, commutation lets you do those
pulls at $\beta$ before its $j$ pulls of $G$. They take $\beta$ once around its loop
and bring it back. So the shared state returns to itself after those $q$ pulls of $F$.
The same argument, exchanging the levers, returns it after $p$ pulls of $G$:
\[
F^{i+q}(\alpha)=F^i(\alpha),\qquad
G^{j+p}(\beta)=G^j(\beta).
\]
I have just proved there are no repeats within either displayed row. The returns must
therefore lie beyond their ends: $i+q>L$ and $j+p>M$. Only the last $q$ entries
of the first row and the last $p$ of the second can be shared. There are at most
$\min(p,q)$ shared states.

Now add the two nonzero lists and both zero rows, subtracting the shared entries once:
\[
|R_T|\ge(r+p)+(s+q)+L+M-\min(p,q)=2T+\max(p,q).
\]
The approach lengths disappear because every pull spent on an approach leaves one fewer
pull for its zero row. If either loop has length at least two, the count is at least $2T+2$.

Only two one-state loops remain: $p=q=1$. If the zero rows do not meet, adding them
without a subtraction gives $2T+2$. If they meet, the crossing restriction puts their
only shared state at both ends. Call it $c$. It is fixed by both levers.
The initial zero state $z$ must now supply another place. To see why, suppose it lay on
one of the rows. Starting there would reach $c$ in at most $T-1$ pulls. The state just
before $c$ on the first row is also reachable by then, and is different from $c$.
The first lever sends both to $c$, violating its promise on $R_{T-1}$.
Thus $z$ lies outside both rows. Count it, and the total is $2T+2$ again.

Finally strengthen the promise: each lever keeps different sources apart everywhere,
even beyond the horizon. A crossing would give the return
$F^{i+q}(\alpha)=F^i(\alpha)$ above. Now you may walk backwards all $i$ steps,
without a horizon restriction, giving $F^q(\alpha)=\alpha$. The left side reads zero
and the right side reads $1$. So in this case the rows cannot cross at all.
Their count with the nonzero lists is $2T+p+q$, which is at least $2T+3$ unless
both loop lengths are one.

In that last case you need one more state. If $z$ is outside the rows, it is the extra
state. If it lies at $F^i(\alpha)$ on the first row, pull $F$ from $z$ another $T$
times. This is allowed from an initial state and reaches $F^{T+i}(\alpha)$.
The whole zero row can never repeat under the global promise, by the same backward
argument used earlier. This new state lies past its displayed end. It cannot be on
the other row either, because the crossing argument still applies, however far you go.
Its zero reading also keeps it off the two nonzero lists. If $z$ lies on the second
row, pull $G$ instead and make the same count. Every case gives at least $2T+3$.
\end{proof}

Build the finite box with two arms and a shared endpoint. The $F$-arm has
$a_0,\ldots,a_{T-1}$; the $G$-arm has $b_0,\ldots,b_T$. Each lever advances its own arm
and fixes the opposite arm. Both fix the common end. Read $a_0$ as $1$, $b_0$ as $2$,
and everything else as zero. Start at those two heads and at $z=b_1$.

At horizon one, there are just four places. Write every arrow down:
\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}ccccc@{}}
State & Tabletop & Pull $F$ & Pull $G$ & Start? \\ \hline
$a_0$ & 1 & end & $a_0$ & yes \\
$b_0$ & 2 & $b_0$ & $b_1$ & yes \\
$b_1$ & 0 & $b_1$ & end & yes \\
end & 0 & end & end & no \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
On the three starts each column has three different destinations.
On the whole four-state carrier each column has a repeated destination.
The horizon promise and the everywhere promise are different. Try both
orders at $b_0$: either order ends at $b_1$. The other three rows also
agree in both orders.
The endpoint first appears at depth $T$. By then every one of the $2T+2$ states has been
reached, and until then each lever keeps its sources apart.

For one-to-one levers on the whole machine, keep the two arms disjoint and let them run
forever. Give them a separate fixed zero state, and start at that state and the two heads.
After $T$ pulls the reachable population is exactly $2T+3$. The same box works at every
horizon.

Change the tabletop and the chairs can fit differently. Give it two bits, with one lever
clearing the first and the other clearing the second. Lay out an infinite grid with
nonnegative integer coordinates $(i,j)$ and a separate blank state. One lever adds one to $i$, the other to
$j$, and both fix blank. Read a grid point as $([i=0],[j=0])$ and blank as $(0,0)$.
Start at blank and the three grid points $(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)$.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth, every node/.style={align=center,font=\small}]
\node (a) at (0,0) {grid $(0,0)$\\reads $(1,1)$};
\node (b) at (4,0) {grid $(1,0)$\\reads $(0,1)$};
\node (c) at (0,-2.7) {grid $(0,1)$\\reads $(1,0)$};
\node (d) at (4,-2.7) {grid $(1,1)$\\reads $(0,0)$};
\draw[->] (a)--node[above] {first lever}(b);
\draw[->] (a)--node[left] {second}(c);
\draw[->] (b)--node[right] {second}(d);
\draw[->] (c)--node[below] {first lever}(d);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
Both orders reach the very same grid point, not just the same reading.
The separate blank state also reads $(0,0)$ but is fixed by both levers;
it is not the grid's origin.

A pull adds one to $i+j$. The three grid starts have sums zero or one, so no word
of length at most $t$ can go beyond $i+j=t+1$. Conversely, the origin is a start. For any
other point in that triangle, start at $(1,0)$ if $i>0$, and at $(0,1)$ otherwise.
Exactly $i+j-1\le t$ pulls reach it. That gives the whole triangle. Its rows have
$1,2,\ldots,t+2$ points. Pair the first row with the last and count, then add blank:
\[
|R_t|=1+\frac{(t+2)(t+3)}2.
\]
Adding to one coordinate is one-to-one on the grid, and neither grid shift reaches
blank. Adding to different coordinates in either order gives $(i+1,j+1)$, so the levers
commute on the whole carrier. The reading follows the two clears because incrementing
a coordinate makes its zero-test false and leaves the other zero-test alone.

This count also meets the lower bound. Each one-cleared fibre starts with one state.
The appropriate clear sends that fibre and at least one $(1,1)$ state into it injectively,
so its population increases by at least one per depth: at depth $t$ it needs $t+1$.
The $(0,0)$ fibre also starts with one. At depth $j+1$, one clear sends both its $j$-depth
population and a one-cleared fibre of at least $j+1$ states into $(0,0)$ injectively.
Its population therefore increases by at least $j+1$. Summing from $j=0$ to $t-1$
gives $1+t(t+1)/2$. Add the one $(1,1)$ state and the two one-cleared populations:
$1+2(t+1)+1+t(t+1)/2=1+(t+2)(t+3)/2$. The three-value box needed extra room for commutation. This two-bit box fits
its best count while keeping commutation intact.

\subsection{The second way out: let the flag come back down}

Take one coin. The rule is: turn it over. Heads is YES, tails is NO. Every move is undoable
(turn it over again), so nothing is forgotten. Tails goes to heads, which is a flip, NO to YES,
and heads goes to tails, so the same move takes the flag back down somewhere else. There are
two states, as finite as it gets, and the move that raises the flag forgets nothing, so a
schedule that charges only for forgetting is allowed to charge it nothing. The move is
injective and can switch the reading both on and off. Pricing the turn at zero
meets merge pricing, since no move merges, and fails the toll.
The premise dropped on this way out is permanence.

There's a fact here sharper than the premise it replaces, and it was the thing
in this section that surprised me. Drop permanence entirely and keep only finiteness, and take
any move that raises the flag anywhere. Then one of two things is true: the move forgets
something, or the same move lowers the flag somewhere else. There's no third option, and the
proof below is a search: go through the finitely many YES states looking for one this move
turns to NO. Find one, and that's the revocation; find none, and the move is permanent at
least for itself, which is all the argument from fresh states needs. So a flag that goes up
without a merge is a flag the same move can take back. A flag that nothing takes back is paid
for. You can't have a raise at zero cost that stays raised, not on any finite machine, not
with any price schedule that charges for forgetting. The sentence is narrower than ``every
certificate costs.'' It's true, and I'll take it.
The broad one would only be mine.

\begin{theorem}[Merge or revoke]\label{thm:merge-or-revoke}
On a machine with finitely many states reading yes (no permanence assumed), if $\mathrm{cert}(s) = \mathrm{no}$ and
$\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{step}(s, i)) = \mathrm{yes}$, then either $i$ merges, or there is a
state $t$ with $\mathrm{cert}(t) = \mathrm{yes}$ and $\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{step}(t, i)) =
\mathrm{no}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Check every yes-state on the finite list for one that $i$ sends to no. If there is one, that
is the second alternative. If there is none, then $i$ keeps every yes-state at yes, which is
permanence for the single move $i$; the argument of Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges} uses
permanence only for the move it is about, so it applies, and $i$ merges.
\end{proof}

I'll give you the three-card version too, because it shows that a move can
be forced to be priced without writing anything permanent, and I don't want you to think the
picture is tidier than it is. There are three cards, T0, T1, T2, with a star on T1.
The rule is that T0 goes to T1, T1 goes to T2, and T2 goes to T1. T0 gains the star (a flip).
T1 loses it (a revocation). T0 and T2 both land on T1 (a merge). So this move is priced, by
the forgetting rule, and yet it writes nothing permanent; it takes a star away in the same
breath. ``The priced moves are exactly the permanent records'' is false, as the three cards
just showed. What's true is one direction: on a finite machine, every permanent raise is a
priced move. The other direction has the three cards standing in it. And ``priced'' here has
an exact meaning worth one sentence: a move is \emph{forced to be priced} when every schedule
that charges for forgetting charges it, and that holds exactly when the move forgets
something, with no finiteness needed at all.

\begin{definition}[Forced to be priced]\label{def:forced-priced}
A move $i$ is \emph{forced to be priced} when every cost function satisfying merge pricing
(Premise~\ref{prem:merge-pricing}) charges $i$ at least one.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Forced price is merging]\label{thm:forced-iff-merge}
A move is forced to be priced exactly when it merges. No finiteness is needed.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $i$ merges, merge pricing charges it at least one, whatever the cost function. If $i$
does not merge, define the cost that is $0$ on $i$ and $1$ on every other move. It satisfies merge pricing, since every merging move is some move other than $i$ and costs one, and it charges $i$ nothing, so $i$ is not forced. \end{proof} A cost here is any rule from move names to whole numbers, so that one is there whether or not anything can tell $i$ from the other names. A test that tells them apart comes in only when a cost has to be computed by a program, and then the program needs it to tell $i$ from the rest.

\begin{corollary}[Permanent records are forced]\label{cor:permanent-forced}
On a finite machine, a move that never turns the reading off and turns it on somewhere is forced to be priced. (By Theorem~\ref{thm:merge-or-revoke} it merges, and merge pricing charges every move that merges, whatever the cost function.) The converse fails: the three cards are
forced, because they merge, and they revoke.\proofclosed
\end{corollary}

\subsection{The third way out: don't charge for forgetting}

The third way out is the easiest to describe and the hardest to argue about, so I'll
describe it and then spend the rest of the section on the argument. Take a sheet of paper and
let its reading be just BLANK or STAMPED. There is one move: stamp it if blank, and leave it
alone if already stamped. It is finite, with two readings. It is permanent, since STAMPED
stays STAMPED. It has a flip, since BLANK goes to STAMPED. Both possible readings now end at
STAMPED. The paper's fibres, the ink and your memory are outside this two-state description;
the merge is a loss from the reading, not the disappearance of every physical trace.
Everything the argument from fresh states needs is here, and the move merges. Now
set the price of that move to zero. The toll fails, and you can watch it fail: the flag went
up at zero cost.
The premise dropped on this way out is the charge on forgetting. (A price of one on that move
satisfies all three premises, so the premises can hold together; the third way out is about
whether they must.) Nothing in counting stops you from setting that price to zero. Only a
claim about the world does. The nearest such claim is Landauer's, and I have to be exact
about the gap between the two: the premise as written charges \emph{every} forgetting move,
whether or not you knew which state you were in, and Landauer's own heat, as the coin under
the cup below will show, is owed only for what you didn't know. Merge pricing keeps only a
yes-or-no distinction: whether any pair can merge. The one-bit reset is where it comes from,
and it measures neither the full worst-case entropy loss nor the heat of any particular
preparation. The counting needs only that rule.

Here is what Landauer said, in 1961, as exactly as I can put it. I went past the
summaries and read the paper itself. A logical operation with no single-valued inverse (a step that
forgets, in this book's words) must produce heat, ``typically of the order of kT'' per operation, where
k is Boltzmann's constant and T is the temperature; and for the specific case of resetting
one bit whose value you don't know, the minimum is kT times the natural log of 2, about 0.69
kT. I want you to hear two things in that. First, ``of the order of'': he was not handing out a
number to three decimals. Second, and this surprised me, he did not measure anything. The
paper is argument, with models. He writes that he can ``show, or at least very strongly
suggest'' the conclusion, and that his reasoning gives ``no guarantee that this minimum is in
fact achievable.'' That's the founding paper of the whole subject, and it's a careful man
saying ``I think this is right and here's why.'' I like him more for it.

Was it measured, eventually? Yes, and only recently. In 2012 a group at the École Normale
Supérieure in Lyon, Antoine Bérut and Sergio Ciliberto's lab working with Eric Lutz, trapped
a single glass bead, two millionths of a metre across, in a
double well made of laser light, and used the two wells as the two values of a bit. Then they
erased the bit, by lowering the barrier, tilting the trap, and raising it again, many times
over, slower and slower, and measured the heat each time. The average heat came down toward
