becomes a condition on rates: the rate of hopping from any state $x$ to any state $y$ is at least
$c$ times $\pi(y)$, for some fixed $c > 0$. Split the rates in two again: a part that, at rate
$c$, forgets where the device was and redraws it from $\pi$, and the rest, which still satisfies
detailed balance. The production rate adds over the two parts, because with detailed balance it's
the rates times quantities that don't depend on the rates. The rest produces nothing negative,
and the redraw part alone produces at least $c$ times the relative entropy still left. So
relative entropy falls at least as fast as $e^{-ct}$. One wrinkle needs its own line. A known
start puts all its weight on one state and none anywhere else, and the logarithms in the
relative entropy go bad at zero. The relative entropy is still continuous at the starting
instant, because each of its terms has the form $u \ln (u/\pi)$, and $u \ln u$ goes to zero as
$u$ does. So adding up the production from the start out to infinity gives exactly
$-\ln\pi(s)$.

I should say what Doeblin's condition costs. It asks for every hop to be possible directly, in
one step or at a positive rate. A device whose states reach each other only through other states
can still settle, and the standard theory of these chains says when: always, for a device that
hops at random moments and can get from any state to any other; and for a chain that ticks, as
long as it also doesn't march round a cycle. Those devices meet the condition for some fixed
stretch of time or number of steps instead of one, and the same argument runs on blocks of that
length, because the relative entropy never goes up in between.

Then come the stretches. The bound used the fact that the long-run chances of up and down stand in the
ratio of the mean stretch lengths, and I took the mean length of a stretch with the flag up to be
the long-run weight of the up-states divided by the flow into them. For a chain that ticks, that's right for the following reason. Start each stretch the way the flow starts them, count the steps until the chain
leaves the up-states, and the average is exactly $\pi(\mathrm{up})$ over the flow. Look at the
long-run weight that has been up at each of the last $k + 1$ ticks. It splits in two: the part
whose stretch began exactly $k$ ticks ago, which is the flow times the chance that a fresh stretch
lasts more than $k$ ticks, and the part that was up one tick earlier still. Add those splits from
$k = 0$ up to some $K$ and the sum telescopes: $\pi(\mathrm{up})$ is the flow times the sum of
those chances, plus the weight that has been up for more than $K$ ticks. The sum of the chances
that a stretch lasts more than $k$ is its mean length. Doeblin's condition makes the leftover die:
from any up-state the next step lands in the down-states with chance at least
$\delta\,\pi(\mathrm{down})$, so the weight that has stayed up for $K$ ticks is at most
$(1-\delta\,\pi(\mathrm{down}))^K$.

With the stretches measured in seconds, when the device hops at random moments, it comes out the
same, by a different route. Ask, for each up-state, how long on average the device takes to
leave the up-states from there. Call that its leaving time. The leaving times are finite: from
every up-state the device hops into the down-states at a total rate of at least
$c\,\pi(\mathrm{down})$, so the chance a stretch is still running at time $t$ falls at least as
fast as $e^{-c\,\pi(\mathrm{down})\,t}$, and no leaving time is more than one over
$c\,\pi(\mathrm{down})$. And they obey one plain rule, which you get by asking what happens in the
first instant: from any up-state, the rate out of it times its leaving time, minus the rates into
the other up-states times their leaving times, comes to exactly one (per second times seconds is a
pure number). Average the leaving times over the way the flow starts stretches, multiply by the
flow, and the rule plus the balance of the steady spread (as much weight flows into each state as
out of it) rearrange the sum into exactly $\pi(\mathrm{up})$, so in seconds too the mean stretch is its mass over the flow. Both of
the bound's premises are proved now, in steps and in seconds, under Doeblin's condition.

One chapter remains in this part, and it's about a different way out entirely. Forgetting has had
its chapter; the question after that is whether \emph{finding out} costs, because the demon's
whole trick was that it knew which way the molecule was going, and I owe you a straight answer
on what knowing costs.

%===========================================================================

\section{Learning borrows, committing pays}
\label{sec:narrowing}
%===========================================================================

I ended the last chapter owing you an answer about knowing. What keeping takes
so far sits on forgetting: under merge pricing, a finite machine's permanent flag-raising
instruction was paid for because it merges two states somewhere. But there's a thing that looks
like the opposite of forgetting and feels like it ought to cost at least as much, probably more,
and that is finding out. Every time a machine rules out a possibility, it knows more than it did. If
forgetting a bit costs, does learning one cost too? I had a strong feeling about this, and you
probably have it too, so I'll say it first: learning is the expensive part. Most physicists had
that feeling as well, for a long time. It's why the demon took a hundred and fifteen years to
exorcise, or didn't. ``Exorcise'' is the word the people who think it worked like to
use. John Earman and John Norton, the doubters from the last chapter, called their two-part
paper on it ``Exorcist XIV: The Wrath of Maxwell's Demon,'' and I read that Roman numeral as a
joke about how many times the demon has been declared gone. So hold the word loosely. This
section is me finding out where the feeling goes wrong, and where it's right. I'll give the answer
up front. Looking can have a physical cost; its value needs a model of the measurement. But it doesn't have to
merge anything, so it owes no floor, and a ledger that charges merges can charge it nothing. What
it does use up is a blank page to write on. Learning borrows that page. Wiping the page to use
it again is a merge, and that's where the floor gets paid. Committing, making a record nobody can
hand back, is paying for good. I'm going to tell you the version where the exorcism worked,
Charles Bennett's,
because it's the version that says where the heat goes, and the third way out in the last chapter, the one Landauer's premise is there to close, stays open behind it.

\subsection{Somebody got there first, goddamn it}

I'd been sitting on this idea that \emph{committing}, making a result stay so it can't be handed
back, is what pays, and learning, writing on a blank page you could hand back, only borrows, and I thought: this
one's mine, I finally had an original thought. Then I found Carlo Rovelli's 2024 paper, ``The
Thermodynamic Cost of Choosing.'' I hadn't. Somebody got there first, goddamn it: a real physicist, with
a real paper, saying that making a choice that sticks dissipates at least the energy Landauer charges
for erasing a bit. He even quotes a German saying, \emph{Wahl ist Leiden}, to choose is to suffer, and at
that point what are you going to do but laugh.

And then, taking him apart properly, it got good, because on its face he contradicts Bennett. Bennett
says measuring owes no floor; Rovelli says any measurement costs. So which is it? Look at what Rovelli
calls a choice. A coin in the air hasn't chosen anything; it has to hit the ground and stop. And
then comes the sentence I'd put on my wall: ``stabilization must be irreversible, otherwise it is not
stabilization.'' Bennett's floorless measurement is one that could still be undone; that's \emph{why} it
owes no floor. It only borrows the page. Rovelli's choice is one that's been made to stay; that's why it costs. The way I read them,
they're standing on opposite sides of the same line: learning, which borrows, on Bennett's side;
committing, which pays, on Rovelli's. (Bennett's demon still pays in the end, when it wipes the page.) Neither of them puts it
that way, so push on it. But if it holds, it's the best sign I've got that the line I'm drawing between finding
something out and making it stay isn't something I made up.

Push on it with his paper open and it gives in four places, which I go through at the end of
this chapter, once the demon has been built. So the two-sides-of-one-line picture is my reading,
not his, and the piece of it that's really his is the one sentence about stabilizing. That
sentence I'll still put on my wall.

So he's my closest neighbour, and the difference between us is exact. His is physics: a dissipation bound,
at least $kT \ln 2$ at the temperature of the recording parts, with no outside heat bath, for a
choice that sticks. Mine is a rule in a model of computation: a charge in
the machine's own count, on the step that flips a permanent reading on, with no temperature anywhere
in it. It's the same instinct in a different place, and I'll take it, because it's annoying to be second
but worse to be alone and wrong. And he's the closest only on choosing. On copying there's an older neighbour, in
the chemistry of copying molecules, and the end of this chapter gets to it.

\subsection{A small being at a small door}

You met Maxwell's demon briefly in Section~\ref{sec:toll}. It gets a whole section here,
because the step it seemed to pay for and the step it actually pays for are what this section
is about.

In December 1867 James Clerk Maxwell, who had published his equations for
electricity and magnetism two years before, in 1865, and to my mind had as good a claim as anyone to being the most important
physicist alive, wrote a
letter to his friend Peter Tait describing a problem he couldn't get rid of. Take a box of gas
at one temperature, with a wall down the middle and a tiny door in the wall. Now imagine, he
said, a ``very observant and neat-fingered being'' sitting at the door, who can see individual
molecules coming. When a fast one approaches from the left, it opens the door and lets it
through. When a slow one approaches from the right, same. Otherwise it keeps the door shut.
It never pushes anything; it only opens and closes a frictionless door at the right moments.
After a while the right side is hot and the left side is cold, and you've got a temperature
difference you could run an engine off, made out of nothing but \emph{looking}. That's supposed to
be impossible; it's the thing the second law of thermodynamics says can't happen, and the
second law is the law physicists are least willing to give up. Arthur Eddington, the English
astronomer, wrote in a 1928 book of popular lectures that a theory
found to contradict it has nothing for it but to collapse in deepest humiliation, and nobody
has had to test that yet.

Maxwell put it in his textbook in 1871, and it got named Maxwell's demon, though not by
Maxwell. William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, called it a demon in \emph{Nature} in 1874, and
Maxwell, in an undated note to Tait headed ``Concerning Demons,'' tried to take the name back:
``Call him no more a demon but a valve \ldots'' Nobody listened, which is probably for the best,
because ``Maxwell's valve'' would not have lasted a century. But keep his correction, because
it's exactly right and it's the whole problem: the being does no work. It opens and shuts a
door. So physicists
spent the next century trying to find where the being was cheating. I want you to feel the
pull of the obvious answer, because I felt it and so did most of them: the being has to
\emph{see} the molecules, seeing costs, and the case is closed. In 1929 Leo Szilard built a one-molecule
version of the box and did the arithmetic, and said the second law survives if finding out
which side the molecule is on costs at least as much entropy as the being gains. In 1951 the French physicist Léon
Brillouin made it concrete: to see a molecule you have to bounce light off it, and the way the
philosopher of physics Jeffrey Bub sums up the result, finding out that way costs at least
k ln 2 of entropy for every bit, which is kT ln 2 of heat, Landauer's number before Landauer, and there was your charge on
looking. For thirty years that was the answer. Information costs because getting it costs.

That's a price on one way of looking, and it doesn't show that every possible way of
making a record has to pay it. A device can burn energy without that being a law.

Szilard is worth one more minute, for a reason that has nothing to do with the demon. Four
years after the one-molecule engine, in September 1933, by his own later telling, he was
waiting at a traffic light on Southampton Row in London, having just read a newspaper report
in which Ernest Rutherford, the physicist who had announced the atomic nucleus in 1911, called the hope of getting power out of atoms moonshine, and as the light
changed it occurred to him that an element which gave off two neutrons when it swallowed one
could keep a reaction going by itself. That's the nuclear chain reaction, thought up crossing
a street. It's his memory of himself, and Richard Rhodes's history of the bomb opens with it, in a
first chapter called ``Moonshine,'' which is where most
people meet it, so hold it as the man's own story, not a record made at the time. Does it change
anything about the demon? No. What it adds is a picture of the man: the same mind looked at one
molecule in 1929 and one neutron in 1933, and both times the question was what a single small
step forces downstream.

\subsection{Bennett moves where the heat is paid}

In 1982 Charles Bennett, who'd already shown in 1973 that computation can be done without
forgetting if it keeps its whole history and pays by taking states it has never used instead, took the demon apart one step at a time. The being looks at a molecule and writes
down which side it's on. Is writing that down a merge? Picture the being's notepad, which
starts blank. After looking, the notepad says ``left'' or ``right.'' There are two possible worlds before
the look (molecule left, pad blank; molecule right, pad blank) and two possible worlds after it (left,
``left''; right, ``right''), so nothing merged: two went in, two came out, and you can read the before off the
after. Copying what you see onto a blank page forgets nothing, and a step that forgets nothing
owes no floor under Landauer's premise. Any finite-time physical cost additionally depends on the chosen dynamics and protocol. But it did use
something up: the blank page. Before the look, the pad was blank and
ready; after it, the pad is full. Brillouin had priced one particular way of looking (bouncing
light) and took it as the price of getting information at all. Bennett gave a way of looking
that, on his account, doesn't pay that price. It borrows a page instead.

So where is the heat floor? The being has one notepad and a lot of molecules. After the first
molecule the page is full, and to do the next one it has to wipe the page. \emph{Wiping} takes two
possible worlds (pad says ``left''; pad says ``right'') to one (pad blank), and that's the merge,
the step with no way back. For a complete reusable engine under the stated thermal assumptions, the
memory reset and the feedback process must be accounted for together. The
cycle cannot turn information about the molecule into net work from a single
bath while restoring every other resource for free. It's the rule from his 2003 notes that I quoted in Section~\ref{sec:toll}: erasing
and merging carry the unavoidable charge, and copying onto a blank place to write doesn't. The
look borrows the page. Resetting an uncertain page without using its
correlation with the molecule has the corresponding entropy-loss floor under
the thermal assumptions. While the molecule is still available, the joint
operation can instead undo the copy; the four-state example below does that.
A blank supplied at the start is an initial condition. To charge its
preparation, specify what uncertain state was reset and how.

Section~\ref{sec:toll} separated making a record from resetting it. Now you can see
exactly which step pays, and why the other one was tempting, because looking \emph{feels} like the active part,
the thing the being does, while wiping feels like housekeeping.
In that reset protocol, the housekeeping is where the entropy-loss floor applies. If there's one sentence in this section I'd want you to carry out of it, it's that one, and the idea in it is Bennett's.

\subsection{Two different things called ``narrowing''}

Here is what I had to get straight in my own head before any of this made sense, and I'll give
it to you as a picture because that's how I eventually got it.

Draw the machine's possible states as a row of dots. Now draw a second row above it: the
dots that \emph{you}, standing outside, still think it might be in. Those are two different rows:
the first is a fact about the machine, and the second is a fact about you, about what you've
seen and what you've ruled out. Both rows can shrink, but they shrink for different reasons, and
only one of them costs.

The machine's row shrinks when two of its states land on the same state, which is a merge, and
a merge is what the price charges. Under the halving rule from Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}, a run can't shrink the
machine's own row by more halvings than it paid for. That's the theorem just below, and
it's that section's halving price run forward along a whole program, where that section took it one step at a time. There is no new idea in it,
only the same counting of states.

To state it exactly, write $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ for the index-bit count of $n$: the smallest whole number
$k$ with $2^k \ge n$, the fewest yes-or-no questions that can guarantee identification among $n$ things
when arbitrary binary splits are allowed. It is $0$ at $n = 1$, and $0$ at $n = 0$ too, since $2^0 \ge 0$; the definition covers empty lists, where the logarithm of zero isn't a number. Wherever I write an ordinary logarithm without the rounding, its argument
is positive. For a run $t$ and a list $D$ of
starting states, let $\mathrm{img}_t(D)$ be the set of states the run can end in, starting
from somewhere in $D$, and write $|\mathrm{img}_t(D)|$ for how many there are (in Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} the
symbol for one move already meant the count; here I need the set and its size both). Let
$\mathrm{cost}(t)$ be the run's total cost.

\begin{theorem}[The machine's own narrowing is priced]\label{thm:machine-narrowing}
If the cost satisfies the halving price (Premise~\ref{prem:halving}), then for every run $t$
and every list $D$ of starting states with no repeats,
\[
|D| \;\le\; 2^{\mathrm{cost}(t)} \cdot |\mathrm{img}_t(D)|, \qquad\text{so}\qquad \lceil \log_2 |D| \rceil \;\le\; \mathrm{cost}(t) + \lceil \log_2 |\mathrm{img}_t(D)| \rceil. \] \end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
After each move, gather the states still possible and count each different state once.
If the first move costs $c_1$, the halving rule says the original count is at most
$2^{c_1}$ times this new count. If the next move costs $c_2$, the new count is at most
$2^{c_2}$ times the count after that. Put the inequalities together: the original
count is at most $2^{c_1}2^{c_2}$ times the count after two moves.

Carry on to the end. The factors multiply, their exponents add, and the added prices
are exactly $\mathrm{cost}(t)$. The last collection is $\mathrm{img}_t(D)$, giving
the first inequality. An empty run contributes no factor and leaves the collection
unchanged, so it fits too.

For the rounded count, let $k$ bits suffice to number all the endpoints.
There are then at most $2^k$ endpoints, and the first inequality gives at most
$2^{\mathrm{cost}(t)+k}$ starts. That many bits therefore suffice for the starts.
This also covers an empty starting collection, whose stipulated index-bit count
is zero, without taking a logarithm of zero.

Rounding throws some information away. Four starts and three endpoints both need
two index bits, so the rounded comparison alone permits zero cost. The unrounded
comparison still sees that four is more than three and forces a positive charge.
\end{proof}

The run itself is the witness;
nothing else is handed in. That will matter in Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}, and I'll say why at the end of this
section.

Your row shrinks when you see something that some of your candidates couldn't have shown you,
and you cross those candidates off. Nothing happened to the machine. It didn't merge anything; it
didn't know you were watching; it would have done the same thing with nobody there. The
physicist Edwin Jaynes had a name for mixing these up, and I think it's one of the most useful
names in all of science: the mind projection fallacy, treating what you know about a thing as
if it were a property of the thing. Your list of candidates is in your head, and the machine's
row is in the machine. The halving price is about the machine's row, and crossing a candidate
off yours doesn't move it.

And here I have to be fair to Jaynes, because he'd argue with where I just took his phrase. In
a 1965 paper on Gibbs's and Boltzmann's entropies he wrote that entropy is ``an anthropomorphic
concept'' (a phrase he credited to the physicist Eugene Wigner), and by that he meant a property
of the particular experiments you or I choose to do on a physical system. On his account the
system alone doesn't carry it. So for Jaynes the second law is
about what's known too, and the line I'd have liked to draw, that the second law has opinions
about the machine and none about you, is exactly the line he'd refuse. Who's right is one of
the oldest fights in statistical physics, Jaynes's reading against Boltzmann's, and I can't
settle it and don't have to. The spreads in Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s entropy
theorems are spreads over the states the device might be in when the step runs, and every
theorem there holds whether you read those chances as ignorance or as physics; ``the floor
comes from what you didn't know'' is the same sentence in either reading, with ``you'' being
whoever built the spread. What I need from the fallacy is only this: the two
rows are different rows, and only one of them is the machine's.

\subsection{The demon on a sheet of paper}

Build it, because the whole claim is four dots and two arrows and you should see it merge or
not merge with your own eyes.

The machine has a hidden bit (think of it as the molecule's side) and a display (the
notepad). It has four states, written as pairs, hidden bit then display: 00, 01, 10, 11. It has two moves.

MEASURE copies the hidden bit onto the display, by adding it in the way that a light switch
adds: if the hidden bit is 1, flip the display; if it's 0, leave it. Draw the arrows: 00 goes
to 00, 01 goes to 01, 10 goes to 11, and 11 goes to 10. Look at the arrowheads: every state has
exactly one arrow landing on it, so nothing merged and MEASURE forgets nothing. Look at the two
states where the display starts blank: 00 goes to 00 and 10 goes to 11, which is the copy onto a blank page, (hidden, blank) to (hidden, hidden), and it's the use that matters here. And the light switch isn't one way of copying among several. A MEASURE that merges nothing, copies onto a blank display and leaves the hidden bit where it was has nowhere else to send 01 and 11: each has one landing left on its own side.

WIPE sets the display to 0 whatever it held. 00 goes to 00; 01 goes to 00 as well. 10 goes to
10; 11 goes to 10 as well. Two arrows land on 00 and two on 10, which is a merge, twice over.

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}ccc@{}}
Hidden bit, display before & After MEASURE & After WIPE \\ \hline
00 & 00 & 00 \\
01 & 01 & 00 \\
10 & 11 & 10 \\
11 & 10 & 10 \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Now follow only the prepared cases: $00,10$ become $00,11$ after the
copy. WIPE sends those two to $00,10$, still two different full states.
The hidden bit retains the distinction. The instruction price nevertheless
charges WIPE because its rule merges other possible pairs, as the full
column shows. That worst-case charge is not a one-bit entropy loss on
this particular correlated preparation.
Under any price that charges per halving, WIPE costs at least one, while MEASURE is allowed to cost
zero. Zero on the price list isn't zero spent: a physical MEASURE can dissipate under its specified dynamics, and it uses up the blank display. What it doesn't do is merge, so it owes
no floor.

Now be the observer. You can see the display and not the hidden bit. What you're shown, the
display here, is what I'll call a \emph{window}: the part of the state an outside observer gets
to see. Section~\ref{sec:windows} is about windows in general; here the window is just the display. The display starts
blank, so your list of candidates is \{00, 10\}: two possibilities, one bit you don't know. The
machine runs MEASURE and you look at the display. If it shows 1, the only candidate that could
have produced it is 10, and if it shows 0, only 00, so your list went from two to one and you learned
the hidden bit. The machine's price for that move, on a list that charges merges, is zero, and
what it spent was the blank display. Its own row of possible states went
from \{00, 10\} to \{00, 11\}, still two; nothing it could have been got merged with anything
else. You narrowed and it didn't. That's the measuring half of Bennett's argument on four dots,
and WIPE's charge is the wiping half. So the demon just broke something: one bit gained, nothing
charged. The thing it broke, written out so you can see exactly where the
crack runs, is this: for every list of starting candidates, every run, and every actual start in the
list, the index bits the observer gains (log2 of the candidates before minus log2
of the candidates after, both rounded up) are at most what the run was charged. On four dots that
sentence is false.

\begin{definition}[What an observer knows]\label{def:knowledge}
Fix a window $w$ from states to what can be seen. Given a list $\Omega$ of candidate starting
states, a run $t$, and the actual start $s_0 \in \Omega$, the observer's \emph{knowledge}
$K(\Omega, t, s_0)$ is the list of candidates $s \in \Omega$ whose run shows the same thing
through the window at every step as the actual run does.
\end{definition}

If that definition looks familiar, it should. It's the standard way logicians of knowledge set
it up: what you know is whatever holds of every case you can't tell apart from the actual one,
given everything you've seen (Fagin, Halpern, Moses and Vardi's \emph{Reasoning About
Knowledge}, 1995, builds a whole subject on it, runs and observations included). And it's the
logically omniscient kind, the kind where knowing some facts means
knowing everything that follows from them, at no extra cost (Section~\ref{sec:established} comes
back to that flaw). I'm using it on purpose, flaw and
all. This section is about learning, and learning in that sense is exactly the thing that
doesn't have to merge. Settling, making a result stay so it can't be handed back, is the separate
act with a price, and nothing in this definition settles anything.

\begin{theorem}[An observer can learn with no merge]\label{thm:observer-free}
There is a four-state machine (the demon), a window (the display), a cost satisfying the halving price, a run of cost
0, and candidates with $|\Omega| = 2$, for which $|K(\Omega, t, s_0)| = 1$. So the claim
``for every $\Omega$ with no repeats, every $t$, and every $s_0$ in $\Omega$: $\lceil\log_2|\Omega|\rceil - \lceil\log_2|K(\Omega,t,s_0)|
\rceil \le \mathrm{cost}(t)$'' is false for that machine and that cost. In the same machine,
every cost satisfying the halving price charges WIPE at least one.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The machine and run are the four dots above: MEASURE is a bijection, so cost 0 satisfies
the halving price; the observer's two candidates show different displays after MEASURE; WIPE
sends two pairs of states to one each, so the halving price needs its cost $\ge 1$.
\end{proof}

The demon is the picture, and the smallest case is smaller than it. The claim as written already fails on
a machine with two states that the window tells apart and every move priced at zero, because the
observer's very first look tells the two apart, and it never fails on a machine with one state. That's why the interesting version is
learning \emph{after} the first look, which is where the three states of
Theorem~\ref{thm:three-states} come in. And WIPE's price needs less than the halving rule: merge pricing
alone charges it at least one.

There is one thing to be exact about. The halving rule is a floor: it says merges cost at least this
much, and it doesn't say anything costs zero. So the theorem exhibits \emph{one} price schedule
that meets the halving rule and charges MEASURE nothing. A different schedule could meet the rule
and still charge MEASURE; nothing in counting forbids overcharging. The claim is that learning
is not \emph{forced} to cost a unit. That's what ``borrows'' in the section's title means: the
look takes a page and pays nothing, and the unit, like the floor, comes due at the wipe.

The physicists had this freedom on the books long before me. Paul Fahn (1996), doing the entropy
accounting of Szilard's one-molecule engine step by step, argued for a symmetry between the measuring step and the erasing step: on his account,
which of the two you charge is partly a choice of bookkeeping, and the
total is what's fixed. Sagawa and Ueda (2009) derived a bound on that total, with the split
depending on the memory. So, on their accounts, ``a schedule could charge MEASURE instead'' is a known freedom in how the books are kept,
and I didn't find a loophole. The other reading is very
much alive too. Ruth Kastner (2025) argues that Brillouin was essentially right after all: once the
physics of a real measurement is put back in, it's measurement that pays and
foils the demon, erasure drops out of the dissipation, and Bennett's floorless copy fails as physics.
The theorem above is about price lists, so it stands either way. What hangs on her is whether a
real demon can look without a floor, which is the same question the next paragraph's doubter presses
on.

And the doubter from the last chapter cuts this side too, so I owe it to you, since I leaned
on him there. In 2013 John Norton argued for a no-go result: at the scale of molecules, thermal
jiggling keeps any process that's supposed to be thermodynamically reversible from ever
actually finishing, and finishing it takes more entropy than Landauer's amount. If he's right,
Bennett's measurement has a floor in practice after all, because it's one of those processes.
The theorem above survives that, because it's about price lists: a schedule that meets the
halving rule isn't forced to charge the copy, whatever a real device spends. What wouldn't
survive is the physics I've been hanging on it, that a real demon's look owes no floor, only the
dissipation of happening that going slowly shrinks. If Norton is right, the line between learning and committing keeps its counting and
loses its physics. I can't referee that one either.

\subsection{Who holds the pen changes who pays}

Now comes the part that I think is the most beautiful fact in here, and you find it by playing
with the four dots rather than by thinking about them. Run MEASURE \emph{twice}. The first copies the
hidden bit onto the display. The second adds the hidden bit in again, and adding a bit twice
with a light-switch add gets you back where you were: the display is blank again. Check the
arrows: 10 to 11 to 10. The display went full and then blank, and nothing merged, and the
price on the ledger was zero both times. So a display that was blank before the first
MEASURE \emph{can} be put back to blank with no merge and no floor, by a second MEASURE, though not
by WIPE. This is the borrowed page being handed back: while the original is still there to check
against, the copy can be un-copied. Each MEASURE still dissipates by happening, and going
slowly shrinks it.

What's the difference? MEASURE \emph{consults the hidden bit} when it clears the display. It knows
what's written there, because it has access to the thing it was copied from, and so it can undo the
copy. Nothing gets erased. WIPE doesn't look. It sets the display to 0 regardless,
and ``regardless'' is exactly the many-to-one. Bennett has the general form of this in the 2003
notes: he lists the ``erasure of one of two copies of data known to be identical'' among the
logically reversible operations, because you're removing a duplicate, and no information is
destroyed. And it goes further than Bennett in
work that came after him: the quantum physicist Lídia del Rio and colleagues argued in 2011
that the floor on erasing a system depends on how much the eraser already knows about it,
dropping to zero, and in the quantum case below zero. The heat of clearing a record falls on
whoever clears it, and its floor is lower the more they know. Try it with a red or blue card
under a cup and a note that is blank or marked.
Start with the note blank. Lift the cup: for red, toggle the note (blank to marked,
marked to blank); for blue, leave it alone. The note now reports the colour. Repeat
that same rule while the card is still available, and the note returns to blank.
Check all four card-and-note combinations: the rule undoes itself, so no two land
together. Erase the note regardless of the card instead, and for either card both
note values land on blank. That rule merges on the full set of combinations. On
the matched pairs you actually prepared, the card still has the information, so nothing is
lost there; the merge is in what the rule has to do to every combination it might be handed,
which is what a rule that doesn't look has to answer for. Cards and paper don't measure heat.
What they show is which information each rule gets to use.

\subsection{The smallest machine that teaches with no merge, and the one that can't}

There are two more small facts, and then the point. The demon measures what you learn by comparing the
start to the end, but an observer's very first look already rules things out before any step
runs, so the fairer question is: after that first look, can a \emph{step} teach you more, at
zero cost? Yes, and the demon still does it. And the smallest machine
that can is three states in a ring: U goes to V, V goes to W, W goes to U, and the window
shows ``true'' only at W. Start with candidates \{U, V\}; both show false. Take one step. From U
you now see false; from V you now see true. One step told them apart, and a ring forgets
nothing, so a zero price meets the halving rule and is the price chosen here.

Two states can't do it, ever, with any arrows, and this is the one that needs no price
premise at all. If a machine has only two states and you can't tell them apart at the first
look, then the window shows the same thing on both, and those two are \emph{all the states there
are}, so the window shows the same thing everywhere, forever, and you never learn anything.
Try to draw a counterexample. You'll draw the
same two dots a few times and give up, and the giving up is the proof. Three is the smallest
number of states on which two states that look alike at the first look can come apart at a
later look, and that's what teaching is.

\begin{theorem}[Three states are the minimum for teaching at zero cost]\label{thm:three-states}
Call a machine a \emph{zero-cost teacher} when it has a cost satisfying the halving price, a list of
candidates with no repeats containing the actual start, and a run of cost 0 after which the
observer knows strictly more than after the first look, $|K(\Omega, t, s_0)| <
|K(\Omega, [\,], s_0)|$. There is a zero-cost teacher with exactly three states, and there is
none with two or fewer.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Three: the ring $U \to V \to W \to U$ with the window true only at $W$, candidates
$\{U, V\}$, one step, cost 0 (a ring is a bijection, so cost 0 satisfies the halving price).
Two or fewer: the actual start is always in the observer's knowledge, so knowing strictly more
after the run needs at least two candidates still left after the first look, which agree there.
On a machine with two or fewer states those two are all
the states there are, so the window takes one value everywhere and no later look can
separate them. This half never uses the price at all.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection*{Finish together, for the first time}

Run the machine from $N$ different starts and photograph its full configuration at
every tick. Put the photographs in rows, one row per start, one column per tick.
Every run finishes for the first time at tick $T$. Through that finish, two different
states in the same column must have different successors.

The sheet has $N(T+1)$ photographs, including the starts and finishes. Could two of
them show the same full configuration? In the same column, cancel backwards and the
starts would have to agree. In different columns, give both configurations the same
remaining steps. One run would finish before its promised first finish. Every photograph
has to show a different configuration.

\begin{theorem}[Room for synchronized first completion]\label{thm:synchronized-room}
Let $F$ be a total rule, $A$ a set of $N$ distinct starts, and $H$ a completion reading.
For every $a\in A$, suppose $F^T(a)\in H$ and $F^t(a)\notin H$ for $t<T$.
Suppose $F$ is injective on $\{F^t(a):a\in A\}$ for each $t<T$.
Then all states $F^t(a)$, with $a\in A$ and $0\le t\le T$, are distinct.
Any carrier containing these runs therefore has at least $N(T+1)$ configurations.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
First compare photographs in the same column. If two showed the same state,
look one column back. The rule keeps different sources in that column apart,
so their predecessors must already have been the same. Repeat until the first
column: the starts agree. Thus different starts cannot give the same photograph
at the same time.

Now compare different columns. Suppose run $a$ at time $i$ shows what run $b$
shows later, at time $j$, with $i<j\le T$. Run $b$ has $T-j$ ticks left before
its first finish. Starting from the identical state, run $a$ must follow those
same remaining steps and finish too. Its time would then be $i+(T-j)$, earlier
than $T$ because $i<j$. That contradicts the first-finish promise for run $a$.

No two places on the sheet can therefore show the same full configuration.
There are $N$ rows and $T+1$ columns, counting time zero, so the machine needs
at least $N(T+1)$ different configurations to hold the sheet.
\end{proof}

That is the room required by the whole sheet of possible runs. The photographs can come
from separate executions of one machine. What keeps different columns apart is the
common first finish: a cycle with no such finish can put the same state in several columns.
\footnote{The count is of full configurations, rather than simultaneously running
machines or newly allocated memory cells.}

\subsection{The certainty bound}

Now I can put the whole path from not knowing to knowing on one page, with what it costs.
 You don't know which state the machine started in. There are a few it
could have been, each with its chance; that's your uncertainty. Run the machine. Every one
of those possible starting states goes somewhere, and only two things can happen to a pair of them.
Either they land on one state, and the difference between them is gone from the machine: a
merge, and the halving price charges for it, at most one bit a unit. Or they land on two
states, and the difference is still in the machine, sitting in its state, kept as two states held apart.
There's no third thing a pair of possibilities can do. So the uncertainty about where it
started splits exactly in two: the part the merges destroyed, paid for in cost, and the part
the end state still holds, paid for by the states it keeps apart.

Now put an observer at the window. Whatever they see is fixed by where the machine
started, so whatever they learn is a fact about the start. And the same split holds for it:
what they learned is either still held in the machine's end state, or it's gone from the
machine and a merge paid for losing it. A run that costs nothing leaves every bit the
observer learned still held in the machine. This is the precise sense of ``learning
borrows'': the observer's copy is a copy, and the machine still holds the original. When
the machine lets go of the original, a merge happens, and the cost comes due.

Said exactly, then: take a spread $p$ over starting states and a run $t$, and write $q$ for the
spread of where the run ends. For an end state $z$ with $q(z) > 0$, the starts that end at
$z$ have chances $p(x)/q(z)$ between them; call that the spread of the start given $z$, and
average its entropy over the ends:
\[
H(\text{start} \mid \text{end}) \;=\; \sum_{z:\,q(z) > 0} q(z)\, H\bigl(\text{start given } z\bigr).
\]
This is how many bits you'd still be missing about the start if someone told you the end. Do
the same for anything $v$ that's fixed by the start, like the whole film of what the window
showed: $H(v \mid \text{end})$ is what you'd still be missing about $v$ once you knew the end.

\begin{theorem}[The certainty bound]\label{thm:certainty-bill}
On a finite deterministic machine with an entropy-priced cost (Definition~\ref{def:u04-entropy-priced}),
take any spread $p$ over starting states, any run $t$, and anything $v$ that the start fixes.
Then
(1) $H(p) = H(\text{start} \mid \text{end}) + H(q)$: the uncertainty about the start is the
part the run destroyed plus the part the end state still holds;
(2) $H(\text{start} \mid \text{end}) \le \mathrm{cost}(t)$: the destroyed part was paid for,
at most one bit a unit;
(3) $H(v \mid \text{end}) \le H(\text{start} \mid \text{end}) \le \mathrm{cost}(t)$: whatever
the end state can't tell you about what an observer saw was paid for in cost, and everything
else the observer learned is still held in the end state. In particular, after a run that costs
nothing, the end state fixes everything the window showed, for every start with a positive chance.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Treat the whole run as one map from starts to ends; the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u04-point-sum} works for any map, so
$H(p) - H(q) = \sum_{x} p(x) \log_2 \frac{q(z_x)}{p(x)}$, where $z_x$ is where $x$ ends. Group
the starts by where they end: for each $z$ the terms add up to
$q(z) \sum_{x \to z} \frac{p(x)}{q(z)} \log_2 \frac{q(z)}{p(x)} = q(z)\, H(\text{start given } z)$.
Adding over $z$ gives $H(\text{start} \mid \text{end})$.
(2) Let the run's moves be $i_1, \ldots, i_n$, and let $q_0 = p, q_1, \ldots, q_n = q$ be the spreads after each step. Entropy
pricing says step $k$ removes at most its own cost: $H(q_{k-1}) - H(q_k) \le
\mathrm{cost}(i_k)$. Add over the steps: $H(p) - H(q) \le \mathrm{cost}(t)$, and by (1) the
left side is $H(\text{start} \mid \text{end})$.
(3) Fix an end $z$. Given $z$, the value of $v$ is a function of the start, so its spread
given $z$ is the spread of the start given $z$ pushed through that function, and by
Theorem~\ref{thm:u04-point-sum} (again for any map) a push never adds bits. So $H(v \text{ given } z) \le
H(\text{start given } z)$ for every $z$, and averaging with weights $q(z)$ gives the first
inequality; (2) gives the second. With $\mathrm{cost}(t) = 0$, $H(v \mid \text{end}) = 0$, so
each end state with a chance leaves one value of $v$.
\end{proof}

Entropy pricing and the halving price are the same premise (Theorem~\ref{thm:one-premise}), so
the theorem holds under either. There are three things it doesn't say. It doesn't say how much heat;
that's Landauer's premise, applied to the destroyed part, $H(\text{start} \mid \text{end})$,
which is the uncertainty the run really removed. It doesn't say the observer's own notes cost
nothing: they need somewhere to be stored, such as a blank page. Supplying
that page is an initial condition; resetting an uncertain page for reuse is
a separate operation. And with a known start, $p$ on one state, every term
is zero: nothing to learn, nothing destroyed, no positive floor from this
premise. To ask what heat the step or the observer actually produces, give
its physical process and preparation. The entropy calculation has not
already charged somebody for knowing.

So the path between uncertainty and certainty runs both ways round. Going in, certainty is
got by narrowing what's possible, and the deterministic calculation separates distinctions lost from distinctions
retained. A copy can put a retained distinction in an observer's memory.
It need not allocate a fresh cell at every step, and an initially held
distinction needs no new crossing. The theorem counts entropy lost under
its pricing premise; it does not put every act of knowing on a heat ledger.

\subsection{What the toll prices, said at last}

Now I can say, more precisely than I could two chapters ago, what the unit of cost in
Section~\ref{sec:toll} is charged for. It is not charged for learning. What you know can be narrowed with
nothing merged, and an honest price list that charges merges can leave it at zero; the demon
is one machine where that happens. It is not charged for looking, or for copying, or for finding out. Their physical dissipation depends on the implementation. In the copying
examples here they use a supplied blank: the demon's blank pad, the
watcher's own notes, a page somewhere that was blank and now isn't. But they borrow that page,
and while the original is still there to check against, the copy can be handed back. The unit is
charged for the one thing in Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} that couldn't be done without merging, on
a machine with finitely many states: raising a flag that stays up, a record nothing hands back.
Learning is the demon writing on a blank pad, which merges nothing. What the demon pays for is
the wipe, a step where two states land on one. The unit in Section~\ref{sec:toll} is charged for the same
reason, because raising a flag that stays up also lands two states on one, but it's a different
step: the demon machine has no flag, and its price list prices merges; commitments never appear
in it. It is the same kind of landing in a different step: learning borrows, and committing pays.

This is also where I settle up with Rovelli, my closest neighbour from the start of this chapter,
because I put him and Bennett on opposite sides of one line: a measurement that can still be
undone borrows and owes no floor, and a choice that sticks pays. I owe you how much of that is
mine. All of the reconciliation is mine. Rovelli's paper doesn't make it, and in four places
his own framing points somewhere else. He reserves ``choice'' for an outcome that is stable and
\emph{not predictable}, and he rules out a thermostat because it runs on a predictable
mechanism; the commit in this book is a step a rule fixes in advance, so by his own definition
his result doesn't cover it. His choice is a branching, one possibility splitting into two,
and he calls choosing in a sense the inverse of erasing, because branching is the inverse of
merging; the toll comes from a merge, the opposite shape. His stability is for a while: he says
stabilization means something only on times that aren't too long next to the time it takes
things to thermalize, and past that nothing stays chosen; my permanence is forever (and the
last chapter owned up that forever is an idealization). And he doesn't stand beside Bennett at
all: he holds that any measurement is dissipative, credits the point to the philosopher of
science Hans Reichenbach, and
doesn't cite Bennett. So what Rovelli and I share is a sentence, that a choice that sticks
costs something like Landauer's heat. There's no shared mechanism. Push on it and his coin hitting the
ground, a fact gained from something nobody could predict, sits closer to what this section
calls learning than to committing. I still think it's the same instinct. This is my reading,
and he doesn't make it; you now have everything you need to disagree with it.

And on one point Rovelli isn't the nearest physics. The nearest I've found is in biology. Thomas
Ouldridge and Pieter Rein ten Wolde (2017) derived what they call the fundamental costs of making a
\emph{persistent} copy of a polymer, one whose sequence stays correlated with its template after
the two have physically come apart, and of destroying one. On their account a copy like that is a state
out of equilibrium, and making it has a thermodynamic cost they measure efficiency against. A companion
paper the same year, with Christopher Govern, does the same kind of accounting for the molecules a
cell uses to read out the state of its receptors, which is a measurement in all but name. The way
I read them, the copy that has to stay is the one that pays, and that's the closest thing in
physics I've found to the line this section draws between finding out and committing. The
differences, so it doesn't get borrowed for more than it is: theirs is work and stored free energy, in chemistry, for a
correlation between two molecules, and their title has the destruction of copies in it too, so
their copies don't last forever; mine is a count in a model of computation, for a reading that
never turns off, with no temperature anywhere. It's the same instinct again, from a different direction.

The chemistry has the sharp form of it, too, and it came two years later. Jenny Poulton, Pieter
Rein ten Wolde and Thomas Ouldridge (2019) studied minimal models of polymer copying, and in
those models, when the copy grows at equilibrium, with the weakest chemical driving, a persistent copy's
accuracy advantage over random copying and the efficiency of storing that
information both vanish. This does not mean every copied site is wrong.
Driving growth out of equilibrium can produce correlations that remain
after the two polymers let go, with chemical work supplied to the process. This is finding out against committing, in chemistry, with the dissipation attached, and I'd
rather say plainly that biology had the distinction before I did. What stays different is the
kind of thing the record is: theirs is a correlation in a chemical ensemble, mine is a reading
enforced by a step in a model of computation.

Two more neighbours have ``learning'' and ``commit'' in their titles, so the slogan shouldn't be
read against them by accident. Sebastian Goldt and Udo Seifert (2017) did the stochastic
thermodynamics of a neural network learning a rule, and argued from it that learning has a thermodynamic cost: on
their account, the entropy the network produces bounds how much it can learn. That doesn't contradict
this section, and the reason is that their learner isn't copying onto a blank page. Its weights are a
driven thermal system, jostled by noise and dragged toward what the data push them to, and what
they price is that physical process. This section's claim is narrower: one way of finding out,
a copy onto a blank, is \emph{allowed} to owe no floor and no cost. It can dissipate under the stated thermal-model assumptions, and it still spends the blank. Nothing here says every way of learning is
cheap, and theirs isn't. From statistics, Aur\'elien Garivier, Tor Lattimore and Emilie
Kaufmann (2016) compare two arms with unit-variance Gaussian rewards and
different unknown means. Their explore-then-commit strategies sample the
arms equally during exploration, then choose one for the remaining horizon.
Within the uniformly efficient classes they compare, the best leading
logarithmic regret is twice that of fully sequential strategies. Whether
the gap between the means is known changes both constants; fixing the
exploration length in advance changes the comparison again. The factor
two belongs to that model and strategy class, not every act called commitment.
That's the closest
published sentence I've found to ``committing costs something'' with a number on it. Their price is
reward lost, which is a different unit from a unit of cost on a ledger, so it's a cousin. A twin would
have to count cost.

So this is exactly what ``No Free Insight,'' the name I gave the toll before I understood it,
covers, because I don't want the name doing work it hasn't earned.
Insight in the sense of \emph{finding out} can come with no merge and no cost; it borrows a
page. The insight the toll prices is the kind
made to stay, written into a record the machine can't silently revise. Whether that
narrower thing deserves the name is a fair thing to argue about; I kept the name because it's
the question I started with, and because the narrowing is the finding. I don't count it as a retreat.

It also tells you how to read a bound that's coming. Section~\ref{sec:entitlement} counts what it takes to narrow a
list of candidates down to a shorter one: at least as many yes-or-no questions as it takes to
point at the survivors among their rivals, a counting fact that holds for anything with a
list in it. Turning that count into a \emph{cost}, saying a run actually paid that many units, is
a different claim, and when the book makes it, for any Thiele machine in Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}, the payment goes in as a hypothesis, in one of two ways: a decision tree (a branching chart of yes-or-no questions, which Section~\ref{sec:entitlement} builds) no deeper than the number of paid steps the run took is handed in, along with the lists themselves and the fact that the tree's leaves cover the narrowing; or the run makes the narrowing itself, with every test step charged at least one and each test it passes keeping at least a set share of the candidates. This section is the reason it has to go in that way. The narrowing alone
doesn't force anyone to pay; the demon just showed you a narrowing charged nothing at all. So
wherever narrowing gets a price in this book, the payment is a premise, and I'll keep calling
it one.

There is one more boundary. This whole section is about a machine that's finite and deterministic
and a watcher who crosses candidates off a list. There's no quantum anything in it. This narrowing has nothing to do with ``observation
collapses the state'': the
narrowing here is bookkeeping in the watcher's
list, the machine never notices, and the result would be the same if the watcher were a
filing cabinet. In 2010 a group in Tokyo (Toyabe, Sagawa, Ueda, Muneyuki and Sano) did
run a real demon, a tiny particle walked up a staircase of potential by feedback on what a
camera saw, and the energy it gained
was paid for by the information the camera took, with no violation of anything. The demon is
real, it works, and it pays. Where it pays is the part that took a century.

What I still owe: everything so far says ``costs at least one'' and I've been keeping the cost
on the side of the page, a running total you tally as you go. Part~II first says what structure
is; then comes the next question (Section~\ref{sec:counter}). What happens when the machine
keeps that total itself, inside its own state, where a step could in principle reach in and
change it? That's the counter, and it's the next thing I have to build.

\part[What structure is made of]{What structure\\is made of}
\clearpage

Part~I found what keeping takes on a single cell and wrote it into a step. Part~II is step three: the rest of
structure is the same thing at a bigger size. It starts with the word itself, structure, and
everyone I could reach who wrestled with it, and comes out where Part~I started, at a sorting of a
pile into groups, a distinction held. Then it asks what follows, on any machine, once a distinction
is kept and the keeping is charged, before I build one. The counter is the ledger, and it uses up states
too: a number that only climbs takes a fresh value for every unit of cost. A window is what's left when you
stop looking at some parts of the state, and it can hide the very distinction that was paid for. Entitlement and
insight ask what a later step may do because a distinction stayed. The latch is the blank cell's
no-to-yes over any machine at all, a reading the machine's own steps turn on and nothing turns off,
and a row of latches is a direction that only goes one way. The diagonal is the wall no level gets
past: no state codes every question about the states (Part~I proved that much), and no machine that
can hand a program its own code, and can run the flip of a verdict as one of its own programs, can
sort all its programs, from inside, by a question about what they do that some pass and some fail.

%===========================================================================
\section{What structure is}
\label{sec:structure}
%===========================================================================

Part~I put a charge beside a new permanent reading under explicit pricing
rules. This chapter starts with one yes-or-no question, states the ruler
under which it is the smallest way to sort, and goes after the rest of it. This whole section is about one word, and I'll give it to you now,
so you can decide whether to stay: structure.

I used that word for most of my life without once looking at it, which I suspect is true of
most people and most words, and it's fine, right up until you do something stupid. The
stupid thing I did was build a machine that keeps a running total of its costs, and the total has one rule I
couldn't talk it out of. You can arrange things however you like, and the ledger lets you put
any price on the arranging, including none; the arranging has whatever physical cost its implementation imposes. But the moment an arrangement has to \emph{stay}, the moment you
ask the machine to keep it, or to vouch for it, to put its own name on the claim that these things
belong together, there's a charge, and it isn't zero. Charged in what? Physical changes have costs determined by the implementation and protocol; keeping something takes more on top, a merge or fresh states. Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} showed there is no other way for a machine that picks its own next step to pay; when the moves are picked from outside, whoever picks them is holding the difference. How much, why I picked
the one I did, and whether I had any business picking it at all: Part~I went through all of that. What was in
front of me, standing there with the thing built, was a model that charges for keeping
structure, and I could not have told you what structure was. It
didn't care. It can't nod along the way a person does. It needed the word to hold still, and
the word had never held still for anyone, least of all me. (The model is already on the
page: five parts and one rule, which you met in Section~\ref{sec:toll}. Part~III builds one small machine
(Section~\ref{sec:smallest}) that meets it, so you can see a complete example. Until then the rule is all that matters.)

So I went looking at the people who'd wrestled it before me. Some of them have been dead two
thousand years and are still, I'd bet money, better at this than I am. I used everything I
had: language models, more than one, books, libraries, my own gut, anything in reach. I don't
know if I found enough. I never do. There's always another shelf behind the one I was
reading. And being dead and famous is not the same as being right, so I pushed on each of
them, and what follows is what I could reach, pushed on as hard as I know how. The one thing
I'm asking is that you push on it with me, out loud, at your own kitchen table, because the
first time through I was the only one checking, and that's not enough people.

The order I ran into them was a mess. Category theory came first, because I'd built one by
feel before I knew it had a name, and everything else came in whatever order the next
question dragged it in. I'm going to put them in the order where each
one leans on the last, which
is mostly the order they happened. And none of it is an oracle. History is where
I start digging. It gets retold, smoothed over, and now and then made up outright
(there's a drowning coming up that nobody can place), so every piece of it is a lead to check,
and I check the parts I lean on.

\subsection{A string, a square, and a drowning nobody can place}

Start with the oldest one, and start by doing it. Take a string. A guitar string, a rubber
band over an open box, anything that twangs. Pluck it. Keep its tension as nearly
unchanged as you can when you stop it at a new point; stretching it tighter changes
the pitch for a second reason. Now stop it exactly at the middle and pluck half.
With the tension held steady, that's the same note an octave up, the one that sounds like the same
note sung higher. Press at a third of the way along and pluck the long side: that's the fifth,
one of the handful of intervals a bugle can play at all, which is why you hear it all through
bugle calls. Half, two thirds: small whole numbers,
and your ear says yes before your brain does. About twenty-five hundred years ago, in the
south of Italy, the followers of a man named Pythagoras are credited with finding exactly that, and it's as true
in your kitchen tonight as it was on their hillside.

I'll tell you what they did with it, as best anyone can tell. Nothing survives that's surely from
Pythagoras's own hand. The earliest fragments are from a later member, Philolaus, and scholars
argue over those. Mostly what's left is Aristotle, one to two centuries later, writing in his
\emph{Metaphysics} about them the way you'd write about the neighbours' religion, and he says they
took the elements of numbers to be the elements of all things: everything is number. That doesn't mean everything can be counted; it means the parts of numbers are the parts of all
things.

Stop and ask what I asked. What does that even mean? Is a chair a number? Does a chair have
a number tucked inside it somewhere? Aristotle doesn't say, and he's reporting a belief he
doesn't hold. So don't take it on his word, or theirs, or mine. But before you push on it,
know what it was holding up, because you can't test a load-bearing wall without knowing what
sits on it. These weren't people doing math for fun on weekends. They were a brotherhood,
with rules about what you could eat and when you had to keep quiet, and that plucked string
was their scripture. Halve the string, hear the octave: to them that was proof that under the
mess of the world there were whole numbers in clean ratios, that the cosmos was a chord and
they'd heard it. ``Everything is number'' wasn't a slogan; it was what they'd organized their
lives around. And that's exactly the kind of sentence you should be suspicious of, mine
included.

Now push, and push where they loved most: the square. Draw one, with a side one unit long,
any unit you like, and draw the line from one corner to the opposite corner. Call that the
diagonal. If everything is number, then the diagonal is some whole number of parts long when
the side is some whole number of parts, so the diagonal divided by the side is a fraction, a
whole number over a whole number. Cancel anything the top and bottom share, the way
four-sixths becomes two-thirds, until they have no common factor left. I'll call the top $p$
and the bottom $q$, and the letters are purely so I don't have to keep writing ``the top'' and
``the bottom.''

You need one fact about squares, and it's the one Pythagoras is famous for. The square built
on the diagonal has exactly twice the area of the square built on the side. If you want to
see it for yourself, cut out two identical squares, cut the second one along both diagonals into
four triangles, and lay one triangle against each side of the first, its long edge on that side. The outline is
the square on the first one's diagonal, and it's made of exactly two of the small squares; it's a
five-minute job with scissors. So $p$ times $p$ is twice $q$
times $q$. People write ``times itself'' as a small raised two, so that's $p^2 = 2q^2$, and that
is the only piece of notation in this argument.

Twice anything is even. So $p$ times $p$ is even. An odd number times itself is always odd: draw that many rows of that many dots,
pair off the columns, then pair the dots in the one column left over, and one dot
remains. The same pairing works for any odd side, so if $p$ were odd, $p$ times $p$ would be
odd too. It isn't, so $p$ itself must be even: it's two
times something, and I'll call that something $r$. Put it back in. Two $r$ times two $r$ is
four times $r$ times $r$, and that equals twice $q$ times $q$. Halve both sides: two times $r$
times $r$ equals $q$ times $q$. So $q$ times $q$ is even, so $q$ is even too, by the same step
as before. But you already cancelled everything the top and bottom had in common, so they
can't both be even. The argument has eaten itself, and when an argument eats itself the
thing you supposed at the start is false. There is no such fraction. The diagonal of a square
can't be named by any ratio of whole numbers, ever. Aristotle reaches for this very argument in
his \emph{Prior Analytics} as his example of proof by contradiction (suppose the diagonal can be
measured, and odd numbers come out equal to even ones), and you just did it with a pencil.

There's a story that a member of the brotherhood named Hippasus let this secret out, and his
brothers took him to sea and drowned him for it. I went and checked, because it's a good story and
good stories are the ones to check. The oldest drownings I could find are in Iamblichus, writing
around AD 300, seven or eight hundred years after Hippasus. In Iamblichus the man drowned by name is
Hippasus, and what he gave away was how to fit twelve pentagons together into a ball, the
dodecahedron. A few pages on, Iamblichus tells it again about whoever first let out the
incommensurable, and that time he names nobody. Carl Huffman, who wrote the Stanford Encyclopedia of
Philosophy's entry on Pythagoreanism, follows the historian Walter Burkert there and finds no ancient
writer who connects Hippasus to this discovery at all. So the version with Hippasus drowned for the
diagonal looks like two old stories stitched together later. It's a legend, but notice that the legend exists.
Somebody, long after, felt that a man \emph{should} have been drowned for this. That's how much
was riding on it. To whoever stitched the story together, the diagonal wasn't a math problem; it was the end of the world.

So the claim is dead, and you killed it. I only handed you the pencil. Now the question that matters: what's left?
Look at your square again. The diagonal is still there. It still stands in a perfectly
definite relation to the side; you drew it, and nobody drowned. That relation was real before
anyone tried to express it as a fraction, and it stayed real after that attempt failed. The relation
came first. The number, when there is one, is a name for the relation, and sometimes there
isn't a name. I'm going to keep that, and I want you to keep it too, because you're going to
watch the same move get made again and again as this book goes on: somebody says ``everything
is X,'' and it's true enough to do real work with, and it sounds right when you pluck it, and
then somebody draws the diagonal. Whether the thing I built survives its own diagonal is a real
question, and Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} answers it.

\subsection{Shapes poured into nothing}

About a century and a half after the brotherhood, Plato, in a dialogue called the \emph{Timaeus}, tried to
build the whole physical world out of geometry. Fire, air, water and earth were four
regular solids (the pyramid, the eight-faced one, the twenty-faced one, and the cube), and the
faces of those solids were built from exactly two kinds of right triangle. You can make one
of each in a minute: cut a square from corner to corner for the first, and cut an equilateral
triangle from a corner to the middle of the opposite side for the second. Everything else, in
Plato's story, was a receptacle, a featureless medium that takes on shape the way wax takes a
seal. Structure, for Plato, is shape laid into something that has no shape of its own.

Why did he care? He wanted a world made on purpose, by a craftsman working from a plan, and
triangles were the plan. Is it true? No, but not for the cheap reason. You can't refute a
claim about what things are made of at the smallest scale by picking one up; the smallest
scale is exactly where your hands don't reach, and Plato knew that. What sank it is that it
made no prediction anyone could check, and the people who eventually did reach that scale,
two thousand years on, found atoms, and atoms aren't triangles. The idea was a guess with no
way to lose, until it lost. But push on it and two things survive. One: structure is something \emph{laid in}, and the stuff it's laid into doesn't carry it
by itself. That's a real idea, and I'd ask you to keep it loosely for now; when the machine
arrives in Part~III, you can ask whether the state it holds is the wax or the seal. Two: Plato put a
crack in his own forms himself, in another dialogue, the \emph{Parmenides}, with an objection that Aristotle later
nicknamed the third man, and it's the most useful mistake in this section. Take all the large
things. Say they share one thing, Largeness. But Largeness is itself large, so now
there's a further thing that all the large things \emph{and} Largeness share, and that one is
large too, and it never stops. The extra move is treating Largeness itself as one more large thing. Grant that
again at each stage and it never stops; refuse it and this particular regress
never starts. The lesson, and I think it's right though Plato never spells it out: the
structure of a collection is not one more member of the collection. The plan isn't a brick.
Hold on to that one.

\subsection{Prove it from what you and I both accept}

Around 300 BC, in Alexandria, Euclid wrote the \emph{Elements}, and the thing to take from it is
not the geometry. It's the method, and the method is the whole reason I trust anything in
this book, so give me a paragraph on it. He starts with definitions (``a point is that which
has no part''), five postulates (things he asks you to grant, like ``to draw a straight line from any
point to any point''), and five common notions (things nobody argues with, like ``things which
are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another''). Then he derives everything else,
four hundred and sixty-five propositions, from only those, in order, each meant to use nothing but
what came before (he sometimes leans on things he never stated, and later geometers filled
those in). He never says ``trust me'' or ``it's well known''; he says, in effect, here are the rules you and I both accept,
now watch. If you've ever been in an argument that ended with ``well, that's just your
opinion,'' Euclid is the man who found a way out of that room, and I'm not embarrassed to say
I learned the way out from someone dead for two thousand three hundred years. Four hundred and
sixty-five times he does the same trick, and the trick is everything.

And then there's the one rule Euclid seems almost embarrassed by, and it's a hole worth falling into. His
fifth postulate, the one about parallel lines, is long and awkward next to the others, and for two
thousand years people tried to prove it from the rest so it wouldn't have to be assumed. Proclus, the fifth-century philosopher who wrote
a commentary on Euclid's first book, tried. Mathematicians in Persia and the Arab world tried. In 1733 an Italian priest named Girolamo Saccheri spent a
whole book assuming it was false so he could watch the contradiction arrive, and he got pages deep
into what is now a perfectly good geometry before declaring that it was repugnant and stopping. A
century later three people, separately, took the step he wouldn't: drop the postulate, and what
you get is other geometries that hold up just as well, and nonsense never arrives. Farkas Bolyai begged his
son János to stay away from the problem, warning that it had swallowed years of his own life; the son went in anyway
and came out with one of those geometries. The part I keep is that they found something real by
refusing to believe one of the rules everyone accepted, and checking what happened without it.
Refusing a rule and checking what happens without it is the push, and this one went on for two
thousand years.

What is structure, to Euclid? Whatever the starting rules force. And when are two shapes the
same? You can do this one yourself: cut out two paper triangles and lay one on the other. If
they coincide, they're equal. That's his fourth common notion, and it's how he proves his
fourth proposition, by picking up one triangle and setting it down on another. Sameness is
coinciding under a move. Keep that; it's about to get very general, and I didn't see that
coming either.

\subsection{The statue and the bronze}

Aristotle, Plato's student, pulled the forms down out of heaven and put them inside things,
which was a bit rude to his teacher and also, I think, correct. His example, from the
\emph{Metaphysics}: a bronze statue is bronze plus a shape. And a circle can be made in bronze or
stone or wood, so, he says, the bronze is no part of what it is to be a circle. The same shape in
marble makes a different statue with the same form.
The bronze is the matter and the shape is the form, and the form is what the thing \emph{is}.

Push on it with two things from the kitchen. A cup can be ceramic or metal and
still hold your coffee. A sandwich carved in wood can keep the outline and fail
to be lunch. The two swaps preserve different things. If the question is shape,
the carving may pass; if the question is whether you can eat it, it does not.

Aristotle already makes a distinction of this kind. In Book VII, chapter 11,
he warns against treating a living animal just like the circle whose bronze can
be changed: its parts must be in a condition to do their work. The sandwich is
a way to make that difficulty visible, not a correction he never considered.

That is the bet I need for the record. Change the material, then check the
operations and the answers again. If they still agree, the record has survived
the change in the respects I promised. Section~\ref{sec:latch} states those
promises over a chosen base; Part~III builds an instance. Neither theorem says
that every material can do every job, or that the price in one material is the
price in another.

\subsection{Where things are, without numbers}

In 1679 Gottfried Leibniz, who co-invented calculus and had opinions about everything, wrote
to the physicist Christiaan Huygens asking for something that didn't exist: a way to reason
about \emph{where} things are directly, the way algebra reasons about \emph{how much}, without ever
laying down coordinates. He called it the analysis of situation. Try it yourself. Describe
where the furniture is in the room you're sitting in without using a single number. ``The couch
is against the wall. The table is between the couch and the window. The lamp is next to the
chair.'' You just did it, and what you used was relations between places and nothing else.
Huygens wrote back that November and was not impressed. It took roughly two hundred years for
Leibniz's idea to become a field, and the field is called topology, and Huygens is remembered
for other things.

What survives the push is the same thing that survived the square, coming at you from the
other side. Position is a relation among places. The numbers you lay on top are a
convenience, and they're a convenience you can take away and still have the room. I'll be
honest about why this one landed for me: the thing I built keeps track of which things
belong together, and I spent a long time thinking that was a list of numbers before I
understood it was a relation that the numbers were merely naming. Leibniz had that in 1679.
Huygens told him no. I'd like to think I'd have sided with Leibniz. I probably would have
sided with the famous guy.

\subsection{Naming a thing by saying when two are the same}

In 1884, in a short book called \emph{The Foundations of Arithmetic}, Gottlob Frege noticed
something you can check in your head right now. ``Line $a$ is parallel to line $b$'' and ``the
direction of $a$ is the direction of $b$'' say exactly the same thing. There is no fact in one
that isn't in the other. But the second sentence has a new object in it, a \emph{direction}, that
the first one doesn't. Where did it come from? From the sameness. Once you can say when two
things count as the same, you've earned the right to name the thing they share. Frege used
exactly this move to say what a number is: the number of things in a pile is whatever every
pile you can match up with it, one to one, has in common. The residue has teeth:
a sameness relation lets you name a new object.

Now push, because Frege pushed too hard, and it cost him. In his formal system, Basic Law V treated value-ranges as objects and
identified them exactly when the corresponding functions agreed everywhere.
Together with his unrestricted comprehension principles, that let the
self-membership construction in. The familiar set version is easier to tell: In June of 1902, a young British philosopher and logician, Bertrand Russell, wrote him a short letter. Consider
the collection of all collections that are not members of themselves. Is it a member of
itself? If it is, then by its own rule it isn't. If it isn't, then it qualifies, so it is. Do
it in your head; it flips every time you look at it, like one of those drawings that's a vase
and then two faces and then a vase. Frege's floor had a hole in it, and he knew it the day he
opened the letter, and his second volume was already at the printer. One repair was Zermelo's 1908 axiom of separation: a property selects
a subset of a set already given. His system also had other existence
axioms, including power set and infinity; separation was not its only way
to obtain a set. What it removed was unrestricted sorting of ``everything.''
You sort a pile. I'll tell you now that this rule shows up again, later, in a place where I
had to obey it or fall through the same hole, and I'll point at it when the book gets there.

Frege's reply is worth hearing, because it's the best example I know of how to lose. He wrote
back within days. He didn't hide it or argue around it. He said, more or less, that arithmetic was
tottering, and in an appendix to the volume that was about to come out he wrote that hardly
anything worse can happen to a scientific writer than having a foundation give way right after the
work is finished. Then he tried to fix it. If I'm wrong about something in this book, and I'd bet
I am somewhere, that's how I'd like to take it.

\subsection{Choose the changes, keep what survives}

By 1872 there were too many geometries. Euclid's, and ones where parallel lines meet, and
ones with no such thing as distance, and nobody could say what made them all geometry and kept
them from being a pile of unrelated hobbies. Felix Klein, twenty-three years old and taking up a
professorship at Erlangen, published an answer in a program paper that people still call the
Erlangen program. Pick a set of allowed changes: rotations, stretches, whatever you decide.
Then a geometry is the study of the properties that \emph{stay the same} under those changes. Pick
a different set of changes and you get a different geometry on the very same page. Euclid's, in Klein's reading, is the one where you may slide,
turn and flip a shape and scale it evenly, and stretching it more one way than another is off limits. And I'd
