underline, if this were my book, which it is, that in Klein's scheme any group of changes can define
a geometry. The choice is yours. Nobody tells you which changes to allow.

You can do this one at your desk. Take any drawing and ask what's still true after you turn
it upside down (lengths, angles), after you stretch it (lengths are gone by then; which lines cross which is still there), after you bend and crumple the sheet without tearing it (which drawn paths remain
connected survives). Two distant ink marks may touch across a fold; that new
physical contact is not a new connection in the drawing. You have to say which
relation you are following. The three changes give three answers and three structures, all from one drawing. The residue is that structure is what survives a chosen set of
changes, and ``chosen'' is doing real work in that sentence. There's no structure of a thing
from nowhere. You have to say what you're allowed to do to it first. I didn't know that when
I started, and I'd been saying ``the structure of'' things for years.

Klein's move has a descendant in logic, and it goes all the way. In a lecture in London in
1966, published only in 1986, three years after his death, the Polish-American logician Alfred Tarski
asked what makes a notion logical, and answered with Klein's recipe at its far end: allow every
one-to-one transformation of the world onto itself, and call logical the notions that survive
all of them. The more changes you allow, the fewer notions are left standing, and with every
change allowed what's left is logic. Tarski's answer is the sentence above, ``structure is what survives a
chosen set of changes,'' with the choice made as large as it can be.

\subsection{An invariance comes with a conserved quantity}

In 1918 Emmy Noether, who at the time wasn't allowed to qualify for a university teaching post
because she was a woman, and for a while taught courses advertised under David Hilbert's name, proved something that physicists still
treat as close to holy. Take a physical system whose laws can be written the way most of
physics is written, as ``of all the paths the system could take, it takes one that makes a
certain total stationary'' (the total is called the action, and stationary means a small change
to the path doesn't change the total to first order; the path needn't make it smallest, and
that's all I'll say about it here). For such a system, every continuous symmetry that leaves the
action unchanged comes with a quantity that is conserved. If the action doesn't change when you
shift everything in space, momentum is conserved. If it doesn't change when you shift everything
in time, energy is. A symmetry isn't decoration. It has a consequence downstream that
you can measure with instruments. I can't hand you this one to do at the table; the proof
needs calculus I'd have to build first and I'd lose you and probably me, and the ``written
as an action'' condition is doing real work that I'm not going to unpack here. What I can hand you is the
shape. Structure, once it's really there and the setting is the right kind, has consequences
you can measure. That's the sentence that made me think a machine could carry a
cost for structure in the first place. Noether makes it reasonable to ask. She doesn't make it true, and
nothing I build in this book is a system with an action.

\subsection{All of mathematics as structures}

Starting in the 1930s, a group of young French mathematicians began publishing a vast
treatise under one made-up name, Nicolas Bourbaki, as if he were a single person. He wasn't.
In 1948 he also applied for membership in the American Mathematical Society, and the application
was quietly turned down, which I find comforting. (The historian Michael Barany has gone through
that application, a second one a year
later, and the letters they set off.) Their goal was to rebuild all of mathematics on one idea: a
structure is a set of elements ``whose nature has not been specified,'' together with one or
more relations on them that satisfy stated axioms. They believed three kinds of structure
were the mothers of all the rest: algebraic, order, and topological.

Push on it. The historian Leo Corry went through the entire
treatise looking for the place where this formal definition of structure actually does any
work, and what he found is that it ``plays no actual role in the presentation of theories within the treatise.'' Outside
the chapter that defines it, it does work almost nowhere. And I found no argument in their writing for why
the mother structures number three. And the chapter on category theory,
which they promised their readers, never appeared; Corry is where I found that too, and Ralf Kr\"omer's 2006 history of Bourbaki and categories in the 1950s follows the attempt. That does not mean Bourbaki left maps out. Their \emph{Theory of Sets}
has sections on morphisms, derived structures and universal mappings
(Chapter IV, sections 2 and 3). Corry's criticism concerns how much their
general formal apparatus was actually used. The lesson I can take for
my own work is smaller: naming a structure is not enough; show which
constructions and comparisons it supports. I learned that one the
slow way, and the origin story at the back of the book (Section~\ref{sec:origin}) tells it.

Philosophers of mathematics took the same idea further and gave it a name, structuralism. In 1965
the philosopher Paul Benacerraf pointed out that the whole numbers can be built out of sets in two
equally good ways that disagree about which set the number three is, and concluded that numbers
aren't objects at all: what arithmetic is about is the pattern, and anything standing in the right
relations to everything else can play the part of three. The philosophers Michael Resnik
(\emph{Mathematics as a Science of Patterns}) and Stewart Shapiro (\emph{Philosophy of Mathematics:
Structure and Ontology}), both in 1997, made the patterns themselves what mathematics is about. The
philosopher Geoffrey Hellman (\emph{Mathematics without Numbers}, 1989) kept the talk of patterns
and did without the patterns, reading each statement as a claim about what would hold in any
system with the right structure, if there were one. The logician Steve Awodey (1996) argued that
category theory says it best, a structure being what its maps keep, which is where this section
goes next. And the philosopher of science James Ladyman (1998) carried the idea into physics: what a
successful theory gets right about the world is its structure. This section's thesis, that
structure is the relations and the things in them don't matter, is theirs. None of the formal
results takes their arguments as a premise, and the bibliography lists them under the same heading
as Bourbaki.

\subsection{A set with some named relations}

What mathematical logic eventually settled on, with the logician Alfred Tarski giving the field its name,
``the theory of models,'' in 1954, is almost boring, and the boring ones are the ones that
last. A structure is a set, called the domain, plus whatever relations and functions a
chosen vocabulary names on it. Pick the vocabulary (Klein again: you choose), and a structure
is anything that gives those names a meaning. Now I want to say ``the smallest one,'' and the
word ``smallest'' has no meaning until I say what I'm measuring, so here is the ruler: count
the names in the vocabulary first; when that ties, count how many things each name takes at
once; when that ties too, count how many answers each name can give. The bottom of that ruler,
for anything that takes things at all, is one name, taking one thing at a time, with two possible
answers, which is a
domain with one yes-or-no property named on it: one question, put to each thing. A single
two-place relation (``these two go together'') can sort a pile too, and so can a single
function that sends each thing to a label, but the first takes two things at once, and the
second can give a different answer for every thing, more than two on any pile of three or
more, so the ruler puts both above one question. There are two
limits, and I'll give them to you
now, so you don't have to find them. A vocabulary with one named
constant (``this one, here'') takes no things at all, so it sits even lower on my ruler, and by itself it doesn't sort anything, so
the claim is ``smallest that sorts.'' Comparing things with the constant takes equality, and I count equality as a name when a
structure uses it, one that takes two things at once. Leave it uncounted, as first-order logic does, and the constant sorts below one
question: ``is it this one?'' splits a pile into that thing and the rest, which is still a split in two, one question whose yes is a
single thing. Plain ``smallest'' would be false. And one question only splits the domain
into two groups when some things answer yes and some answer no; if they all agree there's
one group and nothing was sorted. With those limits said, and with the ruler said: by the
count of names, the smallest structure that sorts anything is one question. Someone with a
different ruler might land somewhere else, and I'd want to see where. Least information lands
one bit lower, on the partition this section ends up starting from: on a nonempty pile of $n$ things a
question can come out $2^n$ ways, and a split into at most two groups with neither one called yes can
come out half as many. The bit between them is the label, which group says yes. Keep it. It's about to turn into the whole
section.

\subsection{The structure is in the arrows}

I met this one first, and backwards. I'd built it by feel, in a rendering engine, as
``digital DNA,'' and only went looking for its name after the thing already ran. In 1945
two mathematicians, Samuel Eilenberg and Saunders Mac Lane, published a paper that founded a field now called
category theory, and they said in plain words that it was a continuation of Klein, which I'd
have loved to know at the time. The move they made was to stop asking what a thing is, and ask how it's
carried. A category is some objects and
some arrows between them, where arrows can be followed one after another and every object has
a do-nothing arrow to itself, plus two rules that make the following dependable: following
three arrows in a row gives the same result whether you pair up the first two or the last
two, and the do-nothing arrow really does nothing when you tack it onto either end, and that's the whole definition. On the page the two rules look like nothing, and they're the part people
skip, so slow down on them for a second, because each one is there for a reason you can see.

Picture three dots in a row, A, B and C, an arrow $f$ hopping from the first to the second and
an arrow $g$ from the second to the third. Composition says there's an arrow taking the whole
stride from A to C in one, $g$ after $f$. Without it, every multi-hop path has to be named on its
own, and the structure falls apart into a pile of unconnected pairs, a phone book without a
search function. Associativity says that with a third arrow $h$ on the end, pairing up the first
two and then adding $h$ gives the same arrow as adding $h$ to the last two first. Both spell the
same three-hop path. With your paper triangle, bracket ``slide, then turn'' before
``flip,'' or bracket ``turn, then flip'' after ``slide'': you still carry out the
same three moves in the same order. Swapping the turn and the flip would be a
different question. If the two bracketings came out different, two people who built the same chain in
different orders would hold two different arrows, which is a bug, because the chain is the thing and
how you assembled it isn't. The identity laws say that tacking the do-nothing loop onto either
end of an arrow gives back the arrow. If the loop changed things, it wouldn't be the loop. Those six
terms, objects, arrows, composition, identities, associativity and identity laws, are all of
Eilenberg and Mac Lane's definition.

Composing relations is older than the definition, too. Who put a name on that move first? I went looking. Augustus De Morgan, writing on the logic of relations around
1860, took the ``is'' out of the old syllogism, put a general relation in its place, and composed
two relations to get the conclusion. The example that gets quoted from that tradition, Peirce's
a decade later, is ``$x$ is the lover of a servant of $y$,'' which is relational composition with better gossip. When exactly
De Morgan read that paper to the Cambridge Philosophical Society, and on which pages it was printed, the
sources disagree, which is a small reminder that history is where you start digging. Then in 1870
Charles Sanders Peirce, an American scientist and philosopher who turns up again in Section~\ref{sec:established}, carried George Boole's algebra of logic (the arithmetic of true and false that Part~III comes
back to in Section~\ref{sec:smallest},
along with the story of Boole himself, a largely self-taught schoolmaster) over to relations, with
composition as one of its basic operations, and he's usually counted as
the real founder of the theory. So following one arrow after another is older than computers,
older than categories, older than Turing's machine: it is a nineteenth-century logician's product of
relations.

And where did they get the word? They didn't get it from mathematics. They borrowed \emph{category} from the
philosophers, from Aristotle and Kant, and \emph{functor} (a map from one whole category to
another) from the philosopher Rudolf Carnap, and then gave both words exact meanings none of
those philosophers had in mind. So Aristotle walks back into this chapter without being asked:
the man who put the form inside the bronze lent his word to the field that keeps track of forms
by their arrows. That doesn't change the laws. It's a reminder that a word can start in
philosophy and arrive in mathematics with a precise meaning bolted on, which is the thing I've
been trying to do with \emph{established} since the start of the book.

What a thing \emph{is} is how it maps. For now the residue is the emphasis I needed: structure
lives in the maps. Nothing later in this book needs more category theory than that sentence, and
the latch of Section~\ref{sec:latch}, where a record is pinned down by the maps between a machine
and the base it extends, is where the sentence does its work.

\subsection{Structure is the part that compresses}

Play this one with me. I write ``th'' and you guess the next letter. You said ``e,'' and you were
right. Now ``the q'': you said ``u.'' Congratulations, you just measured the structure of English.
In 1948 Claude Shannon measured it properly, in a paper that founded information theory, and
found that about half of written English is ``determined by the structure of the language.''
It's the reason a zip file of a long letter is so much smaller than the letter.
Be careful what that says. It does not say that every other letter is fixed by the ones
before it; you just guessed ``e'' after ``th'' and you could have been wrong (think ``than''). It
says that, on average and over long stretches, about half of what's written could be
rebuilt from the rest, so that the text is roughly twice as long as the choices in it. And he said
why that matters in one line that I'd frame if I framed things: the structure ``allows one to
make a saving in time'' (he added ``or channel capacity''). The more you can predict, the less you have to read.

Thirty years later Jorma Rissanen, a Finnish information theorist at IBM's research lab in San
Jose, turned that saving into a price. His idea is called the
minimum description length principle, and it says that the best model of some data is the one
that makes the total description shortest, where the total is the length of the model \emph{plus}
the length of the data once the model has explained what it can. A model is paid for in bits,
and it's worth stating only if it saves more than it costs. Peter Grünwald, a statistician who leads a machine learning group at CWI, the Dutch national
institute for mathematics and computer science in Amsterdam, in a tutorial you can
find online, adds the footnote that keeps this honest: the price of a model depends on the
code you chose to write it in, so the price itself needs a principle behind it, and that principle
is something you have to argue for, not something you're handed.

That's a lot of ``length of'' to swallow in one paragraph, so do one with me, with
numbers small enough to check on the back of an envelope. Every number in it comes from a
code I'm about to make up on the spot, and I'll say every rule of the code out loud, because
Grünwald's footnote is the whole point: change the rules and every number moves.

The data is a row of thirty-two digits, each a 0 or a 1, and you and I agree in advance
that the row is thirty-two long, so nobody has to spend anything saying so:

\[\texttt{0101010101010101 0101010101010101}\]

(The space is only there to rest your eyes.) Every description in the code starts with one
digit that says which kind of description follows: 0 means ``here's the row, written out,'' 1
means ``here's a pattern, then the exceptions to it.'' Each digit is one yes-or-no answer, one
bit, which is what Shannon's unit is. Written out, the row costs that first digit plus the
thirty-two digits themselves, thirty-three bits, and there's no model in it at all. A pattern
description goes like this. First come five digits giving the block length minus one: 00000 means one digit, and 11111 means thirty-two. That covers every allowed length. Then comes the
block itself. The rule is ``repeat the block, then stop at exactly thirty-two digits, cutting off the last repetition if necessary.'' Then come five digits
for how many places the row disagrees with the pattern (up to thirty-one, which is plenty here), and
five more digits for each of those places, numbered zero through thirty-one and listed in increasing order without repeats. At every listed place, flip the predicted digit.

Do it for the row above. The block is $\texttt{01}$, two digits long. So the model costs 1 (which
kind) plus 5 (the block's length) plus 2 (the block), which makes eight bits. Then comes what's left to say
about the data once the model has said its piece: the row disagrees with ``repeat 01''
nowhere, so that's five digits saying ``zero exceptions'' and nothing else, five bits. The total is
thirteen, against thirty-three for writing it out. The pattern pays for itself, with twenty
bits to spare, and Rissanen's sentence has just happened on paper: a model is worth stating when
it saves more than it costs.

Now spoil the row. Flip two of its digits anywhere you like. The model doesn't change, eight
bits, but now the leftover says ``two exceptions, here and here'': five plus five plus five,
fifteen, for a total of twenty-three. It's still cheaper than thirty-three; the pattern still pays, it just
pays less, because the data has more to say that the model can't. Flip four, and the total is $8 + 5 + 4 \times 5 = 33$, a dead tie, and a pattern that saves nothing isn't worth stating. Flip five and it's thirty-eight, and now writing the
row out is cheaper than explaining it, and this particular pattern has lost to writing the row out. Another pattern might
still win. Flip places 6, 12, 18, 24 and 30 of the original row: now the block
\texttt{010100}, repeated and cut off at thirty-two digits, fits exactly.
Its description costs $1+5+6+5=17$ bits. Five changes defeated ``repeat 01''
and produced a better description of their own. The comparison is between
descriptions in the stated code, not a count of spoiled digits alone.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
Message & Original row & Two flips & Five specified flips\\
\midrule
Write all 32 digits & 33 & 33 & 33\\
Repeat \texttt{01}, list exceptions & 13 & 23 & 38\\
Repeat \texttt{010100}, no exceptions & does not fit & depends & 17\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\small For the last column, flip positions 6, 12, 18, 24 and 30.
That defeats one short description and supplies another. Pattern descriptions
include the type bit, length field and exception-count field. The raw row
uses one type bit followed by its thirty-two digits.
\end{center}
 So ``is there structure here?'' has
turned into a question with a number on each side, and a break-even point you can find yourself: four spoiled digits, in this code.

And now change the code, because I promised you'd see the numbers move. Say I'd used seven digits for each exception's place (wasteful, but nobody stopped me). Then three spoiled digits cost $8 + 5 + 3 \times 7 = 34$, one more than writing the row out, where the five-digit code charged twenty-eight and the pattern paid. The pattern stopped paying one spoiled digit sooner. The row is the same, the pattern is the same, the verdict is different, and the only thing that
changed was a convention I chose. That's Grünwald's footnote, and it's why I won't let you
take any of those numbers anywhere else. They're the price of a description in one made-up
code, a length of a written-down message, and nothing more. They are not the charge I opened
this book with. That charge, as Section~\ref{sec:toll} states it, is on one step a machine
takes. How long anybody's description is doesn't enter it, and if the two ever turn out to be related,
that has to be shown. Both of them being counted in whole numbers doesn't get to stand in for the
showing.

Now push, because this is where ``structure means information'' gets born, and it's wrong, and
it's an easy thing to believe. Flip a fair coin two hundred times and write down the string.
Usually there is no substantially shorter way to say that string than to say the whole thing. You can
watch it happen in the little code above, cut to thirty-two digits: a coin-flip row disagrees
with ``repeat 01'' in about sixteen places, which would cost eighty-odd bits to list,
and even the one block guaranteed to fit with no exceptions, the whole row used as its own
block, costs $1 + 5 + 32 + 5 = 43$. The written-out row at thirty-three beats those two descriptions. Another block
could do better; a lucky run of coins can make a pattern, so check it. The general
reason long random rows usually resist substantial compression is a count: put
each short description beside the one row it prints, and there are too few short
descriptions to stand beside more than a small fraction of all the long rows. Nikolai
Vereshchagin, a mathematician at Moscow State University, and Paul Vitányi, a computer scientist at
CWI in Amsterdam, in a 2004 paper on exactly this question, put it without
mercy: every bit of a string like that is ``meaningless information, random noise.'' Such a string carries maximum information and zero
structure. So in this sense structure is the part that compresses, the part where the ``th''
tells you about the ``e,'' and most information and most structure are different things. Hold
that one tightly, because if you built something that charged for information, you'd be
charging for the wrong thing, and for a while I wasn't sure which one I'd built.

And now notice that the word just changed meaning on you,
and on me. I'm pointing at
it so it doesn't slide past. Shannon and Rissanen and Vereshchagin mean \emph{regularity}: a pattern that
lets you say something shorter. Tarski, a few pages back, and Paul Halmos, a Hungarian-American mathematician whose short
textbook on sets is coming up, mean a set with named relations on it, and
those two are not the same thing. You can run the test yourself: number a thousand
objects, flip a coin for each, heads goes in group one, tails in group two. The result is a perfectly
good sorting in the set theorist's sense, every object in exactly one group. And the list of
who went where is a thousand coin flips, which is to say it compresses about as well as a
thousand coin flips, which is to say not at all. Feed it to a code built like the little one,
with the fields widened to fit a thousand, and you get the coin-flip row again, only longer: typically most of the assignment still has to be written down. A lucky pattern
can save some of it; the coin tosses alone do not guarantee there is none. By the set theorist's rule, the sorting
\emph{is} the structure, and it's every bit as much a sorting as ``evens in one group, odds in the
other,'' which compresses to almost nothing. The two are the same kind of object with wildly different
description lengths. So the two meanings don't even rank things the same way: one asks ``is
there a sorting?'' and the answer is yes for both; the other asks ``does a short rule say who
went where?'' and the answer is yes for evens and odds and no for the coins. The coin sorting has structure in the
set theorist's sense and none in Rissanen's. I'll keep both meanings, and I'll try to say which
one I'm using, and when I slip you'll know what to look for.

\subsection{The four parts of every computer}

In 1936 Alan Turing described the machine that every computer you've ever touched is a
version of, and he did it before any of them existed. It's a clerk with a pencil, following a rulebook,
written down as a machine (that clerk comes back in Section~\ref{sec:established}). Write down its parts; there are four.
There's a tape, divided into squares; a head that reads one square at a time and can write on it and
move left or right; a finite list of states the head can be in; and a table of rules: in this
state, reading this symbol, do this. Nothing else is in it, and two different things are true about it
that get run together. The standard effective models compared with it, including register machines and lambda calculus, compute the same partial functions; those are theorems, proved one pairing at a
time, and Turing himself sketched one of them, the pairing with the logician Alonzo Church's lambda
calculus, in an appendix to the 1936 paper. That it also captures everything a person
could ever carry out by rote, everything ``computable'' in the plain-English sense, is a
claim, called the Church-Turing thesis, and nobody has proved it, because the plain-English
side isn't a mathematical object. Turing himself kept those two apart in the 1936 paper, and
so will I. There's a third claim that gets stacked on top, and it's a different kind again:
the physical Church-Turing thesis, that every device you could build out of real stuff
computes no more than this machine does. That one is a claim about physics. No mathematical proof can settle it.
Nobody has built a device that breaks it. Your laptop, your phone, every server in every data
center compute nothing a Turing machine can't; what differs between them is speed, space,
energy, and cost. Hold on to that last word. Cost is where this book lives.

Now do the thing I did, and do it honestly. Look through those four parts for a place that says ``these squares belong
together.'' There isn't one, and that's not me failing to look. Everything the machine is at any
moment is which state it's in, where the head is, and what's on the tape, and the table says what
happens next, and that's the full list. So any grouping has to live in the states and the table, as a
rule, or on the tape, as symbols, which is to say as bytes like any other bytes. The machine can
hold a grouping. It just has no place where holding one is different from holding anything else.

In 1972 David Parnas, a software engineer, wrote a short paper that every programmer should
be made to read and most haven't, on how to cut a program into modules. He took one small
program and cut it two ways. Both worked. But one was easy to change later and the other
wasn't, and the easy one could be ``much less efficient'' if talking between modules cost
anything. His point was that a module is ``a responsibility assignment,'' a decision about who answers
for what, and how you cut decides what every later change costs. If you've ever maintained
someone else's code, you've paid for their cut the way Parnas said you would, probably at two in the morning. What survives
the push is that a division is a commitment: it changes what the work costs, and it is no caption, no
label stuck on afterwards. I'd like to say the thing I built understood that from the
beginning. It didn't. I did, eventually.

\subsection{Laying them all down}

Now lay every one of those on top of the others and see what shows through. I see seven
things. They're my overlay, the places where I see the sources agreeing. The sources never
proved it together; some of them never met, and some of them disagree
(Eilenberg and Mac Lane put maps and their composition at the centre; Shannon's
structure and Tarski's are two different words, as I just showed you). You've pushed on each
source yourself by now, so you're in a position to tell me if I'm seeing things.

A list of seven slogans would be easy to nod at and impossible to check, so I'm going to
carry one thing through all seven and let you watch each one add to the one before it. The
thing is the square you drew for the Pythagoreans, side, diagonal and all. Draw a few more
on the same sheet: one small, one big, the small one again but tilted, and one stretched
out into a long rectangle. You'll want a pile.

Structure is about relations among things, and the things themselves aren't it. You see
that in the diagonal, the bronze, Leibniz's room, Bourbaki's unspecified elements, Tarski's
named relations and the arrows. On your sheet, what makes a square a square was never the
ink. It's that the four sides match and the corners are square, and that the diagonal stands
to the side the way it does whether or not any number names it. Every one of those is a
relation among parts. But on its own this first thing is too loose to use, because a sheet of
paper is drowning in relations: this square is left of that one, this one is nearer the
coffee ring. Which relations count?

Structure is what stays the same under a chosen set of changes. You see that in Euclid's
triangles laid together, Klein's allowed moves, Noether's symmetry, and Frege's direction
that every parallel line shares. This second thing gives the answer the first thing was missing: the
relations that count are the ones that survive the moves you've decided to allow. Slide the
small square across the sheet, turn it, and the diagonal still stands to the side exactly as
before; ``left of the coffee ring'' doesn't make it across. The second thing is a filter on
the first.

The same structure can be carried by different stuff: the statue in marble, or two sets that
answer the same vocabulary the same way. The third thing is the second again with one more change
allowed, which is to swap the material. Cut the square out of cardboard, or lay it out in
string on the table, and if the relations survive, it's the same square in every way you
agreed to care about. Aristotle's bronze is one more thing you agreed not to look at, and the
wooden sandwich is what happens when the material was never on that list.

The first act of structure is a sameness that sorts a pile you were already given. It's there
in Euclid's first common notion, Frege's direction, Tarski's one question, and Russell's
letter, with Zermelo's repair that you must start from a pile. At this point the overlay
stopped being a list for me and turned into a shape, so slow down here with me. Look at your
pile of drawings and say: two of them count as the same when an allowed move, for now a slide
or a turn, carries one exactly onto the other. Watch what happens to the pile. It falls into
groups. The small square and its tilted twin go together; the big one sits on its own; the
rectangle sits on its own. And it falls cleanly, nothing half in one group and half in
another, for a reason you can check. Klein's allowed moves always come with three guarantees:
doing nothing counts as a move, every move can be undone, and two moves in a row is again a
move. Those three are, in different clothes, ``everything is the same as itself,'' ``if this
matches that, then that matches this,'' and ``if this matches that and that matches a third,
then this matches the third.'' Put the last two together and you get Euclid's first common
notion, ``things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another.'' So the
second thing, sameness under chosen moves, \emph{is} a sorting of the pile the moment you ask
which drawings it calls the same. Frege did it with lines and parallels. Tarski's one question
does it in the crudest way there is, by cutting the pile in two. And the pile has to be there
first, because a sameness has to be a sameness among something; that's Russell's letter, and
Zermelo's repair.

Adding structure rules possibilities out. Every one of Euclid's postulates rules one out.
Half of English is already decided. A conserved quantity limits where a system can go. On
your sheet: once the small square and its tilted twin are in one group, you've given up the
right to answer any question the moves respect differently for the two of them. Tell me the
side of one and the diagonal of the other isn't an open question any more. A sorting rules out
a whole bundle of possibilities at once.

Held structure gets used without re-deriving it. You see that in Shannon's saving in time,
Rissanen's compression, Parnas's one-module-at-a-time, and Leibniz's analysis of situation
(reasoning about where things are straight from their relations, with no coordinates laid
down first). The fifth thing pays off here: the possibilities you ruled out are ones you never
have to check again. Know which group a drawing is in and you know everything the group shares
without getting the ruler out, the same way the row of $\texttt{01}$ never needed writing out.
There's one catch, and I'll need a whole section for it: it only pays if you kept the sorting
somewhere you can read it back.

And structure is always relative to a chosen frame, whether that frame is Klein's group, the
vocabulary, the code you compress against, or Parnas's criteria. Nobody gets to say ``the''
structure of a thing without saying from where, and I do it constantly, so watch me for it. On
your sheet: allow stretching as one of the moves and the rectangle walks over and joins the
squares; allow only slides and turns and it doesn't. Same pile, same ink, different groups,
because I chose different moves. The groups were never in the paper. They were in the paper
and the choice, together.

I think the seven hang together this way. Relations are what structure is made of. The
chosen moves pick which relations count, and a change of material is just one more move.
Asking which things the moves call the same sorts the pile. The sorting rules possibilities
out, and what's ruled out is what you get to skip later. And because the moves were chosen,
all of it is relative. Read that way, the fourth thing sits in the middle: it's where the
first three turn into something you can write down, and where the last three get their start.

That's my reason for starting the next subsection with a sorting, and I want to be exact about
what kind of reason it is, because it's mine. None of these people said
``start with a partition.'' Klein would tell you to start with the moves, Eilenberg and Mac Lane
with the arrows, Shannon with the probabilities. What I can actually point at is narrower. In
the framings about when two things are the same shape or the same kind (Euclid laying one
triangle on another, Klein's moves, Frege's directions, Tarski's question) there's a moment
where somebody decides what counts as the same, and that decision, written down, is a sorting
of a pile. In Shannon, Rissanen and Noether I can't find that moment as cleanly, and I'm not
going to bend them until I do. So the overlay doesn't prove that a sorting comes first. It
shows me where the framings I trust most keep putting their first foot down, and I'm putting
mine there too.

I looked for a framing that denies any of the seven and didn't find one, which could mean
there isn't one or could mean I didn't look where it lives. If you know of one, I'd like to
see it.

\subsection{The smallest piece}

Now the sentence I wanted to say at the top and had no right to until here, and even here I
have to split it in two, because half of it is a textbook fact and the other half is me. The
piece of structure I'm going to start from is a partition.

The textbook half: a partition and an equivalence relation are the same object. That's Paul
Halmos, \emph{Naive Set Theory}, 1960, section seven, and you could read that section before
dinner. I'll say it in words first. Take any pile of things. An equivalence relation on it is
a way of saying ``these two count as the same'' that behaves the way sameness should:
everything is the same as itself; if $a$ is the same as $b$ then $b$ is the same as $a$; and
if $a$ is the same as $b$ and $b$ the same as $c$, then $a$ is the same as $c$. Every such
relation sorts the pile into groups, the things that count as the same go together, and every
sorting into groups hands you back a relation, ``same group.'' Do one and then the other and
you land where you started, in both directions. So a partition and an equivalence relation are
one object seen from two sides, and that's the fourth thing on the overlay, the sorting of a
given pile, now with a name and a page number.

I'll give it in the exact form too, since this is the first place the book uses one. A
\emph{set} is a pile, $x \in X$ means ``$x$ is in the pile $X$,'' and a \emph{relation} on $X$
is any rule $\sim$ that, for each pair of things, says whether $x \sim y$ holds. A few more
symbols show up below, and each is a word in disguise. The buckets are written $S_j$, with $j$
saying which bucket (finitely many buckets in every example here, though nothing below needs
that). A cap, $S_j \cap S_l$, is ``what the two buckets share,'' and $\emptyset$ is the empty
pile. And curly braces with a colon, $\{\, y \in X: y \sim x \,\}$, mean ``the pile of every
$y$ in $X$ for which $y \sim x$ holds''; the theorem writes that pile $[x]$, the things that
count as the same as $x$.

\begin{definition}[Equivalence relation, partition]\label{def:equiv-partition}
A relation $\sim$ on a set $X$ is an \emph{equivalence relation} when it is reflexive
($x \sim x$), symmetric ($x \sim y$ implies $y \sim x$), and transitive ($x \sim y$ and
$y \sim z$ imply $x \sim z$). A \emph{partition} of $X$ is a collection of non-empty subsets of $X$,
the blocks, such that every member of $X$ lies in exactly one block. Spelled out, with the blocks written $S_j$: each $S_j$ is non-empty, no two share a member
($S_j \cap S_l = \emptyset$ when $j \ne l$), and together they cover everything (every member of
$X$ lies in some $S_j$).
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Sameness and sorting are one object]\label{thm:equiv-partition}
Every equivalence relation on $X$ determines a partition, whose blocks are the classes
$[x] = \{\, y \in X: y \sim x \,\}$; every partition determines an equivalence relation,
``$x$ and $y$ lie in the same block''; and the two constructions undo each other.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The classes are non-empty ($x \in [x]$ by reflexivity) and cover $X$. If $z$ lies in $[x]$ and
in $[y]$, then $z \sim x$ and $z \sim y$, so $x \sim y$ by symmetry and transitivity, and then
$[x] = [y]$ by symmetry and transitivity again (anything the same as $x$ is the same as $y$, and
the other way round); so two classes either coincide or don't overlap. Going the other way, take a partition and say two things match when they share a block.
Each thing shares its block with itself. If one shares a block with another, the other
shares it with the first. And if $x$ shares with $y$ and $y$ shares with $z$, both
blocks contain $y$. A partition puts $y$ in only one block, so all three share that
block. These are exactly reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity. Going relation to partition to relation returns
``$x$ and $y$ share a class,'' which holds exactly when $x \sim y$ (if $x \sim y$ then $x$ and $y$ both lie in $[y]$; if both lie
in $[z]$ then $x \sim z$ and, by symmetry, $z \sim y$, so $x \sim y$), so it is the original relation. Going
partition to relation to partition returns the original blocks, because the class of $x$ under
``same block'' is exactly the block that contains $x$.
\end{proof}

All of this is textbook mathematics (Halmos, section 7), and the book uses it as a foundation.
I'm claiming nothing new in it.

And the smallest structure that sorts, by my ruler in Tarski's setup, the one question, is
the same object a third time. Put a yes-or-no question to every thing in the pile. The ones
that say yes are one group and the ones that say no are the other. Going the other way, a
two-group partition becomes a question the moment you point at one group and call it ``yes.''
The only thing a question has that the partition doesn't is which group got the label. So the
set theorist's first step and the logician's first step are the same step, and nobody has to
pick a side, which is a relief, because it's an argument you can lose with yourself for a long
time.

So much for the textbook half. The other half is mine, so hold it looser, because Halmos says
nothing about ``smallest'' or ``first'' and I'd be lying if I let his page number carry my
sentence. In what I'm going to build, the order goes: a pile, then groups in the pile, then
whatever connects one group to another, and the groups come first because a question needs
something to be about and a connection needs somewhere to land. That's an order for
\emph{my} construction. It is not a law that every account of structure has to start by
sorting. You could start with an ordering instead (``this one comes before that one''), or with
arrows between the things themselves and no groups at all, and people do, and nothing I've
shown you rules that out. So the honest sentence is: a partition is where I chose to start, it
is the smallest start by the ruler I gave you, and I chose it because it's the first thing that
can be right or wrong about a pile and the last thing I could take away without everything I
build on it coming down. If you have a smaller start by a ruler you can state, I want to see
it. It would change this book.

\subsection{Buckets}

So I'll do the smallest piece once, for real. Take everything in front of you and sort
it into buckets, with nothing in two buckets and nothing left on the floor, and that's the whole
of the definition. It's the thing you do with a kindergartner and a pile of blocks, and I am aware
that I've just marched you past Pythagoras, Plato, Euclid, Frege and Noether to arrive at a
pile of blocks. Keep the blocks anyway. They're about to cost you something.

Take ten blocks, and put the red ones in one bucket, the square ones in another and everything
else in a third. Now a
red square turns up, as they do, and you've got your first crisis: it belongs in two buckets
and the rule says one. So this isn't a partition yet, and you have to decide which bucket
wins. That decision is the whole thing, because a partition is a pile of small rulings like that one,
and once you've made them all, the pile is holding a fact it wasn't holding a minute ago. The
formal version says the same thing with fewer words and more squiggles, and you've already seen
it: it's the definition of a partition in the last subsection (Definition~\ref{def:equiv-partition}), which asks for non-empty
buckets, with nothing in two and nothing on the floor.

The next part isn't kindergarten. Why would that fact cost anything? Watch what it does to one question. Before the buckets, ``are
these two in the same group?'' means working it out: go find the first one, go find the
second one, apply the rule to each, and compare. After the buckets, it's a glance: read the first
one's bucket, read the second one's bucket, and you're done. With each block's address already in hand, and a table that retrieves a label
in one operation, that is two lookups whether the pile has ten blocks or a
billion. Those are access and cost assumptions. A pile with no addresses, or
an index that must be searched, has not been given that same two-lookup rule. What you're looking at is Shannon's saving in time and Parnas's
one-module-at-a-time, the sixth thing on the overlay, showing up in a kindergarten.

Look at what makes that glance possible: a \emph{table}, with a written-down line for each
block saying which bucket it went in. The partition is the fact; the table is one
way of holding the fact so it can be read back fast, and you had to build the table, and
you have to store it, and it has to be the kind of thing you can read in one look (a bucket
number, say; a list of every block in the bucket would have you searching through it
again). Anybody who's used a database has met this table; it's what an index is, and an
index is a thing you build, store, and keep up to date, and every part of that takes something. Take the
table away and keep the partition and you're back to working it out. And
sometimes there was never a search to save: if the rule is ``evens here, odds there,'' you can
answer ``same group?'' by looking at the last digit of each, no buckets needed. What survives is
that holding a sorting in a form you can read back
is worth something, and building that form cost something, and those are already two
different events. Building the table, storing it, checking that it's right, and deciding to
\emph{rely} on it are four different things. The first cost question I want to put to that structure lives in the gap between
the third and the fourth. Nothing in the kindergarten has shown a charge in that
gap. It has separated the acts well enough to ask.

So who, in everything I read, says what has to be paid? I found three answers that come close,
and I'll be exact about how close, because this is the edge of what I know. Rolf Landauer, in
1961, and Charles Bennett after him, say that any step which takes two possible situations
and makes them one, erasing a bit or merging two paths a computation could have taken,
has a heat floor when it removes uncertainty under their thermodynamic assumptions.
That is a physical claim about how the device and its surroundings are prepared, Landauer's
principle, and in this book it is always a premise, never something I prove. It's the place, of all I've found, where a fact about information turns into a fact about
heat, though at room temperature the amount for one bit is far too small to show up on anybody's
electricity bill. In 2012 a lab in Lyon erased one bit, held in a single tiny
bead, and measured the average heat it gave off coming down toward Landauer's floor as the erasing was slowed, and other labs
have found the same since. Not everyone accepts the principle in general, and I'll come back to the
people who don't. Is sending blocks to buckets a step of that kind?
Push on it, because the answer depends on what you keep. If you keep each block and write its bucket next
to it on a spot you knew was blank, you've merged nothing; you can read the block right back off the pair. You
have spent something, though: the blank spot the label now sits on, which the machine hadn't used before, and any heat from the writing depends on its implementation. Bennett's
whole point in his 1973 paper was that a computation which keeps its inputs, and keeps enough
of its working to retrace its steps, can be run without any merging step at all, and it pays
for that by taking fresh states. If instead you throw the block away and keep only the bucket
label, then two different blocks can leave the same label behind, and that is a many-to-one
step, the kind Landauer charges for. Both are things people call ``sorting into buckets.'' Only
the second loses a distinction. So the bucket by itself doesn't hand
you Landauer's heat. The \emph{forgetting} does, when there is forgetting, and keeping instead is paid
for with fresh states. Whether a given machine forgets is a
question about that machine. It has to be answered on the page, and I won't wave at it here.
Rissanen says a model is paid for in the bits it takes to state, and Grünwald says the price
depends on the code. Parnas says a bad cut is paid for later, at two in the morning. And
that's where it stops. Rovelli, back in Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}, prices a choice that sticks, and his
choice is one nobody could predict, which that section showed is a different act. I
couldn't find anyone who says that the moment you \emph{vouch} for a grouping, the moment you stand
behind ``these belong together,'' has a price of its own. Just arranging them that way is a
different act. That could mean nobody says it. It could mean I didn't find
the person who does. I honestly can't tell you which.

So that's where I am at the end of one word. A grouping, the act of making it,
the information kept about it, and a commitment to rely on it are different things.
The blocks let you separate them with your hands. Now take them down to the smallest case there
is, a bucket with two sides, one block, and a ruling that sticks, which is a cell going from blank to
0, the case Part~I started from and showed what keeping it takes. The construction I will study keeps selected distinctions in a state.
Some are there from the start. Some are newly recorded. Those are different
cases: a box that already says YES can sit there forever under a do-nothing
rule, with neither a merge nor fresh states. Part~I's count starts with NO
and follows a new YES that stays under a fixed total rule. That is the case
to which its merge-or-fresh conclusion applies. A grouping by itself does not
supply that run or its price.

%===========================================================================

\section{The counter}
\label{sec:counter}
%===========================================================================

Everything so far has kept the count of cost on the side of the page. You played Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s toy, you made a
tally as you went, and the tally lived in your hand. The machine never saw it. A tally takes a state it
has never used for each unit it records and never goes back to an old one, and putting it inside the machine doesn't change
that; it only makes the machine the one paying with those fresh states. That's fine for a
toy. For anything that's going to run on its own, with nobody tallying, the total has to live
somewhere the machine can reach, which means the machine can, in principle, write it. So
this section is about what a counter has to be before you're allowed to call it a receipt.
I mean the counter of \emph{any} machine whose state carries
a running total that every step bumps by whatever a price list says that step costs. Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s
five parts don't need one (there the total was a sum you did on the side), so this is one
piece added to the five, and the facts below are about anything that has it. I'll give
you the answer first, because it's short, and then spend the section on why each word is
there: a receipt is a total that lives in the state, that only climbs, that equals the sum
of what was charged, and that nothing else could have been.

\subsection{A stick, split down the middle}

The oldest receipt I could find that you can still hold is a piece of wood. From about 1100,
under Henry the First, until 1826, the English treasury recorded what it was owed on tally
sticks: a strip of hazel, notched across with cuts of set widths (the treasury's own handbook
from around 1180, the \emph{Dialogue of the Exchequer}, gives them: a thumb's width for a
hundred pounds, a swollen barleycorn for a pound, a bare cut for a penny), then split lengthwise so that each half carried the
same notches. The payer kept one half, called the stock, which is one story for where the word
stockholder comes from. The treasury kept the other. When the time came to settle, you laid the two halves
together, and only the two original halves fit, because wood splits along a grain nobody can
copy. Add a notch to your half and the other half shows a gap where the partner should be. Try
to remove a notch and you find that wood can't be uncut. When they finally stopped using them,
the clerks burned centuries of old tallies in the furnaces under the House of Lords,
overheated the flue, and burned down the Palace of Westminster, which I mention because it's
the best fact I picked up for this book and because it tells you how many of them there were.

Do it: draw a border round a strip of card, notch it once for every coin you hand a
friend, then split it lengthwise through the notches and keep half each. Don't trim the
edge or swap in a fresh strip. Now add a notch to one half and put them back
together. You'll see the mismatch straight away. And you can't put a cut back: a patch is
just one more thing to look at. The total is the notches, one per coin, and under that
rule the count only climbs. Both halves started with the same count, so if they disagree
now, somebody changed one. The mismatch won't tell you who. What the stick gives you is a
comparison you can make, not an object nobody can forge and not a verdict on who cheated.

Economists read the same stick another way, and they're not wrong either. Alfred Mitchell-Innes
(1913) made the exchequer tally his star witness that money is credit: the crown paid the people
it owed by ``raising a tally'' on some branch of its revenue, a wooden acknowledgment of debt. A
receipt to me, money to him, and it's the same piece of wood. Narayana Kocherlakota (1998) later
proved a version of his point: in a wide class of economies where nobody can be held to a
promise, anything money lets people do, a memory of everyone's past dealings lets them do too.
His title says it in three words: money is memory.

\subsection{Why it has to climb}

Start with the second property, because it's the one that does the most work and the one
people fight hardest. Why can't the counter ever go down?

The answer is in what the toll is for. The floor it buys, back in Section~\ref{sec:toll}, says a run from NO to YES
costs at least one. That
sentence is a \emph{floor}: it says the run paid at least this much. If the counter could come back
down, a run could pay the toll, get its flag, and then take the payment back, and the floor
would be a floor on nothing; ``this run cost at least one'' would be true of a run that ended
having cost nothing. So a counter that can fall is an accountant you can lean on to revise the
books, and a floor stated in terms of it isn't a floor. The counter only climbing is not a flourish; it's what makes ``at least'' mean something.
This ledger records cumulative charges, each a whole number of units and none negative, so it
never decreases. A refundable balance, one that pays money back, would be a different accounting
object with a different invariant, and the floor here says nothing about it. (In Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s abstract theorem the total is
a sum of whole numbers and climbing is automatic; this paragraph is about why a total
\emph{stored in the state}, where a step could in principle write it, has to be designed so that
no step ever lowers it.)

The same rule turns up in two places that have nothing to do with each other, pointing in
opposite directions, and that's a big part of why I trust it. In 1978 Leslie Lamport asked how
a set of computers that pass each other messages, with no shared clock, could ever agree on
what happened before what. His answer is a counter per machine with two rules: add one before
you do anything, and when a message arrives carrying the sender's count, jump your own counter
above it (never below your own). Those counters, he showed, respect cause and effect: if this
caused that, this has the smaller number. And they do it ``with no actual timing mechanism,''
his words; they're clocks only in name. Try it with three people passing notes and you'll see
it work in two minutes, and then let one of them reset their counter to zero after reading a
note, and watch a reply come out numbered \emph{before} the note it replies to. A counter that
goes down can't be leaned on for order.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[thiele]
\node[pipe,text width=3.3cm,minimum width=0pt] (a) at (0,0) {Alice sends\\stamp 2};
\node[pipe,text width=3.3cm,minimum width=0pt] (b) at (5.8,0) {Bob receives\\stamp 3};
\node[pipe,text width=3.3cm,minimum width=0pt] (c) at (5.8,-2.8) {Bob replies\\stamp 4};
\node[pipe,text width=3.3cm,minimum width=0pt] (d) at (0,-2.8) {Alice receives\\stamp 5};
\draw[pipearrow] (a) -- node[above=6pt]{message} (b);
\draw[pipearrow] (b) -- node[left=8pt]{next local act} (c);
\draw[pipearrow] (c) -- node[below=6pt]{reply} (d);
\node[pipe,text width=9.1cm,minimum width=0pt] at (2.9,-5.1)
  {Elsewhere, Carol numbers an unrelated act 1.\\A smaller stamp alone does not prove a causal connection.};
\end{tikzpicture}

\small Start Bob at zero and Alice just after her local act 1. On receipt,
each raises the local count above both its old value and the incoming stamp.
\end{center}

Where did Lamport get it? In the notes he keeps on his own papers, he says the timestamps came
from an earlier note by Paul Johnson and Bob Thomas on keeping copies of a database in step,
whose algorithm wasn't quite right: it let things happen in an order that broke cause and
effect. What let him see the fix, he says, was special relativity, which teaches that the one order of events everybody agrees on
is the order of what could have caused what. And he
passes on a line from Jim Gray, the database pioneer whose commit comes back in Section~\ref{sec:established}: Gray had
heard two opinions of the paper, that it was trivial and that it was brilliant. Lamport's
answer is that he can't argue with the first and isn't inclined to argue with the second.
His account stops at relativity, so the chase does too. It leaves a good picture behind: these update rules put a smaller number on every cause than on its later
effect, without a shared clock. The converse fails: two people can number
unrelated local acts 1 and 2. The numbers alone do not say that the first caused
the second.

Now the other direction. In 1949 Alan Turing, and in 1967 Robert Floyd, each asked how you
prove a program \emph{stops}. Both times the answer was to find a quantity that goes \emph{down} on every step
and can't go down forever (a whole number that can't go below zero, say). If every step
lowers it and it can't fall forever, the steps can't go on forever. Up-only gives you order,
and down-only gives you stopping. They're different rules (one needs the jump-above-the-message
step, the other needs a floor it can't fall below), but they have the same shape, seen from the
two ends: a one-way quantity is something you can build on, and a two-way quantity is a
number that happens to be written down somewhere.

There's also a real-world case where a counter was allowed to go down and got gamed exactly there.
Ethereum, one of the largest blockchains, charges ``gas'' for every step of a program, and for
years it \emph{refunded} gas when a program freed up storage. Someone noticed you could fill
storage when gas was cheap, hold it, and cash the refunds when gas was dear, and a token was
built to do exactly that, and the real work in a block could reach nearly twice the block's
stated limit. In 2021 a change called EIP-3529 cut the refunds sharply (none for
self-destruct, a smaller one for clearing storage, and a cap of one fifth of the gas used).
The written reasons are the gas token and those overfull blocks. I read both as the same
lesson: a counter that goes down was being leaned on at the place where it went down.
Ethereum's gas comes back in Section~\ref{sec:models} as one of five small models of systems people actually run, and
it's the only one of the five that takes a fee at the moment of the write, and it's instructive that the part
they had to fix was the part that could fall.

\subsection{Conservation: the total is the charges and nothing else}

The third property is the plainest one. The counter after a step is the counter
before plus what that step was charged. Add up a whole run and the middle values cancel out,
the way a sum of differences collapses to last minus first, and the total is the sum of the
per-step charges. Why state it?

I state it because it's the property that fails quietly. Say a machine charges one for raising a flag,
and also, somewhere in its error handling, forgets to add the charge when the step fails
halfway through. Or it charges two in one code path and one in another for the same move. Or it
has one step that writes the counter directly. Then the counter is \emph{mostly} the sum of the
charges, and ``mostly'' is the whole gap between a receipt and a note that says ``trust me, about
this much.'' Conservation is the sentence that there is no ``mostly'': every step, every outcome,
every error, adds exactly its charge, and a step that fails is charged the same as one that
succeeds, because the charge is on the attempt. For a machine built the way I'm describing,
that sentence is the rule the counter is updated by, so it can't fail by definition. What can
fail is the claim that a real machine \emph{is} built that way, and checking that means going
through every move it has, the failure branches included, one at a time, which is dull and is
the whole job. The run-long form, counter at the end equals counter at the start plus the sum
of the charges, then follows from the one-step rule by the cancelling sum; it's below. It's
the kind of theorem that looks boring and is the one you'd most want if you were going to
rely on the number.
One thing it doesn't say is that every unit of cost bought something. The ledger is exact about what
was spent. What the spending was worth is another question, and whether a unit of cost bought a real narrowing is
Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}'s question, and it needs a witness on top of the ledger entry.

\subsubsection*{Which mergers does this counter cover?}

Draw the arrows of one run and put a receipt beside each departure. Charge on entry
into a parked state and let the parked state idle free. The charge now depends on where
the step begins. You can check exactly which mergers those receipts cover.

This paragraph changes the accounting interface explicitly. The basic Thiele
definition uses a fixed instruction price $c(i)\in\mathbb N$. Here one autonomous
step $F$ has a source charge $a(s)\in\mathbb N$; with supplied instructions the
broader signature would be $\widetilde c(s,i)$. Its bill must be summed along
the actual run. The same instruction can now cost differently at entry and
at idle. The theorem below states its own charge and coverage premises; it
does not change the instruction-cost definition used elsewhere.

Start at $u$ and follow $L$ steps. The source positions are
$u,F(u),\ldots,F^{L-1}(u)$. Mark a landing state if two different sources in that stretch
lead to it. Count each marked landing once and call the total $\operatorname{Merge}(L)$.
Walking past the same source twice still gives one source. The bill, meanwhile, adds
the charge for every step taken.

The pricing rule is this: whenever two different observed sources share a successor,
at least one of them pays. Give each source its charge $a(s)$ and let the ledger add
exactly that charge. Now every marked landing has a receipt behind it.

\begin{theorem}[Receipts covering the observed mergers]\label{thm:prefix-ledger-bridge}
Let $a(s)\in\mathbb N$ be a source charge and let
$\mu(F(s))=\mu(s)+a(s)$. Suppose every pair of distinct observed sources with the
same successor has a positive charge on at least one member. Then
\[
\operatorname{Merge}(L)\le\sum_{t=0}^{L-1}a(F^t(u))
=\mu(F^L(u))-\mu(u).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Every counted landing state has a paid predecessor. One predecessor cannot belong to
two different landing states, since its successor is fixed. Thus there are at least as
many paid source occurrences as counted landing states, and each costs at least one.
The ledger equality follows by adding its updates.
\end{proof}

Try it with no going to yes and yes going to itself. Charge one at no and zero at yes.
Give those states ledger values zero and one. Entry adds the one; every later idle step
adds zero. The collision is covered and the parked machine can stay parked for free.

Now ask that parked yes-state how many mergers your observation has exposed. After one
step you have seen only no as a source: no merger yet. After two steps you have seen no
and yes, both leading to yes: one merger. The endpoint in your hand is yes both times.
It cannot tell you which observation you made.

Add a clock and you can keep that difference. The endpoints become
$(\mathrm{yes},1)$ and $(\mathrm{yes},2)$. You can read the clock and recover the count
for the old graph. Draw the new full graph, though, and those clock values keep its
states apart. Keep both drawings on the bench so you can see which arrows you are counting.
An external record of the observation length can keep the same missing information.

\subsection{Only one honest count}

The next property surprised me by being provable at all. Suppose you fixed the
schedule: this move costs one, that move costs zero, and so on, for every move. And suppose
someone else keeps their own books: their own function from states to totals, which starts at
zero and, on every step, goes up by exactly what the schedule says. Could their books disagree
with the machine's counter, somewhere, on some state you can actually get to?

No, and the proof is the tally stick. Both totals start at zero. On every step both go up by
the same amount. So on every state you can reach by steps from the start, they're equal.
Nothing more is needed. Agreement at the start survives the first move, then
the second, then every move after it. This way of proving a statement for any
finite number of moves is called induction.
The mathematician's word for this is \emph{initiality}: the counter is the one bookkeeping that
all the others, if they're honest about the schedule, turn out to be. Given the schedule, the
count is forced. There are two things about that sentence I had to be careful with, and they're worth
saying before the symbols. It doesn't assume the other books climb: climbing follows from the
schedule, since the schedule never charges a negative amount, so ``only one honest count'' and
``it only climbs'' aren't two separate demands on the other bookkeeper. And it holds on
\emph{reachable} states only. A state you can't get to from the start is one where it says nothing
about whether the other books agree, which is the right thing for a receipt to say.

I'll state the properties exactly now: first the piece being added to Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s five, a counter and a
price list, and then the two facts about it. A \emph{counter machine} here means a machine that keeps
this ledger. It isn't Minsky's counter machine, the two-counter base Part~I mentioned; the word is the same and
the thing is different, and Section~\ref{sec:smallest} keeps the two apart. The counter gets the Greek letter $\mu$ (mu),
which is the letter the machine in Part~III uses for it (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll}).

\begin{definition}[A counter kept by a price list]\label{def:u06-counter}
A \emph{counter machine} has a set of states, a set of moves, a step function
$\mathrm{apply}$ that takes a state and a move, a start state $s_\mathrm{init}$, a
schedule $c$ giving each move a cost in $\mathbb{N}$, and a counter $\mu$ from states
to $\mathbb{N}$, such that $\mu(s_\mathrm{init}) = 0$ and
$\mu(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) = \mu(s) + c(i)$ for every state $s$ and move $i$, with no
exceptions. A \emph{run} of a list $t$ of moves from $s$ applies them in order, and
$c(t)$ is the sum of their costs. A state is \emph{reachable} when it is the start or is
$\mathrm{apply}(s, i)$ for a reachable $s$ and some $i$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Conservation]\label{thm:conservation}
In a counter machine, for every state $s$ and every list $t$, $\mu$ at the end of the run of
$t$ from $s$ equals $\mu(s) + c(t)$. In particular $\mu$ never decreases along a run.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write the starting counter at the top of a column. Under it write the charge
for the first move, then the charge for the second, and continue to the end of
the run. After the first move the counter is the sum of the first two entries,
because that is its one-step rule. After the second it is that subtotal plus
the next charge. Every further move adds exactly the next entry. With no moves
there is only the starting entry. With any number of moves, the final counter
is therefore the starting value plus their charges, which is $\mu(s)+c(t)$.
Every entry added is nonnegative, so no subtotal is smaller than the one before.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Only one honest count]\label{thm:initiality}
In a counter machine, let $B$ (for ``books'') be any function from states to $\mathbb{N}$ with
$B(s_\mathrm{init}) = 0$ and $B(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) = B(s) + c(i)$ for all $s$ and $i$.
Then $B(s) = \mu(s)$ for every reachable state $s$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Choose a run that reaches $s$ from the start; such a run exists because $s$
is reachable. At the start both books say zero. At the first move both add
the same charge, so they still agree. Whenever they agree before a move,
adding that move's charge to both keeps them equal afterward. Carry this
comparison along the chosen run. The two books agree at its last state,
which is $s$.
\end{proof}

One thing follows that's easy to miss. If a run comes back to a state it has already visited, the
counter is the same both times, so the moves on that loop cost nothing in total. A machine that
keeps its counter inside its state can go round a loop only when the loop costs nothing, and every paid move lands
on a state the run has never been in, because the counter is higher there than anywhere before.
So a counter that only climbs is itself paid for in fresh states: it needs a fresh number for every unit of cost, and it never gets one back. On finitely many states that leaves no paid move at all: play any move over and over from any state, the states come round, and a loop costs nothing, so its price is zero. One move priced above zero takes infinitely many states.

Those two proofs are the whole of it, and they're about any counter machine. They're on
the page, where you can check every line. The machine I build later is one of these, and on
it the run form is a theorem: the ledger after any list of instructions is the start
plus the sum of their costs (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll}). The uniqueness half holds even with
the books' rule asked only of reachable states.

I want to say plainly what initiality does \emph{not} do, because the fact is smaller than the word.
It doesn't pick the prices. The schedule is an input: somebody decided that raising the flag
costs one and adding two numbers costs zero, and nothing here says that decision was right
(Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} is where I argued the floor isn't arbitrary; the rest of a schedule has to be defended by
whoever writes it). It doesn't turn units of cost into anything physical. And it isn't the category
theorist's ``initial object,'' though the word is borrowed for a related reason.

Try the same instruction list on another machine that understands those instructions.
Choose its start. The empty list leaves it there. Append one instruction and its own
rule tells you the next state. Append another and the rule tells you again.
There is only one answer at each stage. So there is only one way to assign a target
state to every instruction list while respecting the chosen start and each appended
move. This walking through a list is often called a \emph{fold}. Nothing in the
argument used a certificate or a price.

Now ask a different question. Can you assign a target state to each \emph{state of the
first machine}, instead of to each instruction list? Two different lists may leave
the first machine at the same state. If those lists leave the target at different
states, the assignment would have to give two answers at that one state. It cannot.

That is the only obstruction. Suppose every pair of lists that agree at the first
machine also agree at the target. To assign an answer to a reachable state, take any
list reaching it and run that list on the target. Choosing another reaching list
gives the same answer, by the supposition. Appending a move respects both machines'
steps because it extends those very runs. The assignment is fixed on every reachable
state, since each comes with a reaching list. This is the \emph{descent} condition:
the assignment can come down from histories to states precisely when the target does
not distinguish histories the first machine has already identified.

A toll does not force that condition. Take a one-bit machine whose set costs one and
whose reset costs zero. Setting its bit once leaves it up. Resetting and then setting
also leaves it up. But a target that keeps the whole instruction list distinguishes
``set'' from ``reset, set.'' Both lists reach the same bit state, and they reach
different history states. The instruction-list assignment still works; the state
assignment fails. That is where the word ``initial'' has to stop.

And the borrowed word has a home. I didn't build it, so I'll point at it. That lists
of moves are the starting object, and that a machine's behaviour factors through its reachable
states exactly when a condition like descent holds, is the theory of minimal realization. Joseph
Goguen put it as a universal property in 1972, in a paper whose title says it outright,
``Realization is universal,'' and Thomas Colcombet and Daniela Petri\c{s}an redid automata
minimization in the same functorial terms in 2020. Their machines can have any output at all,
which is the honest point: the fold and the descent condition never use the record, so the toll
is doing nothing here, just as I said.

The nearest classical parallel to ``only one honest count'' is in thermodynamics. The mathematical
physicists Elliott Lieb and Jakob Yngvason showed in 1999 that once you fix which states of a
system can be reached from which by adiabatic processes, and that relation meets a short list of
axioms, there is an entropy, a function that goes up exactly along the relation, and it is unique
once its zero and its unit are chosen. Their uniqueness, like this one, comes after the fixing:
the order is the input there, the price list is the input here, and in both the count is forced by
it.

\subsection{The toll is an old trick with a new name}

Now for something I first took as a let-down. It would be nice to have a new kind of
cost argument, and this isn't one. The toll is a case of a technique that
algorithm people have used since 1985 and that a mathematician studying the stability of
motion had, in a different form, in
1892. I'm telling you it's old so you don't think I invented it.

The trick is called the potential method, and it works like this. Give every state a
number, call it the potential, that measures how much ``owing'' is stored up in that state.
Then look at each step and ask: does the cost of the step, plus the change in potential it
causes, ever come out negative? If it never does, you've got a bound: any run costs at least
the amount the potential \emph{dropped} from start to finish, because the drop had to be paid for
by the steps along the way. The computer scientist Robert Tarjan set it out in 1985, crediting the potential view to
Daniel Sleator. Tarjan's use goes the
other
way (potential as prepaid credit, to bound a run
from above): he used it to analyse data structures that
are occasionally expensive and usually cheap; and the decreasing-function idea underneath it
is the one the Russian mathematician Aleksandr Lyapunov used in 1892 to prove that a system settles down. Do the coin version,
which runs Tarjan's way, as a ceiling: a stack of coins, PUSH adds one and costs one, POP-ALL removes them all and costs as
many as it removed, potential equals the number of coins. PUSH costs one plus one potential;
POP-ALL of k coins costs k and drops the potential by k, net zero. So any sequence from an
empty stack costs at most twice the number of pushes, however many expensive pops are in it.
The whole method takes three lines.

Push on that 1892 for a second, because a date like that hides a lot. Lyapunov wrote the idea up
as his doctoral thesis, in Russian. A French translation came out in 1907, made by a French
naval engineer, \'Edouard Davaux, and corrected by Lyapunov himself. The English one came
out in 1992, a hundred years after the original, and it was translated from the French: a
translation of a translation. So for most of the twentieth century a reader with only English
met the idea secondhand or not at all. Did the algorithm people of 1985 get it from him? I can't
tell you, and nothing here needs them to have. Whether anybody walked from one to the other on
purpose is a question I'd like answered. What I do have is a picture: the same
idea, a number that only goes one way along a run, turned up in a thesis about whether a moving
system settles down and in a paper about data structures, close to a century apart.

Now point it at the flag. Potential: one if the flag is down, zero if it's up. A step from
down to up drops the potential by one, so for the step's cost plus potential change to be
non-negative, the step has to cost at least one. That requirement is the toll exactly, and the two are the
same statement: the toll holds for a machine if and only if every step has non-negative
amortized cost under the flag potential (``amortized cost'' is just that sum, the step's cost
plus the change in potential). Then the universal floor from Section~\ref{sec:toll}, ``any run from NO to YES
paid at least one,'' is just the potential method's standard conclusion, the drop in
potential from one to zero, and every system with the five parts that obeys the toll is an
instance, which is exactly what a Thiele machine is. Two more facts fall out of the same picture. Under the toll, a run raises the flag
at most as many times as its total cost; each raise uses up a unit and a unit isn't used
twice. And if you demand the upper-bound version too, that the potential before a step covers
its cost plus the potential after, then the two together say every step's cost is exactly the
potential it drops. Go through the four cases. Down to down and up to up drop nothing, so they
cost zero. Down to up drops one, so it costs exactly one. Up to down would have to cost minus
one, and no step costs less than nothing, so the flag never comes down. So the two together
hold exactly when raising the flag costs exactly one, everything else costs zero, and the flag
never comes down. Those prices, a cost of one per raise and nothing on any other step, are rise-only pricing in its tightest form, and I'll call them the \emph{exact schedule}. The flag staying up comes from this ceiling, not from the prices: a ceiling that counts raises instead, which Section~\ref{sec:windows} uses, leaves the same prices and lets the flag come down at cost zero. Notice that Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s two-move illustration doesn't meet it: its
VOUCH move, played from YES, costs one unit although it raises nothing, which the floor allows
and the exact schedule forbids. Part~III's example (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}) doesn't meet it either, and can't; both are still Thiele machines, since the toll is all the model asks.
