The next section answers it: take \emph{any} machine that steps, bolt a record onto it, and see what
shape it's forced into. How a concrete machine hangs actual claims on its parts, a checked
property of one counter at one edition, and where those sit in the state, comes in Part~III (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}).

%===========================================================================
\section{Records over any base: the latch}
\label{sec:latch}
%===========================================================================

The blank cell comes back here, over any machine: a reading that goes from no to yes because the
machine did something, and stays. For the whole book so far I've been building up a thing with a
flag and a counter, and you'd be right to suspect that the whole apparatus is special pleading for one machine, the
one I keep promising to build. So this section answers the suspicion
with no particular machine in it at all, and sees what's left. Take \emph{any} machine that steps deterministically: a Turing
machine, a register machine (a few numbered boxes that each hold a whole number, and a
program that adds, subtracts and jumps), a lambda calculus (Alonzo Church's way of computing by nothing
but plugging expressions into expressions; Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} builds one), anything. Call it the base. Now bolt a record onto it, under rules I'll state,
and ask: what can the record be?

The answer is one shape, and I'll show you the shape first because it's a thing you can
build from a cup and a die.

\subsection{A cup and a die}

Put a cup upside down on the table. The rule is that the first time a coin lands in front of it,
you turn it right side up. There is no rule for turning it back over. Now roll a die, and put a
coin down on every six. Roll twenty times. If a six appears, the cup turns over on the first one and stays
turned over. Write down which roll did it. That number is where the record happened,
and the cup afterward is the record. If no six appears, the cup stays down; a reachable
event need not occur on every trial.

For the deterministic base in the theorem, write the rolls down first and replay them.
The base state is the fixed list and a finger pointing to its next entry; a step moves
the finger one place, regardless of the cup. The event asks whether that entry is six.
Nothing about the cup changes which entry comes next.

The cup is a \emph{latch}. Electrical engineers have had the circuit since 1918, when two British
physicists teaching engineering in London, William Eccles, a radio pioneer, and Frank Jordan,
applied for a patent on a two-valve arrangement that holds whichever state you last put it
in; it became the flip-flop, and the registers and caches in the device you're reading this on
descend from it. Cut its reset wire and what's left has one input, ``set,'' and the rule \emph{new state = old state or set}: once set, it stays set. The cup is that circuit:
a flip-flop with its reset wire cut off.

(Eccles and Jordan didn't call it a flip-flop. Their 1919 paper calls it a \emph{trigger relay}.
Where the newer, sillier name came from I can't source, so I'll leave it at that.)

Is a flip-flop with its reset wire cut off only a picture, or did anybody ever build one on
purpose? Somebody did, and for a reason that's very close to this book's. In the mid-1950s Wen
Tsing Chow, an engineer at the Arma division of the American Bosch Arma Corporation in Garden City,
New York, was asked by the United States Air Force, in the accounts of his career I could find, for
a more flexible and secure way to hold
the fixed numbers, the targeting constants, inside the guidance computer of the Atlas missile.
What he and his Arma colleague William Henrich patented (filed in 1957, granted in 1962, under the
plain title ``Storage matrix'') was a grid with a connection at every crossing, where you set the numbers by
taking out the connections you didn't want, physically or by burning them out with too much
current. The word \emph{burn} is right there in the patent, and people still say they burn a
chip. The descendants are called programmable read-only memories, PROMs, and a fuse blown in
one stays blown: there's no current you can send to grow it back. The grid was a whole memory built out of
cups with no reset wire, made because somebody wanted numbers nobody could quietly change later. That
doesn't prove anything here, because the theorem below doesn't care what a cup is made of. But it's
good to know the shape wasn't invented for a sheet of paper. Somebody needed it, for stakes a
good deal higher than a die.

Now the claim, stated loosely and then exactly: \emph{every base-driven record, over any base, is a cup with no reset wire, turned by some event the base passes through.}

\subsection{What ``base-driven'' has to mean}

The content is in the definition, and I'll give you all five rules, because the theorem is only as
strong as they are.

A machine \emph{extends} a base when there's a map from the bigger machine's states down to the
base's, and that map starts in the base's start states, reaches every one of them, moves in
step with the base (one step up top is one step down below, through the map), and agrees
about halting. The bigger machine may carry as much hidden state as it likes beyond the base,
and that's what the words ``any base'' are about: the base doesn't get to see the extension, and the extension
doesn't get to change what the base does.

The extension carries a \emph{record}, a yes/no reading, and a \emph{ledger}, a counter. It's a
\emph{base-driven record} when five things hold. One: the record's next value depends only on the
base's current state and the record's current value. (I'll call this \emph{driven by the computation}. It says the record answers to what the machine is doing. A clock on the
wall or someone's hand doesn't get a say.) Two: the ledger never goes down (Section~\ref{sec:counter}). Three: the step that turns the
record on costs at least one; that's the toll (Section~\ref{sec:toll}). Four: once on, the record stays on;
that's permanence (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}). Distributed-systems people have a name for a predicate like that. The
computer scientists K. Mani Chandy and Leslie Lamport, in their 1985 paper on taking a consistent
snapshot of a distributed system, called a property \emph{stable} when once it holds it holds
forever after, and stable properties are the ones a snapshot can be trusted to detect. Five: some run from a start state actually reaches a step that
turns the record on; otherwise the record is decoration.

I'll write the rules out exactly. On/off is true/false, $\lor$ is ``or'' (on when either side is
on), and $\mathrm{next}^k$ is $k$ steps.

\begin{definition}[Base, record-carrying machine, cover]\label{def:u11-base}
A \emph{base} $B$ is a set of states with a step function $\mathrm{next}_B$, a set of starting
states, and a halting predicate. A \emph{record-carrying machine} $M$ is a set of states with a step
function $\mathrm{next}_M$, a set of starting states, a \emph{record} $\mathrm{rec}$ from states to
Booleans, a \emph{ledger} $\mu$ from states to whole numbers, and a halting predicate. The cost of a
step is $\mathrm{cost}(m) = \mu(\mathrm{next}_M(m)) \mathbin{\dot{-}} \mu(m)$. A \emph{cover} of $B$
by $M$ is a map $\pi$ from states of $M$ to states of $B$ that sends starting states to starting
states, has every starting state of $B$ as the image of some starting state of $M$, commutes
with the steps, $\pi(\mathrm{next}_M(m)) = \mathrm{next}_B(\pi(m))$, and agrees about halting:
$m$ halts exactly when $\pi(m)$ does.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Base-driven record, latch]\label{def:u11-honest}
$M$ with cover $\pi$ is a \emph{base-driven record} over $B$ when
(R1, driven
by the computation) there is one function $f$ such that, for
every state $m$,
$\mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{next}_M(m)) = f(\pi(m), \mathrm{rec}(m))$; for every state $m$, (R2, ledger)
$\mu(m) \le \mu(\mathrm{next}_M(m))$; (R3, toll) if $\mathrm{rec}(m)$ is off and
$\mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{next}_M(m))$ is on, then $\mathrm{cost}(m) \ge 1$; (R4, permanence) if
$\mathrm{rec}(m)$ is on, so is $\mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{next}_M(m))$; and (R5, a reachable write)
some starting state $m_0$ and some $k$ have $\mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{next}_M^k(m_0))$ off and
$\mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{next}_M^{k+1}(m_0))$ on. An \emph{event} is a function $h$ from base states to
Booleans, and its \emph{latch} is the step $(b, r) \mapsto (\mathrm{next}_B(b),\, r \lor h(b))$. $M$
\emph{factors as the latch of} $h$ when, for every state $m$ (reachable or not),
\[
(\pi(\mathrm{next}_M(m)),\ \mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{next}_M(m))) = (\mathrm{next}_B(\pi(m)),\ \mathrm{rec}(m) \lor h(\pi(m))).
\]
\end{definition}

The theorem says that under those rules the base state and the record move \emph{exactly} as a latch:
the record switches on at the first base state where some event holds, if it started off, and never goes off, and
the event is read off the extension's own rule by asking it what it does when the record is
off (stated exactly below). The theorem is about what the base and the record do together.
The hidden state the extension carries can't push the record anywhere (R1) doesn't allow, since
the record's next value is a function of the base state and the record's own value. The theorem
doesn't say the whole extension is a bare latch machine, and it doesn't make hidden state show up
anywhere in particular: an extension can carry a field that touches neither the record nor the
ledger. And the event is pinned down only on base states that some state with the record off
covers; on a base state with no such state above it, $f(b, \mathrm{off})$ is whatever (R1)'s
function says, and nothing in a run ever consults it.

I promised the content was in the definition, and the proof bears that out: it is a
short case split on whether the record is already on, and it uses only \emph{two} of the five
rules, ``driven by the computation'' and ``permanent.'' The ledger, the toll, and the reachable-write clauses play no part in it. A
latch is what you get from ``answers only to the base'' plus ``never comes back down'' alone. The other three rules matter for the \emph{converse}: for any base and any event the base can reach, the latch of that event, priced at one unit per write, \emph{is} a base-driven record.
The event can be one that holds everywhere, and then its latch is up after one step from every start
and tells no two starts apart. It's still a latch and still base-driven: the converse doesn't ask
the record to distinguish anything. A record that starts off and tells two starts apart at some step has to latch an event that has held along one run by then and not yet along the other, and the latch tells them
apart for as long as that stays so.
Put the two together and base-driven records are exactly
latches: one shape, and no others, over any base.

\begin{observation}[The record is a latch]\label{thm:u11-latch}
Let $B$ be any base, $\pi$ a cover of $B$ by $M$, and suppose $M$'s record is driven by the
computation (R1), through a function $f$, and permanent (R4). Then $M$ factors as the latch of the
event $h(b) = f(b, \mathrm{off})$. In particular every base-driven record factors that way; (R2),
(R3) and (R5) are not hypotheses.
\end{observation}

\begin{proof}
Ask the extension what it would do with the record off above each base state $b$.
Call its answer $h(b)$. Rule (R1) lets you ask that as one function of $b$:
no other hidden field is allowed to change the answer.

Now take an actual state. If its record is off, (R1) gives exactly that answer
$h(b)$ for the next record. If its record is already on, permanence keeps it on,
whatever $h(b)$ says. Together those two cases say ``keep an existing on,
otherwise use $h(b)$,'' which is $r\lor h(b)$.

The cover already says that the base part takes its own next step.
Put that base step beside the record rule just obtained and I have the stated
latch equation. No charge or starting condition entered the argument.
\end{proof}

The latch's nearest neighbours are in verification, and they're old. The computer scientists
Mart\'in Abadi and Leslie Lamport, then at Digital's research lab in Palo Alto, added
\emph{history variables} to specifications in 1991: extra state that records what has happened and
never steers the system, used to prove that one specification implements another. A history
variable that only ever turns on is the cup. Temporal logic has the same record as an operator.
In the past-time temporal logic that Orna Lichtenstein, Amir Pnueli and Lenore Zuck set out in
1985, ``once $h$'' holds now exactly when $h$ has held at some point so far, and a runtime monitor
keeps it in one bit with the update $r' = r \lor h$. Klaus Havelund and Grigore Ro\c{s}u, two
computer scientists working on runtime verification, synthesized monitors of exactly that kind for
safety properties written in that logic in 2002. That update is the latch of
Definition~\ref{def:u11-honest}, word for word. The observation adds the other direction:
a record driven by the computation that never comes down can't be anything else.

One thing about that proof deserves a second look, because it cuts both ways: it never asks what
the base is. The cover decides that: whatever the map sends down is base, and the record's rule is
allowed to read all of it; whatever stays up top is extension, and (R1) keeps the record's rule
from reading it. Draw the line low, so the base is only the computation's own working state, and
(R1) is a real demand. Draw it high, put every table and every refusal bit into the base, and (R1)
is easy to meet, and the latch shape comes out exactly the same. So the theorem holds wherever
you draw the line, and that's exactly why it can't tell you where a record's meaning lives. The
meaning lives in what the event $h$ reads, and that's in the base by construction. On the small machine
of Part~III (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}), the checks that give the flag its meaning sit in the base its
cover picks out. So when that machine arrives, ask it first which parts it puts above the line.

\begin{theorem}[Every reachable latch is a base-driven record]\label{thm:u11-converse}
Let $B$ be any base and $h$ any event. Let $\mathrm{Latch}_h$ have states $(b, r, x)$, starting
states $(b, \mathrm{off}, 0)$ with $b$ starting in $B$, step
$(b, r, x) \mapsto (\mathrm{next}_B(b),\ r \lor h(b),\ x + \delta)$ with $\delta = 1$ when $r$
is off and $h(b)$ is on and $\delta = 0$ otherwise, record $r$, ledger $x$, halting as $b$
halts, and cover $(b, r, x) \mapsto b$. Suppose some starting $b_0$ and some $k$ bring
$\mathrm{Latch}_h$ from $(b_0, \mathrm{off}, 0)$, in $k$ steps, to a state whose record is
still off and whose base state satisfies $h$. Then $\mathrm{Latch}_h$ is a base-driven record
over $B$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The construction keeps a base state, a flag and a tally. Looking only at the
base state gives the promised cover: a start lies over the chosen base start,
every base start has such a flag-down, tally-zero start above it, and each
step advances the base exactly once. Halting is read from that same base state.

The next flag consults only the present flag and the base event, giving (R1).
The tally adds either zero or one and never falls, giving (R2).
If the flag rises, it was off and the event held, exactly the case that adds
one, giving (R3). An on flag stays on under the displayed rule, giving (R4).
Finally the supplied run reaches a state with the flag still off and the event
true. Its next step raises the flag, giving the reachable write (R5).

Whenever a base run reaches the event at all, use its first such visit.
Before that visit the flag remains off, so this is the supplied kind of run.
\end{proof}

What about a base that never merges, a reversible one? It can carry a record, and the next
theorem says exactly what it pays. Keep every earlier record value in a history beside the latch,
one more entry on every step, and the whole step merges nothing either. But that history needs a
fresh slot at every step, forever, so the machine never comes back to a state it has been in,
which puts it in the fresh-state column. On a finite state space there aren't fresh states to go on taking forever, and a permanent record
can't be written by a step that merges nothing at all. A step that merges nothing is
called \emph{injective}: no two states go to the same next state. Keep the old readings on a strip, newest first. If the strip reads
$[\mathrm{off},\mathrm{off}]$ and the current reading is on, the next strip
reads $[\mathrm{on},\mathrm{off},\mathrm{off}]$. The notation $r::H$ below
means exactly that: put the old reading $r$ at the front of the old strip $H$.

\begin{theorem}[Records on reversible machines]\label{thm:u11-reversible}
(1) Let $B$ be a base whose step is injective. The machine with states $(b, r, H, x)$, step
$(b, r, H, x) \mapsto (\mathrm{next}_B(b),\ r \lor h(b),\ r:: H,\ x + \delta)$ ($\delta$ as in
Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-converse}), starting states with $r$ off, $H$ empty and $x = 0$, has an
injective step, never visits the same state twice on a run (the history gets one entry longer on
every step), and under the supposition of Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-converse} it is a base-driven
record over $B$. (2) With finitely many states reading on, a single injective step with a permanent reading never turns that reading from off to on.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Suppose two full states have the same successor. Can you recover what they
were? Their successor base states agree. The base keeps different sources
apart, so their earlier base states agreed too. Their new history strips
also agree. The first entry of each strip is the old record, so the old
records agree; removing that first entry leaves the old histories, which
therefore agree as well.

Those equal old base states and records determine the same charge $\delta$.
Subtract it from the equal new tallies and the old tallies agree. Every part
of the two earlier full states agrees, so they were the same state. The step
is one-to-one.

On a run the strip grows by one entry every tick. A full state cannot recur,
because its strip would have to have two different lengths. Carrying that
strip changes neither the base nor the flag nor the tally rules checked in
the preceding construction, so all five base-driven record conditions still
hold under the supplied reachable-event premise.

(2) Suppose instead there are only $K$ on-states and an off-state enters them.
Permanence sends all $K$ on-states into that same collection, and the entrant
lands there too. A one-to-one step would have to put $K+1$ different sources
into $K$ places. It cannot. Hence a permanent reading with finitely many
on-states cannot rise under a one-to-one step.
\end{proof}

So a base that never merges can carry a record without merging anywhere only by paying in fresh states: once the record is up, the run never comes back to a state it has been in (Proposition~\ref{prop:heat-or-room}). A history that grows by one entry every step is one way to supply them, and a base that never repeats a state, a counter, supplies them already. A machine with finitely many states hasn't got fresh states to go on taking, so it
can't carry one without merging: on a finite machine an instruction that first raises a permanent reading must
merge some possible states. The entering state need not belong to the colliding
pair; Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} prices the instruction under merge pricing.

Process-calculus people ran into the same thing from the other side. Vincent Danos and Jean
Krivine, two theoretical computer scientists in Paris, wanted to pin down what a transaction is. In
2004 they had built a reversible version of CCS, Robin Milner's calculus of processes that talk to each
other, where every step can be rolled back, and in 2005 they modelled a transaction in it as a process that wanders
freely through everything that can be undone until it performs an action declared irreversible,
which is the commit. The way I read it, they start from steps that all come undone and ask what has
to be added before anything sticks, and the theorem above starts from a record and asks what the
step under it must be. In their calculus, as in the theorem, a permanent effect needs a step with no
way back, and the calculus has to say which steps those are. The word I tripped on was
\emph{declared}. Theirs are labelled. Mine, I thought, are picked out by counting, since on a finite
machine the first write merges whatever anyone calls it. Push on that and it gives. I choose the
event $h$, and on a base that grows its history forever the write merges nothing, because it pays in fresh states instead (Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-reversible}), so there my permanence is declared too.

There's an arrow of time in that theorem, and I should say where it came from, because I put it
there by hand. Every starting state has the record off. That's the only reason a raised record
means the event happened: it was down at the start, and only $h$ lifts it. Turn the cup up before
the first roll and it tells you nothing about the die. So the clean start is an assumed ready
state, a past hypothesis in miniature. The past hypothesis is David Albert's name for an assumed
low-entropy beginning of the universe, which several of the accounts below lean records on.
Whether every trusted record leans on it is their argument, and I'm not settling it. Nothing in this book derives one; every theorem here that reads a raised record as news that the event happened assumes its small version and starts from there. The latch observation doesn't need it, and that's why on its own it can't say the event happened.

When I went looking for who else had found the arrow hiding in the start, I got five papers that
read like five unrelated answers. They lined up once I asked each one the same thing: what does
the cup being down at the start rest on? There are two places to put it. You can put it at the
beginning, as a fact about how things started. Or you can put it in the structure of what causes
what. David Wolpert, then a physicist at Los Alamos and the same Wolpert as the free-lunch theorem (Appendix~\ref{sec:whats-mine}),
sorted memory systems in 1992, and one of his kinds works only because it begins in a prepared
state set up by a process that runs one way, which is how it leans on the second law. That's the
cup put down by somebody before the game, at the first place. Wolpert and Jens Kipper, a
philosopher at Rochester, put in 2024 that sorting on a formal footing, and they say plainly that
they have no formal proof this kind can only remember the past. I trust them more for that
sentence. What I think they're saying is that a prepared start buys you a memory, and getting its
direction too takes something they can't yet prove.

Aram Ebtekar, an independent researcher in Vancouver, and Marcus Hutter, who works on the theory of
general artificial intelligence at Google DeepMind and the Australian National University, built in
2024 a reversible toy world, imposed a past hypothesis on it, coarse-grained it, and got records of
the past and none of the future. As I read their route, the clean start doesn't go straight to the
records. It goes through a causal structure first, and the arrows come out of that. Thomas
Blanchard, a philosopher of science at Cologne, got in 2024 the same lopsidedness of knowledge out
of the causal Markov condition, a condition on causal structure. So Blanchard starts at the second
place, which is the middle of Ebtekar and Hutter's road. That took me a while to see, because one
is a toy world and the other is philosophy of causation. They go from the start to causes to
records; he goes from causes to records. The fit is my reading, and it's mine to defend. And Carlo
Rovelli, two years before his paper on the cost of choosing from Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}, studied traces in ``Memory and entropy'' (2022)
and concluded that a memory turns low entropy into available information. He's at the first
place, and he says what the beginning gets spent on. Read against the latch, that's the blank the
record uses up: the flag can say yes once because it started at no.

So does the latch explain why records point backwards? It doesn't,
and I'll say that plainly so it doesn't look
like it does. The step runs forwards and the runs start clean, and a theorem built on those two can
only hand the arrow back. Push further and it gives in a second place. The history that grows
forever looked like a way around the clean start. It starts empty, so it leans on the same blank.
Under a step that forgets nothing, on a finite set, no permanent record can ever be written, past or
future, which is Zermelo again. On the map the book sits at the first place, with Wolpert and
Rovelli, and it sits there by assumption. Ebtekar and Hutter at least imposed their start on a
world with its own dynamics and watched what came out. I wrote mine into the definition.

Constructor theory, which Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} brings in as a neighbour of the
counting argument, has a paper on time (Deutsch and Marletto, 2025) saying that laws stated as which transformations
a device can and can't bring about can't mention time at all, so duration has to come from
relations between physical systems, clocks, that have their own dynamics. What I think they're
saying is that whenever you want a duration you point at a second system and count what it did.
This book is in that position by construction. The step count is the only time in it, and it
comes from the machine's own steps. The next subsection has a record turned at the fifth tick of a
hidden clock, and (R1) throws it out, which read beside them is a rule about which system may be
the clock: the one being recorded. Push on it, though. Their laws have no step in them, and the
paper's work is getting duration and dynamics out of clocks and timers. I put a step,
$\mathrm{next}_B$, into the definition of a base. So I'm in their position only at the far end of
their argument, where a clock already exists. The base is my clock, and I assumed it.

Physicists have built this latch on paper too, in quantum mechanics, and it behaves the way the
last theorem says. The question that sorted them for me is where the cup puts what it forgets,
since a closed quantum system with separate energy levels comes back (Bocchieri and Loinger,
Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}) and the theorem left only
two ways to pay for a record that stays: fresh states, which here mean a history that never ends, or a
merge. Klaus Hepp, a mathematical physicist at ETH
Zurich, wanted a measuring device inside quantum mechanics itself, and studied in 1972 a particle
that flips spins in a long chain as it passes, now called the Coleman-Hepp model (I know Hepp's
paper only from accounts of it), and John Bell (1975) took it apart: the record is exactly definite
only for an infinitely long chain, which is the fresh-state column above, a history that never
ends, in quantum clothes. Jonathan Halliwell, a theoretical physicist at Imperial College London,
used in 1999 a two-state detector that flips once when a particle crosses a point and is kept from
flipping back by a large environment, which is a latch with the environment holding the history.
His abstract calls it \emph{effectively} irreversible, and I like that he puts the word
\emph{effectively} right there where you can see it. And Murray Gell-Mann, the
physicist who named the quark, and James Hartle, of the University of California at Santa Barbara,
gave in 1995 the property a name inside their framework of decoherent histories: the permanence of
the past, past alternatives that stay settled as the story is extended into the future. They name
(R4) for whole histories and leave the cup to others. So Hepp's chain, as Bell read it, is exact and infinite, and
Halliwell's detector is finite and only effectively permanent. Mine is finite, exact and permanent at once, and it
gets there by letting the first write merge. Push on that and it gives: I never say where the
merged state goes. Hepp's chain had to be infinite. Halliwell had to put his in an environment.
Mine just goes, and the toll writes a unit in a counter. That's fine in a model of computation,
and it's exactly where this stops being physics.

\subsection{Both rules do work: the toggle and the timestamp}

A theorem with two hypotheses should have two counterexamples, one for each hypothesis
dropped, and it does, and they're the two ways a record goes wrong in the world.

Drop permanence. Take a base that just counts, and a record that flips at every step: on,
off, on, off. It's driven by the computation; it's not permanent; and it's not a latch of
any event. Such a record is a \emph{toggle}, a piece of working state. A record you
can revoke is working state wearing a record's clothes, and if a revocation has to stick,
that's a \emph{second} latch (``revoked''), which is how certificate revocation lists actually work:
you add an entry; you never delete the certificate. Alin Tomescu, a computer scientist then at
MIT, and his coauthors (2019) built
append-only authenticated sets and dictionaries for transparency logs, and revocation fits that
shape exactly: a revocation goes in once and stays. The pair lemma (stated below) covers two
latches that can each read the other; do it with two cups where the
second only turns over on an even roll \emph{if the first is already up}, and you'll see the
second can never turn before the first.

Dialogue theorists built a version of that two-latch rule for arguments. Give each speaker a row of
cups, one for every claim they've made. Everybody I read in this field is answering two questions
about those cups: whose hand turns them, and can they come back down. C.\ L.\ Hamblin, an Australian
philosopher and logician who also came up with reverse Polish notation for early computers, wrote
\emph{Fallacies} (1970), and it has a chapter on formal dialectic where each speaker has a
\emph{commitment store}, a list of what they're on the hook for, and the rules of the dialogue
update it, while the speaker doesn't. I know that chapter from other people's accounts of it. Hamblin's
store is an answer to the first question, and it's (R1) for arguments: the cup answers to what happened in
the dialogue, and the speaker's hand is kept off it. Henry Prakken, who works on AI and law at
Utrecht, built in 2005 dialogue games for argumentation on stores like that and made commitments
sticky: a claim can be retracted only when it has been challenged, and claims and backtracking
carry a price. He also floats a convention that once a player has retracted a proposition, that
player can't take it on again, which is a revocation that stays revoked, the way an entry on a
revocation list does. Prakken's rules are an answer to the second question, and it took me a second pass to see
that they're two answers: a cup can come down, and coming down costs, and once it
has, the taking-back is itself a cup that stays up. Erik Krabbe, an argumentation theorist at
Groningen, names in 2001 the awkward part of that: retraction is frowned on, and yet resolving a
dispute takes somebody retracting a doubt or a point of view, so the rules have to say when taking a
commitment back is allowed. As I read him, he's standing between the two ends of the second
question. A store that never gives can't settle a dispute, and a store that gives whenever it's asked isn't a store.
The part of all that I'd keep is Hamblin's, that the store belongs to the rules and doesn't belong to the speaker. Take the pen away from the program. And this book answers Krabbe with a price: a
take-back is a second cup, ``revoked,'' and turning it costs at least one like any other write, so a
retraction is allowed, permanent and paid for, which is Prakken's convention with the toll attached.
Where mine gives is his first condition. He lets a claim come down only when it's been challenged,
and nothing in my latch asks why the second cup turned. The pair lemma lets the second cup's event read the
base and the first cup, and nothing in it requires a challenge to be there.

The same field has a notion that looks a lot like earning. In the abstract argumentation of Phan
Minh Dung, a computer scientist at the Asian Institute of Technology in Bangkok (1995), arguments
attack one another, and the \emph{grounded} semantics starts from the arguments nobody attacks and
keeps adding the ones they defend. Look at how it's built: things go in and never come out, which
is a row of cups turned one at a time. Pietro Baroni and Massimiliano Giacomin, at Brescia,
introduced in 2007, and Martin Caminada, then at Aberdeen, revisited in 2014, \emph{strong
admissibility}: a set is strongly admissible when every argument in it is defended by others in the
set that don't lean back on it, so the support bottoms out. Strong admissibility is the argumentation form of an
earned claim. Above the bottom, nothing in it is in by default, which puts it at the far end
from Burge's default on the testimony map in Section~\ref{sec:windows}. Caminada argues it plays a vital part in the dialogue games that decide
grounded acceptance. I've read Caminada's paper; Dung's and Baroni and Giacomin's I know through
what later papers say about them. Notice the bottom, though. An argument nobody attacks gets in
on a check that can't fail, and this book says a check that can't fail establishes nothing
(Section~\ref{sec:established}). Now
turn that on my own cups, because it lands. My first write needs only that $h$ holds, and what $h$
reads sits in the base, where the latch theorem doesn't look. I charge a unit for it, and a unit is a
price, not a check. So my earned records bottom out the way Dung's do, in something let in
without an argument, and the one difference is that mine pays to get in. Whether a machine's
earned record certifies exactly the strongly admissible sets is the kind of statement I'd have to
prove before I said it, and I haven't.

A record that's allowed to change its mind isn't lawless, though; it's somebody else's subject.
Count how many times the cup may be turned. Once, from down to up, is the latch. More than once and
you're somewhere else, and the people who went there sort it two ways: by how many turns are
allowed, and by how long the game runs. The philosopher Hilary Putnam, then at MIT, and E. Mark
Gold, a computer scientist at a research lab in Santa Monica, in back-to-back papers in 1965, looked
at questions a machine answers by guessing and revising, where the answer is whatever the guesses
finally settle on. Putnam's paper says outright that you're never sure you have the correct answer.
That stopped me the first time. What kind of answer can't you ever be sure you have? The way I came
to read it: the cup's position at any moment is the current guess, the answer is where it ends up,
and nobody watching can tell when it's done moving. Yuri Ershov, a logician in Novosibirsk, sorted
those in 1968 by how many revisions they're allowed (that's how his hierarchy is described; I
haven't read his paper). Allow one, from no to yes, and you get exactly the sets a program can list.
That level is in a modern account of the hierarchy by Rod Downey, Carl Jockusch, Timothy
McNicholl and Paul Schupp, four computability theorists, and you don't need their word for it. If a
program lists the set, guess no for every number and flip the guess to yes when the number shows up
on the list. Going back, if every guess flips at most once, from no to yes, run all the guessing
side by side and write a number down the moment its guess says yes. Those listable sets are what a permanent record raised by a search catches. Allow two, three, and so on, and every
extra change buys new sets: the rungs of the ladder are all different. A record that can come back
down lives on that ladder. Now put Putnam's worry on my cup, because it lands. On the bottom rung a
yes is final the moment it appears, and a no never is, since down means not yet. A single cup of mine can
certify that something happened and can never certify that it didn't; a final no would take a second
cup, turned by finding a reason, and that's the pair of latches again. That's what the bottom rung
costs, and I'd rather name it. This book stays on the bottom rung; I'm pointing at the ladder, and I'm
not climbing it.

The ladder doesn't stop at finite time, and the people who followed it past infinity have
names for the two kinds of record I just described. A definition that only ever adds, stage
after stage, and keeps everything it has at each limit, is an \emph{inductive definition}
(the long treatment is a 1974 chapter by Wayne Richter and Peter Aczel, two recursion theorists).
It's the latch run through the infinite, a cup that goes up at some stage and is still up at
every stage after. Let it take things back, and keep what stays put from some stage on, and you
have what John Burgess, a philosopher and logician at Princeton, called in 1986
\emph{quasi-inductive} definitions, which he met in the revision theories of truth that grew up
beside the logician Saul Kripke's 1975 theory of truth, which builds up the true sentences in
stages. Burgess's paper measures how complicated the truths of those theories get. I've read its
abstract, but not the place where he names them. What took me a few reads is that Burgess's rule at a
limit is Putnam and Gold's rule, keep whatever the guesses settled on, applied at every limit stage
along the way. That's my reading of how the two fit. If it's right, the split between a
cup that only goes up and a cup that settles is the same split at finite time and past it: a
permanent record is the first kind, and a toggle that's allowed to settle is the second. Joel Hamkins
and Andy Lewis, two set theorists, let a Turing machine keep running through the ordinals in 2000.
At a limit a cell keeps its value if it settled, and reads 1 if it kept flipping back and forth
forever, and the trick they use again and again is the toggle: flash a flag on and off every time a
guess changes, and at the limit the flag is on exactly when the guess changed infinitely often. A
flag that can come back down is how that machine learns what no finite run could tell it. A
permanent one can't do that trick, because at a limit a cell that only ever goes up just stays up.
So past infinity the toggle is the clever one: a latch tells you a thing happened at least once,
and their flashing flag tells you it happened infinitely often. I threw the toggle out a few
paragraphs back anyway, and I'd do it again, because before the limit its reading can't be relied
on, and nobody using a machine of mine gets to wait for a limit. One finite-time fact belongs beside it, so nobody concludes too much
from permanence. Hao Wang, a logician then at Oxford, described in 1957 a machine whose only write
is to mark a square and which can never erase one, and it computes everything a Turing machine
does. Permanence of a machine's own memory costs it no computing power, given an endless tape: each
mark goes on a square nobody marked before, which is the fresh-state column again. What the book prices is a
permanent reading raised by a step that has to work whether or not the reading is already up, which
is a different thing. So the cost I named a paragraph ago is a cost in what a reading can claim,
and computing power doesn't pay it.

Drop ``driven by the computation.'' Take a base that counts, and a record that switches on at
the fifth tick of a \emph{hidden clock}, whatever the base is doing. It's permanent, and the computation doesn't drive it; such a record is a \emph{timestamp}. A timestamp is not evidence: it says \emph{when} and doesn't say \emph{what happened}, and a record
switched by an outside party or a clock records that party or that clock and leaves the computation
out. Try it with the recorded die list. Keep a second tally hidden beside it, and turn
the cup when that tally reads five before a move; then advance both the tally and
the finger on the list. Run two trials from the same list entry with the cup down,
but start the hidden tally at five in one trial and zero in the other. The next
cup values disagree although everything the base shows agrees, which is the failure
of being driven by the base. If the tally always starts synchronized with the
list position, the position can predict the cup; the distinction matters below.

The two examples do exactly what I said they do: the toggle is driven, isn't
permanent and isn't a latch; the timestamp is permanent and isn't driven. That each also keeps the other rules (the
ledger is the step count, the first switch-on costs one, a run reaches it) is true by
inspection.

Permanent but undriven is a timestamp, driven but impermanent is a toggle, and a record is
the thing that's both. Undriven, for the timestamp, means that along the runs that actually happen the
base state doesn't fix when the record turns; Lemma~\ref{lem:u11-clock-sync} below says why that's
the condition, and what (R1) as written adds to it. That's the whole discrimination, and I think it's the most useful
single sentence in this book for looking at systems other than the one I build, which is
why it's here.

I'll now state the pair lemma and the two counterexamples exactly. The base for both counterexamples is the
counter: states are whole numbers, the step adds one, every state is a starting state, and
nothing halts. Two more bits of shorthand: $\lnot r$ is $r$ flipped, and a statement in
square brackets, like $[k = 5]$, reads on when it's true and off when it isn't.

\begin{lemma}[Two records are two latches]\label{lem:u11-pair}
Let $c_1, c_2$ be two records on $M$, with cover $\pi$ onto a base $B$, such that: there is one
function $F$ with $(c_1(\mathrm{next}_M(m)), c_2(\mathrm{next}_M(m))) = F(\pi(m), c_1(m), c_2(m))$;
the ledger never goes down; a step that turns either record on costs at least one; and each
record is permanent. Then there are $h_1, h_2$ with
$c_1(\mathrm{next}_M(m)) = c_1(m) \lor h_1(\pi(m), c_2(m))$ and
$c_2(\mathrm{next}_M(m)) = c_2(m) \lor h_2(\pi(m), c_1(m))$ for every $m$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Hold the second record fixed and ask what the joint rule does to the first
when the first is off. Call that answer $h_1(b,r_2)$; it is the first
component of $F(b,\mathrm{off},r_2)$. At any actual state whose first record
is off, that is its next value. At any state whose first record is on,
permanence keeps it on. Thus its rule is $r_1\lor h_1(b,r_2)$.

Now hold the first record fixed and ask the corresponding question with the
second off. The answer is $h_2(b,r_1)$, the second component of
$F(b,r_1,\mathrm{off})$. The same off/on argument gives
$r_2\lor h_2(b,r_1)$. The records may affect each other's raising condition,
but neither can undo an on once it is there.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The toggle]\label{lem:u11-toggle}
Let the toggle have states $(n, r)$, step $(n, r) \mapsto (n + 1, \lnot r)$, every state
starting, record $r$, ledger $n$, cover $(n, r) \mapsto n$ onto the counter. It is driven by
the computation, with $f(b, r) = \lnot r$; it is not permanent; and it factors as the latch of
no event.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
At $(0, \mathrm{on})$ the next record is off, which breaks permanence; and any latch gives
$\mathrm{on} \lor h(0) = \mathrm{on}$ there.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The timestamp]\label{lem:u11-clock}
Let the timestamp have states $(b, k, r)$, step $(b, k, r) \mapsto (b + 1, k + 1, r \lor [k = 5])$,
every state starting, record $r$, ledger $b$, cover $(b, k, r) \mapsto b$ onto the counter. It
is permanent and not driven by the computation.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Permanence: $\mathrm{on} \lor x$ is on. Not driven: the states $(0, 5, \mathrm{off})$ and
$(0, 0, \mathrm{off})$ have the same base state and the same record, and their next records are
on and off, so no $f$ of the base state and the record can give both.
\end{proof}

``Driven'' is a condition on every
state. The timestamp makes every state a starting state, so the two states the proof compares are
both ones a run can begin at, even though a timestamp started at $(0, 0, \mathrm{off})$ would never reach $(0, 5, \mathrm{off})$.

That last sentence does more work than it looks, so I'll state it as a lemma. Start the same timestamp
in sync, at $(b, b, \mathrm{off})$ only. On every state its runs reach, the hidden count equals
the base, and the timestamp is exactly the latch of $[b = 5]$. (R1) still rejects it, because (R1)
asks about every state, and $(0, 5, \mathrm{off})$ is a state, though no run from a synchronised
start reaches it. So (R1) as written separates the timestamp from a latch partly by how the cover is
drawn and through states nobody visits. The separation I mean is the one on reachable states:
the timestamp with every state a start fails (R1) even when only states some run reaches are
counted, since two starting states sit over the same base state with the same record and
disagree about the next one. And the latch theorem holds in that reachable form too.

\begin{lemma}[The timestamp, on the states runs reach]\label{lem:u11-clock-sync}
Say $M$'s record is \emph{driven on reachable states} when (R1) holds for every state reached
from a starting state in some number of steps. (1) If $M$'s record is driven on reachable states
and permanent, then on every reachable state $M$ steps as the latch of some event. (2) The timestamp
of Lemma~\ref{lem:u11-clock} isn't driven on reachable states. (3) The timestamp started in sync, with
starting states $(b, b, \mathrm{off})$ and the same step, record, ledger and cover, is permanent,
isn't driven by the computation, is driven on reachable states, and on every reachable state
steps as the latch of $[b = 5]$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(1) is the proof of Observation~\ref{thm:u11-latch}, run on reachable states only. (2) The states
$(0, 5, \mathrm{off})$ and $(0, 0, \mathrm{off})$ are starting states, reached in no steps, and the
proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:u11-clock} applies to them. (3) From $(b, b, \mathrm{off})$ every step adds
one to both counts, so a reachable state has $k = b$ and its next record is $r \lor [b = 5]$. Over
every state, (R1) fails at the same pair as in Lemma~\ref{lem:u11-clock}.
\end{proof}

So ``permanent but undriven is a timestamp'' is a sentence about the timestamp with every state a start,
over the cover that hides its count, and it holds there in the strong form: undriven on the very
states its runs pass through. A timestamp started in step with its base is a latch on the runs it
has, and (R1) throws it out only because (R1) also looks at states those runs never reach.

\subsection{Is there only one such machine? No: one structure, two unforced choices.}

I have to take apart the sentence ``there's only one way to carry a record,'' because three
different things get squeezed into it.

The first claim asks: given the toll and a fixed price list, is there one way to keep the books,
starting at zero and adding each move's price? Yes, on every state reachable from the start;
that's Section~\ref{sec:counter}'s initiality, and it assumes the price list.

The second claim asks: is every base-driven record over a base \emph{the same machine}, charges and all? No,
and the counterexample is embarrassing in its simplicity. Take any base-driven record, give it a new ledger that adds each step's old cost and one unit more,
whatever the step is, and then walk the five rules. The
record still answers only to the base and its own value (R1); the cost never touches it. The
ledger still never goes down (R2); it climbs faster, if anything. The step that turns the
record on still costs at least one (R3), because the toll is a \emph{floor} and a surcharge only
raises the price. Once on, the record stays on (R4), and the same run still reaches the write
(R5). So the surcharged machine is base-driven, and it isn't the machine you started with: wherever
the original sat still at no charge, the surcharged one pays one unit a step for sitting still. Do it
with the cup and the die, and charge one unit for every roll, six or not. The cup turns over on the
same roll as before, so you've changed the cost and nothing about the record. A machine that
charges for CPU time is base-driven and isn't the one that doesn't. The new ledger has to sit beside the old
state and not be read off it. A step's cost is the ledger after less the ledger before, so a ledger read off the
state charges nothing for a step that leaves the state where it was, such as a halted machine stepping to itself,
or for any step on a loop (Section~\ref{sec:counter}). The surcharge is paid in fresh ledger values, the way every
counter that climbs is paid for.

The same base computation and latch are visible after forgetting the new
ledger. The full transition graph can be different: a free self-loop becomes
an endless line of increasing ledger values. So the comparison preserves
base, reading and the stipulated stopping convention, not every full-state
distinction. If the ledger is also observed, these are different contracts.
The construction allows a nonnegative surcharge depending on the current
state in this broader accounting interface. Such a charge is not in general
a price on instruction names alone. The price schedule remains an unforced
choice after the base and event have been fixed.

And then there's the second unforced choice, and this one still surprises me: \emph{which event} is the record?
Nothing in the five rules picks it, beyond (R5)'s demand that it hold somewhere a run reaches; on a base whose runs pass through only one state that leaves one record, and the choice opens as soon as a run passes two states an event can tell apart. The converse above already says so, if you read it
twice: for any event the base can reach, the latch of that event, priced at one unit per
write, is a base-driven record. Do it with the die. One cup turns over on the first six, and another
turns over on the first one. Both are cups with no reset wire; both are base-driven. Roll a one
first, and until a six turns up the two cups disagree about whether anything has been
recorded. So \emph{which permanent reading counts as the record} is a second thing nobody forces
on you. The price list is one unforced choice and the event is the other, and that second choice is the
question Section~\ref{sec:pointer} is about: what, if anything, makes certification the event worth
recording. ``The ledger passed one'' is an event only if the chosen base includes enough
information to decide it. An extension-only ledger is hidden from a base event,
just as the hidden clock was. The unforced choice is among functions of the chosen base.

\begin{corollary}[The event is an unforced choice]\label{cor:u11-event-free}
Let $B$ be any base and $h_1, h_2$ two events, each meeting the supposition of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-converse}. Then $\mathrm{Latch}_{h_1}$ and $\mathrm{Latch}_{h_2}$ are both
base-driven records over $B$. If some run from a start of $B$ reaches a base state $b$ with $h_1(b)$ on and $h_2(b)$ off, and $h_2$ holds nowhere earlier on that run, then after the step from $b$ the same run has the first record on and the second off.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
That both are base-driven is Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-converse} applied twice. Along that run the second record is still off when it reaches $b$, since $h_2$ hasn't held, and the latch's own rule keeps it off, $\mathrm{off} \lor h_2(b)$; the first is on after that step, whatever it was before, since $h_1(b)$ is on.
\end{proof}

Now let the cup wobble. Say whatever turns it over sometimes does and sometimes doesn't, with
odds you could write on a card. Does fixing the price list fix the odds? No, and the
counterexample is two cups with the same price tag and differently loaded coins. I'll set it up
carefully. Let a record be a single bit that moves at random: from each value, a list of weighted next values, every weight positive,
never empty, never leaving on once on, and with the write from off to on charged at least one.
Call such a record a \emph{permanent probabilistic record}.
Call two such records \emph{the same schedule} when the same moves are possible and every move is charged the same, and \emph{the same in probability} when the weighted lists give every move the same odds.

\begin{theorem}[The schedule doesn't fix the probabilities]\label{thm:u11-probabilistic}
(1) There are two permanent probabilistic records with the same schedule that are not the same in
probability. (2) There is a permanent probabilistic record that no deterministic latch on its
current value describes.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) From off, one record moves to off or on with weights $1$ and $1$, the other with weights $1$
and $2$; from on, both stay on with weight $1$; both charge $1$ for the write. Same possible
moves, same charges, different weights. (2) The first record moves from off both to off and to
on, while a latch $r \lor h(r)$ gives one value.
\end{proof}

These are finite-weight models on one bit with no base underneath;
they say nothing about any particular machine.

The third claim asks: is there one state space, up to renaming, that every base-driven record-carrier has
to have? No, because the extension may carry any hidden field it likes, so two carriers over one base can
have state spaces of different sizes, and nothing needs them to match.

\subsection{Bases from outside, and a relation I have to be honest about}

The theorem is stated for any base, so let me put it on three models of computation that other
people built: a small Turing machine (any program); a register machine
of the kind the computer scientists Stephen Cook (of the certificates) and Robert Reckhow described in 1973, with unit-cost indirect addressing (any
program); and a lambda calculus (call-by-value, meaning an argument is worked out before it's
plugged in, and made deterministic by letting a term with no step left to take step to
itself). On each, the latch form holds, by the one generic theorem applied to that base
(the bases are defined below). So a register machine
with a base-driven record is a register machine plus a cup, and so is a lambda calculus. (There's one
more instance, the machine I build later, where a particular flag is shown to
be a base-driven record and the same theorem makes it a latch, in
Section~\ref{sec:smallest}.)

I'll give the three bases explicitly. A base needs a state, a next-state function,
a set of starting states and a halting predicate; the latch theorem asks for nothing
else about its instruction vocabulary.

\begin{definition}[Three concrete bases]\label{def:u11-concrete-bases}
The \textbf{tape base} has a finite Boolean list $t$, a head index $h$, a program counter
$q$ and a natural-number cost field. Reading beyond the list returns false. Writing
at $h$ extends the list with false cells if needed, then changes that cell.
Moving right increments $h$ and extends the list through the new head position.
Moving left decrements a positive $h$; at $h=0$, it prepends a false cell and keeps
the head at zero. A fixed finite program contains these instructions:

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.482\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.482\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Instruction} & \textbf{Next state} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
Write a bit & Perform the write and advance $q$ by one. \\
Move left or right & Perform the move and advance $q$ by one. \\
Branch to $j$ & Set $q:=j$ if the current cell is true; otherwise advance $q$ by one. \\
Halt & Leave the entire state unchanged. \\
ClaimTapeIsZero with a label $\ell$ & Advance $q$ by one and do nothing else. \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

An out-of-range program fetch is Halt. Every state is allowed as a starting state,
and halting means the fetched instruction is Halt. The cost field is preserved by
every instruction in this base. In particular, its ClaimTapeIsZero instruction
neither erases the tape nor charges the cost field; neither the name nor the label supplies any
semantics.

The \textbf{random-access base} has a register function $X:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ and a
program counter $q$. For a fixed finite program its instructions are:

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.482\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.482\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Instruction} & \textbf{Next state} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
Constant $(i,c)$ & Set $X(i):=c$. \\
Add $(i,j,k)$ & Set $X(i):=X(j)+X(k)$. \\
Subtract $(i,j,k)$ & Set $X(i):=\max(0,X(j)-X(k))$. \\
Indirect load $(i,j)$ & Set $X(i):=X(X(j))$. \\
Indirect store $(i,j)$ & Set $X(X(i)):=X(j)$. \\
Positive branch $(j,a)$ & Set $q:=a$ if $X(j)>0$; otherwise advance $q$ by one. \\
Jump to $a$ & Set $q:=a$. \\
Halt & Leave the entire state unchanged. \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

Each register-writing instruction advances $q$ by one; its operands are evaluated
in the old state, and all other registers are preserved. A fetch outside the program
also leaves the state unchanged. Starting states have $q=0$ and arbitrary register
contents. A state is halted when it fetches Halt or is outside the program.
Unit cost here counts instructions. It has nothing to do with the record's ledger.

For the indirect instructions, draw boxes 1, 2 and 3 and put 2, 7 and 0 in them.
Indirect load $(3,1)$ first reads the 2 in box 1, uses it as an address, and copies
box 2's 7 into box 3. Now put 9 in box 3 and execute indirect store $(1,3)$:
the 2 in box 1 tells it where to put the 9, so box 2 changes and box 1 stays 2.
An address is being read from a box; it is not necessarily the box's own number.

The \textbf{lambda base} uses the terms and weak call-by-value rule defined in
Definition~\ref{def:u12-L}. To compute its next state, first try to reduce the function
part of an application. If that part cannot step and is an abstraction, either
substitute an argument that is already an abstraction or take a step in the
argument. If neither applies, the term cannot step. Variables and abstractions
cannot step by themselves, and there is no reduction under an abstraction.
The base leaves a term unchanged when it cannot step and calls precisely those
terms halted. Every term is allowed as a starting state, including open terms.
\end{definition}

So all three are bases in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:u11-base}, and the latch theorem
applies to each. It says nothing else about them, nothing about what they can compute or how fast.

There's also a relation defined between bases, \emph{weak base equivalence}: two bases are
equivalent when some correspondence covers their start states both ways, related states agree
on an observation and on halting, and one step on one side is matched by some number of
steps, possibly zero, on the other. That ``some number of steps'' is the \emph{stuttering} idea
Leslie Lamport (the same Lamport as Section~\ref{sec:counter}'s message counters) put forward in 1983: a fine-grained machine and a coarse one shouldn't count as
different because one takes three ticks to do what the other does in one. The relation
carries no cost; a machine that multiplies huge numbers in one step and a Turing machine
differ in price. The relation never looks at price, so on what it does look at they can match. It's proved to be an equivalence relation, and the latch
form is preserved across it.

Draw a coarse machine $0\to1$, with 1 halted, and a finer one
$a\to b\to c$, with $c$ halted. Let $a$ and $b$ both show 0 and $c$ show 1;
halted states stay where they are. Relate 0 to both $a$ and $b$, and 1 to $c$.
The fine move $a\to b$ changes nothing visible, so the coarse machine matches it
by taking no step. Its move $b\to c$ matches $0\to1$. Starting from $a$, the
coarse move is matched by two fine steps. ``Possibly zero'' allows this;
the relation is about matching observations and halting, not matching the number
of ticks or their cost.

There is a limit to that statement. The ``preserved across it'' proof throws away its equivalence hypothesis; the latch holds
on every base regardless, so the preservation is true for a boring reason. And nowhere in this
book are \emph{two} of the bases actually related by this relation. The relation is
defined, it's an equivalence, and it is not used to connect the Turing machine to the
register machine to the lambda calculus, or any of them to the machine of Section~\ref{sec:smallest}. It would be
easy to read that list as if it did. The honest sentence is the one that's proved: each base, separately,
carries a latch.

\begin{definition}[Weak base equivalence]\label{def:u11-weak-equiv}
Bases $B_1$ and $B_2$, with observations $o_1$ and $o_2$ into one common set, are \emph{weakly equivalent} when some relation $R$ relates every starting state of each to some starting state
of the other, and any related $x$, $y$ have $o_1(x) = o_2(y)$, the same halting, some $n \ge 0$
with $R(\mathrm{next}_{B_1}(x), \mathrm{next}_{B_2}^n(y))$, and some $n \ge 0$ with
$R(\mathrm{next}_{B_1}^n(x), \mathrm{next}_{B_2}(y))$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Outside bases, and the relation]\label{thm:u11-four-bases}
(1) Weak base equivalence is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. (2) If two bases are weakly
equivalent, Observation~\ref{thm:u11-latch} holds over one exactly when it holds over the other.
(3) Observation~\ref{thm:u11-latch} holds over each of the three bases in
Definition~\ref{def:u11-concrete-bases}, for every fixed program where the base has one.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) A base matches itself by pairing each state with itself and matching one
step with one step. Reverse any matching between two bases and it gives a
matching in the other direction.

For three bases, pair a state of the first with a state of the third whenever
some middle state matches both. A start on either outside has a middle start
beside it, and that middle start has a start on the far side. Observations
and halting agree across the first pair and then across the second, so they
agree across the outside pair too.

Follow one step on the first base. Its match supplies a finite sequence of
middle steps. Match the first of those steps on the third base, then the
second from where that match ended, and continue. Joining the finite
sequences gives a match for the original step. If the middle sequence is
empty, take no step on the third base. Do the same in the other direction
for a step on the third base. This checks both stepping requirements and
proves transitivity.

(2) The latch argument uses only a base step and the stated record rules.
It therefore holds over both bases, whether or not they are matched.
(3) Each of the three displayed constructions supplies that step, its starts
and its halting reading. The same latch argument applies separately to each.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Records with more than two values}

A cup has two positions, and some records have more: a counter of how many checks passed, or a level
that only rises. The same reasoning goes through one threshold at a time. For each value $a$,
``the record has reached $a$'' is a yes/no reading, and each of those readings is a latch. What
doesn't go through is squeezing the whole record into one cup. ``Rises'' needs one word of explanation: the
values come with an order $\le$, ``is at or below,'' which needn't compare every pair (that's
what makes it a \emph{partial} order), and $[a \le x]$ is the yes/no reading ``$x$ has reached $a$.

For example, keep separate records that an experiment was repeated and that its
calculation was checked. ``Repeated only'' and ``calculation checked only'' are
different places; neither includes the other. ``Both'' is above each. In this
order, moving up means retaining what was already done and possibly adding
another act. The order also has three rules: a place includes itself, inclusion
carries through an intermediate place, and two places including each other
are the same place. Those are the rules the proof below uses.''

\begin{definition}[A growing record]\label{def:u11-growing}
Let the record take values in a set $A$ with a partial order $\le$ decided by a Boolean test. A
record $\rho$ on $M$, with cover $\pi$ onto a base $B$, is a \emph{base-driven growing record} when: there
is one function $f$ with $\rho(\mathrm{next}_M(m)) = f(\pi(m), \rho(m))$; it grows,
$\rho(m) \le \rho(\mathrm{next}_M(m))$; the ledger never goes down and every step that changes
$\rho$ costs at least one; and some run from a starting state reaches a step that changes it.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Growing records are families of latches]\label{thm:u11-growing}
(1) For every base-driven growing record there is an $h$ with
\[
[a \le \rho(\mathrm{next}_M(m))] = [a \le \rho(m)] \lor h(a, \pi(m), \rho(m))
\]
for every value $a$ and state $m$: each threshold is a latch, whose event may read the current
value. (2) The thresholds determine the value: if $[a \le x] = [a \le y]$ for every $a$, then
$x = y$. (3) For a growing record, charging every change is the same as charging every threshold
that switches on. (4) One latch is not enough: a three-valued record that climbs
$0 \to 1 \to 2$ over a one-state base, each climb charged one, is base-driven, and no single Boolean
latch with a decoding from the base state and the latch reproduces it. (5) A chain of distinct
$k$-bit words, each word's set bits contained in the next one's, has at most $k + 1$ members.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Fix a threshold $a$. If the old record has already reached it, growth
keeps it reached. If it has not, the cup rises exactly when the next record
$f(b,x)$ reaches it. Define the event to say both things: ``not reached at
$x$, reached at $f(b,x)$,'' or
$h(a,b,x)=[a\not\le x]\wedge[a\le f(b,x)]$.
Keeping an existing yes and otherwise using that event gives the stated
latch equation.

(2) Suppose $x$ and $y$ give the same answer at every threshold. Ask the
threshold named $x$ itself. The record $x$ has reached it, so $y$ must have
reached it too: $x\le y$. Ask the threshold named $y$ and get $y\le x$.
The order's third rule says those two records are the same.

(3) If the value stays put, every threshold gives the same answer before
and after. If it grows from $x$ to a different $y$, look at the threshold
$y$. It is reached afterwards. It was not reached before: $y\le x$,
together with growth $x\le y$, would force $x=y$. Thus some threshold
switches on exactly when the record changes. Charging those steps is the
same requirement in either wording.

(4) Keep the base at its sole state and let the record move from zero to
one, then two, then stay at two. Add one to the tally at each climb.
The record rule consults only its present value, keeps it growing and pays
for both changes, so it meets the requirements. A single flag over that
unchanging base offers a decoder only two inputs, flag down and flag up.
It cannot reproduce the three different record values just visited.

(5) Lay the distinct bit words out in their increasing order. At each move
to the next word, at least one bit that was zero must become one; no one
may become zero. Across the whole chain there are only $k$ bits available
for those changes. There are therefore at most $k$ moves between distinct
words, or $k+1$ words including the first.
\end{proof}

I have two cautions about that. In (1) each threshold's event may read the record's current value, so
the events aren't all functions of the base alone. And (3) charges a step when it switches some
threshold on: a step that switches on three thresholds at once owes at least one, and nothing
here makes the charges add up per threshold.

The order need not be finite;
(5) is the finite-memory bound.

\subsection{What leaving the base open buys you}

The reason this section exists is to answer the suspicion I started with. The record isn't
special pleading for one machine. Over any base that steps deterministically, under rules you can read, a record that
answers to the computation and never comes down is a latch on an event, and the proof
doesn't care what the base is. What a particular machine adds on top of the latch is a
\emph{choice of price list} and a \emph{choice of event}, and both are choices. That is why the permanent-flip theorem in Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} never needed the word certify: it forces a
merge in whatever stays. The surcharged cup
shows the first: the cost can change and the record not notice. The two cups on one die show
the second: the rules are happy with either event. Any machine that meets the model will have to make both
choices, and whether its choice of event is the right one is a question I'll get to
(Section~\ref{sec:pointer}), and won't claim to have settled. Before that, a record can have
more than two positions. Earlier in this section a record that rises got cut into one cup
per threshold; the next section asks how much of the rest of the book survives once a record has
more places to be than up and down.

\subsection{What it takes to be complete}
\label{sec:complete}

The latch left two choices open, the price list and the event. A machine I can hold up against
everything else has to make both, and a name for ``this machine computes, and its record keeps
something'' has to ask for more than the toll does. The toll alone is a low bar. A machine that
charges one for every step it takes is a clock bolted to a computer, and it obeys the toll for any
record at all: every raise costs at least one because every move does. And a machine whose record
never goes up obeys it too, because a toll on a raise that never happens is never broken. The clock-priced machine may keep useful records; its prices simply do
not distinguish computing from recording. The constant reading can keep no
new yes/no distinction. The toll permits both.

I'll give the names now, all of them, once, with the reason for each, and they work the way
Turing's do.
\emph{The Thiele Machine}, with capitals, is the model: a computer with a reading that can go from
no to yes, natural instruction prices and the toll. The reading may also
be constant or revocable. An internal ledger is extra structure. \emph{A Thiele machine}, lower case, is any particular system
that fits the model, the way one rule table is a Turing machine. That bar is low on purpose, and a
clock clears it. \emph{Thiele-complete}, defined next, is the bar worth meeting, the way
Turing-complete is: a machine that computes anything, with its record kept apart from its computing
and able to tell starts apart. Part~III adds one stricter bar, \emph{certified Thiele-complete},
for a record that, from a clean start, goes up only on a claim that was checked, committed and certified. And
Appendix~\ref{sec:universal-machines} names a \emph{universal Thiele machine}: one machine that
runs the others, the way Turing's universal machine runs every Turing machine. Those are all of
them: the model, the systems that obey it, the ones that compute and keep, the ones whose keeping
is earned, and the one that runs them.

The bar comes in four clauses, and nothing in it mentions what the record is about.

\begin{definition}[Thiele-complete]\label{def:thiele-complete}
A machine with the five parts is \emph{Thiele-complete} when it can be read through an \emph{interface} that
hands over three things: a universal base, a split of its moves into \emph{computing moves} and
\emph{marks}, and a \emph{ledger}, a whole number for each state. A \emph{universal base} is a way
of reading each state as a configuration of a machine that runs every program (I use Minsky's two
counters, Section~\ref{sec:counters-origin}), a class of \emph{live} states, a computing move for each of that machine's instructions that does to the configuration exactly what the instruction does from every live state and keeps it live, and, for each start, a live loaded state showing that start. The interface has to meet four clauses.
(A) \emph{Computing can't reach the record, and the record stays.} No computing move changes the
record, and a record that's up stays up under every move.
(B) \emph{Starts are blank.} Every loaded state has the record down.
(C) \emph{Computing costs nothing, marks cost one.} Computing moves cost 0, every other
move costs exactly 1, and each move adds its cost to the ledger.
(D) \emph{The record tells starts apart.} Some run, the same list of moves, ends with the record
up from one loaded state and down from another.
\end{definition}

Read the clauses as four plain sentences, with the universal base underneath them: the machine
computes anything a Turing machine can. (A) The computing never touches what's kept, and what's
kept stays. (B) Nothing is kept before the run starts. (C) The
ledger counts the marks, and only the marks. (D) What's kept depends on where you started: there's
a run whose record says something about its start.

(D) is the clause where distinction comes in, and it's a low bar: a mark that reads one bit of the
input meets it. What it excludes is a record that ignores the start. A record that goes up on every
run from every start keeps a before and an after, and nothing about where the run began. (D) doesn't
ask that every raise tell starts apart; it asks that the machine can. A machine may have a mark that
raises the record from any state at all; it pays one for it, like every raise, and (D) is still met
by some other run. Which runs a machine wants its record to tell apart is its own choice, and
Part~III makes one.

The name echoes Turing-complete, but this is a specification a machine meets, not a class closed
under simulation: a machine is held up against it through an interface, and changing the unit of
price drops a machine out.

\begin{theorem}[What every Thiele-complete machine has]\label{thm:tc-has}
Let a machine be Thiele-complete through an interface. (1) It obeys the toll, and the move that
raises its record is a mark, never a computing move, and costs exactly one. (2) Along any run, the
ledger rises by exactly the number of marks in it. (3) From any state with the record down, every
run that ends with the record up raises the ledger by at least 1. (4) Some run from some loaded
state raises the record. (5) Every move costs 0 or 1, and some move costs 0. (6) Its base runs
every two-counter program step for step from every live state, and halting from a loaded state
matches halting from the configuration it shows.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) If a computing move raised the record it would change it, against (A); so the raising move is
a mark, and a mark costs one by (C). (2) is (C) added up along the run. (3) Somewhere along the run
the record goes from down to up, and that move is a mark, by (1), so it adds one. (4) is (D), and by (B) the record started down. (5)
Every move is a computing move or a mark, and the universal base supplies computing moves. (6) is the universal base, one instruction at a time, from a loaded state that is live and shows its start.
\end{proof}

The floor is one, and one is reached: the lift below gives a machine whose record goes up after a
single mark.

\begin{observation}[A clock is a Thiele machine and isn't Thiele-complete]\label{obs:tc-clock}
Take the two-counter machine, let every move cost 1, and take as the record any yes/no question
about its configuration; or a flag that switches on, and stays on, the first time a chosen test of
the configuration says yes. It obeys the toll and has a two-counter machine inside it, and it isn't
Thiele-complete. No machine whose every move costs at least 1 is.
\end{observation}

\begin{proof}
A Thiele-complete machine has a move priced 0, by Theorem~\ref{thm:tc-has}(5), and this one has
none.
\end{proof}

A two-counter base priced 0 with a record that's down at every state obeys the toll and meets (A),
(B) and (C), and isn't Thiele-complete either: (D) asks for a run that raises the record.

\begin{theorem}[Each of the four clauses is needed]\label{thm:tc-clauses}
For each clause there's a machine that meets the other three through some interface and is
Thiele-complete through none. Two of them are built on the two counters with two marks, one that raises
the record when $A$ is 0 and one that always raises it, and a ledger beside them that each move adds its cost to. (A) fails: that machine, and one more move,
priced 0, that puts the record back down. (B) fails: the two counters, every move priced 0, with
a record that no move ever changes, up at the starts where $A$ is 0 and down elsewhere. (C) fails:
the two counters with two marks, every move priced 1. (D) fails: the two counters, every move priced 0,
with a record that's always down.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Each machine meets the three by construction. The first fails (A) through every interface, because
a move lowers the record, so the record doesn't stay. The second: every one of its moves costs 0,
so (C) makes every move a computing move under any interface; then by (A) no run changes the
record, and with every start blank by (B) no run raises it, so (D) fails. The third has no move
priced 0, so it fails by Observation~\ref{obs:tc-clock}. The fourth never raises its record.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The record can't be read off the window]\label{thm:tc-window}
Let a machine be Thiele-complete through an interface. (1) Every configuration is shown, at no
cost, with the record down, by one computing move from some loaded state. (2) Some loaded state
has two runs that end on the same window, one with the record up and one with it down, and their
ledgers differ by at least 1. (3) So no rule that reads only the window says, at the end of every
run from every loaded state, whether the record is up, and none says what the ledger reads.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) From the loaded state $(1, x+1, y)$, the computing move ``DEC $A$ to line $p$'' shows
$(p, x, y)$, costs nothing by (C), and leaves the record down by (A) and (B). (2) Take the run (D)
gives, from the loaded state where it raises the record. Its end shows some configuration. From
the same loaded state, computing moves alone reach any configuration at all: count each counter
down to zero, count it up to the value wanted, and jump to the line wanted. That run ends on the
same window, and it's all computing, so by (A) and (B) its record is still down and by (C) its
ledger hasn't moved, while the first run's ledger went up by at least one, at its raise. (3) A rule
that reads the window gives one answer for one window, and (2) has one window with two answers.
\end{proof}

Part~III proves the same blindness for its certified machines (Observation~\ref{thm:u34-tc-window}),
with a gap of three, because a certified raise costs three. Here the gap is one, and one is
reached.

\begin{theorem}[Every universal base becomes Thiele-complete]\label{thm:tc-lift}
Take any machine with a universal base and any events on its states, and add a record, a ledger and, for each event, a
mark that costs one and raises the record exactly when the event holds; computing moves cost nothing
and leave the record alone, and every move adds its cost to the ledger. If some run of computing moves makes some event hold from one loaded
state and not from another, the result is Thiele-complete, its computing is the original machine's
step for step, and its record goes up after a single mark from any state where the event already
holds.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(A): computing moves are the original's and don't touch the record, and a mark only adds to it.
