(B): the record starts down. (C): by construction. (D): run the moves that make the event hold
from one loaded state and not the other, then the event's mark. Step for step: a computing move
acts on the original part and nothing else. And a mark from a state where its event holds puts the
record up.
\end{proof}

One mark on ``$A$ is at least 1'' always works: the starts with $A$ at 0 and at 1 already differ
on it, so that mark alone, run from each, tells them apart. So Thiele-complete isn't a property only a special
machine has. Any model with a universal base becomes Thiele-complete by adding marks, and needs no
claims and no checker to do it; a model that simulates the two counters some other way does so once
its moves are grouped into ones that carry out a counter instruction each (Theorem~\ref{thm:lift-models}). Two kinds of base don't lift, whatever the
events: one whose moves don't depend on the state it's in, and one whose moves lead from each state
to only finitely many next states. A universal base needs, from one state, a move at no cost to
every line of a program, and that's infinitely many places to go.

Some Thiele-complete machine runs every Thiele machine a program can describe.
Appendix~\ref{sec:universal-machines} defines a \emph{universal Thiele machine} and builds hosts
that run any machine a program can describe, in order, carrying its reading as a latch and matching its ledger up to a surcharge of at most three, with every
computing step done by counter moves on the host and every rise of the host's record placed by its
program. None of that needs certification: the presented host's own program, read on a host with no claims, no checker and no table of facts, and one paid mark that raises the record when a register is at least 1, meets the definition too.

The rest of the book holds machines to this bar. Part~III gives one example that clears it,
and then asks for the stricter certified bar: that from a clean start its record go up only on a claim that was checked, by a
checker proved to mean it, and then committed, and that some claim's check can come out either
way. Asking that is a choice of what the record answers to, the second of the latch's two open
choices, made one way, with clean starts and three priced acts added (Theorem~\ref{thm:tc-decomposition}).

%===========================================================================
\section{The whole direction}
\label{sec:direction}
%===========================================================================

I have a hunch I can't fully back up, and Part~III tells where it came from
(Section~\ref{sec:established}): \emph{established} doesn't feel like a switch to me. It feels
like a direction with lines drawn across it, and the switch is just the first line. The one piece
of that I can settle is that a single switch isn't enough once there are three or more stages. I
settle it in this section, and find out how much of the rest survives being pushed on.

A row of cells that only ever go from blank to written is a direction: you can tell how far
along it a state is, and nothing walks it back. The cup of Section~\ref{sec:latch} has two positions. Definition~\ref{def:thiele}
already lets the record sit in any order; the proofs so far were done for the cup. Everything the book has proved about the
toll so far (the universal floor, the merges, the squeeze, the windows) was proved for a cup. The question
for this section is blunt: if the record has more places to be than up and down, how many of
those results come along, and which ones break?

\subsection{A row of cups}

Get four cups and a pencil. Write five stages of an experiment on a strip of paper,
left to right: \emph{proposed}, \emph{set up}, \emph{run}, \emph{read}, \emph{recorded}.
Agree to do them in that order. Put an upside-down cup between each pair of neighbours.
The first means ``the setup happened,'' the second ``the run happened,'' the third
``the result was read,'' the fourth ``the result was recorded.'' As you complete a
stage, turn over its cup. Cups only ever get turned right side up; none has a reset
wire. These are records of completed acts. A fourth cup up does not make a false
conclusion true, and a different experiment may need a different order.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[thiele]
\node[pipe,text width=3.4cm,minimum width=0pt] (a) {proposed\\\texttt{0000}};
\node[pipe,text width=3.4cm,minimum width=0pt,below=0.55cm of a] (b) {set up\\\texttt{1000}};
\node[pipe,text width=3.4cm,minimum width=0pt,below=0.55cm of b] (c) {run\\\texttt{1100}};
\node[pipe,text width=3.4cm,minimum width=0pt,below=0.55cm of c] (d) {read\\\texttt{1110}};
\node[pipe,text width=3.4cm,minimum width=0pt,below=0.55cm of d] (e) {recorded\\\texttt{1111}};
\draw[pipearrow] (a.south) -- (b.north);
\draw[pipearrow] (b.south) -- (c.north);
\draw[pipearrow] (c.south) -- (d.north);
\draw[pipearrow] (d.south) -- (e.north);
\end{tikzpicture}

\small Read down the drawing. Zero means cup down, one means cup up. Four cups give five stages
along this run because each new stage turns up one unused cup.
\end{center}

Two things to notice with the cups in front of you. Each cup by itself is exactly the cup of
Section~\ref{sec:latch}: it reads yes or no, and once yes it stays yes. And four cups were
enough for five stages. Try it with three, and you'll find you can't: three cups that only ever
turn up, in order, give you at most four different arrangements along the way. I'll prove both of
those in a minute, and the proof is about as short as the experiment.

Now a harder strip. Some checks don't line up. One person repeats the experiment;
another independently works through the calculation. Neither act includes the other.
Draw a diamond: \emph{neither} at the bottom, \emph{experiment repeated} on the left,
\emph{calculation checked} on the right, \emph{both} at the top. There are two ways
up, and the middle points don't compare, which is what a \emph{partial} order allows.
Put a cup on each point except the bottom, one for the repeat, one for the calculation,
one for both. Each cup is still a latch. The three cups tell you which acts have
happened. They do not decide whether the experimental model or the calculation's
premises were appropriate.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[thiele]
\node[pipe,text width=3.6cm,minimum width=0pt] (n) at (0,0) {Neither act\\\texttt{000}};
\node[pipe,text width=3.6cm,minimum width=0pt] (r) at (-3.2,2.6) {Experiment repeated\\\texttt{100}};
\node[pipe,text width=3.6cm,minimum width=0pt] (c) at (3.2,2.6) {Calculation checked\\\texttt{010}};
\node[pipe,text width=3.6cm,minimum width=0pt] (b) at (0,5.2) {Both acts\\\texttt{111}};
\draw[pipearrow] (n) -- (r);
\draw[pipearrow] (n) -- (c);
\draw[pipearrow] (r) -- (b);
\draw[pipearrow] (c) -- (b);
\end{tikzpicture}

\small Read the cups as repeat, calculation, both. Neither middle point
includes the other. The third cup repeats information already supplied by
the first two; it is useful for showing thresholds, not needed for storage.
\end{center}

Whatever the shape of the strip, a straight line of stages or a diamond or something with a
hundred points, I'll call the set of places the record can be the \emph{direction}, and each
question ``has the record reached at least this place?'' a \emph{line} across it. One line is
one cup.

\subsection{The order, said exactly}

The strip and the diamond each come with an order you can see by looking: whether one place is at
or below another. Said exactly, the order is a test. For any two places $x$ and $y$ it answers ``is
$x$ at or below $y$?'' with yes or no, and I write a yes as $x \le y$. The test has to obey two
rules: every place is at or below itself, and if $x \le y$ and $y \le z$ then $x \le z$. An order
that obeys just those two is called a \emph{preorder}. If it also obeys a third rule, that $x \le y$
and $y \le x$ together force $x = y$, it's a \emph{partial order}, and that third rule is called
antisymmetry. The two-point order, no below yes, is the cup. The whole numbers in their usual order
are a straight strip that never ends.

The cups say the same thing in their own terms. For a place $a$, the cup for $a$ asks ``has the
record reached at least $a$?'', so with the record at $x$ it's up exactly when $a \le x$, and I
write its answer as $[a \le x]$. In the row of cups I said the cups together tell you which place
the record is at. On the strip and the diamond you can check that with your eyes, and part (2) of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-growing} already proved it whenever the order is partial, though I hadn't asked
what in that proof was doing the work. My first guess was that it held for every order.

Why bother with the bare preorder at all, when every strip on the table is a partial order? I bothered because
I wanted to see what the third rule was doing, and the way to see what a rule does is to take it
away. Take a preorder with two places, call them \emph{left} and \emph{right}, where each is at or
below the other. There are two cups, one asking ``at least left?'' and one asking ``at least
right?'', and both are up at left and both are up at right. Look at the table and you can't say
where the record is. Now build a record that swaps between left and right on every single step and
charges nothing. Every rule I'm about to state is satisfied. The record never drops below anywhere
it was, because each place is at or below the other. No cup ever moves, so the toll in the next
subsection has nothing to charge. The record moved on every step and nothing on the table noticed.

\begin{theorem}[The cups fix the place, and only with antisymmetry]\label{thm:dir-lines}
(1) In a partial order, if two places $x$ and $y$ leave the same cups up, $[a \le x] = [a \le y]$
for every $a$, then $x = y$. (2) In a preorder that isn't a partial order this can fail: there's a
preorder with two different places that leave the same cups up, and a record over it, driven by
the computation and growing in that preorder, that changes on every step while no cup moves.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Look at the cup for $x$. It's up when the record is at $x$, since $x$ is at or below itself,
so it's up at $y$ too, and that says $x \le y$. The cup for $y$ gives $y \le x$ the same way.
Antisymmetry gives $x = y$. (2) Left and right above, with the record swapping every step.
\end{proof}

So in a partial order the cups are the place, and in the preorder I built they aren't. That second
half holds in every preorder that isn't partial, by one line: if
$x \le y$ and $y \le x$ with $x \ne y$, then a cup that's up at either one is up at the other, by
transitivity. So the cups fix the place if and only if the order is partial. My first guess was right on every
strip I could draw, and it was right because of a rule I hadn't noticed I was leaning on. On a
bare preorder, putting two places on the same rung tells the toll not to care about moves between
them, and it doesn't. I don't think that's a defect; it's the order telling you what you agreed to
count.

\subsection{The toll, over the whole direction}

One cup had one rule: the step that turns it right side up pays. Now there's a row of cups, or a
diamond of them, and a single step can turn over several at once. The rule I'd guess first
turns out to be the right one: \emph{a step that turns over any cup pays at least one.} A step
that turns over three cups at once still only has to pay one. The rule asks whether a step turned
something over. It doesn't ask how many.

That rule buys the same thing one cup bought. Take any run, and suppose some cup is up at
the end that was down at the start. Somewhere along the run a step turned that cup over, and that
step paid. So the run paid at least one. Count the same way and you get more: the run paid at least
once for every step that turned anything over.

Now look at what that argument didn't use. It didn't care whether the cups sat in a row or a
diamond or something with a hundred points. It didn't care how many there were. It didn't even use
the fact that cups never get turned back down. If something could knock a cup back over, the
argument still works, because all it needs is the one step where that cup went up.

To say it exactly I want to translate it into places. The cup at a place
$a$ is up exactly when the record is at or above $a$. Say a step takes the record from $x$ to $y$.
The cup at $y$ is up afterwards, since $y$ is at or above itself, and it was down before exactly
when $y$ isn't at or below $x$. And if $y$ is at or below $x$, any cup that's up at $y$ was already
up at $x$. So a step turns over some cup exactly when it lands somewhere that isn't at or below
where it started. The same reasoning says a run ends with some cup up that was down at the start
exactly when it ends somewhere that isn't at or below where it started.

\begin{theorem}[The toll over any direction]\label{thm:dir-toll}
Take a machine whose record is a place in any preorder, and say a step \emph{turns a cup over} when
it takes the record from $x$ to a place that isn't at or below $x$. (1) Every step that turns a cup
over costs at least one exactly when every run, from whatever state it starts, that ends somewhere not
at or below its start costs at least one. (2) When that holds, a run costs at least the number of its
steps that turn a cup over. (3) It holds exactly when every cup, on its own, obeys the toll of
Section~\ref{sec:latch}: for every place $a$, a step that turns the cup at $a$ from down to up costs
at least one. The universal floor of Section~\ref{sec:toll} (Observation~\ref{thm:universal-floor}) is (1) with one cup.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) and (2) are the walk above. For the other half of (1), a run of one step that turns a cup over
ends somewhere not at or below its start. (3) is the translation above.
\end{proof}

When the cups only ever go up, as on the strip and the diamond, a step that turns a cup over is
just a step up.

That surprised me a little, because I'd filed the floor away as a fact about one bit, and nothing in it was
about one bit. It was about one cup going up, and anything you build out of cups has that.

\subsection{One line isn't enough}

Now comes the payoff I promised at the start of this section. Could a cleverer single cup do the job of all four, with one latch and some decoding that reads the record's place off the
latch and whatever the machine shows? Section~\ref{sec:latch} already ruled that out in the
smallest case: over a machine with one visible state, a record that climbs through three places can't be
produced by one latch and a decoding, because one latch and one visible state make two outcomes and
the record has three.

So try a second guess, closer to the cup's own rule. The cup's rule was ``new value is old value
\emph{or} the event.'' The obvious rule for a whole row is ``new place is old place \emph{joined
with} the event's place,'' where joining two places means going to the lowest place at or above
both. On the row, the event names a place, and you turn up every cup as far as that place. To see
it break, take the strip $0 < 1 < 2$, a cup at $1$ and a cup at $2$, over a machine with one
visible state, so the event has to be one fixed place. Let the record jump from $0$ straight to $2$,
turning up both cups in one step, and stay put at $1$ and at $2$. From $0$ the event has to turn up
both cups, so the fixed place is $2$. From $1$ the same event would turn up the second cup as well,
and the record stays at $1$.

What works is giving every cup its own event, and letting the event for a cup look at where the
record already is. Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-growing} said exactly that, and this is why it had
to say it. That leaves the question of how many cups. In the row of cups I asked you to try five stages with three
and said you couldn't. Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-growing} (5) already bounded the chain from above.
The count behind that bound comes again below, with the matching example added, and with an arrangement of
$k$ cups read as a $k$-bit word, a one for every cup that's up.

\begin{theorem}[Lines a direction needs]\label{thm:dir-bits}
(1) A list of different arrangements of $k$ cups, each keeping up every cup the one before had up
(a chain of different $k$-bit words in which each word's set bits are among the next word's), has
at most $k + 1$ members, and for every $k$ there's such a chain with exactly $k + 1$. So a straight
strip of $n + 1$ stages needs exactly $n$ cups. (2) Over a machine with one visible state, take the
record on the strip $0 < 1 < 2$ that jumps from $0$ to $2$ and stays put at $1$ and at $2$. It
grows and is driven by the computation, and no rule of the form ``join the record with a fixed
place'' reproduces its steps.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Going from one arrangement to the next, which is a different one, turns up at least one more
cup, and there are $k$ cups, so there are at most $k$ steps and $k + 1$ arrangements. For the
matching chain, take no cups up, then the first, then the first two, and so on, packed to the
left: that's the row of cups. (2) Joining $0$ with a fixed place $g$ gives $g$, and from $0$ the
step has to give $2$, so $g$ is $2$. Joining $1$ with $2$ gives $2$, and from $1$ the step has to
stay at $1$.
\end{proof}

So five stages need four cups, and neither one nor three will do it, as long as the cups only turn
up. An ordinary binary counter holds a thousand stages in ten bits, because its bits go
down as well as up, and the theorem says nothing against that. The switch isn't wrong:
it's the first line, and a straight strip with more than two places needs more of them, exactly one
fewer than it has stages. A direction that branches needs at least as many cups as the steps in its longest strict climb, and at least as many as it takes to tell its places apart, the rounded-up logarithm of how many there are. Put three places above a bottom, none of them above another: the longest climb is one step, and one cup can't tell four places apart, so it takes two, and two do it, though not two lines: one cup that goes up at the first and the third, and one that goes up at the second and the third. It can need more than both. Take two places each below two others: one step of climb, four places, and two cups still won't do, because both upper places would have to keep up every cup either lower one has up, and two cups allow at most one arrangement like that besides the lower places' own.

People got here before me, and from a direction I didn't expect, which was programming for many
processors at once. Lindsey Kuper and Ryan Newton's LVars (2013), ``lattice-based data structures
for deterministic parallelism'' in their own title, are memory cells whose value only climbs in an
order, where a read can't ask for the value and can only ask whether it has climbed past a
threshold. That's a cup. Writers running side by side can push the value up in different orders,
and a threshold once passed stays passed. Their deterministic behaviour also depends on
which reads and updates the language permits. Permanence alone would not do it: a program
allowed to ask whether the cup is up \emph{yet} could still see another writer's timing. Amin Timany and Lars Birkedal (2021), coming at it from proofs about programs,
show, as I read their paper, that any preorder at all can be carried as monotone ghost state
in a program logic. That's the closest thing I've found to somebody else arriving at the decomposition into
lines.

The two rest on the same thing, a value that only climbs and a question that only asks whether it's
past a point, and they use it for opposite jobs. In an LVar the threshold read steers the program.
Ghost state, as far as I understand the term, lives in the proof, and the running program never
reads it. Here the record is never allowed to steer the base computation, so that particular restriction sits closer to the ghost state. Push on
that and it gives a little: Section~\ref{sec:structure}'s glance, the whole reason to keep a record,
is a read. What keeps me on that side is that a glance worth trusting gives the answer the long way
would have given. Their purposes aren't mine, but the shape is theirs first. What I can't find in
either is a price on crossing a line.

\subsection{Why crossing a line has to cost}

Part~I showed that the cup's toll isn't an arbitrary rule. It's forced by three premises, and the
argument that ties them together was the
pigeonhole: on a machine with finitely many states, the move that raises a record that goes up and stays up has to land two
possible states on one state (Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges}), and a step that
lands two states on one is a step that forgets which one it came from. Does that survive the whole
row of cups? Mostly, and the parts that don't survive are the interesting ones.

The counting needs a flag, because what it counts is the collection of states with that flag up, and now there are many cups, each one a yes-or-no reading that could serve as the flag, so the first job is to pick one. My first guess
was the cup for the place where the record starts. That goes nowhere: the starting state
already has that cup up, so it's already in the collection, and there's no state coming in from outside. The cup
that works is the one the step turns over, the cup for the place where the record lands. It's up
after the step, since a place is at or above itself, and it was down before, which is what turning a cup
over means. So the collection is every state with that landing cup up, and the state the step
starts from is the one coming in from outside.
If the move keeps every state in the collection inside it and never lands two states on one, the states already inside use up every state in the collection between them, and there's none left for the newcomer. So one of two things
happened. Either two states landed on one, or some state that was in the collection got moved out, which
means its landing cup went back down. I'll call that second thing a \emph{revocation}.

\begin{theorem}[Turning a cup over merges]\label{thm:dir-merge}
On a machine with a record in any preorder, where each place has finitely many states with its cup up: (1) if a move turns a cup over
at some state and lands the record at a place $a$, then either the move merges two states, or
there's a state with the cup at $a$ up that the same move takes to a state with the cup at $a$
down, which is a revocation; (2) if the record only grows, so that no cup ever goes back down, the
move merges; (3) if the record only grows, the toll holds exactly when every move that turns a cup
over at some state, and merges, costs at least one, so merge pricing gives the toll.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Gather every state with the cup at $a$ up. There are finitely many. If the move keeps each of
them there and is injective, it maps that collection into itself without two landing on one, so it
hits all of them, including the state it sends the starting state to; injectivity then says the
starting state was in the collection already, and it wasn't, because its cup at $a$ was down. So
either some state in the collection has its cup at $a$ knocked down, or the move isn't injective. (2) Growth rules out the
knocking down. (3) If the toll holds, every move that turns a cup over somewhere pays, merging or
not. The other way, a move that turns a cup over merges by (2), so the hypothesis charges it.
\end{proof}

It's the old counting argument again, run once for every cup.

Each premise there can be knocked out, and I wanted to see each one go, because a premise you've
never seen fail is one you don't understand yet.

Knock out finiteness. Take the whole numbers as the states, which gives a row of cups that never
ends, and let the record be the state itself, one more on every step, at no charge. Every step turns
up one more cup. The step never merges anything: different numbers go to different numbers. Merge
pricing holds, because there are no merges to price, and the toll fails on every single step. The
counting broke at the one place it needed the collection to be finite. Every state moved one along, and there was
always another state to move to. That's Charles Bennett's 1973 construction in miniature: a machine that
keeps its whole history never has to forget, so it never has to merge. It hasn't got out of paying.
Every step lands it on a state it has never used, and that's the fresh-state column. The toll fails here
because merge pricing only charges merges and this machine pays by taking a state it has never used, which that price list
doesn't charge. Take the infinity away and the supply of fresh states goes with it.

Knock out growth. Take a two-state machine whose record flips back and forth between two places, so
a cup goes up on one step and gets knocked back down on the next. The two states just swap with each other,
so nothing merges, and the price list is honest about merges. The step that turns the cup up
pays nothing. It takes the other branch of (1) and revokes: the state that had the cup up gets moved to where it's down.

Knock out the price on merges. A two-state machine that stamps every state with yes turns the cup
up wherever it was down, merges at the stamp, and charges nothing. Of course the toll fails; nobody
asked the merge to pay.

\begin{theorem}[Each premise does work]\label{thm:dir-escapes}
(1) There's a machine with infinitely many states, a growing record and an honest merge price on
which every step turns a cup over and the toll fails. (2) There's a two-state machine with an
honest merge price whose record doesn't grow, which turns a cup over and fails the toll. (3)
There's a two-state machine with a growing record whose merges aren't priced, which fails the toll.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The three machines above, in order.
\end{proof}

So
the toll over a whole direction rests on exactly the three things the cup's toll rested on:
finitely many states with each cup up, a record that doesn't come down, and merges that pay. Nothing extra got
smuggled in when one cup became a row, and nothing the one cup needed got left behind.

I'd half expected the diamond to need something new, some extra rule for the two middle cups that
don't compare. It didn't. Every cup gets its own collection of states, and the argument on each is the old one.

%===========================================================================
\section{The shadow, exactly}
\label{sec:shadow-exact}
%===========================================================================

Section~\ref{sec:windows} put the machine behind a window and asked what an outsider could tell.
It found that two states can look the same through the window and differ in what matters, and that
a price computed from the window can't be exact if the window has a collision
(Observation~\ref{thm:shadow-price}). That was for one cup. With a whole row of cups in hand I can ask
the sharper version of the same question, which is also the one I actually care about. Take the
ordinary machine, the one with no cups and no ledger, and let it look at itself. What's the shape
of everything it can't see, and what does the toll cost in terms of that shape?

\subsection{The ordinary machine is a shadow}

Take any machine with a record and a ledger, and sweep both off the table, the cups and the
counter. What's left is a machine that steps the same way and knows nothing about either, provided
the step's effect on everything else never depends on the cups or the counter: sweeping them off
has to commute with the step. A system whose control reads its record or its ledger has no shadow
in this sense. Where the premise holds, call what's left the \emph{shadow}. Over any one state of the shadow there's a pile of full states, all casting that same shadow and
differing only in their record and their ledger. Section~\ref{sec:windows} already called the pile over a point the
\emph{fibre} over it. The shadow is one particular window, the one that shows everything except the
cups and the ledger.

The shadow has its own fibres, and every move has piles of its own too: the states a move sends to
one landing spot. I'll call those the move's \emph{landing piles}. A fibre is everything that looks
the same before anybody moves. A landing pile is everything that ends up in the same spot after one
move. Keep the two kinds apart, because the whole section turns on how they meet.

\subsection{Pricing from the shadow}

First the window question, over a whole row. A \emph{window price} charges each step from what the
window shows before and after it. It meets the floor if it charges at least one for every step that
turns a cup over, and it's \emph{exact} if it also charges nothing for any step that turns no cup
over. A \emph{collision} is two steps that look the same through the window, where one turns a cup
over and the other doesn't.

With one cup, the fix in Section~\ref{sec:windows} was to put the cup in the window. So my first
guess for a row was that the window has to show some of the cups. Try the smallest version: a
record in the whole numbers, and a window that shows only the first cup, the one that asks ``at
least one?'' Let the record rise on some steps and hold still on others. Once it's past one, that
cup is up before and after both kinds of step, so a step that turned over a cup further along looks
exactly like a step that turned over nothing, and the two make a collision. So then, I thought, the window
has to show every cup. That's wrong too, from the other side. Take a record in the whole numbers
with two moves, one that adds one and one that leaves it alone, and a window that shows only
whether the record is even, which on the row is whether an even number of cups are up. You can't
read the record off that window, and no flat charge is exact, since some steps turn a cup over and
some don't. But the evenness changes on exactly the steps that turn a cup over, so charging one
exactly when the evenness changed is exact.

\begin{theorem}[Window prices over a direction]\label{thm:dir-window}
(1) If the window has a collision, every window price that meets the floor charges at least one for
some step that turns no cup over, so no window price is exact. (2) An exact window price exists exactly when the window has no collision; on a machine with finitely many states and moves, whose views can be told apart by a yes-or-no test, it can also be computed. (3) Along
any run, a window price that meets the floor charges at least the number of steps that turn no cup
over but look, through the window, like a step that does. Some window price meets the floor and, among the steps that turn no cup over, charges one on exactly those, so that number is the least overcharge; when it can be decided, for each pair of views, whether some step showing them turns a cup over, that price can be computed. (4) A window can
price exactly without showing where the record is: there's a record in the whole numbers with a move
that raises it and a move that leaves it alone, and a window that shows only whether the record is
even; the evenness changes exactly on the rises, no charge that is the same for every step is exact,
and charging one exactly when the evenness changes is exact, although no rule reads the record off
the window. (5) There's a record in the whole numbers and a window
that shows only the one cup ``at least one,'' and that window has a collision.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) The two colliding steps get the same charge. The floor makes it at least one because of the step
that turns a cup over, and the other step pays it too. (2) Without a collision, ``does some step
that looks like this turn a cup over?'' is a question about what the window shows; charge one exactly when the answer is yes. On a finite machine you can answer it for every pair of views. (3)
A step that turns no cup over but looks like one that does gets that step's charge, which is at
least one by (1)'s argument; add along the run. For the other half, charge one exactly when the
answer to (2)'s question is yes, which needs that question to be decidable, and count the
overcharge. (4) A rise changes the evenness and the other move doesn't, so the window sees exactly
the steps that turn a cup over; a flat charge either charges nothing for a rise or charges something
for a step that turns nothing over; and 0 and 2 look the same through the window. (5) The first cup, as above.
\end{proof}

Item (4) changed how I think about this. I'd assumed a window had to see the cups to price them. It
doesn't; it has to see them \emph{move}. A window that cannot tell you your exact place, but detects every rise and every pause,
can charge the right amount every time.

\subsection{What a priced move destroys}

Now the fibres. Part~I showed that the move raising a permanent flag on a finite machine lands two
possible states on one state, and Theorem~\ref{thm:dir-merge} showed the same for a step that turns any cup
over, once the cups only go up. Which two? It matters a great deal. If they're in different shadow
fibres, then the ordinary machine lost a distinction too; the record may also differ between them. If they're in the same
fibre, the ordinary machine lost nothing, and what got destroyed was only ever off the table: two
states that cast one shadow, told apart by their cups or their ledger, crushed into one.

My first guess was that it's always the second kind, because the cups are where everything
happens. It isn't always. It depends on whether the ordinary machine forgets anything on its own.

\begin{theorem}[The toll prices a collapse inside a fibre]\label{thm:dir-fibre}
On a machine with finitely many states and a growing record: (1) a move that turns a cup over
somewhere sends two different states to one landing spot; (2) if the shadow exists, so that sweeping commutes with the step, and the shadow's step for that move
forgets nothing, sending different shadow states to different shadow states, then those two states
are in the same shadow fibre, and every landing pile of the move lies inside one fibre; (3) without
that premise it can fail: there's a two-state machine whose two states sit in different fibres and
whose shadow step forgets, so the merge at the step that turns the cup over lands two states from different fibres
and no fibre loses a point. (4) The halving price, which says a move of cost $c$ shrinks any finite
collection of states by at most a factor of $2^c$, holds exactly when every landing pile has at most
$2^c$ states, on a machine of any size.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) is the counting argument of Theorem~\ref{thm:dir-merge}, with growth. (2) If two states land on one spot,
their shadows land on one shadow spot, and the shadow's step tells shadows apart, so the two states
cast the same shadow to begin with. (3) The stamp of Theorem~\ref{thm:dir-escapes}, with the record's value also shown in the
visible part, so each state is its own shadow: both states land on yes, and so do their shadows. (4) is the worst pile-up of
Premise~\ref{prem:halving}. Any $2^c+1$ states of one landing pile would be a collection that lands
on a single spot, which the premise caps at $2^c$, so no pile has more; and any finite
collection is at most the number of spots it lands on times the biggest pile. Neither half needs the
machine to be finite.
\end{proof}

So on a machine with finitely many states and a record that only grows, when the ordinary machine forgets nothing,
the toll is a price on crushing a fibre: on taking
two states that cast one shadow, which only what's off
the table told apart, and making them one.
The last of those premises is the one I just showed you failing.

\subsection{How much gets destroyed, on average}

The halving price is a worst case, because it prices the largest landing pile a move can have. The next question is
the average one: if I don't know which state the machine was in, cups and all, but I have some
spread of chances over the states, how much do I lose, on average, about which state it was, once
I know where it landed? Shannon's conditional entropy measures exactly that (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}
built the entropy from scratch, so I won't do it again here), and I'll write it in bits.

\begin{theorem}[The halving price in bits bounds the average loss]\label{thm:dir-bits-loss}
Take any spread of non-negative weights over the states, uniform or not, with finite total weight, on a machine
of any size. (1) If every landing pile has at most $N$ states, with $N\ge1$, the weighted conditional entropy of
the state given its landing spot is at most the total weight times $\log_2 N$ bits. (2) So on a machine with the
halving price, that weighted information loss is at most its cost in bits times the total weight, even when the
spread's own entropy is infinite. For a probability distribution, the total weight is one and the average loss is
at most the cost. (3) If a landing pile has $2^c$ states, the uniform probability distribution on it loses exactly
$c$ bits and attains that bound.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Look at one landing spot. Suppose the sources that land there carry total
weight $w>0$. Divide each source's weight by $w$. Those shares now add to one:
they describe the uncertainty about the source once you know this landing spot.
There are at most $N$ possible sources. The logarithm argument in
Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} says the uncertainty is greatest when those
possibilities have equal shares, and is then at most $\log_2 N$ bits.
Multiply by $w$ to put this pile back into the whole spread. Its contribution
is at most $w\log_2 N$. A pile with zero weight contributes nothing.

Add the contributions. The pile weights add to the original total weight,
so the same $\log_2 N$ multiplies that total. Under the halving price,
$N=2^{\mathrm{cost}}$, whose base-two logarithm is exactly the cost.

Infinitely many piles cause no subtraction of one infinite entropy from
another. I am adding the nonnegative uncertainties inside the piles.
Every finite collection contributes at most its weight times the bound,
and its weight is at most the total. Taking the largest value approached
by those finite sums keeps the same bound.

Finally put all probability on one pile of $2^c$ sources, equally shared.
Before landing there are $2^c$ equally possible origins; afterwards the
landing spot distinguishes none of them. The uncertainty left about the
origin is $\log_2(2^c)=c$ bits. That attains the bound.
\end{proof}

Where does it stop? My first guess was one place, a landing pile with infinitely many states, and
that the average would blow up there right along with the worst case. That's half right, and the
half that's wrong surprised me. No finite charge satisfying the halving price can price a move that sends infinitely many states
to one spot. The weaker merge price could still charge one, since it does not measure the pile's size. But the average depends on the spread. Put weight $\tfrac12$ on
the first state, $\tfrac14$ on the next, $\tfrac18$ on the next, and so on, and the information lost
by crushing the pile never reaches 2 bits, however many of its states you count. Under that spread,
a two-bit information budget covers the average, though no finite budget covers the worst case. So I went looking
for a spread that does blow up, and it took a nastier one: blocks of states, block $k$ holding
$2^{2^k}$ states and a share $\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)}$ of the weight, which adds up to one. Under that
spread the loss grows past every bound, and no finite information budget covers that average loss.

You can generate the first spread by tossing a fair coin until the first head.
Zero tails names state 0, one tail names state 1, and so on. State $j$ has chance
$2^{-(j+1)}$, and identifying that outcome takes $j+1$ toss-results, so its entropy
term is $(j+1)/2^{j+1}$. Add these by counting each possible toss position:
the first is reached with chance 1, the second with chance $1/2$, the third with
chance $1/4$, and so on. The total is $1+1/2+1/4+\cdots=2$; every finite partial
sum of the state terms is smaller. Resetting all those outcomes to one box can
lose only those two bits on average, despite having infinitely many possible starts.

For the block spread, split each block's weight equally among its states. The block
weights sum to one because $1/((k+1)(k+2))=1/(k+1)-1/(k+2)$. Within block $k$,
there are $2^{2^k}$ equally likely choices, so just identifying a state within that
block contributes $2^k/((k+1)(k+2))$ to the average bits. Those contributions grow
without bound as $k$ grows, and forgetting which block it was only adds to the loss.
And no finite worst-case price can handle an infinite pile: for any proposed cost
$c$, select $2^c+1$ different states in it. They all land together, violating the
halving rule's maximum of $2^c$.

\begin{theorem}[An infinite pile]\label{thm:dir-infinite}
(1) A move that sends infinitely many states to one spot isn't priced by the halving price at any
finite cost. (2) Under the halving spread $2^{-(j+1)}$, crushing the pile loses exactly $2$ bits, and counted over its first $n$ states, less than $2$ for every $n$. (3) Under the block spread, the information lost
grows past every bound, so no finite bit budget covers it.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The three computations above.
\end{proof}

And heat? Part~I already said where the line is, and it's the same line here. Landauer's
principle, that crushing $c$ bits' worth of possibilities gives off at least $c\,kT\ln 2$ of heat on
average, is a premise from physics, and a contested one (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}). Nothing in
this section proves anything about heat. What the counting does give is that, under that premise,
on a machine with the halving price, a move's cost priced at $kT \ln 2$ per unit,
times the weight of the piles, is always enough
to cover the minimum the premise would
demand, for every spread of finite total weight.  If the premise falls, that sentence falls
with it, and every theorem above it stands, because none of them used it.

\subsection{What the shadow is}

Put the two sections together and you get the shape I've been circling since the Flatland night (the night a video about
\emph{Flatland} gave me the hunch behind this book; Section~\ref{sec:origin} tells it).
The ordinary machine is the shadow of a machine with a row of cups beside it. Over every shadow
state there's a whole fibre, a pile of states that differ only in their cups and their ledger, and
the ordinary machine can't tell them apart, on a machine whose step never looks at the cups. On a machine that obeys the toll, a
step that
turns a cup over costs, whichever cup it is and however many it turns, and on a machine with finitely many states whose record
only grows, when the
ordinary machine forgets nothing, what that cost pays
for is exactly crushing two states of one
fibre into one. A window can charge the right cost without seeing the cups, if it sees them move.
And on a machine with the halving price, where each unit of cost pays for at most one halving, the
cost in bits, times the weight of the spread,
is never less than what got crushed on average.

What I haven't shown is that any of this is out there in the world, that nature keeps a direction
like this over its own shadows. That's a belief of mine, and nothing in this book proves it. What
I've shown, and you can check, comes with its premises showing. A machine whose record is driven by
the computation and climbs a partial order is a row of cups, one latch for every line. If it also
has finitely many states, never lets the record come down, and prices its merges, it has to pay this
way. And when its ordinary machine forgets nothing, what it pays for is exactly this. It's less than the
Flatland night promised me. It's also the part of it that held when I pushed.

\subsection{Shortcuts}

There's a question every machine with a record runs into once its programs can be handed their own code. A cup is worth turning over because something later glances at it
and doesn't have to work the thing out again, the way Section~\ref{sec:structure}'s glance reads
a block's bucket off the table without applying the rule from scratch. Call any move like that a \emph{shortcut}, and
call it \emph{sound} when it gives the answer the long way would have given. (That gloss is about cost, leaning on what
was done so nothing is redone, and the wall I'm about to show you doesn't look at cost at all;
the next section says exactly what it does look at.) So can a machine like that \emph{decide}, from inside, whether its own shortcuts are sound? That question runs into a wall, the same wall Kurt Gödel and Alan Turing hit, and
I have to show you that it's there before I show you anything that pretends to be on the other side
of it.

%===========================================================================
\section{The diagonal}
\label{sec:diagonal}
%===========================================================================

In Section~\ref{sec:structure} I said you'd watch the same move get made again and again as the book went on:
somebody says ``everything is X,'' it's true enough to do real work with, and then somebody
draws the diagonal. I owe you the diagonal itself now, because Sections~\ref{sec:latch} to~\ref{sec:shadow-exact} just handed a record, and a whole
direction of them, to \emph{any} system that steps, and the next thing anyone wants from a system with a record is for
it to tell sound shortcuts from unsound ones by itself. Before I let anything claim that, I
have to show you the wall every such claim runs into, and then show you exactly where a
system with a record stands relative to the wall. It doesn't stand on the far side, because nobody's on the far
side. A record keeps a distinction and pays for it. What it can't do is the judging: no machine
that can hand a program its own code, and can run the flip of a verdict as one of its own
programs, can sort all its programs, from inside, by a question about what they do that some
pass and some fail. So the record carries a commitment, and somebody still
has to make it.

\subsection{Five names and a table}

Do this first, with a pencil, because the whole family of arguments is this one trick and
you should own it. Write five friends' names down the left of a page. Next to each name,
write a five-digit string of zeros and ones, anything you like. Now build a new string: its
first digit is the \emph{opposite} of the first digit of the first row; its second digit is the
opposite of the second digit of the second row; and so on down the diagonal. Look at what
you've made. It differs from row one in position one, from row two in position two, from
every row at that row's own position. So it's nobody's string, and your table of five missed
something.

With five rows and five digits that's a cute fact. Georg Cantor, a mathematician working out how to compare infinite
sets, made the point in 1891 that it works for \emph{any} list, however long, even infinite: hand me a complete list of all infinite
strings of two symbols, I'll walk the diagonal flipping as I go, and I'll hand you back a
string that's on no row. So there is no complete list. There are more such strings than there
are places on any list, and that's where ``some infinities are bigger than others'' comes
from. (He wrote the two symbols as m and w, where I'd write 0 and 1, and that paper wasn't even his
first proof of the fact. The first was in 1874, by a harder road through the real numbers, and in
1891 he called the new one much simpler. The diagonal was him finding the easy way.)

Now look at what the argument \emph{did}, because it's going to do the same thing again and again,
in new clothes, and I want you to recognise it each time. (Not every name below is a
flipped diagonal in the table sense. Kleene's theorem is the tool that makes the diagonal
buildable, Rice's is the general form, the one from Ken Thompson, who built the
original Unix operating system at Bell Labs, is an attack that uses the same
trick, and the last, Lawvere's, is the theorem that makes them all one.) There was a table: rows are the things being
listed, columns are questions, each cell says ``does row i do column j.'' There was the
diagonal: the cells where a thing is asked about \emph{itself}. There was a flip: something with no
fixed point, like turning yes into no, applied along the diagonal. And the thing that got
refuted was \emph{the assumed object}, the complete list. Nothing outside the assumption was
touched. Hold on to those four: a table, a diagonal, a flip, and the assumption eating itself.

\subsection{The same move, again and again}

Russell, 1902, from Section~\ref{sec:structure}: the collection of all collections that don't contain themselves.
It's Cantor's flipped diagonal with ``contains'' as the table, and Russell said as much, in
\emph{The Principles of Mathematics} in 1903. He got there, he wrote, by running Cantor's argument
on a supposed collection of everything, which ought to be the biggest collection there is. What got
refuted was the assumed object, the collection of everything, and Zermelo's fix was to stop
assuming it. I promised in Section~\ref{sec:structure} that I'd come back to this here. Every reading in this book is a yes or
no question on the states of one machine, a collection cut out of a collection I was already
given, and never a sort of everything. When Part~I asked for one state that codes every question
about the states (Section~\ref{sec:what-a-chair-is}), the same flip refuted it.

Jules Richard, a French mathematician who taught at the lycées of Tours, Dijon and Châteauroux,
took his doctorate in Paris in 1901 and wrote mostly on geometry. In 1905, in a short note, a
letter to the editor of a French science review, he observed: some phrases (his were in French) define real numbers (``the ratio of a circle's
circumference to its diameter''); there are only countably many phrases, so list the numbers
they define in order; run Cantor's diagonal down their decimal expansions and you get a real
number no phrase defines, except that you just defined it, in the phrase that describes the
diagonal. The lesson I take from that one is the lesson this whole
section turns on: keep apart the language a system \emph{talks in} and the language you use to
talk \emph{about} it. Mix them and the diagonal bites you.

Richard's paradox has a cousin small enough to do at the table, and it comes with a footnote I
can't resist. Russell, the first to put it in print, in 1906, credited it to G. G. Berry, a
junior librarian at the Bodleian Library in Oxford. The paradox has outlived empires, and it
came from the library desk. In the version in \emph{Principia Mathematica} it's about syllables. Take
the phrase ``the least integer not nameable in fewer than nineteen syllables.'' There are only
so many phrases shorter than nineteen syllables, so they name only so many numbers, so some
least number is left over, and the phrase picks it out. Now count the phrase: the, least,
in-te-ger, not, name-a-ble, in, few-er, than, nine-teen, syl-la-bles, and it comes to eighteen. In eighteen
syllables it has named the number that can't be named in fewer than nineteen. It's the same lesson as Richard's, in a smaller coat: ``nameable'' is a word about the
language, used inside the language, and that's where the bite is.

Kurt Gödel, 1931, with an improvement in 1936 by Barkley Rosser, a logician who had studied under
Alonzo Church at Princeton and whose trick lets the theorem assume only that the system is
consistent: the big one, and I'll say exactly
what it says, because every word of it is carrying weight. Take any consistent formal system with a mechanically checkable list
of axioms that can do a bit of arithmetic. Then there are sentences it can neither prove nor
refute. The engine is a lemma that lets you build, for any property you can write down, a
sentence that the system proves \emph{equivalent} to that property holding of the sentence's own
code number. Apply it to ``not provable'' and you get a sentence equivalent, inside the
system, to its own unprovability. The table is the sentences listed by code, the diagonal is a sentence about its
own code, and the flip turns provable into not-provable. The Stanford Encyclopedia stresses two cautions, and
I'll repeat them. The sentence doesn't literally ``say'' anything about itself. It's provably
\emph{equivalent} to a claim about its code, which is less mystical and more exact. And the
theorem doesn't say the sentence is unknowable. It says \emph{this one system} can't settle it.

And how did the world take it? Mostly, at first, it didn't. Gödel, twenty-four years old,
announced the first theorem during a round-table discussion on the last day of a conference in
Königsberg in September 1930, and by the account of Solomon Feferman, one of the editors of
Gödel's collected works, the room met it with general incomprehension, except for one man. John
von Neumann pulled Gödel aside to talk about it, kept thinking about it, and a couple of months
later saw that the argument gave something more: a consistent system of this kind can't prove
its own consistency. He wrote to Gödel with it in a letter dated 20 November 1930. Gödel had
already got there. His paper had reached the journal three days earlier, with that
second theorem announced in it, and von Neumann left the credit with Gödel. It's the
``somebody got there first'' shape from Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}, with one difference: here the man
who got there second was von Neumann.

Alan Turing, 1936. I'd always taken it that Turing proved the halting problem undecidable, and
here I had to go and look. The set theorist Joel David Hamkins and his coauthor Theodor Nenu went
back to the 1936 paper and report that the word ``halting,'' the modern statement, and the
self-referential proof everyone teaches are all, strictly speaking, absent from it. What Turing
proved undecidable were two other questions about his machines (whether a machine prints
infinitely many digits; whether it ever prints a given symbol). The second is \emph{equivalent} to
halting and the first is strictly harder. So their answer cuts both ways, and they say so: Turing
never stated the halting problem, and he essentially proved it, because his second question is a
short translation away from it. The name came later. Martin Davis seems to have been the first to
write ``halting problem,'' in a book of 1958, and Stephen Kleene had already stated the problem,
without that name, in his 1952 textbook \emph{Introduction to Metamathematics}. The textbook version is still right as mathematics, and it fits on two index
cards. Card A is the Checker: hand it any program card and it announces ``halts'' or ``runs
forever.'' Card B is the Contrarian: ``Hand me to the Checker. If it says I halt, run forever.
If it says I run forever, stop.'' Hand B to A, and either answer is wrong, so there's no Checker.
The table is programs against programs, the diagonal is a program run on itself, and the flip turns halt into loop.

Stephen Kleene, 1938, the logician whose textbook I just mentioned, and this is the one that turns the paradox into a tool, so slow down.
Everything above needs the self-referring object to \emph{exist}: Gödel's sentence has to be
buildable, the Contrarian has to be able to ``hand me to the Checker.'' Kleene's second
recursion theorem says: for any transformation of programs you can compute, there's a
program that behaves exactly as if it had been handed its own source code. Any program may
be written as though it already had a copy of itself in hand. He stated it almost in passing, in a paper
on something else, and proved it in the last two lines of one of its sections. I have that count
from Yiannis Moschovakis, a logician at UCLA and Athens who wrote a 2009 paper on it, expanded in the Bulletin of Symbolic Logic in 2010, called
``Kleene's Amazing Second Recursion Theorem,'' and he calls it a little
gem. It's the reason ``programs that print their own source'' exist in every ordinary programming language: one that can compute whatever a Turing machine can and can build, from a program and an input, a program that runs the first on that input (they're called quines, after a philosopher I'll come to in a moment; try ``Print the
following twice, the second time in quotes: `Print the following twice, the second time in
quotes:'\,'' and obey it). Self-reference in computation isn't a paradox but a construction.
The paradoxes happened only when someone assumed an \emph{unrestricted} collection or language;
the theorem happens when you build the self-referrer honestly.

And where does the word quine come from? The philosopher didn't coin it himself. Douglas Hofstadter
coined it in 1979, in \emph{Gödel, Escher, Bach}, in honour of Willard Van Orman Quine, who had
made a long study of self-reference that works indirectly. Quine left a sentence you can take
apart at the table, from a 1962 essay on paradox, and in full it reads: ``yields falsehood when
preceded by its quotation'' yields falsehood when preceded by its quotation. Do what it says.
Take the part in quotation marks, put a quoted copy of it in front of itself, and look at what
you've built: it's the whole sentence, word for word. So the sentence says that it itself is
false. It's the liar paradox, but look at how it got there: no ``this sentence'' anywhere, no
pointing at itself, just an instruction to quote and copy, the same move as the print-twice
instruction above. Quoting and copying is Kleene's trick in plain English, and it's why the paradox and the tool
look so alike. The paradox is what you get when the copy asserts something about its own truth.
The tool is what you get when the copy just does something.

Henry Rice, 1953, whom you met briefly in Section~\ref{sec:windows}: the general form. Any property that depends only on what a program \emph{does},
whatever its text, and that's true of some programs and false of others, has no
algorithm that decides it for all programs. ``Does this program halt'' is one such property.
``Does this program ever output 7'' is another. ``Does this program contain an if-statement''
isn't, because that's about the text. One standard proof goes straight through Kleene.

And the one that's actually an attack: Ken Thompson, in his Turing Award lecture, published in 1984.
Build a compiler that, when it compiles the login program, plants a back door, and when it
compiles \emph{a compiler}, plants both habits into that one too. Then delete the trick from the
source. The compiled compiler still carries it, and recompiling a clean source with the
poisoned binary re-plants it, forever. Reading the source never reveals it. A locksmith
teaches an apprentice to cut a spare for every town-hall key and to teach \emph{that} to every
apprentice they train, and never to write it in the manual; years later the manual is
spotless and every locksmith in town cuts the spare. Thompson's compiler is the recursion theorem with a
knife in it, and his moral was that you can't trust code you didn't write entirely yourself.

And Thompson wasn't first either, and he said so. Pull on the lecture's acknowledgment the way
Section~\ref{sec:established} pulls on Bitcoin's footnotes: he writes that he first read of the
possibility in an Air Force critique of the security of an early implementation of Multics, a
time-sharing system from the 1960s, and that he couldn't find a more specific reference to it,
and he asks anyone who can to send him one. The critique is Paul Karger and Roger Schell's 1974
security evaluation of Multics, which already described a trap door planted in a compiler that,
because the compiler is written in its own language, keeps itself alive. So the knife was in the drawer
ten years before the lecture was printed. Then comes the obvious next question, whether there's any way out or whether
``trust no binary you didn't build'' is the bottom. There's a partial answer, and it took a while.
David A. Wheeler, in a 2005 paper and a 2009 dissertation at George Mason University, worked out
\emph{diverse double-compiling}: compile the suspect compiler's source with a second,
independently made compiler, use the result to compile that source again, and compare the
output bit for bit with the suspect binary. If they match under Wheeler's assumptions, that gives a source-to-binary
correspondence. The second compiler must correctly translate the relevant
source, the execution and comparison environments must be trusted for these
runs, and the build's language and environmental effects must match the
conditions of the argument. Two compilers having different authors is useful
evidence for trust, not a substitute for those premises. The question has
moved to a boundary where we can name what we trust.

Bill Lawvere, in 1969, proved a fixed-point theorem that, as I read it, makes all of these one theorem in disguise: if a set can be mapped
onto all the functions from itself to some target, then every function on the target has a
fixed point; so if the target has a function with no fixed point (a flip), no such covering
exists. Cantor, Russell, Gödel and halting all come out as instances of one shape. Noson Yanofsky retold it
in 2003 without the category theory. I mention it because ``it's the same wall'' is a claim I
make below, and I want you to know it's fair at the level of \emph{proof shape}, and that every
instance has its own boundary of \emph{who counts as a decider}, and that boundary is exactly
where most overclaims live.

\subsection{Applying the diagonal}

Before applying the diagonal to a system with a record, identify who the proposed decider
is and what it must decide. Four familiar applications show why those details matter.

``Gödel shows minds aren't machines.'' John Lucas, a philosopher who spent thirty-six years as a
fellow of Merton College, Oxford, argued it in 1961, in a paper called ``Minds, Machines and
Gödel.'' Roger Penrose, the Oxford mathematical physicist who later shared a Nobel prize for his
work on how black holes form, revived it twice, in two books, \emph{The Emperor's New Mind} in 1989
and \emph{Shadows of the Mind} in 1994. I'm sure of who argued it and when. Whether they're right is
the question, and the standard replies, as far as I can tell, have held up: the Gödel sentence is true \emph{only if the system
is consistent}, so a human who ``sees'' its truth has to know the system is consistent, which
is the hard part; and nobody can build the Gödel sentence of a system they can't specify, so
humans might be machines too complicated to diagonalise. The theorem has a conditional in it
and the argument drops the conditional.

And the part that's easy to miss is that Gödel himself didn't go as far as Lucas. In a lecture
on the day after Christmas in 1951, at a meeting of the American Mathematical Society at Brown
University, he drew from his own theorems only an either-or. Either the human mind, even inside
pure mathematics, infinitely surpasses the powers of any finite machine, or there are problems
about whole numbers, of a certain simple kind, that no proof the human mind can conceive will
ever settle. Feferman, writing about that lecture, says Gödel privately believed the first half
and still stated only the disjunction, because he didn't have a knock-down argument against the
machine side. Gödel wrote soon afterward that he meant to publish the lecture, and never did; the
text sat among his papers until after his death. So the man whose theorem gets quoted for
``minds aren't machines'' stated an either-or and left the deciding to whoever came next. The
conditional is there again, kept by the person with the most right to drop it.

``Undecidable means unknowable.'' Two senses share the word: a problem with no single
algorithm correct on every instance, and a sentence independent of one particular system.
Neither means nobody can know a given answer. Any single instance is decidable, trivially:
for any one program, one of ``say yes'' and ``say no'' is right. What's ruled out is one
\emph{inside} procedure that's right on \emph{every} case.

``Everything interesting is undecidable.'' Rice is about behavioural properties over \emph{all}
programs. It says nothing against checking the text, nothing against deciding for specific
programs, nothing against analyses allowed to say ``I don't know,'' nothing against finite-state
model checking or type checking. Real compilers and analysers live with Rice by being sound but
incomplete, and what limits them in practice is mostly cost. The diagonal shapes them; it doesn't stop them.

``Self-reference is a paradox.'' It's a theorem with a construction, as Kleene, the quines and Thompson show.

\subsection{Now point it at the record}

The question Section~\ref{sec:shadow-exact} left open can be asked with nothing in it but what Parts~I and~II have built. A
system steps; a record rides along and latches on an event (Section~\ref{sec:latch}); when the event is a
certification, Section~\ref{sec:entitlement} said the reading, with its object and its paid event behind it, is what lets an
auditor treat a claim as established, and for a claim that a shortcut is sound, that's what
makes the shortcut \emph{admissible}. Can a system like that have, as one of its own programs, a procedure that
correctly decides, for every program, ``does this program admit a sound shortcut''? A procedure like that
would be autopilot: hand it any program and it says yes or no, and it's always right.

The exact statement is narrower than the question in plain words, so I'll give it
before the proof. In the theorem, ``admits a shortcut'' is any property of programs with two
features: two programs that behave alike agree on it, and there's one program that has it
and one that doesn't. Those two features are all the argument gets to look at. The diagonal doesn't see
soundness. Each system that wants the wall picks its own property, and whether that
property lines up with being entitled to soundness in Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}'s sense is a separate fact about that system,
checked one system at a time if it's checked at all. A procedure that returns soundness
records for some programs, or only for restricted inputs, or with outside evidence, is not
what the wall rules out.

So in the theorem ``shortcut'' is a label. The plain-words gloss at the end of
Section~\ref{sec:shadow-exact}, leaning on a record so the thing isn't worked out again, is about
\emph{how} a program gets its answer, and how is exactly what extensionality throws away: the
theorem only gets to see what programs do, and it treats any two that do the same as one. A
question like ``is there a cheaper program that gives the same answers?'' isn't the theorem's
question, and a wall for it would need a different theorem. The nearest thing I know of is Manuel
Blum's speedup theorem, from 1967, and it goes somewhere stranger: there are computable functions
with no fastest program at all, where every program for the function has another that's faster on
all but finitely many inputs. Blum's theorem is a fact about cost, not a wall about deciding, and nothing
in this book proves anything in that territory. Each use of the wall also names its sameness. In
the substrate theorem it's the substrate's own $\simeq$; on L it's what a term computes; on the
host of the small machine Part~III builds, in Appendix~\ref{sec:small-diagonal}, it's the partial function a program
computes (Theorem~\ref{thm:host-wall}). A particular notion of shortcut gets the wall only after someone proves it
behaves alike on programs that are the same in the sense in use, and holds of one program and
fails of another.

The answer is no, under premises. The proof is the two index cards, and I'll give you the
premises because they're the whole content. Suppose there were such a decider, one that says yes
exactly when a program admits a shortcut. Build the
flip: ``if the decider says yes about me, behave like a program that admits no shortcut; if
it says no, behave like one that does.'' If the system has a recursion theorem (a program
can be handed its own code), and if that flip is one of the transformations the system can
carry out, and if ``admits a shortcut'' depends only on behaviour (two programs that behave
the same agree on it), and if there's at least one program each way, then there's a program
that behaves exactly like its own flip, and whatever the decider says about it is wrong.
Both cases close in a line each. This rules out a decider that says yes if and only if a program admits a shortcut,
for any substrate with those parts. (A substrate here is the mathematical structure just described: programs, a run that may fail
to give back a state, a counter with a step relation it never goes down along, an
encoding of programs as data, a notion of ``representable'' transformation, and the recursion
theorem for those. It says nothing about what the states are made of. A small instance is the nat family below.) It's Rice's trick one floor over, and I should be careful
with that. Rice stated his theorem for classes of recursively enumerable sets, the sets a program
can list, and it's usually taught now for the functions Turing machines compute. This wall is
the same diagonal with different premises: it carries its own recursion theorem and its own
list of representable transformations, and it picks the property. So it isn't a corollary
of Rice as Rice stated it, and it doesn't show that any property is harder or easier to decide
than classical halting. And
I want you to have one thing about its proof: it never touches the counter,
the toll, or the step relation. It uses the recursion theorem, representability of the flip,
the two witnesses, and extensionality, and nothing else.

I'll set out the setting and the wall now, with every word pinned down so you can poke at it.

\begin{definition}[Substrate]\label{def:u12-substrate}
A \emph{substrate} has a type of states, a type $\mathrm{Prog}$ of programs, and a run map that
takes a program and a state and either gives back a state or gives nothing. It has a counter
$\mu$ on states and a step relation along which $\mu$ never decreases; an encoding
$\mathrm{enc}$ of programs as states with a decoder $\mathrm{dec}$ such that
$\mathrm{dec}(\mathrm{enc}(p)) = p$; and a predicate $\mathrm{Rep}$ on maps
$f: \mathrm{Prog} \to \mathrm{Prog}$, the transformations the substrate counts as its own.
Two programs are \emph{equivalent}, $p \simeq q$, when $\mathrm{run}(p, s) = \mathrm{run}(q, s)$
for every state $s$. The last condition is the \emph{recursion theorem}: for every $f$ with
$\mathrm{Rep}(f)$ there is a program $p$ with $p \simeq f(p)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Shortcut predicate]\label{def:u12-shortcut-predicate}
A \emph{shortcut predicate} on a substrate is a property $A$ of programs with two programs $y$ and
$n$ such that $A(y)$ holds, $A(n)$ fails, and $A$ is extensional: $p \simeq q$ implies
$A(p) \iff A(q)$. For a Boolean function $d$ on programs, its \emph{flip} is
$f_d(p) = n$ if $d(p)$ is true and $f_d(p) = y$ if $d(p)$ is false.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[No inside decider]\label{thm:u12-no-inside-decider}
Let a substrate carry a shortcut predicate $A$ with witnesses $y$ and $n$. Then for every Boolean function $d$ on programs with $\mathrm{Rep}(f_d)$ there is a program $p$ with $p \simeq f_d(p)$, and $d(p) = \mathrm{true} \iff A(p)$ fails at that $p$. So no such $d$ is right about $A$ on every program. \end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Hand the proposed judge $d$ to the flip construction. The flip is an allowed
program transformation, so the recursion theorem supplies a program $p$
that behaves exactly as its own flip tells it to behave. Now ask the judge
about that particular program.

If the judge says yes, the flip sends $p$ to the no-example $n$. Thus $p$
and $n$ behave alike. The question depends only on behaviour, and $n$ fails
it, so $p$ fails it too. The judge's yes is wrong.

If the judge says no, the flip sends $p$ to the yes-example $y$. Now $p$
and $y$ behave alike. Since $y$ passes, $p$ passes too. The judge's no is
wrong. Those are its only answers.

I used the recursion theorem to obtain this one self-matching program,
the two examples to give the flip somewhere to go, and the rule that alike
behaviour gets the same verdict. The counter, the step relation and the
encoding played no part. Any setting supplying that same fixed point for
the flip gives the same contradiction.
\end{proof}

So what's ruled out is a $d$ that says true exactly when $A$ holds, and whose flip the substrate can represent. Every part I named is a premise, and the theorem covers every substrate that supplies them all.

So the wall is there. The part I have to be honest about is \emph{who counts as a decider}. The theorem rules out
a decider whose flip the substrate can itself represent. It says nothing about a decider
standing \emph{outside}, and an outside decider can exist for the very same property, correct on
every program. The line between inside and outside is the boundary of the sentence, and the boundary is
Richard's lesson: the language you talk about a system in is a different language from the one it
talks in.
You'll see it in miniature in a minute, on the nat family, with a pencil.

Two forms of the wall live in this section, and they're honest in different ways.

The first is the \emph{nat family}, a tiny substrate built so that program two is the
Contrarian for a given candidate decider d, and for every d, d is wrong about program two. It's
a \emph{family}, one instance per d, and its recursion theorem holds by construction. It's the
index cards made formal and nothing more.

\begin{theorem}[The nat family]\label{thm:u12-nat-family}
Fix any Boolean function $d$ on $\mathbb{N}$. Let the substrate $N_d$ have programs and
states $\mathbb{N}$; program 0 returns 1, program 1 returns 0, program 2 returns 0 if $d(2)$
is true and 1 if it is false, whatever the input state, and every other program gives nothing;
each program is encoded as itself; $\mu$ is constantly 0, so any step relation will do;
$\mathrm{Rep}(f)$ holds when $f(p) = 1$ for every $p$ with $d(p)$ true and $f(p) = 0$ for
every other $p$; and $A(p)$ holds when program $p$ returns 1 on input 0. Then it is not the
case that $d(p) = \mathrm{true} \iff A(p)$ for every $p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The recursion theorem of $N_d$ holds with the fixed witness 2: for a representable $f$,
$f(2)$ is 1 or 0 according to $d(2)$, and program 2 returns exactly what that program
returns. The witnesses for $A$ are 0 and 1, and $A$ is extensional because it reads only what a
program returns. The flip of $d$ is representable by the
definition of $\mathrm{Rep}$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:u12-no-inside-decider} applies to $d$ itself. Directly:
$A(2)$ holds exactly when $d(2)$ is false.
\end{proof}

Now push on it once more, because the nat family shows the outside decider in three lines,
and you can do them yourself. Stand outside $N_d$, knowing $d$. Write down a new decider
$e$: say yes on program 0, say ``not $d(2)$'' on program 2, and say no on everything else.
Check it against $A$. Program 0 returns 1, so $A(0)$ holds and $e$ says yes. Program 1
returns 0, so $A(1)$ fails and $e$ says no. Program 2 returns 1 exactly when $d(2)$ is false,
and that's what $e$ says. Every other program gives nothing, so $A$ fails and $e$ says no.
So $e$ is right about every program. Does that break the wall? It doesn't, and the reason is the part that
matters: in $N_d$ a flip is representable only if it says 1 exactly where $d$ says yes, so
the flip of $e$ is representable only if $e$ and $d$ agree everywhere, and they disagree at
program 2. The correct decider exists; its flip just isn't one of the substrate's own moves.
(It's three lines and a pencil, and you just did it.) One and the same property is undecidable from inside and decided cleanly from outside, at the
same time. That's not a paradox, because it's two different people asking.

The second form is the one where the recursion theorem is \emph{proved} from the reduction rules rather than assumed.
It's on \emph{L}, the weak call-by-value lambda calculus that Yannick Forster and Gert Smolka presented in
2017 as a model of computation, and which a group at Saarland has since used as the
seed of a whole library of undecidable problems. Here L is built from its reduction rules. The recursion theorem is proved, Rice's theorem follows, halting
follows, and the diagonal is reproved in the shape of the substrate
theorem, for any property of programs that depends only
on what they compute and that holds of one program and fails of another. The statement
mentions no shortcut. So on L the result is the diagonal for one fixed model, and I don't plug L into the
substrate theorem, for this reason: a substrate's run map has to answer, with a state or with nothing, and for L that map is the halting function itself, which no term of L computes. Using it would take something from outside L, and L is in this book as the model where nothing is taken from outside. So on L I run the argument again from
scratch instead of applying the general one. Both are true; they're different sentences.

I'll say what that string of words means, because L is the strangest thing in this book that
computes, and the smallest. The lambda calculus is Alonzo Church's, from the 1930s, and it's
a programming language with one idea in it: functions. A term is one of three things: a
variable; a function, written $\lambda$ followed by its body, the body saying what to do with
whatever you hand it; or one term applied to another, written side by side. Running a program
is one move, over and over: when a function meets an argument, put the argument into the body
where the variable was. The lambda calculus has no numbers, no memory, no instructions, and in 1937 Turing published a proof that
it computes exactly what his machines compute. ``Weak call-by-value'' is two house rules about
the order of moves: an argument is run down to a finished function (a \emph{value}) before it's
put in, and nothing runs inside a function that hasn't been handed anything yet. Variables
are written as numbers counting how many $\lambda$s back they were bound (a trick of Nicolaas
de Bruijn; it means two variables can never get mixed up by sharing a name), and a term is \emph{closed}
when every variable in it is bound inside it, so it leans on nothing outside. Last, to
hand a program to a program, L needs a way to write any term as data, the way a program's
source is a string you can pass around. The one used here is the \emph{Scott encoding}, named for
Dana Scott, a student of Church's who went on to build mathematical models of the lambda calculus
itself. As far as I can trace it, the encoding first appeared in lecture notes of his from Berkeley
in 1962 that he never published, as a way to write data; Torben Mogensen carried it over to
lambda terms themselves in 1992, and that's the form used here. All you need about it is that every term $t$ gets one \emph{code}, written
$\ulcorner t \urcorner$, and the code is itself a closed value. Two tools get built on top of
that in the proof: a \emph{quoting} term $Q$ that takes the code of a term to the code of that
code (a program that prints its own source needs exactly this move), and a \emph{fixed-point
combinator}, a term that lets a function call itself, which is how $Q$ works its way through
a code of any size.

Do two of these on paper before I give you the general rule. Write
$I=\lambda x.x$: its instruction is ``return whatever you were handed.'' Hand
