$I$ its own card and you get $I\,I\to I$, and it stops. Now write
$D=\lambda x.x\,x$: ``make two copies of what you were handed and apply the first
to the second.'' Hand it its own card. Putting $D$ in for both copies of
$x$ gives $D\,D\to D\,D$. You're back at exactly the same instruction and
argument, so the rule never finishes. Both arguments were already
functions, so neither example sneaks any work under a function that hasn't been handed anything.

The variable numbers are what keep the copying from getting confused. In $\lambda x.\lambda y.x$,
the last $x$ points past the nearest $\lambda$ (the one for $y$) to the one before it, so its number
is 1; in $\lambda x.\lambda y.y$ the last variable has number 0. Rename $x$
and $y$ however you like and neither recipe changes. The codes below are a way of putting a whole
recipe on a card that another recipe can read.

\begin{definition}[L, as built here]\label{def:u12-L}
A term of L is a variable (a de Bruijn number), an application $s\,t$, or an abstraction
$\lambda s$; the values are the abstractions. One step is weak call-by-value, left to right:
$(\lambda b)\,v$ steps to $b$ with $v$ substituted when $v$ is a value, a step inside the
left part of an application is a step of the application, and so is a step inside the right
part once the left part is a value. A term $s$ \emph{evaluates to} $v$ when $s$ reaches $v$ in
some number of steps and $v$ is a value; $p \equiv q$ when $p$ and $q$ evaluate to the same
values. Every term $t$ has a code $\ulcorner t \urcorner$, its Scott encoding, which is a
closed value. A map $f$ on terms is \emph{L-computable} when some closed value $s$ has
$s\,\ulcorner p \urcorner \equiv f(p)$ for every $p$. A term $D$ \emph{decides} a property $P$ of
terms when, for every $p$, $D\,\ulcorner p \urcorner$ reaches $\lambda\lambda.1$ (true) if
$P(p)$ holds and $\lambda\lambda.0$ (false) if it fails. $P$ is \emph{extensional} when
$p \equiv q$ and $P(p)$ give $P(q)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Recursion, Rice and halting for L]\label{thm:u12-L}
(1) For every closed value $s$ there is a closed term $t$ that reaches
$s\,\ulcorner t \urcorner$; so every L-computable $f$ has a term $p$ with $p \equiv f(p)$.
(2) Let $P$ be extensional, with $P(y)$ and not $P(n)$ for closed terms $y$ and $n$. Then no
closed term decides $P$. (3) No closed term decides halting, the property of evaluating to
some value.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) First build a program that can assemble the code of the very application
I am about to run. The quoting program $Q$ takes a term's code and returns
the code of that code. Appendix~\ref{sec:quoting-construction} gives the idea of its
construction, and the companion volume follows it through the three kinds of term. The program
$\mathrm{mkapp}$ takes two codes and joins them into the code of an application.

Make $A$ do this when handed a code $x$: quote $x$, put that quoted code
beside $x$ using $\mathrm{mkapp}$, and hand the result to $s$. Written out,
\[
 A=\lambda x.\,s\,(\mathrm{mkapp}\ x\ (Q\,x)).
\]
Now run $A$ on its own code, and call that whole application $t$:
$t=A\,\ulcorner A\urcorner$. The first step puts $\ulcorner A\urcorner$
where $x$ stood. Quoting it supplies the code of $\ulcorner A\urcorner$;
joining the two codes supplies the code of
$A\,\ulcorner A\urcorner$. That is the code of $t$ itself. The computation
therefore reaches $s\,\ulcorner t\urcorner$, as promised. All the pieces
were closed, so $t$ is closed too. If $s$ computes $f$, the resulting
behaviour is exactly $f(t)$.

(2) Suppose a closed program $D$ decides $P$. Build another program that asks
$D$ about the code it receives, then runs the no-example $n$ after yes and
the yes-example $y$ after no. In this language you must keep the two branches
wrapped as functions until the answer chooses one; otherwise call-by-value
would try to run them before choosing. The following term does that:
\[
 \lambda x.\,D\,x\,(\lambda\_.\,n)\,(\lambda\_.\,y)\,(\lambda z.z).
\]
The final identity function is the harmless argument that opens the selected
wrapper. Thus a true answer runs $n$, and a false answer runs $y$.

Apply part (1) to this program, obtaining its self-matching $t$. If $P(t)$
holds, the judge says true and $t$ behaves like $n$, where $P$ fails. If
$P(t)$ fails, the judge says false and $t$ behaves like $y$, where $P$ holds.
Either answer contradicts the requirement that alike behaviour has the same
verdict. No such $D$ exists.

(3) Halting depends only on which values a term reaches. The identity
$\lambda z.z$ is already a value. The term
$(\lambda x.\,x\,x)(\lambda x.\,x\,x)$ takes a step back to itself each
time, and is never a value. These supply the yes-example and no-example
for part (2), so halting has no closed decider either.
\end{proof}

The construction in that proof isn't mine, and the credit belongs right here. Forster and Smolka's
L development of 2017 has the Scott encoding of terms, a closed quoting term with exactly this
specification, the code of a term to the code of its code, and a fixed point built the same way:
their $t$ is $C\,\ulcorner C \urcorner$ with $C = \lambda x.\, s\,(A\,x\,(Q\,x))$, so their $C$ is
my $A$, and their $A$, which builds the code of an application, is my $\mathrm{mkapp}$. They say they
follow the proof in the Dutch logician Henk Barendregt's textbook on the lambda calculus (1984),
where statement (1) is the full lambda calculus's second fixed-point theorem, and part (2) is what
they call Scott's theorem. The term construction is given in the companion volume, with its idea in Appendix~\ref{sec:quoting-construction};
the route is theirs, and Barendregt's before them.

So I've given the wall on paper, on a family built to fit it, and on one outside model.
The machine built in Part~III (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}) fills in this same shape: on
its host machine, the one the universal program of Appendix~\ref{sec:universal-host} runs on, which has a counter for every whole number,
programs are numbers, Kleene's recursion theorem is a theorem, and so is Rice's, and the fixed point
can be taken to agree on what the program computes and also on the ledger and the flag at the end of every run where they stop (Appendix~\ref{sec:small-diagonal}).

The table below lines up the picture all of that fills in against Turing's, one column per axis.

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.482\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.482\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Time axis} & \textbf{Structural axis} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
counts: steps & counts: $\mu$ \\
asks: does it halt? & asks: does it admit the shortcut? \\
the wall: no Turing machine decides halting & the wall: no decider whose flip is representable, under a recursion theorem \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

Read the table as two uses of one diagonal, each under its own premises, and as saying nothing more than that.
The structural wall never uses $\mu$; the $\mu$ entry only says what that axis counts. The
nat result is a family indexed by the candidate decider, and L's results are about one fixed
model and properties that mention no shortcut. Neither hands you a second fixed undecidable
problem, and neither separates Turing degrees: a property can sit behind the wall from inside
and be decided cleanly from outside, as the pencil argument on $N_d$ showed. And ``admits the
shortcut'' in the right-hand column is the theorem's sense, any behavioural property with a yes and
a no. ``Has a cheaper way to the same answer'' is a second question, and the column has no wall for it.

\subsection{Where the diagonal applies}

The three versions put the candidate procedure in different places. In the general
substrate argument, the substrate must represent the candidate's flip. In the natural-number
family, each candidate $d$ supplies the substrate whose predicate defeats it. In L, the
candidate is a closed term and the question is a nontrivial extensional property of closed
terms. The reduction rules and recursion argument give Rice's theorem there.

The pencil calculation on $N_d$ is useful precisely because it is outside that substrate.
To run the diagonal inside, I need the representability and recursion conditions stated
in the theorem.

\subsection{What this does to the book}

It does two things. It keeps me honest: nothing in what follows claims that a system with a
record can check its own shortcuts on autopilot, because that's a wall, the same wall, and I
showed you the bricks. And it tells you what a record \emph{can} do, which is the thing Part~II
has been about since the counter: it can carry a shortcut \emph{with its receipt}, so that the question
``was this earned'' is answered by an event you can point at. No decider has to exist for that,
which is lucky, because on a system with a recursion theorem no inside one can. The
diagonal says such a system can't automate the judgement from inside, for any behavioural property with a yes and a no. The latch
says you can record the commitment. Those are different jobs, and a record does the second.

The diagonal has a famous cousin that looks as if it ought to bite a record too, so let me walk
right up to it. Gödel's second theorem says a consistent system strong enough for arithmetic can't
prove its own consistency, and Martin Löb, a logician answering another logician's question, sharpened that in 1955: if such a system proves ``if this
is provable, it's true,'' it already proves the thing itself. So can a record vouch for itself, and
does Löb stop it? My first guess was that Löb stops it, since a record looked like a system talking about itself.
I landed somewhere else, and mostly it's a relief. Hold two things side by
side: ``there's a receipt for this somewhere,'' and the receipt in your hand. Löb's theorem is
about \emph{provability}, the bare claim that some proof exists, the receipt somewhere. A raised Boolean flag is not, by itself, the receipt in your hand. From a
clean start the earned-history theorem says there was a passing check,
commitment and certification in that order. The flag does not identify
the claim or the steps, and it need not store a proof of the checked claim.
The native table and channel carry more information; exporting a proof
requires an interface that actually supplies one.

Sergei Artemov's distinction between implicit provability and explicit
proof terms is useful here, but neither a flag nor the word ``receipt''
turns one into the other. The guarantee in this book comes from an external
proof about the checker, the clean start and every permitted operation.
It is not an internal proof of the system's own consistency, and does not
evade Gödel's or Löb's hypotheses.

Push on that and it gives, because a receipt is only as good as whoever wrote it. Its trust rests
on the checker meaning what it says, and that gets settled once, from outside the machine.
That's where I chose to stop this machine's chain of reasons. Gödel's second theorem does not
forbid a machine from checking a proof about a checker. What it limits is a system's ability to prove \emph{its own} consistency, when the system
is strong enough to do arithmetic and its axioms can be listed by a machine. Eliezer Yudkowsky and Marcello Herreshoff's 2013 draft on agents that trust their
own rewrites describes a related problem, the Löbian obstacle: how an agent can justify
trust in a successor's proofs. That's a cousin of this question, and it doesn't settle it, and it doesn't make
my design the only one possible. So I didn't get rid of the receipt somewhere. I moved it out of the
machine and handed it to whoever reads the record.

One more thing follows from the same picture, by a short argument. Can a record rest on itself, the way the sentence ``this
sentence is certified'' would like to? It can't if it's earned and permanent. The check behind the certificate that put the record up happened while the record was still down, because the record goes up only after that check passes, and once up it never comes back down, so it goes up only once. So no claim whose truth needs the record already up can be the claim the record went up on. (A later certificate, with the record already up, can stand on such a claim; it raises nothing.) Saul Kripke's 1975 theory of truth calls a sentence like
that, one that only ever leans on itself, ungrounded, and earned records are grounded in his
sense: every one bottoms out in a check that didn't lean on it. Caspar Oesterheld's 2019 work on
programs that cooperate by simulating each other needed a grounding step of the same kind to stop
an infinite regress. I haven't written this argument out anywhere else; the claim is exactly what this
paragraph says, and it's short enough to check by hand.

I want to draw one last distinction, because the two are easy to conflate and conflating them is the
easiest way to misread this book. There's a \emph{second} wall, nothing to do with the diagonal.
It's Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s kind of wall, a window with a colliding pair in it. Two states that differ in their
certification reading can look identical through a window that doesn't show that reading,
the stamp inside the closed drawer and the drawer opened and shut, and then no function of
the window recovers the reading (Theorem~\ref{thm:fibre}: a decoder has to give one answer on
everything the window lumps together). This wall comes from missing information. Nothing about it is undecidable; it holds for finite things with
nothing to compute; and it sits \emph{beside} Rice. None of Rice is underneath it. The property the diagonal uses (any behavioural property of programs with a yes and
a no) is a different kind of thing from the reading the window hides, and nothing here says
the two are the same. So there are two walls, on two different axes. The diagonal is about what no inside procedure can
decide. The window is about what no outside observer can see. I'll need both, and I'll try
not to call one by the other's name again. The machine I build later has a colliding pair of
exactly that kind (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-separation}).

\part{Established}
\clearpage

Part~III is step four, the sharpest case. A record that a claim was checked and closed is a
distinction that stays, so it pays what Part~I found keeping takes, and it's the case where you can point at the
kept 0 and at what it cost. It starts with what \emph{established} means, and why two computers
with the same bits can differ in it. Then it builds the smallest example I could find that meets the definition: an ordinary computer of two
counters, with a record layer on top whose flag is the blank cell, six kinds of instruction in all.
Read through its window, the line and the two counters, it's the ordinary computer again, run by its
moves for the instructions and blind to the record and the ledger: the record layer is the part the
slice forgets, and the appendix proves that every computer with a move for each two-counter
instruction is the slice of a certified Thiele-complete machine (Theorem~\ref{thm:slice}). The
step that raises the flag is the write of a 0, a merge in the record layer, and that's why it's
charged; the order the step enforces, check, then commit, then certify, is what makes this
record's raise mean a claim held. That's what I mean by certification, and it's the layer this part adds to the bar
Part~II set. Then how far the example reaches, the real systems that already put a price on a write,
the thesis about which kept distinction is worth paying for, and what the example's counter has to do
with heat. Those claims are about the model; the example is where you can check them line by line. The ordinary computer's own steps merge too (counting a counter down lands two states on
one), and their physical costs depend on the implementation; the ledger leaves them alone.

%===========================================================================
\section{What established means}
\label{sec:established}
%===========================================================================

Parts~I and~II were about any kept distinction at all. This chapter picks one: the distinction
between an answer that was checked and the same answer that wasn't. It's the case the first pages of
the book called the sharpest, and it's sharp because the two answers are the same bits, and everything that differs
is in what was kept.

\subsection{Two computers that end up the same}

You met these two computers in one paragraph at the start of the book. Now I'll take them slowly:
what an ordinary computer does about what Part~I found keeping takes, and why that matters to anybody who isn't a
physicist.

Put two computers on a table. Hand each of them the same list of a thousand numbers.

The first one sorts it. It compares, swaps, walks the list again and again until nothing is out of
order. Then it does one more thing: it walks the whole list front to back and checks that every
number is no bigger than the one after it. That check could have failed. It passes. Then it tidies
up after itself, wipes its scratch work, and leaves the sorted list in memory. (That check compares
neighbours, so what it settles is that the output is in order. That the output holds your
thousand numbers and no others is a second claim, and it would take a second check comparing the
output with the input. When I say sorted below, I mean in order.)

The second one never looks at your list. Somebody typed the sorted version into it earlier, same
thousand numbers, same order, and it puts them in memory.

Now wait until both are done and read the retained digital state we have
chosen to compare: the list, the working registers and the control position.
Arrange for both programs to finish at the same control point and clear the
scratch fields. Those endpoints can agree. The first compared the entries
and checked their order. The second loaded the same answer without doing
either. Wheel the boxes out, swap them and bring them back. From those fields
alone, neither of us can tell which run happened.

That is a construction with a specified observation. It does not establish
that every microscopic state of two physical computers agrees: the room,
heat, clocks or retained logs may carry other evidence. And ordinary computers
can keep a checked flag or a protected log. These two programs were arranged
to erase the distinction from the fields being read. That choice, and what
it prevents the next reader from answering, is the example.

Who cares? Anybody who's been handed a sheet that says ``all tests passed.'' Anybody who's looked at
an inspection sticker on a windshield: the sticker looks the same whether somebody checked the
brakes or somebody sold the sticker. An audit, a proof, a ledger, an AI that sounds very sure of
itself: every one of them is a pile of bits that could have come out of either computer, and the
question that matters is the one the bits can't answer. Did something establish this, or did it just
print it? I'll come back to every one of those later in this chapter and say which of them this
book actually helps with, and I'll warn you now that it's fewer than you'd hope.

I'm going to call the first run's relation to that answer \emph{established}: it
checked the order of this list. The second run has the answer without that relation.
The list's order is there either way. What can a machine keep of the difference
between the runs? The rest of this chapter takes that question apart.

It belongs in a book about a 0 because a record that the check ran would be a distinction that
stays, a 0 in some cell that says ``checked.'' These two computers did not keep that
record. A machine that does keep it gives you something more to inspect.

\subsection{Look harder}

The obvious answer is: just look harder. Don't look at the end, look at everything. So make the
computers as lookable as computers get. Scale them up to the size of a warehouse, every wire a
lamp that's lit or dark, every switch something you can walk up to and touch. Nothing is hidden in a
chip too small to see. Put both of them side by side and walk the floor.

While they run, sure, you'd see the difference. One has a whole wing lighting up, comparing and
swapping, and the other just copies. But they finish, and the comparing wing goes dark. Now walk the
floor and look at every single lamp. The sorted list is spelled out in lit and dark lamps in both,
the same pattern, and everything else is dark in both, because both cleaned up.

There is no lamp anywhere that says ``a check ran here and passed.'' It isn't hidden, and it isn't encrypted; it just
isn't there. You can see every retained digital field in this drawing, and none records the earlier check. Looking harder doesn't help, because the problem isn't that you can't see enough. It's that
nothing was kept.

The shape I want you to carry through the rest is that the problem was never visibility; it's keeping.

\subsection{So keep the trace}

Then the fix is obvious, isn't it? Don't let the run go. Keep the trace: every comparison, every
swap, the check and its answer, written down as it happens. Wheel the computers out on the cart and
back, read the traces, and you'll know which one sorted. Problem solved?

It's the right instinct, and it gets most of the way to this book. But take it apart, because
``just keep the trace'' has three things wrong with it, and each one is a piece of
what comes later.

First, a trace is bits, and bits can be typed in. Whoever typed the sorted list into the second
machine can type a trace in too: ``compared, swapped, checked, passed,'' a few thousand lines of
it, every one of them plausible. A trace written by a program is something the program produced,
unless some enforced rule constrains how the program can write that log. So keeping the trace doesn't
answer the question; it moves it. Did something establish this trace, or did it just print it?

Second, the way out of that is to take the pen away from the program. Don't let the program write
its own trace. Have something underneath it write the trace, one step at a time, as the steps
actually happen, so nothing a program does can add a line that didn't happen or erase one that
did. Airplanes do a version of this. Flight recorders go back to a prototype David Warren built in
Melbourne in the 1950s. He was an Australian scientist at the Aeronautical Research Laboratories,
working on jet fuel, and after a string of unexplained airliner crashes he wanted a box that would
hold the instrument readings and the voices in the cockpit for whoever came looking afterwards; I
know his story from museum and encyclopedia accounts, and I haven't read his own report. The
recorders that came out of that idea preserve instrument data and cockpit sound.
The sound can include a person's account, correct or mistaken. A recorded
sensor reading can also be wrong about the aircraft. What the recording
supplies is evidence of what those channels carried, subject to the recorder
and sensors working as specified. Crash protection helps that evidence survive. The flight recorder has the right shape, and that shape isn't mine. Later in
this chapter it gets its name from computer security, a reference monitor, and I'll say outright
that a machine built that way would be doing what this book describes. What the book adds is
narrower than a rulebook for everything underneath. It's about the records that go up and never
come back down: what that something has to keep for good, and what keeping it takes.

Third, a fixed memory cannot retain every possible history of unbounded
length with exact recovery. Give the run one independent yes-or-no choice per
tick: after $n$ ticks there are $2^n$ histories to distinguish. A fixed number
of bits eventually runs out. A completed finite trace can fit, and a predictable
trace can compress. The obstruction needs unbounded independent possibilities,
not just the word ``trace.''

Flight recorders make a practical choice about the history to retain. A voice
recorder loops, replacing older sound when its capacity is reached. Thirty
minutes, two hours and twenty-five hours are different retention windows;
the applicable requirement depends on the aircraft and rule. The FAA's
\href{https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-02-02/pdf/2026-02110.pdf}{2026 final rule}
extends twenty-five-hour recording to specified newly manufactured aircraft.
Whatever window is chosen, it is a window. It does not imply that no other
machine can store an entire finite run.

The fingerprint is the sharpest reply, so take it seriously. Fold every new line of the trace
into a fixed-size scramble of everything before it, and you've got a hash chain. The timestamps of
Stuart Haber and Scott Stornetta, two cryptographers at Bellcore whose story comes later in this
chapter, work that way; so do the audit logs the cryptographers Bruce Schneier
and John Kelsey designed in 1999; and so do the measurement registers in the security chip a lot
of computers carry, the TPM. For the PCRs and lifecycle under discussion, an extend folds a measurement
into the previous value. Reset permissions depend on the register, platform
and locality; some PCRs are resettable during operation. A claim about an
unbroken history must specify which resets and writers its policy permits. That really does keep something about the whole trace in a few dozen bytes. But look at
what it keeps: it keeps a binding, and the content isn't in it. To read the history you still need the trace
stored somewhere, and the fingerprint only tells you whether a copy somebody hands you is the one
that went in. The binding holds only because nobody knows how to find two traces with the same
fingerprint, which is a bet on how hard a search is. No law of nature backs it. That part isn't only my opinion.
The computer scientists Moni Naor and Guy Rothblum proved a sharp version of it in 2005, and they even call the thing a
fingerprint: keep a small private fingerprint of a big file somebody else stores, check the file
by reading only a little of it, and against an opponent with unlimited computing the size of the
fingerprint times the amount you read has to be on the order of the whole file. Do even slightly
better than that against an opponent with limited computing, and you've shown that one-way
functions exist, which is the hardness bet in its barest form. Their setting is a stored file. A
growing trace is a different setting, but it's the same bet, with its terms written down. And squeezing traces that keep
growing into a fixed number of bits has to land many traces on one fingerprint, and that's a merge, hidden behind how hard it is to find which traces land on the same fingerprint. It's the
same merge as in the example of Part~I (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}) where four people have to sit in three chairs. Fingerprints are great, but they're not a way out of forgetting; they're a very clever way of
forgetting.

So the real question was never ``save everything.'' The real question is:
what's the smallest thing worth keeping for good, and what does keeping it take? The answer this
book ends up with is the commitment, in the database's sense, a question closed, and the trace
drops away. (The cryptographer's sealed envelope also goes by the name commitment. It's a different
thing, and both come up later.) What's kept for good isn't every comparison the sort made, just the
one fact that a check of this very claim passed and the question got closed. And the part
that matters most is that keeping even that one fact for good takes something on every machine. It's paid by
forgetting something somewhere else or by taking fresh states the machine never gets back, and on a
finite machine the fresh states run out, so it's the forgetting. That's Part~I's counting of states again, and Part~I
counted the fresh states.

So the premise was never that computers can't keep records. They keep records all day. It's that
nothing in the rules of an ordinary computer makes the record paid for, permanent, or earned, and
those three come in at different places, so I'll say where. Paid for is the model's one rule: in the
Thiele Machine, the step that raises the record has to cost something. Permanent is a premise, the
one Part~I's counting of states needs, and one of the conditions Part~II puts on a record. Earned, meaning a check
of this very claim passed first, isn't in the model's core at all. It's what the step of the small
machine in the next chapter enforces, proved for that machine and every program on it run from a clean start. One more word rides
along with permanent, and it'll come up when I line my record up against other people's: dated. A
record that goes up and stays up went up at one particular step of the run and not another,
even though the record doesn't write down which step. So dated, in this book, means it has a
place in the run's history. Carrying a timestamp is something else, and my record doesn't do it. A machine that charges one for every step it takes meets the first rule, and the charging does
nothing toward
the others, and I'll keep pointing that out.

\subsubsection*{Open the gauge wider}
\label{sec:history-capacity}

Go back to the Sorter. It checked the order of the list. Now ask it another question:
did it also check that none of the original numbers went missing? The list on the screen
can be the same whether that second check happened or not. One lamp saying ``checked''
will not tell me which work was done.

Put a sheet beside the scratchpad, with a named box for each check. Order gets a box.
Membership gets a box. Each other check you want to remember gets its own. When I come
back, I want to know which boxes were ticked. If two runs tick different boxes and leave
the same working value, the full machine has to leave me something that tells them apart.
That is more of the fibre above the same tabletop picture, brought within the question.

Here are the moves. WRITE puts a value $b$ on the scratchpad and starts a fresh sheet,
even if I write the same value again. CHECK $i$ tests its named predicate $P_i$ and records
its name when it passes. A failed check changes nothing in this monitor. IDLE leaves both
scratchpad and sheet alone. The reader can see the working value and ask about every
check name: did it pass since the last WRITE? The sheet must answer yes when it did and
no when it didn't.

Take a finite list of named checks, and let $m(b)$ count the ones whose predicates are
true at $b$. Each of those can be run or left unrun. The truths themselves may overlap;
it is my choice to perform each check that is independent. Four true predicates give
sixteen possible ticked sheets above the same value. The general count follows in the
same way.

\begin{theorem}[Exactly how many current sheets]\label{thm:current-sheet-capacity}
For a finite nonempty working set $B$ and this WRITE/CHECK/IDLE interface, an exact host
needs at least $2^{m(b)}$ reachable full states above each $b$. The minimum total reachable
state count is
\[
\sum_{b\in B}2^{m(b)}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Hold the working value fixed and start with two named checks that would pass
there. Run neither, the first alone, the second alone, or both. The working
value is the same in all four cases. The required answers are not. In particular,
the first-only case and the second-only case cannot finish at the same full
state: ask whether the first check ran, and that one state would have to answer
both yes and no.

Each further check that would pass doubles the choices. For every sheet you
already had, you can leave its new box blank or run that check and tick it.
Starting from one empty sheet, $m(b)$ such choices give $2^{m(b)}$ sheets. Every
sheet is reachable: WRITE the value $b$, then perform exactly the checks whose
boxes it ticks. Any two different sheets disagree at some named box, so they
need different full states. States showing different working values are also
different. Add the required states for each value to get the displayed sum.

Now build a machine with exactly that many states. A state consists of the
working value and its ticked sheet. Include every sheet that ticks only checks
true at that value. WRITE replaces the value and clears the sheet. CHECK ticks
its own box if its predicate is true, and otherwise leaves the sheet alone.
IDLE changes nothing. These rules never produce a forbidden sheet.

Start with the empty sheet. After a WRITE it is empty again, exactly as the
task requires. After a successful CHECK it has precisely that success added;
a repeated success changes nothing further. A failed CHECK adds nothing, and
IDLE adds nothing. If the sheet described the history correctly before a
command, it therefore describes it correctly afterward. Following any finite
list of commands proves the promised answers. The WRITE-and-check runs above
reach every state I included. The lower count is attained.
\end{proof}

Try it with just one box. The workspace holds false or true, and CHECK asks whether it
is true. The whole monitor fits in three states: false, true-unchecked, true-checked.
WRITE false goes to the first. WRITE true goes to the second. CHECK moves the second
to the third and leaves the other two alone. IDLE leaves all three alone.
Start at false. WRITE true reaches true-unchecked, and then CHECK reaches true-checked;
all three states are reachable. Now take any word of instructions. A WRITE makes the
verdict false and starts a new sheet, even if it writes the same value. A CHECK on false
leaves the verdict false; a CHECK on either true state makes or keeps the verdict true.
IDLE preserves it. These are all the cases, and each matches exactly what happened since
the last WRITE. Applying that argument after each instruction proves the promise for
every finite word. In particular, the first arrival at true-checked must use CHECK:
neither WRITE nor IDLE can enter it from another state.

The two true states also show you the merger. CHECK sends true-unchecked and true-checked
to the same next state, right above the same working value. A larger implementation can
move that merger later: let CHECK enter a finite region of accepting states in the fibre
and keep it there, and some two distinct states must share a CHECK successor. WRITE can
still clear the current sheet. Permanence under that one check and permanence under every
instruction are different promises.
 Call that finite accepting region $H$ and the entering state $u$.
The move sends all of $H\cup\{u\}$ into $H$. There are $|H|+1$ distinct sources
and only $|H|$ possible targets, so two sources share a successor. The move preserves
the working picture, so both sources and their common successor lie in that same fibre.

\subsubsection*{Keep the old receipts when the page is wiped}

Now wipe the scratchpad and use it again. I still want the receipt for the first page.
Then use it a third time. I want that receipt too. Think of carbon copies filed before
each sheet goes in the bin. On the tabletop, you can be back where you started. In the
file, you have a past you didn't have before.

On each of $n$ editions, give me the choice to certify it or leave it uncertified.
Bring every choice back to the same final working picture $b$. Then ask the machine
about any edition I name. It has to answer whether that edition was certified. Two
histories that disagree on that answer need two different full states, however alike
their tabletops look. There are $2^n$ possible yes-or-no lists to distinguish.

\begin{theorem}[Room for independently retained editions]\label{thm:edition-fibre-capacity}
Under those realization and exact-query requirements, the fibre above $b$ contains at
least $2^n$ reachable states. If one fixed host meets the requirements for every finite
$n$ at that same $b$, no finite set covers its reachable fibre.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Two different lists of length $n$ differ at an edition. Equal endpoints could not answer
that edition's query differently, so the endpoints are distinct. A putative finite cover
of size $K$ fails once $2^n>K$. Every endpoint being counted has the same working view $b$.
\end{proof}

You can build the witness directly. Keep a Boolean workspace, the answers for the
completed editions, and the current stage of CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY. On a true
workspace, run the chain for an edition you choose to certify, or skip it for one you
don't. Then WRITE true to start the next edition. Every choice brings you back to the
same true workspace and a fresh current stage. Open the file and the choices are still
there, in exactly the places you made them.

Put the whole machine on the table. There is the current page, holding false
or true. There is a marker beside it, with four positions: raw, checked,
committed, published. And there is a numbered file of yes-or-no answers for
pages already put away. Start with a true page, the marker at raw, and an
empty file.

CHECK can move the marker from raw to checked, but only if the page says true.
COMMIT can move it from checked to committed. CERTIFY can move it from
committed to published. Press any of those buttons at another stage and it
leaves the arrangement alone. IDLE always leaves it alone. Those are all the
ways to move the marker without replacing the page, so there is no shortcut
from raw to published.

WRITE does three things, in this order. It files yes if the marker is at
published and no otherwise. It puts the requested value on the page. Then it
returns the marker to raw. The answer goes into the file before the marker is
reset, and no command alters an answer already filed.

Check what that means after any command. CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY move the
current page through exactly the named stages; they do not touch earlier
pages' answers. IDLE leaves both alone. WRITE closes the current page with
the answer its stage warrants, then opens a raw page. Start with no earlier
pages and follow those rules one command at a time: the file always answers
the completed-page questions correctly, and the marker gives the current
page's stage.

To file a yes, run CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY, then WRITE true. To file a no,
use WRITE true alone. Either choice leaves a true page with the marker at
raw, ready for the next choice. After $n$ choices the page and marker are
identical in every run, while the file holds exactly the $n$ answers chosen.
Every yes-or-no list is possible, and different lists are different full states.

Keep asking for another edition, with the same freedom of choice and the same right to
read back every answer. Whatever finite number of full states you offer above $b$, a
long enough history outruns it. The tabletop can keep coming back to one picture.
The machine that keeps all those choices cannot fit its reachable fibre into a finite set.
That is where the infinity comes from.

The old yes-or-no gauge still has a job. Ask whether the file contains any certification
at all and it becomes a permanent lamp: once yes, always yes. Ask whether today's sheet
is certified and wiping that sheet starts the answer over. The small native machine in
the next chapter has the permanent lamp. I will look behind it at the whole native state,
then count which publication histories even that larger view leaves out. That camera sees
more than the working value here; the next count will name its fibre just as explicitly.

\subsection{Computed, stored, established}

Three words get used like they're one.

\emph{Computed} is about the steps. The first machine computed the sorted list. The second didn't.

\emph{Stored} is about the bits. Both machines stored it.

\emph{Established} is neither, and that's the whole problem. It isn't the steps, because they're gone. It
isn't the bits, because they're identical. It's something like this: the first machine has a right
to lean on ``this list is sorted,'' because it ran a test that could have failed, the test passed, the
test was about this very list, and then the question got closed. The second machine has the same
sentence and no right to it. That's a true fact about the two of them, and it's written down
nowhere, in either one. (Whose right, strictly? A machine doesn't lean on anything, any more than a
filing cabinet does. It's the right of whoever reads the first machine to lean on what it says, and
the machine is where the grounds for that right would have to be kept. ``The machine has a right''
is shorter, so I'll keep saying it, and now you know what it's short for.)

I'll hold four words still from here on. A \emph{check} is the test, the thing that could say no. A
\emph{commit} is the closing, the question shut for good, about that edition of that thing. The
\emph{record} is whatever stays behind to say so. And \emph{established}, in the sense a machine can
carry, is all three, about one thing. The first machine had the check and the closing and kept no
record of either, which is the problem above. Where the closing and the record are one act, as in a
database's commit, writing the record is the closing. The small machine keeps them apart, a
commitment the next one replaces and a certificate that stays. The book cashes this working sense at three depths: a paid closing in the bare model; an
object with a checked relation and a paid event, in Part~II (Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}); and the
whole chain on the small machine, in the next chapter. Each place says which one it means.

That raises a fair question: what if the second machine, handed the typed-in list, runs the check
on it? Then it has what the first machine had, and if it closes the question and keeps the record,
it has established that the list is sorted. It didn't do the sorting and it
doesn't need to. The line I'm drawing is between checked and unchecked. Whether the list was
computed or copied doesn't enter into it, and ``without doing either'' up there was about the copier that never looked. So whatever this
book ends up counting, it isn't how hard anybody worked.

People say ``a right to lean on it'' about a lot of things that turn out to be vibes, so I had to find
out whether this one was anything. I went looking, and I'll go through what I ran into.

\subsection{The clerk who forgets everything}

The picture of a computer I used in Section~\ref{sec:structure} is a person with a pencil, a
strip of paper and a short list of rules. So I went back to the source, Alan Turing's 1936 paper, to see how far he actually
takes it.

He takes it a long way. Back then a ``computer'' was a job, a human doing sums by hand, and Turing
modelled that person. He's careful with the person's mind: whatever the clerk knows, beyond a
handful of states, has to go down on the paper. Then he goes all the way. He imagines the clerk
getting up, walking off, forgetting everything, and coming back later. To pick up where he left
off, the clerk leaves himself ``a note of instructions,'' and Turing says that note \emph{is} the clerk's
state of mind, as far as the computation is concerned. Marks on paper and a note are the whole
state.

My two computers are sitting right inside that. Suppose the clerk didn't write the note. Somebody
slipped it under the door, in the right form, with the right instructions. He comes back, reads it,
carries on, and every mark he makes from then on is exactly what he'd have made if he'd written it
himself. Turing's model can't tell the clerk who did the work from the clerk who was handed a note
saying he did. It was never asked to. Turing wanted something you could check without crawling into
anybody's head, and a note on a desk is about as checkable as it gets. That's why the paper still
works ninety years later. The chosen note omits its provenance. A Turing machine can retain additional provenance fields, and its transition rules can restrict how those fields are written. The omission belongs to this note, not to the reach of the model.

So the founding picture of computing is a man who leaves his desk, forgets everything he was doing,
and trusts a sticky note. I relate to him deeply.

And now the question nobody needs answered to follow the argument, which is exactly the kind I
can't leave alone: who were those clerks? They were real people. In the late 1800s the Harvard Observatory hired rooms full of women to
do the arithmetic of the sky, cataloguing stars by hand for a fraction of a man's wage, and some of
them made discoveries of their own, Henrietta Leavitt's way of telling how far away a star is among
them. (I took the wages and the discoveries from Dava Sobel's history of those women, and from the
historians at the American Institute of Physics, who put the men's hourly pay at nearly five times
the women's.) Rooms like that ran artillery tables in both world wars; that part I took from David Alan Grier's history of human computers. So when Turing modelled ``the computer,'' he was modelling somebody's actual
afternoon. That doesn't change the argument a bit. It changes the picture, though, for me anyway: the
sticky note was always a person trusting another person's work, and the question of whether the
work behind it was really done is older than any machine.

\subsection{Information doesn't have it either}

My next guess was information: one machine got some, the other didn't. That one died fast. Claude
Shannon, who turned information into a number in 1948, says on his first page that the meaning of a
message is ``irrelevant to the engineering problem.'' His entropy depends on the probabilities of the possible messages. With an
even spread it is the logarithm of their number; with an uneven spread the
number alone is not enough. Fix the same distribution and the same message
and the information assigned to that message agrees for both computers.
That calculation has not included which history produced it.
He'd give them the same number if one of them got hit by lightning and came out right by luck.

Fine, forget the set and look at the one message. In the 1960s three people, separately, worked
out how to measure the information in one string: Ray Solomonoff, an American who was after a theory
of guessing what comes next from what came before; Andrei Kolmogorov, the great Soviet mathematician; and Gregory Chaitin, an Argentine-American mathematician who later worked at IBM. Their measure is
the length of the shortest program that prints the string. The same two computers hold the same string and get the same number. And
then there's the thing in that theory I keep going back to and standing on, to see if it creaks.
Running a program can't add this kind of information. What comes out can't hold more than what went
in plus the program, give or take a little. Leonid Levin, who studied under Kolmogorov in Moscow and
later left the Soviet Union to teach at Boston University, proved a general version of this, and he has
a one-liner for it that's too good not to repeat: you can torture an uninformed witness all you
want, you won't get information about the crime.

The bound says that an effective sorting procedure does not create
unbounded algorithmic description complexity from that input. It does not
say that sorting tells a person nothing. A person with limited time may now
see the smallest entry immediately. Description length, useful access and
a record that a particular check ran answer different questions.

Logic says the same thing in a different coat. The standard logic of knowing, the
one the Finnish philosopher Jaakko Hintikka worked out in 1962, has a property people call logical omniscience: if you know
some facts, you automatically know everything that follows from them. So by that logic, once you
knew every number on your list, you already knew whether it was sorted. Hintikka flagged the problem
himself, in the same book, and people have been trying to fix it since. The fixes read like a pile
until I asked each one the same thing: when it lets you write \emph{known} next to ``sorted,'' what
does it make you write in the margin? Hintikka's margin is empty. Each fix writes one thing there.

The fix that comes closest to me is from 1995, by Sergei Artemov, a logician at the City University of New York
who studied under that same Kolmogorov (the 1995 report came out of Cornell). He wanted a logic that could
name the proof itself. What I think he's saying: you only get to know a thing if you've built an actual
justification for it, and the justification rides along with the claim. That's a reason traveling with the claim, which is almost a record, but only almost, because it's a way of writing things down and reasoning about them, and nothing in his margin says the reason was ever run, or when.
People have taught it to count, too: Ho Ngoc Duc, a logician at Leipzig, in 1997, made knowing
take reasoning steps, and Artemov and Roman Kuznets, a logician then at Bern, in 2014, asked how big a justification can get before knowing by it
stops being feasible (Part~II weighed both properly, in Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}). I took those for rivals at first. As I read them now, Duc counts the
steps the knower takes and Artemov and Kuznets weigh what you'd hand somebody to check it, one
distance from two ends. It has a computational side, too: Francisco Bavera and Eduardo Bonelli, two Argentine computer
scientists who work on what programming languages mean, in 2018 turned justification logic into a lambda calculus whose terms carry, and can inspect, the
history of the computation that made them, and Samuel Bucheli, Meghdad Ghari and Thomas Studer, three logicians, Studer the head of the logic group at Bern, put justifications on a time line in 2017, where they persist and change.

Line that up against the margin this book wants: earned, paid for, permanent, dated. Artemov's
reason is nearly earned, the steps and the sizes are prices, the time line is a date. Their
time line keeps its dates. Mine is dated only in the execution history: the raise happened at a
definite step, and the record doesn't keep the step number. What none of it has
is the closing of a question as a step with a price. Their prices are on reasoning, and the Bern
justifications change, the one thing a closed question doesn't do. Push on mine, though, and it gives twice. Artemov's margin holds the reason itself, and mine only
says a check passed. And their prices grow with how hard the thing was to know. This book charges the
step that raises the record, and how long the checking took never enters it, so for a measure of
effort, read theirs.

So the two most careful accounts I could find, one about bits and one about knowing, say the same
thing: the sort added nothing.

And yet you know something after the sort that you didn't before. You can read the smallest number
off the first slot. You can stop worrying. Something happened, and that's the clue, the first
solid thing I've got: whatever
\emph{established} is, it isn't new bits. It's the same bits, \emph{settled}: a question sorted into yes and no, with yes made to stay. It's the 0 again, about a claim.

\subsection{The guy who got closest}

Somebody had that clue before me, and on that clue he's the closest neighbour I've found, so he gets the most space
and the hardest push.

Bennett again, the one from Part~I's counting of states and the demon, wrote a paper in 1988 that starts where I just ended up:
information isn't the same as value. His example is an almanac of where the moon and planets will
be every day for a hundred years. It has no more information than the equations it was calculated
from, but it saves you doing the calculating. So the value is the work. He called the amount of
work a thing carries its \emph{depth}.

Was this my idea, already done, by a guy at IBM? The only way to find out was to find where it
parts from mine, because if I couldn't find that place I'd just be renaming his idea. And it's one
word: \emph{plausibly}. Depth is the amount of work a thing was \emph{plausibly} made with. Bennett says
straight out that you can't know how a message actually came to be; for all you know it came from
flipping coins. Depth is read off the finished thing, the way a fossil's age is read off the
fossil.

Bring the two computers back. The sorted list in the first one has some depth. The identical list in
the second has exactly the same depth, because depth looks at the list and nothing else. A
photocopy of a deep thing is just as deep. Depth tells you what work a plausible way of making the thing would take.
It's not a record that \emph{this} machine did it, and it's not a receipt for what doing it
cost.

So Bennett's standing right next to the line, on the other side of it, and as far as I can tell he
got his own question right. He asked how much work a thing embodies. I'm asking who has the right to
lean on it and what they paid to get there. His answer lives in the object. Mine, if I've got one,
has to live in the machine.

\subsection{Statues that walk off}

If it isn't in the information, maybe it's in the knowing, so I went and read the philosophers.
And there it was again: people had been arguing about the difference between having the right
answer and knowing it for a couple thousand years.

Plato's version is a joke about statues. There was a story that the sculptor Daedalus made statues
so lifelike they'd walk off if you didn't tie them down. Plato says true opinions are like that:
they wander off, and they're not worth much until you tie them down with the reason why. Once
they're tied down, they're knowledge, and they stay put. Knowledge tied to a reason, and knowledge that stays: of everybody I'd have bet on to hand me that shape, Plato wasn't on the list.

Then in 1963 Edmund Gettier, whose trap Part~II played with cups (Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}), broke the tidy version in three pages. Smith and Jones are up for the same job. Smith has good reason to think
Jones will get it, and he's counted the coins in Jones's pocket: ten. So Smith figures, with good reason, that
the man who'll get the job has ten coins in his pocket. Then Smith gets the job, and, unknown to
him, Smith also has ten coins in his pocket. Smith had a belief that was true and backed by a reason, and it still wasn't knowledge. He
was right by luck, because his reason was about the wrong pocket.

Gettier's case is the push that matters for a machine. Checking one pocket and committing to a claim about
another is right by luck. So whatever a machine commits to, the check underneath has to be about
\emph{this very claim}, and I'd better say exactly what that means, because it carries a lot of weight
later.

A check is about this very claim when four things hold. It tests the same property the commit names.
A cousin of that property won't do. It tests that property on the same thing the commit names, and
the thing next to it won't do either. Nothing has written to that thing between the check and the commit, so it's still the same
edition the check looked at. And the check is honest: it says yes when the property is true and no
when it isn't, on every value it could ever be handed, this one and all the others. Break the first three and
you're Smith with his ten coins. Break the fourth and the check is just a rubber stamp. The next
chapter builds a machine whose step won't let a commit through unless the first three hold, and whose
checks come with a proof of the fourth.

Two notes on those four, because they matter later. The fourth asks for more than it needs. To rule
out luck, a check only has to never say yes when the property is false; saying yes every time it's
true is a bonus. And the third is a very old bug in computing wearing Gettier's coat. Security people
call it time-of-check-to-time-of-use: check a file, use it, and something swaps the file in between
(Matt Bishop and Michael Dilger, two computer security researchers at the University of California,
Davis, wrote up how to hunt for it in 1996). Databases guard against the
same thing by making sure, just before a commit, that nothing they read has been written since;
H. T. Kung and John Robinson, two computer scientists at Carnegie-Mellon, called that optimistic concurrency control in 1981. A philosopher's
pocket and a sysadmin's race condition are the same bug. One limit, said now: a machine can only promise
``nothing has written to that thing'' about its own memory; for brake pads or a voter roll the
third condition becomes a premise about whoever measured (Section~\ref{sec:models}).

At this point I went further than this chapter needs, because the obvious next question is:
does anything fix Gettier? People tried for years. The first patch is ``no false steps in the
reasoning'': Smith's mistake was believing Jones would get the job, so rule that out. Then a
philosopher named Alvin Goldman came back with barns, and he credits the barns to Carl Ginet,
another philosopher working on what it takes to know something. You're driving
through a county that, unknown to you, is full of fake barns, just painted fronts propped up to look
like the real thing. You look at the one real barn in the county and think ``that's a barn.'' It's true, you believe it, you have a good
reason, your own eyes, and there's no false step anywhere. And still you were lucky: if you'd glanced at
the next one over you'd have believed the same thing and been wrong. Every patch gets a new barn,
and as far as I can tell the arguing hasn't stopped. That tells me something I'll keep: whether a
check was good isn't only about this one case. It's about what the check would have done on the
cases next door. Hold on to that, because it's the next section.

\subsection{What ``could have failed'' means}

I keep saying the first machine's test \emph{could have failed}. Take that apart, because it's the
piece everything else hangs off.

The machine is deterministic. Given your list, the check was always going to pass. So in what sense
could it have failed? By ``could have failed'' I mean this: hand the checking stage an out-of-order
candidate output and it says no. I do not mean hand the whole sorter an unsorted input; putting
that input in order is its job. The relevant counterfactual is a defective candidate reaching the
checker. An ordinary unsorted input reaching the sorter isn't it. Chance has nothing to do with
it. The copier that never checks has no corresponding rejection.

A check is a question asked of every possible input, and it splits them into two
piles: the ones it says yes to and the ones it says no to. ``Could have failed'' just means the no
pile isn't empty. A check that says yes to everything has an empty no pile, and it distinguishes no
inputs, however long it runs and however official it looks. It can still be sound, when its
property holds of everything, and then it's sound and tells you nothing you didn't have. A philosopher, Robert Nozick, made a
version of this a condition for knowing, in 1981: you know a thing only if, had it been false, you
wouldn't believe it.

``Could have failed'' describes the
\emph{procedure}, about what the check would have done on other lists. It isn't a fact about the end
state at all. Look at the first machine's memory when it's done: a sorted list. Nothing in those
bits says ``and whatever made me would have caught a mistake.'' The warehouse comes back here, every
lamp visible and none of them saying it. The one thing that makes the first machine's answer
worth more is exactly the kind of thing those bits can't hold: the copier ends with the same
bits, and neither machine kept anything else. An end state can hold more than the answer, and the
only way a machine can own this
is to write something down at the moment the check passes, and to have that something mean what it
says. More than anything else in this chapter, that's why I ended up needing a record. A better
answer wouldn't have done it. Even then the record only carries half of it. It can say a check ran on an
edition and passed. That the check would have said no on a bad list is a fact about the checker,
and that half rides on a proof about the checker; on this machine that proof sits outside, and
whoever reads the record reads and accepts it. Where that kind of chain of reasons stops is the swamp of the philosopher Karl Popper, a little further down.

One more thing that tripped me up and then didn't. Rig a check to pass only on your one list. Is
that cheating? No. It's a perfectly honest check of a different claim, ``this is that exact list,''
and it has a big no pile: every other list. It establishes exactly that and nothing more. What a
check establishes is whatever it's honest about.

Put that next to the empty no pile and the two fit together: a check establishes what it's honest
about, and a check with an empty no pile is honest only about what you already had. One
thing I'll say plainly now, so it doesn't ambush you in the next chapter: the example I build there
doesn't police this. Its step makes sure a commit was checked first, about the same thing, by a
checker proved honest. It doesn't stop you asking a question that can't come out no, like ``is this
number at least zero.'' Ask one and the whole chain runs, it costs three, and nothing is
established but the chain. The certificate I show off there asks one that can fail.

\subsection{Settled, whether it's true or not}

Then I ran into Charles Sanders Peirce again, the one from Section~\ref{sec:structure}, in an 1877 essay called ``The Fixation of Belief.'' He was asking what inquiry is for, and his answer named the thing I'd been running together without noticing. The point of inquiry, he says, is to get out of doubt and settle on a
belief. And when someone objects that surely what people want is a \emph{true} belief, he answers like a
guy who's watched a lot of arguments end: ``as soon as a firm belief is reached we are entirely
satisfied, whether the belief be true or false.''

That's funny, and then it isn't, because he's right. Settling and being right are two different
events. A question can be closed on a wrong answer, and once it's closed it acts closed. Peirce cares
a lot about which ways of settling hold up (science wins, for him, because it has to answer to
something outside any one person), but the settling itself, the question snapping shut, is there
every time, and it never comes with a guarantee.

Karl Popper came at it from the other side. He was a philosopher from Vienna asking what separates
science from everything else, and in his 1934 book, the one that came into English as \emph{The Logic
of Scientific Discovery}, he says every test has to stop somewhere, at some
statement somebody decides to accept, and nothing in the evidence forces you to stop there instead
of one step further. You stop when you're satisfied. His picture is a jury: the verdict is a
decision about what happened, and the jury deciding it doesn't make it true. Science, for him, is a
building on piles driven into a swamp, and the piles stop where somebody's satisfied they'll hold.
They never reach firm ground.

A real jury has a problem Popper doesn't mention, because a real jury is twelve people.
Lewis Kornhauser and Lawrence Sager, two law professors writing in the Yale Law Journal, noticed in 1986 that a court that votes by majority on
each premise of a case and also on the verdict can end up contradicting itself: every judge
is consistent, and the court isn't. Christian List and Philip Pettit, two philosophers writing
in Economics and Philosophy, turned that in 2002
into a theorem. No way of combining people's yes-or-no judgments on connected questions
meets a short list of conditions that each look harmless on their own and always hands back a consistent,
complete group judgment. A group's settling is a rule's settling, and which rule you pick
decides which of the honest settlings sticks. Try the problem with three ballots and a rule that a payment is due only if a contract
was signed and a deadline was missed. One voter says yes to both, one says signed but
not missed, and one says missed but not signed. Each voter applies the rule consistently.
Count separately: a majority says signed, a majority says missed, and a majority says
no payment. You can point to the disagreement on the paper without blaming any one
voter's logic. I haven't tried to put a group on the machine, and that's where I'd
expect the first wall to be.

Popper's swamp sent me further down, because it's the oldest problem in the book and it doesn't have a
bottom. Ask why you believe something and you get a reason. Ask why you believe the reason and you
get another one. Sextus Empiricus, a skeptic and doctor who lived probably in the second or third century and
whose whole method was holding off judgment, wrote down the ancient version, credited to someone called
Agrippa, and in 1968 the German philosopher Hans Albert, who with Popper led the school called critical rationalism, gave it a name with a joke in it: the
Münchhausen trilemma, after the baron who claimed he pulled himself out of a swamp by his own hair.
Every chain of reasons does one of three things. It goes on forever. It loops back on itself. Or it
stops somewhere, because somebody decided it stops. People have argued for a very long time about
which of the three to live with. So ``when do I actually know, and when am I done checking?'' doesn't get a clean answer
from anybody. What you can do is be honest about where you stopped and why. That's a lot of what
the rest of this book is: every place it stops is written down, with its name on it, so you can
decide whether you'd have stopped there too.

Lay Peirce and Popper on top of each other and what shows through is that the check is one act and the stopping
is another. The check can run as long as you like and it never \emph{makes} you stop; at some point
something decides, and the deciding is its own event. That's the second machine's whole trick: it
skipped the check and kept the answer.

And a logician said the part I didn't expect a logician to say. Per Martin-Löf, a Swedish logician, says a proof is an act, and once it's done it's done. His
words, from lectures he gave in Siena in 1983: ``a proof is, not an object, but an act \ldots{} Only
secondarily, and irrevocably, does it become the act that has been performed.'' That took me a few
reads, and the tenses unlocked it: first the act being done, then, for good, the act that has been
done. You could say that's true of everything that ever
happened, and I'd grant it, but it's the two computers again: the first machine's check happened, irrevocably,
and the machine right now carries no trace of it. The past can't be undone. The \emph{record} of it can
be lost, unless something keeps one. That gap is where this book lives.

Then the intuitionists got there first, which by now I should've expected. The Dutch mathematician L.~E.~J. Brouwer, who held that a mathematical truth is something a mind
makes evident, argued from 1948 on about an idealised mathematician working in stages, the creating
subject. The people after him only came clear to me once I sorted them by three words: the act, the
object, and the trace the act leaves behind, which Martin-Löf's sentence has no room for. The logician Georg Kreisel (1967), Austrian-born and then at Stanford, wrote it down as a formula: the subject has evidence for
$A$ at stage $n$. That's a trace, something you can come back and ask about after the act is over. Anne Troelstra (1969), a Dutch logician who studied under Brouwer's student
Arend Heyting and became one of the leading authorities on intuitionism, added that the
subject never forgets what it has made evident, so the trace never fades. That's how Mark van Atten (2018), a philosopher in Paris who has spent years on Brouwer, credits it; the
Stanford Encyclopedia's entry on intuitionism lists the never-forgets axiom among Kreisel's own, and I
haven't settled which is right. Van Atten, going through the whole history, reads the formula as ``by stage $n$ the Creating Subject has made $A$ evident.'' Look at the
tense. \emph{Has made} is Martin-Löf's ``the act that has been performed,'' reached from the other
end. And look at
what that carries. It's tied to a stage; at any stage you can ask whether it's happened yet; it
never goes away; and it's never wrong. Van Atten even says the subject can't just accept a proof
handed to it from outside: it has to go through the steps and rebuild the evidence itself, which is
the copier who runs the check. And then there's G\"oran Sundholm, a philosopher of logic at Leiden. He has long kept a proof as an act
apart from a proof as an object (1998), and, as I understand his work, apart from its trace as well.
In a 2014 paper he worked through how Brouwer's theory of the creating subject sits beside the thesis
that every effective procedure is a program, which is the side this book's machines live on. I
know that second paper only by what it sets out to do, so I lean on it lightly.

Set their trace beside my record and the columns nearly all fill: their stage is my dated, their never
forgetting my permanent, their never wrong my earned. Their stage is written into the trace,
though, and my dated is only a step in the run that the record doesn't keep. The empty one is the price, and I think
I see why. A mind with unlimited memory pays for never forgetting by taking states it has never used, and an idealised
mind has endless fresh states to take, so nobody charges it for that. On a finite machine the fresh states run out, and
writing a record that stays up forces the instruction to merge some states. Charging for that
merge is a further premise. The forcing is Part~I's counting of used and fresh states, and the charging is the price rule Part~I sets.
So it's the closest thing to my \emph{established} that I've found. The formula is around sixty
years old, and the idea under it, Brouwer's creating subject, is older than that. Push on my side
from theirs, though, and it gives twice. Van Atten's subject won't take a proof from outside,
and my machine takes exactly one: its checker is trusted on a proof about the checker that somebody
did outside every run. And their evidence is never wrong because, for Brouwer, made evident is what
true means. Mine is right only as far as that checker is honest. Where they differ, the difference is honest: their subject is an idealised mind with
unlimited time and memory, and mine is a machine with a finite table that establishes only the
claims its program checks.

\subsection{Not a switch}

So far I've been talking about \emph{established} as if it were a light switch: on or off, the first
computer on and the second one off. That bothered me the whole time I was writing it, and for a
while I couldn't say why. It felt too small, the way a word can be technically right and still not
cover what you're pointing at. I don't trust that feeling on its own, because I've had it plenty of
times about things that turned out to be nothing. So I went looking for something outside my own head
that would either give the feeling something to stand on or show me I was imagining it.

I didn't know what I was looking for, at first, beyond a rough shape: two things that look exactly the
same and differ in how far something about them has been settled. So I started collecting anything
that seemed to have that shape, and most of what I collected fell apart as soon as I looked at it
closely. How each one fell apart taught me more than the thing itself did, so I'll go through them
in the order it happened. Every story below is the version I could piece together from the records I
could reach, and where I couldn't reach a record I'll say so. Check me.

The first batch was all hidden things. A pea under one of three cups. A tree, whose age you can't see
from the outside. A forged painting that looks right until somebody tests the paint. A glass of gas,
where the thermometer shows one temperature and underneath there are uncountably many arrangements of
molecules that would all show the same reading. Plato's prisoners in the cave, who see shadows on a
wall. The things casting them stay behind their backs (Section~\ref{sec:windows} tells their story). Every one of these looked promising for about a minute. Then I noticed they
all fail the same way: look harder and the hidden thing shows up. Lift the cup. Cut the trunk and count
the rings. Run the paint test. Look at the molecules, at least in principle. Turn around in the cave.
In each case the hidden part is a fact about the object that better eyes could find. That isn't what
the two computers have. You can see every lamp in the warehouse and not find the check.

That failure gave me the first real tool I had, and it's a crude one. Give an observer perfect vision of
the visible thing, as much detail as they want, and ask whether they could read the difference off it.
If they could, it's something hidden, and that's not what I'm after. If they couldn't, it might be. I
should say how much weight that test holds. It's a judgment, and I'm the one making it, so it's a
way of sorting my own examples, not a verdict. If you find a case it sorts wrongly, that tells me
something about the test and about me.

The second batch got past that test and failed a different way. A clock face reads three o'clock and
doesn't show how many days have gone by; no amount of staring at the face tells you. And a computer can
keep a complete history of what it did. It's Bennett's 1973 machine from Part~I's counting of states, and the
story is better than I let on there. Landauer had argued in 1961 that real computers throw
information away all the time, and Bennett, his younger colleague, asked whether they had to. His answer, in a 1973 paper, was no. A machine can write down
every step it takes, copy out its answer, and then run itself backward, retracing its steps and wiping
the history as it goes, until it holds only the input and the answer and has never thrown anything
away. It takes a forward run, a copy of the answer and a backward run, with scratch space for the history. Bennett thanks
Landauer at the end for raising the question in the first place, which I like: the man whose principle
says forgetting gives off heat is the one who asked whether you could get out of it. The history it keeps along the
way is real extra information, sitting out where anyone could read it, so it isn't a hidden fact
of the first batch's kind. Keeping it and unwinding it throws nothing away, so by Landauer's own
reckoning there's no floor under its heat: run it slowly and the heat comes down as near nothing
as you like, though never to nothing for a run that finishes, which Part~I proved for Bennett's
own model (Theorem~\ref{thm:time-bill}). What it spends besides is fresh states, the scratch space the history sits in. And it can be
run back down. Neither of those two, the keeping that merges nothing and the running back down,
fits what happened to the first computer, which did something that can't be undone and paid for
it. If the standing I'm after could be put up and taken back down with nothing kept and no floor
either way, it would just be bookkeeping. So that batch taught me what else I needed: something that only moves one way, and costs
something to move.

The third batch came closer and still didn't quite fit. In 1782 James Six, a Canterbury man from a
family of silk weavers who had taken up watching the weather, described a thermometer for the Royal
Society. He wanted the coldest moment of every night, and he'd found that with an ordinary thermometer
you had to be looking at it when it happened, because, in his words, ``if it be not immediately
noticed, it can never after be known.'' His fix was two little steel markers in the tube that the column
pushes up and that stay where they're left. The markers make a record that only moves one way. Then he spoils it,
for my purposes, in the same paper: every evening he wrote the numbers down and slid the markers back
with a magnet, ``without a touch.'' A record anybody can reset with a magnet is not the thing I'm after,
and Six would have been the first to say he wasn't the first to build one; his paper lists the
thermometers that came before his.

Since 1996, starting with oral polio vaccine, vials of vaccine bought through UNICEF have carried
a small sticker, a square inside a circle. The square darkens as the vial takes on heat, and the darkening doesn't undo when the vial cools.
When the square matches the circle, the vaccine shouldn't be used. It only moves one way, and it can't be reset. But
it's chemistry. The reaction in the square is chosen to run about as fast as the vaccine itself spoils,
so the sticker is really reading the vaccine's own condition by a proxy. Nobody ran a check; the heat
did.

Closer still: the International Vocabulary of Metrology, the reference book that measurement
laboratories work from, says a result is traceable only if it ``can be
related to a reference through a documented unbroken chain of calibrations, each contributing to the
measurement uncertainty.'' That's a lot like what I want, a standing earned by checks, step by step. The
same document adds that traceability ``does not ensure \ldots that there is an absence of mistakes,''
which is the true-versus-established split written into an international standard. And the top of the
chain wasn't fixed either. When the official copies of the kilogram were compared with the prototype in
1889, 1946 and around 1991, they had drifted apart by tens of micrograms over the century, and nobody
can say which one moved, because the prototype was the kilogram. In 2019 the kilogram was redefined by
fixing a constant of nature, Planck's constant, instead. A chain like that can also lapse: if the calibrations stop, new
results stop being traceable. The standing has to be kept up, which my record doesn't.

The rules of chess have the shape too. The current Laws of Chess of FIDE, the international chess
federation, say in Article 9.2.3 that two
positions are the same only if ``the same player has the move, pieces of the same kind and colour occupy
the same squares and the possible moves of all the pieces of both players are the same,'' and they spell
out that a king that could still castle and one that can't are in different positions, even on an
identical board. That passes the perfect-vision test. And the official text says why it passes: the
castling right changes which moves are legal. So the hidden part steers the game: it decides what can
happen next. In the example machine, the flag never steers. It never touches the ordinary computing at
all. The table and the trap that give the flag its meaning do steer, and Section~\ref{sec:smallest}
says where that line falls. Each of these got something right and missed something else.

The one that fit best, and I want to say clearly that it only fit best among the ones I found, was the
standing of a mathematical statement. I'll go through how it went for one statement, as far as I could follow it.

In 1611 Johannes Kepler, the emperor's mathematician in Prague, owed his friend and patron Johann Matthäus
Wackher von Wackenfels a New Year's present and, he said, had nothing to give. Wackher, Kepler wrote,
loved \emph{nothing}, for the games you can play with the word, so Kepler wrote him a little pamphlet about the nearest thing to nothing he could find,
a snowflake, which had landed on his coat as he crossed a bridge. Why six corners? Kepler couldn't say
in the end. But along the way he stacked equal balls in his head and asserted that one way of stacking
them, the way grocers stack oranges, packs them so tightly that, in the 1966 English translation, ``in
