no other arrangement could more pellets be stuffed into the same container.'' He didn't prove it. He
said it.

Then the sentence sat. In 1831 Carl Friedrich Gauss, reviewing somebody else's book on a piece of
number theory, proved what amounts to the special case of stackings laid out on a regular grid. In 1900 David Hilbert put the general question of packing equal spheres
on his famous list of problems for the new century, without mentioning Kepler. In 1953 the Hungarian geometer
László Fejes Tóth showed how the whole thing might be cut down to a problem with finitely many numbers in it, and a decade
later he guessed that computers might one day finish it. Thomas Hales, a mathematician then at the University of Michigan, started on it in earnest in 1994,
and in August 1998 he and his student Samuel Ferguson announced a proof that leaned on a great deal of
computer work. The Annals of Mathematics gave the paper to a panel of twelve referees, led by Gábor
Fejes Tóth, László's son. They ran seminars on it for years. A journalist, George Szpiro, later reported
that by July 2002 they were 99 percent certain it was right; I couldn't find those words in anything the
referees wrote themselves. What Szpiro printed in \emph{Nature} in 2003 was the editor's letter as
Hales reported it: the referees had ``not been able to certify the correctness of the proof, and will
not be able to certify it in the future, because they have run out of energy \ldots'' The Annals printed the human part in 2005, and the whole
proof appeared in 2006. Hales started the Flyspeck project in 2003 to supply a fully explicit derivation of the entire argument. It was finished on 10 August 2014.

Lay those dates out on the table and look at what moved. The sentence never changed. Hilbert's version
of the question didn't even name the man who first said it. Whether it's true never changed, as far as
anyone can tell. What changed was how far it had been established, and it changed in stages, each one
paid for by somebody's work: a guess, a special case, a place on a list, a plan, an announcement, a
panel's reported ninety-nine percent and their exhaustion, a printing, a machine check. A perfect reader of the
sentence can't see which of those acts has occurred. An act already completed stays in the history; confidence in the argument can still fall. A place on a famous list is recognition, not itself another proof step.

Then I tried to break that one too, because by this point I'd watched a lot of good-looking examples
fall over, and there's an obvious place to push. Standing can fall. In 1852 a student named Francis
Guthrie, colouring a map of the counties of England, noticed that four colours always seemed to be
enough to keep neighbouring counties different. The question passed to his old teacher Augustus De
Morgan, who wrote to the Irish mathematician William Rowan Hamilton that a student had asked him for ``a reason for a fact which
I did not know was a fact,'' and that he didn't know it yet either. In 1879 Alfred
Kempe, a barrister who did mathematics on the side and sang counter-tenor, published a proof, and his
description of finding it is wonderful: ``After a somewhat arduous search, I have succeeded, suddenly,
as might be expected, in hitting upon the weak point \ldots'' The journal's associate editor, William Story,
added a note saying Kempe had ``substantially proved'' the theorem, and tightened the counting part of
the argument. Eleven years later Percy Heawood, a lecturer at Durham who by one account brought his dog
to his lectures, showed that one step of what he called ``the now apparently recognised proof'' doesn't
work. Kempe swaps colours along two chains at once, and swapping the first can spoil the second.

So standing can fall. Story's published note strengthens the counting; that
alone does not establish exactly which other steps he privately examined.
What Heawood exposed is enough for the comparison: an accepted argument had
an invalid step. Human acceptance and a proved sound checker are different
premises. The example machine below is given the second one. Its theorem
cannot turn the historical acceptance of Kempe's argument into a sound check
by calling the overlooked part unearned.

And then came the part I didn't expect. The four-colour statement was true all along. Kenneth Appel and
Wolfgang Haken, two mathematicians at the University of Illinois, proved it in 1976 with a computer, and the proof was met with suspicion for years; a
cleaner version came in the 1990s; and in 2005 Georges Gonthier, a computer scientist at Microsoft Research in Cambridge, finished a proof of the whole thing
checked by a small proof-checking program. So this one statement stayed true the entire
time while its standing went up in 1879, came down in 1890, went up again in 1976 against a lot of
doubt, and went up further in 2005. The fall wasn't a fall of the truth. It was a fall of how far the
truth had been established, and it was the right fall to have, because what had been established was
less than anyone thought.

Laying all of that out together is what changed my picture. If there are stages, then at each one
there's a line, and the line has two sides: not this far yet, and at least this far. Each line amounts to
its own yes-or-no question. But choose the question carefully. ``Do I still trust this
proof?'' can turn back to no, as Kempe's did. ``Did I carry out this particular check?''
asks about a completed act. Cross out the acceptance and the act still happened.
To keep that answer, the machine has to keep a record of it and have no move that knocks
the record down. A check that could have failed doesn't give you that by itself.
Maybe the switch wasn't wrong. Maybe it was just incomplete, the first of many lines, and the
real shape is a direction with lines drawn across it. I've gone
around many times on whether the lines create the direction or the direction comes first and the lines
are just places where you cut it, and on whether yes and no are even different from each other until
something draws the line between them. I don't have an answer to that. The one part I could actually
settle is that a single switch isn't enough once there are three or more stages, and Part~II proved it
(Section~\ref{sec:direction}). Everything else in this paragraph is me thinking out loud.

Flatland, where this hunch started (Section~\ref{sec:origin}), turned out to belong in the first batch. It's a novel Edwin Abbott published in 1884, narrated by a square who
lives in a flat, two-dimensional world (Section~\ref{sec:windows} says more about him and it). When a sphere passes through the flat world, the narrator sees a line whose ends fade wrong and whose
length keeps changing, and only when he feels it does he find a circle, a perfect one. Then the
sphere tells him it will rise, and he watches it dwindle to a point and vanish, and come back larger
and larger. The hidden direction
leaks into his view. Even an exact cross-section does not locate it uniquely:
for a sphere of known radius, equal distances above and below the plane give
the same circle. A known direction of travel or another observation is needed
to choose between them. In this machine two states can sit at different places along the
established direction and agree on every bit of the ordinary machine (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-separation}). That may be exactly why the
ordinary machine can't see it. It may also be why, if the direction is worth having, someone has to build
it in on purpose and keep it on purpose. Keeping it is paid for; Part~I's counting of states says so. What's still open is what has
to be kept, and that's what the rest of this chapter is for.

Those readings helped me separate the jobs. A Thiele machine keeps a distinction about a
claim. Its step determines how that distinction is established, its record keeps
it through later work, and its schedule counts the charge. The next few sections put
those jobs in computing's own words; the next chapter builds one example.

\subsection{Computing already had a word for it}

Computing already has a word for this and uses it every
day. Anyone who's used a database has seen it: COMMIT.

A database does a pile of tentative work, and then there's one moment, the commit, written to a log,
after which the change counts. Jim Gray, who more or less built the theory behind that, opens his
1981 paper on it by saying the idea comes from contract law, and his example is a wedding. People
negotiate, somebody asks, two people say ``I do,'' and from then on it's binding. If it was a mistake, you don't erase
it. You do another transaction to fix it, the way a bad contract gets a second
contract. Nobody reaches for a time machine.

The wedding was a philosopher's example first. The Oxford philosopher J. L. Austin, lecturing in 1955, said ``I do''
\emph{makes} a marriage. It doesn't \emph{describe} one, and sayings like that aren't true or false. They can misfire
(the wrong person says it, a step gets skipped). They can't be false. A commit works exactly the same way.
Writing the commit record doesn't report that a question got closed. Writing it \emph{is} the closing.
And a commit can't be false. It can misfire: committed without the check, committed about the wrong
pocket. Those two misfires are Gettier and Peirce again, coming in from a third direction. Then somebody else reads the record, and
for them it stops being a performance and turns into a report: ``this was checked and closed.'' A
report can be false. On the small machine of the next chapter it can't be, about the machine's own history:
if its flag is up from a clean start, some claim was checked and closed, and that claim held of that
edition when it was checked. That's how this book ties a commit to the truth, on that machine and
the ones built on it, and it took a proof to do it.

Robin Milner, building a proof checker in the 1970s, ran out of memory, so he decided to keep only
the finished theorems and throw the proofs away, like a teacher rubbing out the blackboard to make
room. The obvious worry is forgery: if the proofs are gone, what stops someone just writing a
theorem down? His answer was beautiful. Theorems got their own type in the programming language, and
the only way to make one was through the rules of logic. You couldn't forge one because the language
wouldn't let you build it any other way. He named that language ML, for Meta Language. I wanted to
call my machine the meta machine. I'm choosing to treat that as a coincidence. Calling it a sign would be more my
style, so this is more restraint than I usually manage.

Bitcoin is a modern version of keeping a history costly to replace. A returning
node checks the candidate chains against its rules and follows the valid one
with the most accumulated proof of work. ``Longest'' here means that work,
not simply the most blocks. Replacing an old block requires replacing the work
that binds the later blocks to it. The protection depends on the adversary,
network and mining assumptions; a recently accepted history can be reorganised.
The clerk is still reading a note, but now has a specific test for the note and
a resource behind the difficulty of replacing it. That resource is not the
abstract unit charged by this book's toll.

Making a settled fact expensive to fake is a different job from the one this book's price does, the unit of cost it charges for raising a
record. Bitcoin makes it tempting to read the toll of Section~\ref{sec:toll} as a deterrent, so I'd
rather say this here. One unit of cost deters nobody. Bitcoin's work is tied to something
scarce, electricity and hardware; a unit of cost in this book is tied to nothing. Eric Budish, an economist
at the University of Chicago, built a model in 2025 of what that tie has to cost. As I read him, for
Bitcoin's kind of trust to hold, the honest work has to stay expensive at every moment compared with
what an attacker could win, and the expense grows in step with the value being protected. A flat charge of one unit can't do that job, and it isn't trying to. It's a count, not a lock, as the start
of the book put it: the lock is the order rule, check, then commit, then certify, and it would work
at a price of zero. The price is there because nothing is kept for free: Part~I's
counting of states shows that a machine with finitely many states that prices its merges
can't avoid it. Scaring anybody off has nothing to do with it. The machines I actually build have
counters with no top, endless fresh states, so Part~I's counting of states doesn't reach them whole. It reaches the flag: CERTIFY sends its two readings to one, the same counting run on a set of two. The charge comes from pricing that merge in the record's own part of the state, a premise I choose
(Theorem~\ref{thm:record-merge-toll}), and the
size of the charge is my choice too (Section~\ref{sec:smallest} says why).

And Bitcoin wasn't first. Pull on its footnotes: three of the eight
references in the paper that started it point to Stuart Haber and Scott Stornetta, who in 1991
worked out how to stamp a document with a time nobody could fake later, by chaining each stamp to
the ones before it. A company built on their idea, Surety, printed a short fingerprint of its chain in the classified
ads of the New York Times once a week from 1995, and it was still doing it in 2018. I found that in
a piece the journalist Daniel Oberhaus wrote that year, which says the ad runs under ``Notices \&
Lost and Found.'' Think about that for a
second. To make a record nobody could quietly rewrite, they put it somewhere a million people would
keep a copy of without even meaning to. A physicist named Wojciech Zurek has spent decades arguing that the world does the same thing with a measurement, copying the result into so many places that nobody can take it back. I'll get to him properly later in this part (Section~\ref{sec:pointer}).

There are more fences like these: logs that can't quietly change, certificates you can check. Later
in this part, Section~\ref{sec:models} takes five of
them apart. I lean on all of them. They work. I want that said plainly, because the next thing isn't
``they're broken.''

The next thing is where they sit. The database's commit is bits in a log, kept by a database
program, on a machine whose own step will overwrite those bits the moment some instruction says to.
Milner's guarantee is a type checker; it holds inside programs written in his language and nowhere
else. Bitcoin is a protocol on ordinary computers that will do whatever they're told. Every one of them is a program or a rule, on top of a
machine that can't tell my two computers apart. The machine underneath keeps nothing and charges
nothing for what got settled.

The obvious comeback: so put the rule one level lower, in the operating system, or what security
people call a reference monitor, the small always-on piece everything has to pass through. Yes,
exactly that: a monitor that wouldn't let any program raise its record without paying would be doing
the thing I'm talking about. In this book's words it would be \emph{implementing} the model, and I'd
count that as agreement. What I care about isn't who builds the fence. It's what the fence has to
obey, wherever it's built, and whether that's forced or just a good idea.

That comeback has a history, and it's older than me by a lot. In 1972 James P. Anderson's planning
study for the US Air Force described a reference monitor: a piece every access has to pass through,
that can't be tampered with, and small enough to check. In 2000 Fred Schneider, a computer scientist at Cornell, argued that a monitor that only watches a
run as it goes can enforce only rules whose breaking shows up at some finite point, the kind
computer scientists call safety rules. ``No certificate without an
earlier passing check and a commit'' is one of those. And in 2015 Arthur Azevedo de Amorim, a computer scientist then at the University of Pennsylvania, and six
coauthors built monitors that check a rule at every single instruction, and proved them correct. So putting a rule under every program, so nothing can
get around it, is their move. I didn't invent it. What I'm putting under that move is narrower: a record that
has to be paid for, on the small machine one that has to be earned, and a reason, from counting,
why a finite machine that prices its merges can't make the price of a record that never comes down zero.

\subsection{What settling looks like}

The chapter on what structure is (Section~\ref{sec:structure}) ends with a pile of things sorted
into buckets. Settling a question is that, plus one more thing, and it's the 0 from the start of
the book at a bigger size.

Picture every state the machine could be in as a field of dots. A yes-or-no question about the state
splits the field into two parts: yes and no. That split is a sorting, the smallest one there is. And
remember the no pile: if one of the parts is empty, there's no sorting at all, just a field. Now the
extra thing that makes it a settlement: once the machine is in the yes part, \emph{no step it can take
leads back out}. The door opens one way. A settled question is a sorting plus a door that only
swings in.

At its best, what goes through the door is a relation: these numbers are in this order, these two
things belong together. Sultan, the chimpanzee of Section~\ref{sec:insight}, fitted two short
sticks into one long one and reached the food. Nothing new got added to the cage. Two sticks became
one tool. That's what I'd want the door to be for.

But the door doesn't care, and this is the honest edge of the whole picture. Hook the door to a
check that says yes to everything and the machine walks through even when the claim
is false. The question is settled either way,
true or false, like Peirce said. A door that only swings one way tells you a question was closed. It
doesn't tell you it was closed right. Price and correctness are two different books, and I keep
both, separately.

One more edge, the one Gray's wedding already hinted at. What stays shut for good is that the
question got closed, about that edition of that thing. Whether the claim is still true is another
matter. Change the list after the commit and the record still says, truthfully, that the old
edition was checked and closed. And if the claim turns out bad, the fix is another act on top, a
second record that says ``withdrawn.'' The first one never quietly comes back down. So ``entitled
to lean on it right now'' is three things at once: closed, not withdrawn since, and the thing
unchanged.

\subsection{What the Thiele Machine is}

So I'll set out what I built, and which parts I was pushed into and which parts I chose, because you
should know which is which.

You've had the model since the start of the book: five parts (states, moves, a step, a price on
each move in whole units, and a record that sits somewhere in an order; here the order has two
places, no and yes), one rule, the toll, and a counter and a window
when a result needs them. You can't buy it in a box. It isn't a device, a CPU or an instruction set;
those are things you build to carry it, and the next chapter builds one, as small as I could make
it. It counts what a computation makes the case, and this chapter's case is the sharpest one: the
reading is a record that says whether something's been established, and the toll is what the first page
of the book said about records, nothing becomes something for free. The event it accounts for
happens on any computer, whether anybody keeps track of it or not, and the record exists only if
something keeps it. The window earns its place here too, because the two computers already showed
you the problem: the usual window, the bits, can't see the record.

A unit of cost isn't a joule or a dollar; whether it's worth anything physical is Landauer's assumption,
named, and nowhere else. And one unit is just the floor: Part~I shows that if you charge one unit per
halving, a step that squeezes a lot together pays at least the logarithm of the squeeze, roughly how
many times it halves the number of states it can tell apart. Don't read that backwards, though. One
unit isn't one halving. A single state flipping into a big set of states that already read yes,
with every state in play equally likely, squeezes things together only a little, much less
than a halving, and the whole-number count rounds that up to one. Read in the worst case over what the
machine might be holding, the same flip can remove a full bit; Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}
has both readings.

\emph{What ``new model of computation'' means here.} The Thiele Machine takes distinctions I
choose and writes them into the state, the step and the price. In the case on the table that
means which thing a check was about, which edition of it the check saw, and which later act
gets to lean on it. A record keeps some of that. A window decides how much of it somebody
looking in can get back. Change what's kept, or what the window shows, and you change which
questions the end state can answer. The machine underneath does the computing. The record adds
no function it couldn't already compute.

Which leaves a fair question hanging: if it computes nothing new, does it even get to call
itself a model of computation? It does, for the reason the start of the book gave: the
random-access machine computes exactly what Turing's does, the cell-probe and input-output models
leave the computing between the moves they count out of the count, and each is worth having for
what it counts. So are the energy-aware random-access machines of Demaine and his
coauthors (2016), which count the bits destroyed. Add one more to that family,
the bulk-synchronous parallel model of Leslie Valiant, a computer scientist at Harvard (1990), which
charges for rounds of communication between processors. Closest in kind are Blum's axioms, also from
the start of the book, which constrain every cost the way the toll constrains every price list
on the model. The Thiele Machine's own axis is what a run made the case, and what that
cost. Part~II laid the toll over a register machine of Cook and Reckhow's kind, and over a Turing
machine and a lambda calculus, and none of them computes one function more afterward
(Section~\ref{sec:latch}). What each of them gains is a record and a cost.

The opening split what I found from what I assumed and what I chose, and the choice that matters
most here is the first on its last list: the count goes inside the step.

About the name. I named it after myself, on purpose. Half of that is a joke and half of it is a
stake in the ground. Turing got a machine, so here's mine. The longer story,
meta machines and all, is in the afterword, ``How I got here'' (Section~\ref{sec:origin}).

The names are the ones Section~\ref{sec:complete} set out, and they work the way Turing's do. A
clock is enough to make something a Thiele machine. It isn't Thiele-complete, because it charges
for computing, and neither is a machine whose record never goes up. The small machine of the next
chapter is held to a higher bar,
\emph{certified Thiele-complete}: on top of all that, from a clean start the record goes up only
after a passing check of a claim, by a checker proved to mean what the claim says, then a
commitment to that same claim, then a certificate, one unit each; and some claim's check, commitment and certificate raise the record from some starts and not from others, exactly where the claim holds. A \emph{universal} Thiele machine runs any machine of a stated class as a
guest, with every computing step done by its own counter moves and every rise placed by its
program; a certified one also earns each guest's record again. The end of this chapter pins every
one of these words down (Section~\ref{sec:layers}).

\subsection{The two computers, put back together}

I'll tell the two-computer story again, rebuilt as Thiele machines, with the record and the counter
written out, so you can watch it happen. You don't have to take my word. The prices are the ones on the smallest
machine, which the next chapter builds: one unit each to check, to commit, and to certify (raise the record), and
nothing for ordinary work like moving numbers around.

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.205\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.097\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.097\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.097\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.097\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.097\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.097\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{step} & \textbf{sorter does} & \textbf{record} & \textbf{counter} & \textbf{copier does} & \textbf{record} & \textbf{counter} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
start & nothing yet & no & 0 & nothing yet & no & 0 \\
1 & sorts (lots of ordinary steps) & no & 0 & copies in the typed list & no & 0 \\
2 & checks ``sorted'' on this list, this edition: passes & no & 1 & (no check) & no & 0 \\
3 & commits to ``sorted,'' about this list, this edition & no & 2 & tries to commit: nothing checked, refused & no & 1 \\
4 & certifies & \textbf{yes} & 3 & tries to certify: nothing committed, refused & no & 2 \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

At the end, the bits on both machines are still the same sorted list. Everything else differs. The
sorter's record is up and its counter reads 3. The copier's record is down, and it's paid 2 for two
refusals, because on that machine a refused attempt still costs what it costs. (Read those as two
separate attempts. Written as one stored program, the copier would stop at its first refusal and
pay 1.) Nothing the copier
can do raises its record without first running a passing check of the claim it then commits to. And no
outside window that only shows the list can tell you which is which; the difference is all in the
part the window doesn't show. Walk that warehouse now and there's finally a lamp that's lit in one
and dark in the other.

Now, how literally should you take that table? It's a picture of the chain, and the chain is what's proved.
The small machine's own checks are three questions about one counter: is it zero, is it even, is it
at least some number. What its proofs need from the questions is a checker proved to say yes
exactly
when the answer is yes, and an exact test for telling two questions apart. That's enough for ``sorted'': a version of the machine that takes
any questions with checkers like that proves the same chain once for all of them, and with a list
packed into one counter it certifies a sorted list for a cost of three and refuses an unsorted one
forever (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}). Without a proved checker for ``sorted,'' the chain would be honest about a
counter and only by convention about your list, which is Gettier's pocket again, one level down.

And a lamp for whom? The record is bits too. It's a lamp on the machine, for anybody walking that
warehouse. Hand somebody a printout of it across a desk and you're back at the sticker on the
windshield: they have to trust whoever hands it over, or have some way to check the box that says
it ran. That crossing is a different problem with its own tools, signatures, attestation and proofs
a stranger can check, and this book doesn't solve it. Section~\ref{sec:windows} says what those
tools rest on, and the small machine's record, like any record kept in a machine's state, carries
nobody's signature. What the step changes is the question, from ``did it run?'' to ``do I trust
the box that says it ran?'' That's a smaller question, but it isn't no question.

So, back to the list from the start of this chapter: the test sheet, the sticker, the audit, the ledger,
the proof, the confident AI. I'll give the straight answer on which of those this helps. The sticker
is a question of whether a piece of paper is genuine, and nothing here touches it. The ``all tests
passed'' sheet fits only if the test is a checker proved to mean what it says, in the machine's own
language; a set of tests that can miss a bug certifies ``this procedure said yes,'' which is true
and smaller. An audit and a ledger get the test sheet's answer: kept by a program on an ordinary
computer, they're bits the program wrote, and they fit only where the step underneath keeps the
record and refuses to raise it without the check. A proof is one example: checking its steps is a
procedure that can reject them. Whether its statement says what you meant is still yours to read.
The AI that talks as if it's sure of itself isn't addressed at all. Section~\ref{sec:scope}, under
``Outward consequences,'' says how little of the outside world I've reached.

Now comes the honest half. Take away the small machine's rules and keep only the bare toll, and the copier
has an easier move: pay one unit, flip the record to yes, and that's the whole move. The toll is satisfied
and the receipt is real, but it's a receipt for nothing. The bare toll prices the closing of the door, and the check
behind it goes unpriced.

\subsection{What putting it in the step buys}

The hardest objection is one I'd rather make myself. You defined a flag and a charge,
then proved the charge gets paid when the flag goes up. That's your definitions agreeing with each
other.

On the bare model, that's fair, and the copier's receipt for nothing is the proof. What makes the
record mean \emph{established} is the small machine's step, which won't let a commit through unless a
check of that very claim passed, meeting the first three of the four conditions from Gettier's
pocket, with the fourth, an honest checker, proved about the checker separately. And what it proves
isn't about one program: on \emph{every} list of instructions anybody can write, starting
clean, if the record is up, then somewhere earlier a check of some claim, about some edition,
passed; then a commit of that same claim; then the certificate; with nothing touching the
thing between the check and the commit.

So a raised flag, from a clean start, tells you some claim went through a passing check, a
commitment to it about the same edition, and a certificate. That piece of history is what the
flag keeps, and only that. The channel names the latest commitment that got through, which
needn't be the one the flag first went up on, and in general you can't read off the end state
which claim was certified at that first rise, or when. And the flag doesn't say the claim still
holds, at the certificate or at the end, because the counter can change after the commitment.

That ``every'' is what the operation-by-operation proof buys. A log written
by one program inherits that program's correctness conditions. A database
or reference monitor can instead enforce rules over every operation its
interface permits. The small machine does that too: its invariant covers
every string of its instructions from a clean start, including hostile
strings. The coverage comes from those restrictions and their proof; it
does not follow just from calling the record part of the step. And the tie
between a check and the thing it checked gets a job: the step reads it, and refuses a commitment
when it no longer fits, so the structure is doing something in the machine instead of sitting in a note
beside it.

There are two limits on that ``every,'' and I'll say them now so you don't have to find them later. First, it's every program,
not every everything. The guarantee covers any list of instructions, run from a clean start, one step at
a time, on a step that does what its definition says. Hostile programs are inside it. A hostile start
(a table of facts nobody checked, a reset), hostile hardware (a soldering iron on the flag's bit,
a second writer the step can't see) or a hostile reader isn't; Section~\ref{sec:scope} lists the
whole fence. The guarantee has the same shape as a database or reference monitor's:
it covers operations mediated by a faithful enforcing layer. How large that
class is depends on each interface; being a database does not make it a
one-program guarantee.

Second, the flag and the ledger on their own are what people who verify programs call ghost state:
erase them and every program computes exactly what it did before (Section~\ref{sec:counter} has
where that idea comes from). What isn't ghost on the small machine is
the table of checked facts, which the step reads and refuses on, at run time, for every program. And
the move of putting a rule under every program isn't mine either. It's the reference monitor's,
and its history is a few sections back.

\subsection{The record, the checker and the host}

Take the flag and ledger off the small machine's drawing. The core follows the same steps:
neither field tells it what to do next. Put them back and you can read whether certification
occurred and what the instruction schedule charged. That is the passive record's job. The
latch argument in Section~\ref{sec:latch} gives its form over any fixed base when the record
is driven by that base and never comes down.

The checker has another job. CHECK of ``$A\ge m$'' tests the counter in one instruction;
a program using only the two counter moves would have to work through their operations.
A step comparison therefore starts with the instructions each machine is given. Every
checker built in this book is a program. The abstract certified interface also admits a
supplied checker, so its computational power includes whatever that checker can do: supply
a halting oracle and CHECK can answer halting questions. The effective implementations here
use effective checks.

Now put a guest program inside the host. A guest that can write any value into its own
``checked'' variable can write YES without checking. The host I build gives the guest three
entry points instead: CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY. Its step rule controls those entry points
for every allowed guest program. The fact table and channel determine whether the next act
is permitted; the flag and ledger record the result. An ordinary universal machine can
implement these rules. The work is in preserving them through every guest instruction.

The universal program in Appendix~\ref{sec:universal-host} does that work with the small
machine's six instruction kinds on a host with more counters. It fetches a guest instruction,
decodes it, and carries it out. At matching points the guest and host ledgers agree. The
host halts exactly when the guest halts, keeps the guest's answer in its counters, and raises
its own flag exactly when the guest raises its flag, through its own earned chain. Its guests
are the small machine's programs from clean starts, with Minsky's encoding supplying their
universal computation. Appendix~\ref{sec:simpler-host} gives a simpler picture with a guest-step
operation supplied directly; the instruction-by-instruction construction shows how to build it.

Add a one-unit PAY instruction and the host can also follow a computably presented Thiele
machine: its selected moves, transitions, prices and total yes-or-no reading are all given
by programs. Appendix~\ref{sec:presented-universal} constructs that interpreter. Starting
with the guest's reading at no, the host follows its ledger with at most two extra units at
the raise. Starting with the guest already at yes, the clean host must establish its own
flag immediately and spends three. The same clean-start three-act count explains the
surcharge when the guest certifies with a whole ledger below three.

\subsection{Two layers, and the names}
\label{sec:layers}

\emph{The layers, once.} The core definition (Definition~\ref{def:certsys}) is a Thiele
machine: states, moves, a step, a cost for each move, a yes-or-no reading, and the toll. Everything
else is added on top, and each theorem names what it adds. First come extra structures and
requirements: a ledger that sums the costs, a window, permanence of the reading, a price on
merges. Then an earned implementation, the small machine of the next chapter, with a checker proved sound
and a provenance theorem. Then two interfaces any machine can be read through: Thiele-complete,
about computing and a record that tells starts apart, and certified Thiele-complete, which adds the
earned chain.
Then a universal interpreter for a stated class of guests. The bare definition doesn't ask the step
to be computable, so when I say the record adds no computing power, I mean relative to a fixed
base.

\emph{Substrate versus scaffolding.} Two layers run through the book, and confusing them makes
the theorems quietly stop meaning what they say. The \emph{substrate} is the shape: a kind of
state and a rule for stepping. Different theorems ask that shape for different extra pieces,
and the pieces aren't the same. The universal floor (the ``pays something'' result of Section~\ref{sec:toll})
asks for a yes-or-no reading and the toll on it. The counter's uniqueness (only one
count fits a chosen start and price list) asks for a starting value and a schedule of
increments; Section~\ref{sec:counter} gives the argument, a short induction that works for any system with
those two pieces, and on the small machine of the next chapter the ledger is the sum of the charges by
theorem (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}). The diagonal asks for a recursion theorem for the transformations the substrate can express, and needs no toll and no encoding at all. ``Substrate-level''
doesn't mean one fixed set of parts that every theorem shares. A theorem only gets to use the parts
it asks for. Ask it what it needs and it'll tell you, and whatever else is lying around the
workshop isn't the theorem's. So each result is stated over exactly the extension it uses. The substrate with the extension a theorem names is what I
mean by \emph{the model}, and the name Thiele Machine belongs to the model. The \emph{scaffolding} is
everything that holds the shape up so you can touch it, and when I say \emph{my machine}, \emph{the
small machine}, \emph{the machine I build} or \emph{the build}, this is what I mean: the machine
of the next chapter, with its two counters and their versions, its table of checked facts, its channel,
trap, ledger and flag, its six instruction kinds and their prices, the host with a register for every
whole number, and the universal programs that run on that host (Appendix~\ref{sec:universal-host}). The build fills in several extensions at once and borrows, for any one theorem, only
the extension that theorem names. Let that line blur and a theorem stated over one extension
starts reading as if it carried premises it never uses. ``Substrate'' never means the build,
and it never means the side of a simulation doing the stepping; for that I say ``the machine
doing the stepping,'' as against ``the program it runs.''

So the book keeps the two apart: Parts~I and~II were about any system with the
pieces each result names, and their pictures were small worked instances you could hold (two boxes on a sheet of
paper, chairs in a room, a row of dots). The example machine wasn't one of them; where they said something
about it, they pointed ahead, and the next chapter builds it. Every Part~II claim that has a machine instance gets that instance there
(Section~\ref{sec:part3-on-machine}) or in Appendix~\ref{sec:universal-host}, with
its own theorem, and Part~II said so in one sentence at most. When the origin story
(the afterword, Section~\ref{sec:origin}) says the shape ``was the substrate the entire time,'' it means this layer, the model's shape.
It doesn't mean any piece of the build. The same goes for two more of its words. When it says ``the
machine'' about the thing it named the Thiele Machine, or calls that thing a meta machine, it
means the model; ``my machine'' is the build of the next chapter.
And when it lists what the model asks for (a state, a step, a record, a ledger, a window), read the
ledger and the window as two of the extra pieces: a result asks for them only if it uses
them.

The build is one piece of scaffolding, and I'd rather you know up front that it is one instance, chosen to be small enough to inspect.
Section~\ref{sec:smallest} builds the smallest honest machine I could: two counters, six
instructions, a table of checked facts, a ledger and a flag. Earned commitments are proved there
(a flag raised from a clean start was
checked, then committed, then certified, on the same
edition, with nothing touching
that thing between the check and the commit), and so is universality, through Minsky's two-counter machines and his halting result, through the counter constructions of Forster, Larchey-Wendling and their coauthors, set out in Appendix~\ref{sec:counter-constructions}. Then one fixed program, on a host made of the same
kinds of instruction with more counters, runs every program of it, and with one paid move added,
every computably presented Thiele machine (Appendix~\ref{sec:universal-host}). None of that is the model. It shows the model fits in
six instruction kinds.

The names again, with every part of the certified one pinned down, because I'll hold to them for
the rest of the book. A Thiele machine is any particular system that fits the model's core
definition, its five parts and its toll (Definition~\ref{def:certsys}); the toys on paper in
Part~I count, and so does the small machine, with its toll proved. \emph{Thiele-complete}
(Definition~\ref{def:thiele-complete}) says nothing about what the record is about.
\emph{Certified Thiele-complete} asks for four things of its own
(Definition~\ref{def:u34-thiele-complete}), and it is exactly Thiele-complete with clean loads, the
earned record and a claim that can fail added (Theorem~\ref{thm:tc-decomposition}). The first of the four is a
universal base whose moves can't touch the record, and a record that stays up once it's up. The second is a record that, from a clean start, rises
only after a
passing check of a claim, then a commitment to that same claim with nothing it's about changed in
between, then a certificate, with the checker proved to mean what it says. Over a language fixed first, the claims and what they mean are that language's, and the proof is that the checker's yes makes the claim true in its sense; every instance in this book is stated that way (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-tc-over}). The third is exact prices: one
unit for each of those three acts and nothing for anything else. And the fourth is a claim whose check, commit and certificate
raise the record from a loaded start exactly when the claim holds there, with the claim holding
at some loaded starts and failing at others. Every clock-style machine fails the definition, because it charges for computing, whatever its
record, and every machine that meets the definition hides its record and its ledger from its own window, both by theorem.
That's about an observer who sees only where a run ended; one who also has the program and the
start can work both out.
None of the four clauses is there for decoration: for each one there's a machine that meets the other three and fails it, each of them a
Thiele machine with a two-counter machine inside that no interface makes certified Thiele-complete (Theorem~\ref{thm:tc-independent}). The small machine
meets it, and so does the same machine over any properties with an exact test for telling two of
them apart and a checker proved to say yes exactly when the property holds, as long as one of them can come out both ways, sorted lists included. A
\emph{universal} Thiele machine is one fixed machine running one fixed program that runs any
machine of a stated class as a guest, with every step of the guest's computing done by the host's
own counter moves and every rise of its record put where its program put it; a certified one also
earns each guest's record again by its own check, commit and certificate. Nothing is left to the
guest's good manners. Appendix~\ref{sec:universal-host}
builds one, $U$: a fixed program in the small machine's own six kinds of instruction, on a host
with more counters, with no step of any guest built in. Its guests are the small machine's
programs, so every computation runs on it under Minsky's $2^n$ encoding, done outside the
machine, and it matches each guest's halting, answer, flag and
ledger exactly, raising its own flag by its own check, commit and certificate. Then $U_P$, the
same program with one more handler for a paid move that does nothing else, takes as its guests
every computably presented Thiele machine, one whose next move (picked by a driver), step,
prices and reading are computed by programs, with the reading decided on every state. It matches the guest's halting, raises its
own flag on its own earned chain exactly when the guest's reading has said yes, and keeps the
guest's prices to within a surcharge of at most two when the guest's reading
starts at no, which no program on that host, run from a clean start, can avoid in general.
And a computer that runs the small machine, your laptop say, isn't the small machine. Read through the emulator's prices and flag it's a Thiele machine, a finite one, like the toys of Part~I, but it isn't Thiele-complete, because its counters stop somewhere and a universal base needs every configuration. It implements the small machine, inside bounds, the way a laptop implements a Turing machine.
Push on that comparison, because it's loose, and the looseness is the
point. Does a laptop implement a Turing machine? Not exactly. Turing's tape never runs out,
and a laptop's memory does; strictly, a laptop is a very large machine with finitely many
states, and it behaves like a Turing machine only on computations that fit. Nobody minds,
because the bound is known and most computations people care about fit inside it. That's the
same deal any device running the small machine gets: its counters stop somewhere, and the
theorems speak only for runs that fit. The bounds aren't fine print. They're the whole
difference between implementing a model and being one.

How much can a difference in width matter? There's a famous answer, and it's worth the
detour. On 4 June 1996 the first Ariane 5 rocket lifted off and broke apart about forty
seconds after its engines lit. The inquiry board, chaired by the mathematician Jacques-Louis
Lions, traced it to one conversion in the inertial reference software: a sixty-four-bit
floating-point number, an alignment value called BH that's tied to horizontal speed, squeezed
into a sixteen-bit signed integer. On Ariane 4, where the software came from, that value
could never get big enough to overflow, because of how that rocket flew in its first forty
seconds. Ariane 5 flew differently. The value got too big, the backup unit failed on it, the
main unit failed the same way one cycle of its software later, seventy-two thousandths of a second, and the function doing the
converting didn't even serve a purpose once the rocket had lifted off; it was kept for
commonality with the old rocket. The board's report says the assumption that made the conversion
safe had been agreed on and then, not on purpose, kept out of sight of any outside review. A width premise that holds on one machine is a fact
about how that machine gets used. The code doesn't carry it, and yet it travels with the code without
anybody noticing. The only defence I know is the dull one: write the premise into every
statement that needs it, where the next person will trip over it.

%===========================================================================

\section{The earned-chain counter example}
\label{sec:smallest}
%===========================================================================

The chapters before this one never built a machine you could program. They said ``any states, any steps,'' and whenever a
picture was needed, a board or some chairs or a cup stood in. Now I have to build a
machine, and the first question is about the one I built before it. I built a big
one first, on the way here (the Afterword, Section~\ref{sec:origin}, tells that story), with dozens of instructions,
some picked for reasons and some picked because I had to pick something, and theorems held of it.
What does that show? That the model works, or that I'm good at stacking instructions until the
proofs go through? A big machine is a wonderful place to hide a mistake. It's a garage so full
of stuff that you could lose a car in it.

So the example machine in this book is a small one. I want the state and every way of
changing it where you can inspect them. There are six instruction kinds, and you can follow how
a check stays tied to an object, how a change makes it stale, and how the next move
uses that relation. Each kind takes operands, a counter or a property or a line to
jump to, so there are unboundedly many instructions. It's one way of building the
model, not the only one, and the theorems will say which facts hang on these particular choices.
I built it by throwing things out until nothing more would go. I haven't got a
proof that nothing smaller works, and I'm not claiming one.

\subsection{What the model asks for, and the example that meets it}

The model asks only for states, moves, a step, a price on each move and a yes-or-no reading, with the toll. Before any of its parts, I'll give the example that meets it in three sentences. It's an ordinary computer, two
counters and a jump, with a record layer on top. The flag in the record layer is the blank cell,
and raising it is the write of a 0, a merge in the record layer (flag down and flag up land on the
same state), which is why the step that raises it is charged once merges in that layer are priced
(Theorem~\ref{thm:record-merge-toll}, in Part~I). And the order rule, check, then commit, then
certify, is what makes a raised flag mean something.

Parts I and II define the model by five parts and one rule. The example meets them with the smallest \emph{record} there is, a flag that reads
no or yes and, once yes, stays, which on a machine is the blank cell's 0. Here yes means ``certified,''
because that's the event I picked (Section~\ref{sec:pointer}, later in this part, asks whether anything outside the rules picks it out). It adds a \emph{toll}: the step that raises the flag costs something
(Section~\ref{sec:toll}). And it adds a \emph{ledger}, the running total of those costs, a whole number that only climbs (Section~\ref{sec:counter}).
And Section~\ref{sec:latch} proved the thing this whole chapter stands on: over any base at
all, a base-driven record is a \emph{latch}, a bit that switches on at an event the base decides and
never switches off (Observation~\ref{thm:u11-latch}). The record watches the base. It doesn't
compute anything the base couldn't compute without it.

Push on that for a second, because it cuts the job in half. If the record adds no computing
power, then all the computing power comes from the base, and the question ``how small can
the machine be'' splits into two questions that don't touch each other. For the base: what's
the smallest thing that can compute everything there is to compute? For the record: what's
the smallest set of pieces that makes the flag \emph{mean} something?

There's one honest asterisk on ``don't touch,'' because the machine below makes it matter. What's
blind is the flag and the ledger: the base never reads either of them. But the pieces that
make the flag mean something (a table of checked facts, a slot for a commitment, a trap that
stops a refused run) have to sit where the step can read them, which is in the base, and they
do steer the run: a failed check stops a program dead. The latch theorem holds wherever you
draw the line between base and record, which is exactly why it can't tell you where the
meaning lives. On this machine the meaning lives on the base side of that line, in the bookkeeping, and the flag on top reports it. That line has to sit at the core: the step reads the table, the channel and the trap, so a map that hid any of them wouldn't move in step. The record-layer merge of Part~I draws a lower line, with only the line number and the two counters below it, and what the premise charges moves with that line. Drawn there, all three record acts merge in the record's part and the premise charges each of them; drawn at the core, it charges only CERTIFY.

The record question, the second of those two, is the one Part~II left to the machine, on purpose. Section~\ref{sec:insight} said that
testing a claim and committing to it are two different acts, and that nothing in the five
parts of the model makes the second wait for the first. Read Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s definition again with that
in mind: a machine where you pay one unit and raise the flag over nothing in particular
obeys every rule in it. That machine is honest about the price and silent about what was
bought: it's a receipt for nothing. The toll alone can't fix that, because the toll is a rule
about \emph{cost}, and ``was this earned'' is a question about \emph{order}: did a check happen, of
this claim, before the commitment, with nothing changing underneath in between?

This machine is my attempt to make the order part of the machine, in the smallest place I
could find to do it. I'll show you the pieces, then the proofs, then the places it falls
short, which there are, and which I'd rather you hear from me.

\subsubsection*{The blown fuse cannot be hidden from every future move}

Blow the fuse and pull the lever. Nothing moves. Replace the fuse, start from the same
counter values, and that lever can turn the gears. The fuse decides what the next pull
does, whether the camera can see it or not.

That is what a failed CHECK does here. It traps the core, and every free instruction
then leaves the whole state alone. Suppose I hide the failed check from the camera and
still demand that the next picture depend only on the present picture and the free move.
The live and trapped pictures agree. The camera's rule must give them the same next
picture. Since the trapped box stays still, the projected live box has to stay still too.

\begin{theorem}[A globally check-silent native shadow is static]\label{thm:native-static-shadow}
Let $\pi$ be any projection from native full states, with any target type. Suppose every
CHECK preserves $\pi$, and each zero-cost instruction $i$ has an autonomous projected
rule $h_i$, so $\pi(\mathrm{exec}(s,i))=h_i(\pi(s))$ for every state. Then
$h_i(\pi(s))=\pi(s)$ for every $s,i$. If $\pi$ is onto, each $h_i$ is identity everywhere.
The conclusion also holds on the reachable states from a fixed start when those same
laws hold throughout that reachable domain.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Stand at any native state $s$ and read counter $A$. Ask CHECK whether that
counter is at least one greater than the number just read. It is not, so
this check leaves a trapped state $t$. In symbols, the chosen question is
$A\ge A(s)+1$.

By the proposed silence rule, the failed check has not changed the picture:
$\pi(t)=\pi(s)$. Now choose any free instruction $i$. At the trapped state
it changes nothing at all. The camera's rule $h_i$ must therefore leave
that picture alone. But it is also the picture of $s$, and $h_i$ receives
only the picture, not a choice between the two boxes. It must leave $s$'s
picture alone too. Written as one chain,
\[
 h_i(\pi(s))=h_i(\pi(t))=\pi(\mathrm{exec}(t,i))=\pi(t)=\pi(s).
\]

You could begin at any $s$ and choose any free $i$, so every free projected
move is still on the whole image. If every base picture occurs, that is
the whole base. I did choose a different failing question for different
counter values; the premise allows every CHECK at every state, so it
allows each of those choices. Finally, if $s$ was reached from the fixed
start, append this CHECK to that run to reach $t$. Both boxes remain inside
the reachable domain, and the same argument applies there.
\end{proof}

The fuse belongs with the gears that read it. The certificate and ledger can sit beside
them unread. The later slice follows the computing moves while the machine is live;
a failed check takes it out of that working domain. That is where the line goes on
this machine.
\footnote{A view that exposes refusal, or a machine with a different failure rule,
would supply a different interface. The obstruction concerns the native failure
semantics and a globally CHECK-silent autonomous projection.}

\subsection{Where the counters come from}
\label{sec:counters-origin}

The base first, and the base isn't mine. It's Marvin Minsky's. In a 1961 paper in the
\emph{Annals of Mathematics}, and then in his 1967 book \emph{Computation: Finite and Infinite
Machines}, Minsky studied a machine so bare it's almost a joke. Picture a few bins of
pebbles and a numbered list of instructions. There are only two kinds of instruction: put
a pebble in bin $c$ and go to the next line; or take a pebble out of bin $c$ if there's one to
take, and go one way if there was and another way if the bin was empty. There's nothing else: no memory but
the bins, no tape, no arithmetic beyond plus one and minus one. When the line you're on has no
instruction, the machine stops.

What Minsky proved is that two bins are enough to compute anything a Turing machine can
compute, as long as you're willing to pack the input in a strange way. The trick is to keep
many numbers inside one number, as the powers of different primes ($2^x 3^y 5^z$ holds
three numbers in one), and to do arithmetic on the exponents by multiplying and dividing
with the second bin as scratch space. Packing numbers that way can turn a modest input
into an enormous pile of pebbles, handled one at a time, so it's no way to build a fast
machine. It's a way to settle a question: with that packing, the two bins can do every
Turing computation. What the bins give me here is a base whose ordinary moves you can see
all of. Each of the earlier results says which properties of a base it needs, and
Appendix~\ref{sec:every-model} carries the earned layer over to other bases once you've named
what they have to supply.

Who cares? Minsky did, because the question then was where the edge of computation sits and
how little machinery reaches it. You should, because it means the base of this chapter's
machine hides nothing: if it can compute everything with plus one, minus one and a jump,
then nothing about the record can be smuggling computing power in through some instruction
I made fancy. For this construction I use Minsky's two-counter halting result and the counter constructions of Forster, Larchey-Wendling and their coauthors. Appendix~\ref{sec:counter-constructions} sets out the reduction; the step-for-step connection to this machine is the part I have to establish.

And the pebbles aren't only my picture. They were somebody's actual machine, the same year.
In one issue of the Canadian Mathematical Bulletin, September 1961, Z.~A. Melzak, a
mathematician at the University of British Columbia, described a
computer made of distinguishable holes and an unlimited supply of pebbles, with one
three-place operation, and a few pages later Joachim Lambek, a mathematician at McGill
University, trimmed it to two moves: put a
pebble in hole $X$; take one out of hole $X$ if there's one to take. He called it an
\emph{infinite abacus}, and early on he writes ``Our method is probably not new,'' which is
a hard sentence to beat. He also tells anybody who distrusts infinity not to worry
about all those holes, since any one computation only ever uses finitely many of them.
Is that two inventions or one? Lambek says his was a modification of Melzak's, so call it one
and a half, with Minsky's as a separate find the same year. And then Lambek went somewhere
you wouldn't guess: in 1986, with Philip Scott, a logician who had come to McGill to work with
him and later taught at the University of Ottawa, he wrote a book whose first part, as the
publisher describes it, shows that typed lambda
calculi and a certain kind of category are essentially the same thing. He went from pebbles to category
theory in one career, twenty-five years end to end. Does any of it change the argument? No. The
machine uses Minsky's version and Minsky's name. But a bare machine that several people
reach for in the same year looks like a shape that was sitting there. It doesn't look much like
anybody's invention.

The title of Minsky's 1961 paper is the clue I can't leave alone. It's about ``Post's problem of
tag.'' Who's Post, and what's tag? Emil Post was a logician, a fresh PhD from Columbia, who in
1921, on a fellowship at Princeton, was playing
with about the simplest rewriting game there is. Take a word of 0s and 1s. Look at its first
letter, chop the first three letters off the front, and stick something on the end:
\texttt{00} if the letter you looked at was 0, \texttt{1101} if it was 1. Repeat, and stop when
fewer than three letters are left. Try it at the table. Start from \texttt{1000}: you get
\texttt{01101}, then \texttt{0100}, then \texttt{000}, then \texttt{00}, and it stops. Start from
\texttt{100}: you get \texttt{1101}, \texttt{11101}, \texttt{011101}, \texttt{10100},
\texttt{001101}, and then \texttt{10100} again, and it goes round forever. Post wanted a rule
that tells you, for every starting word, which of those happens. He worked at it for months and
later called it hopeless, and as far as I can tell it still is: a hundred years on, nobody knows
whether that one little game, with that one rule, can be decided. Stephen Wolfram, the physicist
who built Mathematica, wrote a 2021
article on it that tells the Princeton story, and it's where I'd start. In his 1961 paper Minsky proved
that tag games in general can compute anything, which is why Post's name is on it. It didn't settle Post's
own game. And the chase goes one step further. In 2008 Liesbeth De Mol, a historian and philosopher
of computing who wrote her doctoral work on tag systems, turned
the famous $3n+1$ problem (halve an even number, triple an odd one and add one, and ask whether
you always get down to 1) into a small tag game of the same kind. So is Post's game secretly as
hard as everything, or just stubborn? I can't tell you, and as far as the published work goes,
nobody can yet.

None of that changes the machine below. It changes the picture. The two-counter machine came
out of a hunt for the smallest thing that can't be predicted, and the smallest things are exactly
where the open questions are still sitting.

There's one word clash to settle before it bites. Minsky's machine is usually called a \emph{counter machine},
and its bins are \emph{counters}. Section~\ref{sec:counter} also had a counter: the ledger $\mu$, the number that only
climbs. It's the same word for two completely different things, and I'd love to say I set that up on
purpose. In this chapter, \emph{counter} means one of Minsky's two bins, called $A$ and $B$, and
the climbing total is always \emph{the ledger} $\mu$.

\subsection{The example machine, piece by piece}

I'll go through the whole state a piece at a time, in words first.

\begin{itemize}
\item Two counters, $A$ and $B$. Each holds a whole number, with no upper limit.
\item A \emph{version} for each counter, also a whole number with no limit. It starts at 0 and goes
up by one every time its counter is written. Think of it as the counter's edition number:
a new value is a new edition.
\item A \emph{line number}, which instruction comes next, counting from 1
(more on that choice just below).
\item A \emph{fact table}: a list of facts. A \emph{fact} is three things stuck together: a property, a
counter, and a version. ``$A$ is even, as of edition 3'' is a fact. The table has room for
sixteen. Why sixteen? It's a pick, with no derivation behind it, and what the pick gives up is set out
in the subsection near the end of this chapter on what the machine doesn't do.
\item A \emph{channel}: either empty, or holding one fact. This is where a commitment sits.
\item A \emph{trap}: one bit, down at the start. When it goes up, the machine has refused something,
and it stays up.
\end{itemize}

Counting lines from 1 looks like the least interesting choice in the chapter, and it's one of
the oldest arguments in programming, with a famous referee. Edsger Dijkstra was a Dutch computer
scientist, one of the generation that founded the field, and for over forty years he mailed
numbered notes to a few dozen colleagues. In 1982 he wrote one of them, EWD 831, titled ``Why
numbering should start at
zero.'' His case goes through ranges first. Of the four ways to write ``2 up to 12'' with
less-than signs, he picks the one that takes the bottom in and leaves the top out,
$2 \le i < 13$: two ranges that meet end to end then share one number written once, and the
length is just the top minus the bottom. Start a sequence of $N$ things at zero and it's
$0 \le i < N$, and each thing's number is how many things came before it. He reports that
programmers on the language Mesa, which allowed all four conventions, found the other three a
steady source of clumsiness and mistakes, and he points out that FORTRAN starts at one. Does that
settle it? It settles which convention is tidier, by an argument you can check. It doesn't settle
which convention somebody else's work used, and that's the catch: the two-counter
machine used by Forster, Larchey-Wendling and coauthors numbers its lines from 1, and so does this machine,
because matching it line for line is worth more here than tidiness. Is zero the right place to
start counting? Dijkstra's title says it is, and I can't tell you more than that. What his note
carries is an argument about which way makes fewer mistakes. That part you can check for
yourself, and it's the more useful thing to have.

Everything in that list is the \emph{core}, the part the base moves. Outside the core sit the two
pieces from the model: the ledger $\mu$ and the flag. The machine never reads either of
them to decide what to do next. I'm not asking you to take that on trust: it's how the step is
written, and it shows up as a theorem below.

The properties a fact can name come from a tiny fixed language with three words: \emph{is zero};
\emph{is even}; and \emph{is at least $n$}, for any whole number $n$ you like. Each one comes in two
forms. There's the \emph{checker}, a little program that computes yes or no: compare with 0,
look at the last bit, compare with $n$. And there's the \emph{meaning}, the plain arithmetic
statement the checker is supposed to be checking: the number is 0; the number is two times
something; $n$ is less than or equal to the number. Why both? Because a checker is code, and
code can be wrong in ways that look right, and ``the checker says yes'' is only worth
anything once somebody has proved it says yes exactly when the meaning is true. That proof
is one line per property, and it's the first block below.

Why can a machine check a claim at all? Because a claim with a precise meaning is something you
\emph{evaluate}: plug in the values and turn the crank. George Boole worked out in 1847 that you
can do arithmetic on claims this way, treating ``and'' like multiplication and ``or'' like a kind
of addition. Why multiplication? Try it at the table. Write 1 for true and 0 for false, and
multiply: one times one is one, and anything times zero is zero. That's ``and'' to the letter.
Then comes the stranger thing Boole noticed. Say ``x and x'' and you've said nothing new; it's just x.
In numbers that's $x \times x = x$, and he made it a law of his system, and it's a law ordinary
numbers mostly break. Which numbers equal their own square? Two times two is four, no. A half
times a half is a quarter, no. Zero, yes. One, yes. That's the whole list. So when Boole wrote his
bigger book in 1854, \emph{The Laws of Thought}, he asked you to imagine an algebra whose letters
take the values 0 and 1 and nothing else. Every checker on this machine answers in that algebra.

And the 1847 book has a backstory worth a detour, which I found in the Stanford Encyclopedia of
Philosophy's entry on Boole. Boole was largely self-taught and spent
about fifteen years as a schoolmaster, and what pulled him back to logic, early in 1847, was a
loud public quarrel between Augustus De Morgan and the Scottish philosopher Sir William
Hamilton over who had first thought of a small technical idea in the old logic of
syllogisms. Two well-known men fighting over credit, and a schoolmaster watching from the side
picks up the subject and writes the little book this paragraph is about. Few people remember
what the quarrel was over. Every checker in this chapter runs on what the bystander wrote.

Then push on it, because Boole's ``or'' isn't quite the one a checker uses. His plus only made
sense for things that can't both hold at once, so ``x or y'' with both of them true had no
meaning in his system. William Stanley Jevons, an English economist who also worked on logic, read
``or'' as ``either or both,'' which gives ``x or x is x,'' the same trick as before. He wrote to
Boole in 1863 saying plus ought to work that way, and in 1864 he put it in a book called
\emph{Pure Logic}. Boole wouldn't have it, since it broke the
tie to ordinary algebra his whole system stood on. The ``or'' in every programming language I know
is the inclusive one Jevons argued for. Does that change anything about the checker? No; the crank turns the same way. It
changes the picture: the ``or'' a checker uses is the one the man who invented the algebra
turned down.

Hanging a checked claim on a point in a computation is an old move too. Tony Hoare, in 1969,
built a whole way of reasoning about programs out of it: attach a claim to a \emph{point} in a
program (``whenever execution reaches here, this is true''), and reason forward from claim to
claim. Robert Floyd had done it two years earlier on flowcharts. Their claims were checked on
paper by the person writing the proof. This machine's version is a property of one counter at
one edition, checked by a step while it runs.

And is two years earlier the bottom? Not even close, and the next step down is a paper this
book already leaned on. In June 1949, at a Cambridge conference held for the new EDSAC
computer, Alan Turing gave a talk three pages long, ``Checking a large routine,'' the same note
the counter chapter used for stopping (Section~\ref{sec:counter}). Stopping was the second half
of it. The first half is this move, twenty years before Hoare: the programmer should make
``definite assertions which can be checked individually,'' and the correctness of the whole
should follow from them. His example program computes a factorial using nothing but addition,
and his picture for why you'd bother is one you can do on the back of an envelope. Add up a long
column of four-digit numbers and hand someone only the total, and they have to redo the whole
sum at one sitting, because the carries tie every column to the one before it. Hand them the
total of each column as well, and the job falls apart into small checks they can do one at a
time. Each column total is a claim hung on a point in the middle of the work, so the person checking never
has to hold all of it at once. The paper got its due mostly later: in 1984 two computer scientists, F. L. Morris of Syracuse
University and C. B. Jones of Manchester University, who had worked on it together at Oxford,
republished it, with its misprints corrected, as an early program proof by Alan
Turing. Theirs is the text I read, and the column of numbers is Turing's own example in it. Does any of that change the machine? No. It changes the date on the idea, and it tells
you something I like: the first person to ask how you'd check a program put the claims in the
middle of it. He didn't save them for the end.

The machine has six instruction kinds.

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.242\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.344\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.344\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Instruction} & \textbf{What it does, when the trap is down} & \textbf{Cost} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
INC $c$ & Adds one to counter $c$, adds one to its version, goes to the next line. & 0 \\
DEC $c$ $j$ & If $c$ is above 0: subtracts one, adds one to its version, jumps to line $j$. If $c$ is 0: just goes to the next line. & 0 \\
HALT & Nothing. A program that reaches it stops. & 0 \\
CHECK $p$ $c$ & Runs the checker for $p$ on $c$'s value. If it says yes and the table has fewer than sixteen facts, writes the fact ($p$, $c$, $c$'s current version) into the table and goes to the next line. Otherwise, trap. & 1 \\
COMMIT $p$ $c$ & Looks in the table for exactly the fact ($p$, $c$, $c$'s current version), field by field. If it's there, puts it in the channel and goes to the next line. Otherwise, trap. & 1 \\
CERTIFY & If the channel holds a fact, preserves that channel, goes to the next line, and the flag goes up. Otherwise, trap. & 1 \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

The first two are Minsky's machine, and HALT lets a program say it's done. It says it by doing nothing: HALT leaves the state where it is. If it put the trap up instead, it would land a live state on its trapped twin, a merge in the record's part, and the record-layer merge would charge it. The last
three are the record's, and they read as a chain: you can only certify with a commitment in the
channel, you can only commit to a fact in the table, and the only way into the table is a
check that passed. The chain has three links, and each one costs.

One of what? One unit of $\mu$, the same unit as Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s toll. Why one? Why would ten be worse? Because one is the least each of these three acts can cost once a merge in the record's own part of the state is priced, as the end of this paragraph says, and Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} is where that pricing comes from. The argument for a whole finite machine doesn't reach this one: these counters have no top,
and some of the base moves merge states at a price of zero. What does reach it is the
record-layer merge named at the start of this chapter (Theorem~\ref{thm:record-merge-toll}, in Part~I), which
gives the toll once you've agreed to price a merge in the record's own part of the state. Agreeing to that is my choice. Once I have, one unit on each of the three acts isn't: COMMIT and CERTIFY merge when they pass, and all three merge when they fail, because a failure puts the trap up and changes nothing else, so the failed state lands where the same state with the trap already up lands. What I pick is one rather than more.

The whole numbers have a history of their own. In 1888 the German
mathematician Richard
Dedekind published a little book whose title asks what numbers are and what they're for, and in
1889 the Italian mathematician Giuseppe Peano published a booklet, written in Latin, that set out
the axioms for the whole numbers in the form people still teach: there's a first number,
and every number has a next one, and a few rules about how ``next'' behaves. I had the two of
them down as working independently. I went looking, and the Stanford Encyclopedia's entry on
Dedekind says Peano acknowledged Dedekind's priority, which is why the axioms often go by both
names. (Peano's booklet is also where the
sign $\in$ that you met in Section~\ref{sec:structure} comes from: he wrote it as a Greek epsilon,
for the Latin \emph{est}, ``is.'') Start from zero and take ``the next one'' three times, and you have three.
Once prices are whole numbers, one is the smallest price that isn't nothing.

The zeros matter just as much:
computing costs nothing on this ledger. Plus one, minus one and jumping around cost zero,
with physical costs left to an implementation model.
Only the three acts that make a claim cost, and each of them costs whether it passes or traps. Failing is not a discount.

\textbf{The version rule.} Some numbers show why versions exist. Start with $A = 4$, version 0.
CHECK \emph{is even} $A$ passes, and the table gets the fact (\emph{even}, $A$, 0). Now INC $A$: $A$
becomes 5, and its version becomes 1. Now COMMIT \emph{is even} $A$. The machine looks for
(\emph{even}, $A$, 1), the claim about the current edition. The table only has (\emph{even}, $A$, 0).
There's no match, so the machine traps. The old fact is still sitting in the table, still true about edition 0,
and completely useless for committing to anything about edition 1. A fact is about one
edition of one counter, and an edition never comes back, because versions only go up and
never wrap. The version rule is the whole trick against stale evidence: you can't check a number, change it, and then commit to the check. And the never-wrap part isn't a convenience. INC $A$, then DEC $A$ back to the same line, puts the line and both counters exactly where they were, at no cost, and once record-layer merges are priced neither move may join two states that agree on those. If the record had only finitely many settings over one line and one pair of counters, enough round trips would bring the whole state back to where a CHECK left it, with $A$ touched in between and its COMMIT still passing. Under those free-move, injectivity and continued-use requirements, the
record fibre cannot be finite. This machine supplies fresh editions without
a bound. A bounded implementation can instead stop before wraparound or
change its invalidation and pricing rules; that changes the contract.

What the version rule stops is the time-of-check-to-time-of-use bug from Section~\ref{sec:established}, the file checked and then swapped,
and the database answer to it is Kung and Robinson's: at commit time, check that nothing you read
was written in the meantime, and back out if something was. The version rule is that check, done
by the step, on one counter. It also shows where the guarantee ends. It works because one step does
every write and every write bumps a version. A second writer that changed a counter without
bumping its version, a second processor or a device writing memory on its own, would walk
right around it, and none of the theorems below are about a machine with one of those.

Processor designers put a cousin of this check in silicon. Jensen, Hagensen and Broughton, at
Lawrence Livermore in 1987, described a pair of instructions now called load-linked and
store-conditional: the load reads a word and the processor starts watching it, and the store
goes through only if nothing has written that word since; otherwise it fails and the program
tries again. It's tempting to say CHECK is the load and COMMIT is the conditional store, and
it's wrong in two places. COMMIT doesn't write the counter it checked, and the thing doing the
watching, the fact, sits in a table the step keeps. No single processor holds it. The hardware
version does cover the second writer, because the watching happens on the memory everyone
shares, which is exactly the case the version rule leaves out.

The real kinship is older, and it's somewhere else. Picture the table and the counters shared
by many processors, with CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY each done as one indivisible step. Maurice
Herlihy (1991), a computer scientist who has spent his career on how many processors can share
memory safely, ranked shared objects by how many processors each one can bring to agree on a
single value with nobody ever waiting on anybody. Test-and-set, an instruction that writes a
cell and reports what was there, brings exactly two. A sticky bit, the idea of Serge
Plotkin (1989), a Stanford computer scientist working on distributed algorithms, is a cell the
first writer jams for good, with the first writer's value, and everyone after can read it; it
brings any number. I guessed that the shared object would sit at the top with the sticky bit,
