so ends at least 200, still nonnegative. So every store leaves the appropriate line true. Carry the two-line test
through the list of stores: if the final value is nonzero, the net charge is
at least 20000. A cold access adds another 2100, once, on the first store.
Keep that extra charge in a separate column; later updates are exactly the
ones just checked and do not depend on the accumulated total. A nonempty
run from a cold slot therefore pays that 2100 on top of the bound, giving
at least $20000 + 2100$ when it ends nonzero. (2) Direct
computation: $2100 + 20000 = 22100$ for the first store, $100$ for the second, refund
$19900$, and $22200 - 19900 = 2300$.
\end{proof}

The fragment covers one slot in one transaction, with the gas and refund arithmetic copied out of the
Ethereum execution specification's storage instruction and gas table, at a named commit. It has no stack, no call context, no other
slots, and \emph{no refund cap}, the one-fifth rule applied at the end of a transaction.

Then comes the wrapper, which is a different kind of object, and the walk near the end is about
exactly that difference. It's a \emph{gas schedule} in the abstract: any states, any steps, a cost
per step, a yes/no commitment flag, and a charge predicate saying which steps get charged. It
formalises no EVM (the Ethereum virtual machine) at all. It is Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s result
with the whole-run ceiling, the one that pins the amount as well as which steps pay, under a new
name. Its two halves are worth reading separately. Leave one
committing step uncharged, and a one-step run commits at no charge, so the floor fails outright; one missed commit
is enough. Charge one step that doesn't commit, and the schedule charges more than the number
of commits on that one-step run, so the ceiling fails. And
the class isn't empty: in any system, the price that charges one exactly on a step that raises
the flag and nothing on any other meets both halves (Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s step price).

The wrapper itself is the cleanest thing in this section and has the least
Ethereum in it.

\begin{definition}[A gas schedule]\label{def:u13-gas-schedule}
A \emph{gas schedule} has states, instructions, a step, a cost $c(s, i) \in \mathbb{N}$ that may
depend on the state, a Boolean commitment flag on states, and a Boolean charge predicate
$\chi(s, i)$, with two premises: a charged step costs at least 1, and an uncharged step costs
0. A step \emph{commits} when it takes the flag from false to true. For a run $t$ from $s$, let
$c(t)$ be its total cost and $n(t)$ its number of committing steps. The schedule has the
\emph{floor} when $c(t) \ge n(t)$ for every run, and \emph{no overcharge} when $c(t) \le n(t)$ for every
run. It has \emph{unit pricing} when $c(s, i) = 1$ if $\chi(s, i)$ and $0$ otherwise.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Gas schedule exactness]\label{thm:u13-gas-exactness}
For every gas schedule: it has the floor and no overcharge if and only if $\chi(s, i)$ holds
exactly when the step from $s$ by $i$ commits, and it has unit pricing. Moreover, (1) if some
committing step from an uncommitted state is uncharged, that one-step run costs 0 and the
schedule fails the floor; (2) if some charged step does not commit, the schedule
overcharges.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The equivalence is Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s characterization with the whole-run ceiling, under another name. From right to left, each step's cost is 1 on a committing step and 0 otherwise, so a
run's cost counts its commitments. From left to right, apply the floor and no overcharge to
one-step runs: a committing step must cost at least 1, so it is charged; a charged step costs
at least 1 and may not exceed its commitment count, so it commits and costs exactly 1. Parts
(1) and (2) are those one-step runs read the other way.
\end{proof}

Gas prices storage growth and computation. It says
nothing about whether what's stored is true.

\subsection{Attestation: hash chains, and a quote about the past}

A trusted platform module keeps platform configuration registers, or PCRs.
An extension hashes the old value together with a new measurement digest.
A quote signs selected PCR values and challenge data supplied by the asker;
the verifier must check the signature, challenge and expected measurements.
That can establish a fresh report of those values. It does not establish
that every relevant fact about the machine was measured.

PCR reset permissions depend on the register, locality and platform rules.
Some reset at startup; some support permitted resets during a boot. Thus
``you can only extend'' describes an interval with those resets excluded.
Intel SGX uses enclave measurements and attestation reports for a related
purpose, but it does not use this PCR-extension interface.

What does the specification price on the registers? Nothing: no fee, no bond, no budget. Within the stated reset and access restrictions, forging a different
measurement history that passes verification relies on defeating the
cryptographic assumptions or trusted components. Authorized resets are a
separate operation, not an attack that requires breaking a hash. Expensive against infeasible is the difference between a price and a wall, and
it's easy to blur, which is why the definition at the start of the section leaves walls out.
What stands behind a cost can come in three currencies. It can be economic, a fee or a deposit
the protocol takes (Casper and gas are here). It can be cryptographic, a reversal made
infeasible by a hardness assumption, which makes it a wall with no exact price on it (attestation and
transparency are here). Or it can be physical, energy spent or hardware worn, which none of these five
specifications charges as a fee or a bond; the nearest thing is the chip's write budget, below. And the record's permanence is only as long as the register lives: a
register's continuity lasts only through the interval allowed by its
reset rules, not necessarily an entire boot.

Why the registers, then, when something that lasts would make a better record? Because the quote is what a remote asker
reads, and the registers are what it signs. The same chip has longer-lived records, and they're
closer to the latch than anything else in this section. Version 2.0 of its specification has
storage slots of a kind it calls a bit field, changed only by a command that ORs new bits into the
old value. During that index's lifetime the command can set a bit and
cannot clear one, the OR rule from Section~\ref{sec:latch}. Deleting and
redefining an index is governed by separate authorization and policy; it
must be included in any claim about persistence across that lifetime. It also has counters advanced by an increment command. On first use,
a new counter starts above the values previously held by counters on that
TPM, so deleting an index and making a new one does not restart the count
at zero. This is a guarantee of the specified chip, not protection against
replacing it with another chip. And those slots are rationed. Bryan Parno and his
coauthors, building a system called Memoir in 2011, noted that the specification of the day only
required a counter to be able to tick once every five seconds, and that the chip's storage was
expected to survive about a hundred thousand writes in its whole life, so writing once a second
would wear it out in under twenty-eight hours. Memoir writes to it twice per boot. Those figures describe the hardware assumptions discussed in Memoir, not
a universal write quota for every TPM. Endurance and throttling constrain
real use, but an expected endurance figure is not itself an enforced
protocol budget. The quoted PCR interface supplies no such numerical price. On the bit field it's the budget of Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-growing}'s chain
of $k$-bit words, which can only climb $k$ times. Phones and small controllers go one floor further down,
to fuses like the PROMs in Section~\ref{sec:latch}: a version number kept as a row of fuses, one
more blown at each security update, and boot code that refuses anything older. An industry guide
on it, Rob Smart's 2021 explainer for PSA Certified, a security certification scheme for chips and
devices, tells designers to make sure there are enough fuse bits to last the number of updates
expected over the device's lifetime, which is part (5) of that same theorem, written as a design
rule.

What all of this is for is \emph{rollback}. Memoir's example is a password checker restored to an
old saved state to undo a user's password change, and in 2017 a system called ROTE did the same
job for Intel's enclaves by having several machines vouch for each other's counters, with the
stated result that the only way left to break it is to reset every one of them to its start.
In 2016 Raoul Strackx and Frank Piessens's Ariadne got that job down to flipping a
single bit of non-volatile memory per state update, which they call the theoretical lower limit.
Notice who the attacker is in every one of these: whoever gets to put an old state back. A bad
program doesn't come into it. A record kept by the step can't see that attacker. Every guarantee the small machine gives about a record's earned history (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}) is stated from a clean start; put back a state the machine really reached and each one still holds of it, through the run that reached it first, and none of them can say that nothing came after it. The per-step toll still holds after a restore; it just can't tell you what happened before it.

Replicated services put the same kind of record somewhere else: inside each replica, where a
replica that's been taken over still can't make it say two different things. Byung-Gon Chun and
coauthors' attested append-only memory (A2M, 2007) is a log a replica can only add to; Dave Levin
and coauthors' TrInc (2009) shrinks that to a trusted counter; MinBFT (Giuliana Veronese and
coauthors, 2013) uses a trusted counter to reach agreement with $2f+1$ replicas when $f$ of
them can lie, where the usual count is $3f+1$; and Damysus (Jérémie Decouchant, David Kozhaya, Vincent
Rahli and Jiangshan Yu, 2022) has a small trusted service, the Checker, that keeps a monotonic
counter of where the protocol is. Allen Clement, Flavio Junqueira, Aniket Kate and Rodrigo
Rodrigues (2012) worked out, with proofs, what such a record buys, and as I read their result it's
a good warning for this book.
On its own, stopping a replica from saying two different things doesn't lower the $3f+1$ bound
in an asynchronous network at all. Add signatures that a third party can check, and it turns any
protocol that survives crashes into one that survives liars, with no extra replicas. The way I
read it, a record helps the others only as far as they can check what it says, which is
Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s point from the other side.

There's a fourth currency under those three, the logical
kind, and it's the one every permanent record on a finite chip pays in: Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s counting of used and fresh states applies to any of these records. With only finitely many states holding the record on, a step that switches it on somewhere, and never switches it off anywhere, forgets something.
Forgetting alone doesn't single out a record write: any step that overwrites a field able to hold
two values forgets something too. What singles it out is where the forgetting lands. Take the
states the record already reads yes on, together with the one the step switches on. The step
sends every one of them to a yes state, and it can't keep them apart, so what it destroys is a
distinction on the record's own yes side: two states it already vouched for, or the state it just
raised and one that was up already. Any overwrite merges states somewhere; a permanent write is
forced to merge them on that side.
That needs no premise about money, keys or heat. The economic, cryptographic and physical
payments each need a premise of their own about their kind (a fee rule, a hardness
assumption, Landauer's principle), and they hold exactly where that premise holds.

\begin{theorem}[A permanent write forgets on its own yes side]\label{thm:u13-logical-payment}
For any states $S$, instructions $I$, step and Boolean reading: suppose a duplicate-free list names
every state, the instruction $i$ never turns the reading from on to off, and $i$ turns it on
at some state $s$. Then the step by $i$ is not injective. More: the step by $i$ sends every state
that reads on, and $s$, to a state that reads on, and it is not injective even on those states.
\end{theorem}

Count the on-states and call their number $K$. The list of all states is
finite, so this count is finite too. The instruction keeps each of those
$K$ sources on, and it also sends the additional off-state $s$ to on.
That gives $K+1$ distinct sources with only $K$ on-states available as
landing places. Two sources must land together. Both came from the stated
collection, so the failure to keep sources apart already occurs there.
Permanence of any other instruction was never needed.\proofclosed

What the quote can do is say what was \emph{measured}.
It can't say the measured code is correct, and it can't say anything about runtime state
that was never folded in. A correctly measured buggy program attests beautifully. The
fragment proves that exact limit: one register, a hash about which nothing is assumed, a quote as a pair, and no
function of the quote decides a runtime flag the quote ignores, which is Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s cube again. And a second small result shows
that a sign-and-verify interface \emph{alone} gives no authenticity (a scheme where verify always
says yes passes the interface), so a cryptographic premise has to be added; the fragment
doesn't model signatures, formats, or a freshness check (the nonce is just a field the
verifier fixes).

The same limit, turned outward, is the honest edge of the four conditions of Section~\ref{sec:established}.
Every one of them is about a thing the machine holds: same property, same thing, same edition,
honest check. For a claim about the world (the oven is hot, the parcel arrived) there's no edition
the machine controls. Whatever reads the world is a window onto it, and ``nothing changed between
the check and the commit'' stops being something a step can enforce and becomes a premise about
the sensor. So a record can establish claims about the machine's own state, and claims about the
world only through named premises about whatever measured them. A correctly recorded sensor
reading establishes what the sensor reported. Whether the oven was hot
still depends on the sensor and the connection between its report and the world.

\begin{definition}[Platform and quote]\label{def:u13-quote}
Fix any functions $H: \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ (the extend hash) and
$\delta: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ (the digest); nothing is assumed about either. A
\emph{platform} is a measurement log (a list of numbers) and a Boolean runtime flag. Its register
is the log folded from 0 by $H$. The \emph{quote} with nonce $n$ is the pair
$(\delta(\text{register}), n)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The quote cannot attest unmeasured state]\label{thm:u13-quote}
For every nonce $n$ there is no function $D$ from quotes to Booleans with
$D(\mathrm{quote}_n(P)) = \mathrm{flag}(P)$ for every platform $P$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take two platforms with the empty log, one flagged true and one false. Their quotes are
equal, since the quote never reads the flag, so $D$ would have to return both values on one
input.
\end{proof}

Anything that depends only on $\delta(\text{register})$, the quote can answer; that's what it's
for. And the second result is the one I mentioned: a ``signature'' scheme whose check always says yes
fits the sign-and-verify interface perfectly and accepts a signature no key ever made, so the
interface on its own promises nothing.

\subsection{Certificate transparency: visible, unpriced}

The certificates that make your browser show a padlock are issued by hundreds of
authorities, and a bad or compromised one can issue a certificate for a domain it shouldn't.
Certificate Transparency puts certificates in public append-only logs built
as Merkle trees. An inclusion check ties a certificate to a particular root;
a consistency check ties a later root to one the reader already has. It was specified in RFC 6962 in 2013 and revised as
RFC 9162 in 2021. I went looking for which one the running logs follow, and it's still 6962:
Mozilla's reference for web developers says browser implementations are based on 6962, and as late
as November 2025 Chrome's team was only proposing to drop its rule that every certificate carry a
timestamp from at least one 6962 log. The fragment I
transcribe is 9162's. A Merkle tree is Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s hash chain folded into
a tree: hash each certificate (those are the \emph{leaves}), hash the leaf hashes in pairs, hash
those in pairs, and so on up to one \emph{root} hash. To prove one leaf is in, the log hands you
only the few hashes sitting beside the climb from that leaf to the root, the \emph{path}, and you
redo the climb yourself. A second check, \emph{consistency}, shows that a bigger tree is a smaller
one with leaves added on the end and nothing rewritten. The record is a leaf in the tree.

The data structure has a history of its own in security. The computer scientists Scott Crosby and
Dan Wallach, at Rice University, built tamper-evident logs on the same kind of tree in 2009, with
a proof that an entry is in the log and a proof that a later version of the log extends an earlier
one, each a logarithmic number of hashes. A rewrite that fails to extend a
previously witnessed root is caught by the consistency check.

The RFC prices nothing, and it says in its first section that logs let interested parties \emph{detect} misissuance
afterward. They don't \emph{prevent} it. And a log that shows different views to
different people (a \emph{split view}) can defeat the auditing, so logs are still trusted parties.
What it buys is visibility.

Which raises the obvious question: if the specification prices nothing, why does any authority bother logging?
Nothing in the RFC makes it. The answer is a browser. Chrome's team set the rule, enforced from
Chrome 68 in July 2018, that every certificate issued after 30 April 2018 had to meet its
transparency policy, and a
publicly trusted certificate that doesn't is simply not trusted by Chrome: the visitor gets a full-page warning in front of the site. So there is a price after
all, though it isn't anywhere in the specification: it lives in one vendor's browser, and it's the price of being shown to that
browser's users at all. Is that the bottom? Not quite, because it means the strongest lever on
this record is a policy one company can change, which is a fact about who holds the stamp. The
tree has nothing to do with it. That policy changes nothing in the table at the end of this section, which asks what
each specification prices. But it's worth keeping two sentences apart: ``the specification
prices nothing'' and ``nothing is priced.''

Do the inclusion proof by hand. Lay out seven cards $d_0$ through $d_6$,
each standing for one leaf hash.
Join neighbours with paper brackets: $a=\nu(d_0,d_1)$,
$b=\nu(d_2,d_3)$ and $c=\nu(d_4,d_5)$. The last card stands alone.
Next join $a$ to $b$, giving $L=\nu(a,b)$, and $c$ to $d_6$, giving
$R=\nu(c,d_6)$. The root is $\nu(L,R)$. Here $\nu$ means ``put these two
expressions, in this order, inside one labelled bracket.'' Equal symbolic hashes
must have exactly the same bracket structure.

To check $d_3$, keep only that card and the three siblings $d_2,a,R$.
Combine $d_2$ on its left to recover $b$, then $a$ on the left to recover $L$,
then $R$ on the right to recover the root. You never needed to open the cards
inside $a$ or $R$. Those three siblings are the inclusion path.

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}cll@{}}
Step & What is supplied & What is rebuilt \\ \hline
Start & card $d_3$ & starting leaf hash $d_3$ \\
1 & $d_2$ on the left & $b=\nu(d_2,d_3)$ \\
2 & $a$ on the left & $L=\nu(a,b)$ \\
3 & $R$ on the right & root $=\nu(L,R)$ \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Swapping left and right changes the bracket. The path has to carry the
correct order as well as the correct siblings. The hashes here are brackets, not numbers,
so what you just checked is how the tree is put together; a real log uses short hashes, and
``two different trees can't give the same root'' is then a separate promise from the
cryptography. Nothing in this fragment signs anything, no auditors talk to each other, and no
log misbehaves.

\begin{definition}[Inclusion check, RFC 9162 section 2.1.3.2]\label{def:u13-inclusion}
Given a leaf index $m$, a tree size $N$, a leaf hash, a root hash and a path, the check
rejects unless $m < N$. Otherwise start counters $f=m$, $s=N-1$ and an accumulated hash $r$ equal to
the leaf hash. For each path element $p$, reject if $s=0$. If $f$ is odd or
$f=s$, replace $r$ by $\nu(p,r)$; in this branch, while $f$ is positive and
even, halve both counters with rounding down. In the other branch replace
$r$ by $\nu(r,p)$. After either branch halve both counters once more. At the
end accept exactly when $s=0$ and $r$ is the claimed root. A \emph{symbolic hash}
makes a leaf hash $\ell(x)$ and a node hash $\nu(a,b)$ distinct constructors:
two hashes are equal only when their entire constructions agree.

The consistency check used here takes old and new sizes $M,N$, roots $u,v$ and
a path, and rejects unless $0<M<N$. If $M$ is a power of two, prepend $u$ to
the path. Reject an empty resulting path; otherwise its first element seeds
two accumulated hashes $r_\mathrm{old},r_\mathrm{new}$. Start $f=M-1$, $s=N-1$,
and halve both while $f$ is odd. Process each remaining path element $p$:
reject if $s=0$; when $f$ is odd or $f=s$, put $p$ on the left of both
accumulated hashes and halve both counters while $f$ is positive and even;
otherwise leave $r_\mathrm{old}$ alone and put $p$ on the right of
$r_\mathrm{new}$. After either branch halve both counters once. Accept exactly
when $s=0$, $r_\mathrm{old}=u$ and $r_\mathrm{new}=v$. All halvings round down.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The RFC's own examples pass]\label{thm:u13-ct-examples}
With the symbolic hash, in the RFC's seven-leaf tree with leaves $d_0, \dots, d_6$ (writing
$d_k$ also for its leaf hash $\ell(d_k)$), the inclusion check accepts leaf 3 with path $[d_2, \nu(d_0, d_1), \nu(\nu(d_4, d_5), d_6)]$, and
likewise leaves 0, 4 and 6 with their paths; the consistency check from size 4 to size 7
accepts. For every input with $m = N$, the inclusion check rejects.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Use the brackets $a,b,c,L,R$ built above. For leaf 3, the counters start at
$(3,6)$: put $d_2$ on the left, leaving $(1,3)$; put $a$ on the left, leaving
$(0,1)$; put $R$ on the right, leaving $(0,0)$ and root $\nu(L,R)$.
Leaf 0 has path $[d_1,b,R]$ and three right combinations. Leaf 4 has path
$[d_5,d_6,L]$: right, right, left. Leaf 6 has path $[c,L]$:
left, then left; its first branch shifts $(6,6)$ to $(3,3)$ before the ordinary
halving, which accounts for the unpaired last leaf. Each reconstructs the same root.
For consistency from 4 to 7, the old root is $L$ and the supplied path is $[R]$.
Prepending $L$ seeds both hashes with $L$; shifting the initial $(3,6)$ gives
$(0,1)$, so the sole remaining element leaves the old root alone and makes the
new root $\nu(L,R)$, with final counters $(0,0)$. The boundary case $m=N$
fails the first test $m<N$.
\end{proof}

And the append-only part of the fragment is as plain as it sounds: the history is a list,
and adding to the end of a list leaves every old entry where it was.

\subsection{Proof-carrying code: no price, no permanence}

Necula's idea, from Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}, is to ship untrusted code with a proof that it obeys the host's policy; the
host computes what would need to be true and checks the proof with a small checker. The
record is the checked proof or the result of checking it. An implementation
may retain either. Proof-carrying code does not by itself require a permanent
latch or assign an abstract toll to acceptance. Producing and checking the
proof both take computational work; that work has not been identified with
the unit charge in this book.

The fragment is a three-instruction
memory-bounds language with the policy ``every address is below the limit'': the checker
accepts exactly when the condition holds, and a certificate implies the condition. One example
sits on top of that, a computation you can do in your head: a program that reads address two under a limit of two is rejected.
The fragment isn't the paper's real case study, and nothing connects it to anything else in this book. And it has a limit: a
program that writes garbage to address zero passes if zero
is below the limit. The proof is of the stated policy and nothing else.

And what was the paper's real case study, the one my fragment isn't? It was network packet filters, the
little programs an operating system runs on incoming network traffic to decide which program
gets to see which packet. They run inside the kernel, the most trusted part of the system, and
they have to be fast, so they're exactly the code you'd most like to take from a stranger and
least like to trust. In the 1996 paper that first set out the idea, Necula and Peter Lee wrote
several filters by hand in the assembly language of a DEC Alpha, shipped each with its proof,
and reported a one-time cost of 1 to 3 milliseconds to check the proof, after which the filter
ran with no checks at all. Those milliseconds put a number on ``checking is cheap by design''. What the paper reports changes
nothing about my fragment, which still isn't that case study, and it doesn't add a price: the
milliseconds measure the checker's work in that experiment. They are not
a per-crossing toll theorem, whether or not an implementation saves the result.

\begin{definition}[The bounds fragment]\label{def:u13-pcc}
Instructions are READ $a$, WRITE $a\ v$, and HALT. For a memory limit $L$, the policy allows
READ $a$ and WRITE $a\ v$ when $a < L$, and always allows HALT. The \emph{verification condition}
of a program is that the policy allows every instruction in it. A \emph{certificate} is a list of
per-instruction policy facts, one for each instruction in order. The \emph{checker} tests the
policy on each instruction and returns the conjunction.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The checker is the verification condition]\label{thm:u13-pcc}
For every limit $L$ and program $P$: the checker accepts $P$ exactly when the verification
condition holds; any certificate for $P$ gives the verification condition; and with $L = 2$
the checker rejects READ 2 followed by HALT.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Lay the instructions in a row. For each READ or WRITE, compare its address
with $L$; put yes beneath it exactly when the address is smaller. Put yes
beneath HALT without asking about an address. The checker accepts exactly
when every mark in that row is yes. The verification condition asks for
exactly those same per-instruction facts. An empty row has no failing
instruction, and extending the row preserves acceptance precisely when
the new instruction also passes. This covers programs of every finite length.

A certificate supplies one policy fact at each place in the same row.
Reading them in order gives every fact the verification condition asks
for, so it implies that condition too.

With limit two, the first instruction READ 2 asks whether $2<2$. It does
not. The later HALT is allowed, but cannot undo that failed comparison,
so the checker rejects the two-instruction program.
\end{proof}

\subsection{One example, three levels}

Before I lay all five side by side, let me walk one of them up and down the three levels from
the start of the section, because every claim in here lives at exactly one level and it's
easy to let a claim slide up a floor without noticing. I'll take gas, since it's the one place all
three line up. Think of a restaurant's real recipe, my photocopy of one page of it, and a
cookbook chapter on what any recipe has to contain. I can check my photocopy line by line.
That tells you nothing about what the kitchen cooks tonight.

Start with the real specification. Ethereum's execution specification says, in a document that runs real
money, what a storage write costs, what clearing it refunds, and how the refund is capped at
the end of the transaction. None of what I proved is at this level. What the network
actually charges is whatever the clients people run actually compute, and the evidence for
that is the clients and the chain. This book has none of it.

Next comes the transcription. I copied one mechanism out of that document, one slot in one transaction,
gas and refund arithmetic only, at a named commit
(Definition~\ref{def:u13-slot}, Theorem~\ref{thm:u13-sstore}). What the result tells you: \emph{if} the
storage rule is what I copied, then leaving a fresh slot set costs at least twenty thousand,
and set-then-clear nets twenty-three hundred at the counter. What it can't tell you: anything
about the refund cap (not copied, which is why what a real set-then-clear pays came out so different from the counter
earlier), the stack, calls, other slots, or whether any client implements the rule as written.
The boundary of the claim is the edge of the copy.

Last comes the wrapper. The gas schedule of Definition~\ref{def:u13-gas-schedule} isn't Ethereum. It's any
system with steps, a cost per step and a yes/no commitment flag, plus one thing \emph{stipulated}:
a charge predicate, with the premise that a charged step costs at least one and an uncharged
one costs zero. That premise is the whole of what the wrapper adds, and it's added by
hand; no specification supplies it. Given it, the theorem says every run costs exactly its number of commits, never letting a commit go unbilled, never billing one twice and never billing a non-commit, exactly when the charge predicate is the commit predicate at unit price. What that tells you is what exact pricing would have to
look like, in any system. It doesn't say Ethereum meets it, and Ethereum doesn't: real gas
bills computation that commits nothing, which the transcription shows in numbers. So the
wrapper prices a definition, the transcription prices a copied rule, and neither prices the
chain.

The other four sit on the same three levels, and only one more wrapper is spelled out in this
section. Casper's transcription is the accountable-safety proof above; its wrapper is a small
gadget with the stake at risk handed in. A finalize step that risks nothing turns the record
on at no charge, which breaks Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s toll, and one that risks at
least one unit has a floor. It records exposure to loss (no collateral is destroyed in it), has no Casper
checkpoints in it at all, and is priced by stipulation, the same way the gas wrapper is.
Attestation, transparency and proof-carrying code have transcriptions that prove what their verifiers do and no price theorem, because no specification of theirs puts a price on the verdict. Their
wrappers, which I don't spell out here, are Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s verifier argument told in each system's vocabulary,
with a colliding pair behind each one, and that argument is all they carry here.

The book's rule is that every claim gets a way to break it, so I'll say how to knock down the four claims with the most weight on them.
For the gas transcription: a list of stores from a fresh slot that ends nonzero with net charge under 22100. For the gas wrapper: a schedule in which every run costs exactly its number of commits, whose charge predicate still differs from the commit predicate at some step. For the finality gadget: a finalizing trace from unfinalized to finalized whose
charged stake is zero while the gadget claims a floor. For the attestation fragment: a
verifier reading only the quote's fields that decides a runtime flag the quote ignores.

\subsection{The same table, five ways}

Lay them out by the one definition of price from the start of the section. Casper puts a bond
behind the write and takes it on \emph{reversal} (slashing). Gas takes a fee at \emph{the write} (and refunds the
revocation, capped), and rations writes with a gas limit per block. Attestation prices \emph{nothing} on
the registers the quote signs, and puts a budget on its longer-lived slots and counters.
Transparency prices \emph{nothing}. Attestation and transparency make reversal
infeasible or visible. Proof-carrying code prices nothing and keeps nothing.

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.15\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.16\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.16\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.19\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.21\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{System} & \textbf{Fee at the write} & \textbf{Bond} & \textbf{Budget} & \textbf{What the transcription proves} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
Casper finality & none & the deposit, taken on a contradicting vote (slashing) & none & a finalization fork means a slashable third \\
Gas & 20000 for a fresh slot, mostly refunded on revocation, up to a cap & none & the gas limit of each block & a persistent write to an empty slot nets at least 20000 \\
Attestation & none; reversal is infeasible & none & none on the registers; a write budget on the non-volatile slots and counters & the quote can't decide what it never measured \\
Transparency & none; misissuance is visible & none & none & the RFC's own inclusion examples pass \\
Proof-carrying code & no required persistent latch & none & none & the checker is the verification condition \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

Each row proves what its own transcription says, and no more. To read a row as a claim about
the running system you'd need evidence from that system, and no row shows that certification
is the one event every model has to price.

So the thing the toll charges for, the moment the record is written, is charged a fee in one of the five
specifications I read, and in that one the designers had to patch the place where the charge
could be clawed back. I find that neither a vindication nor a refutation. It's a fact about
what people built, and what they built was mostly walls (hash chains, signatures) and
penalties for contradiction. Tolls on commitment were rare. Whether a toll on commitment is a
\emph{better} design than a wall is not something I can prove, and I won't pretend the five say
so. What I read in them, and it's a reading of five fragments I chose, is that each has a condition treated as a record, though the conditions differ in durability, and that the price axis is
mostly empty. With one definition of price fixed before the survey, that last part is a count:
of fifteen cells in the table, four are filled (one fee, one bond, two budgets), and only gas
takes a payment at the moment of the write.

That leaves the question Section~\ref{sec:latch} raised and Section~\ref{sec:pointer} has to face. The five systems have five different
events chosen as ``the record'': finalized, committed, attested, logged, checked. Is there
anything that picks out one event as \emph{the} one worth recording, or is it an unforced choice every
time? The pointer thesis is my proposed answer, and the next section gives the evidence it asks for.

%===========================================================================

\section{The pointer thesis}
\label{sec:pointer}
%===========================================================================

Everything so far leaves one choice open. A permanent record driven by the machine is a
latch on an event, and the event is yours to pick (Section~\ref{sec:latch}, the two
cups on one die). Five real systems each picked a different one
(Section~\ref{sec:models}), and for the machine in this book I picked certification.
So I owe you an answer to the obvious question: is that just my choice, or is there
something about how people and machines lean on records that picks this event out?

What I have is a thesis, in the sense the Church-Turing thesis is one
(Section~\ref{sec:structure}): a claim tying defined things to the world, which no proof
can settle. Whether it stands or falls is what decides whether the choice of event has a reason behind it.
Nothing before it depends on it; the latch, the windows and the counting arguments hold
whichever event a system records. What follows is the claim, where I got it, and how its terms apply to the systems being described.

\subsection{The claim}

Of all the events a machine could put on its ledger, the ones its price list charges for and
its counter adds up, certification is the one whose records
get \emph{copied and relied on by parties who didn't produce them}: checked, stored, and acted on
across independent places that share no other state. Copying alone can't be the test. A
replicated system copies everything it holds to every node, the gas used in a block header as
faithfully as the word final, so rival events get copied too. Reliance does not
automatically separate them either. In Ethereum, the previous block's gas use
helps determine the next block's base fee: another party reads it and acts on
it. That is an explicit rule in \href{https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1559}{EIP-1559}.

So the examples cannot establish that certification alone is copied and acted
on. The thesis asks whether a separately justified class of reliance selects
it, and whether that selection gives a reason to charge its establishment.
The formal toy below fixes its readers and actions in advance. It can test
those choices, but it cannot choose the real readers for us. Both the claimed
selection and its connection to prices remain to be justified.

There's a second handle on the same question, and it comes from Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}. The permanent-certificate
theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges}) never uses the word certification for anything special: given Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s rule that
forgetting is charged, it prices any yes-or-no reading that, once on, stays on, on a machine
with finite memory. So it points at a narrower
candidate: the events to price are the ones that write a record no later step can take back.
Certification is one of them. As an exact answer that candidate is false, because a merging
step can also revoke (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s three cards). Whether the records that are copied and relied on are the permanent ones, and
whether being copied and relied on picks out anything the merge criterion doesn't, is what the two handles
have to settle between them.

I can see two holes in that from here, so you don't have to find them for me. The first
is a missing premise. Even if the world copies certification records more than any other kind,
``copied'' doesn't give you ``priced'' on its own. Something has to connect them, and the best
candidate I have is a premise about incentives: a record that many independent parties copy and
lean on is exactly the record worth forging, so it's the one where a price buys the most
protection. That's a reasonable premise, but it's still a premise. The thesis's second half states the
connection as a claim to be tested; it doesn't explain it, and nothing in this book supplies the explanation. The second hole is a circle. If ``certification'' just means ``the record other
people rely on,'' then of course it's the one that gets relied on and copied, and the claim says
nothing. So the event has to be picked out without mentioning reliance: here it's a reading going
up for good right after a check of the same claim passed, which you can find in a run without
asking who reads it. Whether the world copies \emph{that} event more than its rivals is then a real
question, and it could come out no.

The thesis says no more than that, and what's left is the rest of what a thesis owes you.

\subsection{Where the shape comes from, and how much of it survived}

The shape is from physics, and I want to tell you where exactly, because I borrowed a word
and I didn't get to keep the whole thing.

Quantum mechanics has a famous problem: a system can be in a blend of states, and when you
measure it you find one definite state, and nobody agrees on what ``measuring'' did. In 1981
Wojciech Zurek asked a sharper question: of all the ways a measuring device \emph{could} end up,
why does it end up recording one particular kind of quantity (the position of a pointer on a
dial, say)? Why never some blend? His answer, developed over twenty years and summarised in a
2009 paper called ``Quantum Darwinism,'' is that the \emph{environment} decides. The air, the light,
the table, everything the device touches, is constantly interacting with it, and only
certain states of the device survive that interaction; those are the \emph{pointer states}. More
than that, the environment selects them, and then it \emph{copies} them. The light bouncing off a
dial carries the dial's reading to every corner of the room, redundantly, so that a thousand
observers can each read a different scrap of the environment and all agree on where the
pointer is, without touching the dial. Objectivity, on this view, \emph{is} redundancy: a
property is objective when many independent fragments of the world each carry it.

Zurek isn't the only one behind it. Fernando Brand\~ao, Marco Piani and
Pawe\l{} Horodecki (2015) prove an approximate statement about most small
fragments of a large output: their channels can be approximated by measuring
the input in one common way and preparing fragment states from that result.
The error and the exceptional fraction are part of the theorem. Agreement on
outcomes also needs the fragments to carry enough information about them.

Xiao-Liang Qi and Daniel Ranard (2021) strengthen the bound on the exceptional
region. Outside a region whose size is controlled by the input size, allowed
error and size of the fragments being examined, locally accessible information
is approximately classical. This does not say that every observer gets an
exact record, or any useful information at all. My definitions below ask for
exact Boolean answers from specified observers. That is a simpler chosen
contract, not the quantum theorem with its qualifications removed.

What I borrowed is that shape. Certification is to a machine's ecosystem (the machine plus everything around it that
reads, stores and relies on its records) what the pointer
reading is to the room: the thing that gets copied everywhere. It's a good shape and I think
it's the right intuition. I'm going to be exact about what survived into the definitions below,
because the word ``redundant'' is doing less than it does for Zurek.

Zurek's redundancy is \emph{graded} (each fragment carries almost all the information, with some
small loss) and it requires the fragments to be \emph{disjoint}: different observers reading
different parts of the environment. The definition below is the zero-loss case with \emph{no
disjointness at all}. An ecosystem is a state type, some number of observers, and one bit
per observer; an observer \emph{records} an event when its bit is true exactly when the event
holds; an event \emph{proliferates} when every observer records it. Nothing in that says two
observers draw on separate parts of the state. They could all be reading the same bit, and the definition permits it. So I kept the word and dropped the independence that makes Zurek's version
mean ``objective.'' That leaves a gap between the thesis's prose and that first formal object, and the
prose is where the thesis lives. The definitions under the thesis below close part of the gap:
they define independent carriers, and the definition turns out to force something
(Theorem~\ref{thm:u14-independent-constant}).

The independence I dropped is exactly what the thesis's closest published neighbour keeps.
Jess Riedel, Zurek and Michael Zwolak (2016) took histories of a closed quantum system, the
story a whole sequence of events tells, and asked which of them the world keeps records of in
many separate pieces of the environment. As I read their paper, redundant records in separate pieces make a history
consistent, so ordinary yes-or-no reasoning about it works, and they pick out a small set of
histories from the huge number that are merely consistent: in their words, an objective past.
Their result is ``what proliferates is what counts'' in quantum form, with the disjointness in it, and it
came before this book. Halliwell, in a second 1999 paper, ``Somewhere in the universe,'' had already carried the link between records and
consistent histories from pure starting states to mixed ones, where the records still exist but
are necessarily imperfect.

There's a deeper mismatch in the borrowing, and it runs against the book, so it goes here. In
Zurek's picture the whole thing, system and device and environment together, evolves by quantum
mechanics' rule for closed systems, and that rule never sends two states to one; every step can
be run backwards. So, seen from the whole, the environment's copying is just that, copying: the
dial's reading gets written onto fresh light, and no two states anywhere are merged. A simple copying model sends each new copy to a previously unused carrier.
That is a use of fresh space, like Bennett's blank page. It is not a proof
that every closed quantum evolution visits a new state forever; finite closed
systems can recur.

Looking only at the dial discards the correlations with the light. In an ideal
complete-dephasing channel, distinct input phases can give exactly the same
reduced output. In gradual decoherence they may only become harder to tell
apart; they need not become exactly equal at any finite time. An exact merge
in a reduced description, approximate loss of accessible coherence, and a
heat transfer are three different claims. To obtain a heat floor one still
needs the physical preparation, the relevant entropy change and the thermal
premises. Copying alone supplies none of those conclusions.

That is the difficulty for the borrowing. The thesis points at copies being
kept and used. The quantum account explains particular ways information can
spread and become accessible. It does not attach this book's toll to that act.

A published no-go cuts closer still. Philippe Allard Gu\'erin, Veronika Baumann, Flavio Del
Santo and \v{C}aslav Brukner (2021) gave an argument that, under assumptions that look natural in quantum
mechanics, an observer's own perceptions of her outcome at two different times can't share one
reality: no joint chance for the two, depending linearly on the starting state, reproduces what
unitary quantum theory predicts for each. A record that persists, for the one holding it, is
exactly what gets into trouble once the whole is treated as one-to-one. It isn't a theorem
about my machine, which isn't quantum. It's still the strongest published reason I know to hold
the word ``permanent'' loosely when a physicist is in the room.

Which leaves the question to ask of any borrowed shape: has anybody checked the original? For a
long time quantum Darwinism was a theory without a lab. Then, in 2018 and 2019, three groups
working separately, in Italy, China and Germany, went looking for its fingerprint, as Philip Ball's 2019 report in \emph{Quanta Magazine} tells it. The German
one, at Ulm, with Zurek among the authors, watched the spin of a single defect inside a diamond
and the carbon atoms around it, and saw the redundancy the theory predicts: the defect's state
turned up copied in its surroundings, and it didn't take much of the surroundings before more of
them told you nothing new. The other two did it with photons. Is that the bottom? It isn't, not by a long
way, and the people involved said so. Zurek himself pointed out that the photon experiments make
their copies artificially and that the diamond's environment is small, and others noted that all
three are schematic versions of a real environment and don't rule out rival accounts. So the
shape I borrowed has passed some first tests in a lab, at the scale of a handful of atoms or
photons, with the caveats written on it. None of that touches the thesis here, which is
about machines and never rested on quantum physics. It changes the picture: what I borrowed is a
lead somebody is checking. It isn't settled, and I don't get to lean on it as if it were.

\subsection{What's proved}

This section has definitions, two toys, a theorem about independence, a survey, and two refutations of things that would have been stronger.

The definitions are the ones above, plus ``unique pointer among rivals'': the event proliferates and none
of a listed set of rival events does. Uniqueness is \emph{relative to the list}, necessarily,
since any event that holds on exactly the same states as a proliferating event proliferates
whenever it does: the same fact under another name, so someone has to say which names count
as rivals. And the first criterion is stated
as a schema: for every ecosystem in some class, its metered event is the unique pointer among
its rivals. The class and the rivals are inputs. Nothing about them is proved. A second set of
definitions, after this one, tightens ``proliferates'' to ``copied and relied on'' and drops the
rival list.

The formal object is small enough to hold in one hand.

\begin{definition}[Ecosystem, records, proliferates, pointer]\label{def:u14-ecosystem}
An \emph{ecosystem} is a type of states, a number $N$ of observers, and for each observer $i$ a
Boolean fragment $F_i$ on states. Observer $i$ \emph{records} an event $E$ (a property of states)
when, for every state $s$, $E(s)$ holds exactly when $F_i(s)$ is true. $E$ \emph{proliferates} when
every observer $i < N$ records it. $E$ is the \emph{unique pointer among} a list of rival events
when $E$ proliferates and no rival in the list does. Given a class $C$ of ecosystems, and for
each member a designated metered event and a list of rivals, the \emph{pointer criterion holds}
for $C$ when every member's metered event is the unique pointer among its rivals.
\end{definition}

Nothing in the definition makes two fragments read different parts of the state, and
``metered'' is only a label: the definition has no metering in it.

One bit per observer can't even state the objection a replicated system raises. Every full
node of a blockchain holds the whole shared state, so every fact about it, ``gas used is at least
one'' as much as ``final,'' sits on every node. The tightened definitions give each observer
whatever it holds, an action it takes on what it holds, and a flag for whether it produced the
record.

\begin{definition}[Copied and relied on, independent carriers, the pointer]\label{def:u14-reliance}
An \emph{ecosystem with reliance} is a type of states, a number $N$ of observers, and for each
observer $i$ a view $V_i$ (a function from states to some type of things an observer can hold), an
action $a_i$ (a Boolean function of the view) and a producer flag. Fix a set $R$ of reachable
states. An event $E$ is \emph{copied} on $R$ when for each $i < N$ some Boolean function $d$ of the
view has $E(s)$ exactly when $d(V_i(s))$ is true, for every $s$ in $R$. Observer $i$ \emph{relies on}
$E$ when $a_i(V_i(s))$ true gives $E(s)$ for every $s$ in $R$, and $a_i(V_i(s))$ is true for some $s$ in
$R$. $E$ is \emph{relied on by parties who didn't produce it} when some observer $i < N$ is not a
producer and every such observer relies on $E$; it is \emph{copied and relied on} when it is both.
$E$ is the \emph{pointer} on $R$ when it is copied and relied on, and every event that is copied and
relied on holds at every state of $R$ where $E$ holds. The carriers are \emph{independent} under a family of relations $P_i$ (states that agree on
observer $i$'s own part of the world) when each view gives equal values on states related by its
$P_i$, and for any two observers $i \ne j$ below $N$ and any states $s$, $t$ there is a state $u$
with $P_i(u, s)$ and $P_j(u, t)$: the two parts can be set separately.
\end{definition}

Two pointers on the same $R$ agree on every state of $R$, so the pointer is unique with no list
of rivals. And the definition of independence has a consequence I
didn't put in on purpose.

Put one yes/no card in front of each of two readers. If the cards can be set
separately, all four arrangements are allowed: no/no, no/yes, yes/no and yes/yes.
Ask each reader to recover one shared event using only their own card. Suppose
that event is false at no/no and true at yes/yes. At no/yes, the first reader
sees exactly what they saw in the false case, while the second sees exactly
what they saw in the true case. Their answers conflict. That mixed arrangement
is exactly what the independence condition hands the proof.

Now impose a copying procedure that only leaves no/no or yes/yes. On those
reachable arrangements each reader can report the shared bit correctly.
Separate cards are things that \emph{could} carry a copy; what makes them copies is that
the arrangements you actually reach have the two agreeing. The theorem below is about
recovering the event exactly on \emph{all} arrangements, the mixed ones included, which
the copying never leaves behind.

\begin{theorem}[Independent copies on every state: the event is equivalent at any two states]\label{thm:u14-independent-constant}
In any ecosystem with reliance whose carriers are independent and which has at least two observers,
an event copied on the set of all states holds at one state exactly when it holds at any other,
so it holds at every state or at none.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let observers 0 and 1 decide the event by $d_0$ and $d_1$. Given states $s$ and $t$, take $u$ with
observer 0's part from $s$ and observer 1's from $t$. Then the event at $s$ is $d_0$ of observer
0's view, which is the same at $u$, so it equals the event at $u$; and the event at $u$ equals the
event at $t$ the same way through observer 1.
\end{proof}

So
separate parts of the world can each carry an exact copy of a real record only on the states the
world actually reaches, where the copying made them agree, and that's why the definition asks for
copies on a set $R$ of reachable states. Zurek's copies are the same: the light carries the
dial's reading because the dial put it there.

\begin{theorem}[A replicated header: copying doesn't separate, reliance does]\label{thm:u14-ledger}
Let the states be a block header (a finalized bit, a gas-used count) and three nodes' copies of it,
with $R$ the states where every copy equals the header; node $i$'s view is its own copy, its part of
the world is that copy, node 0 is the producer, and every node acts exactly when its copy says
finalized. Then the carriers are independent; ``finalized'' and ``gas used is at least one'' are
both copied on $R$; ``finalized'' is the pointer on $R$; and ``gas used is at least one'' is not
relied on by parties who didn't produce it.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Independence: to give node $i$ the copy from $s$ and node $j$ the copy from $t$, overwrite node
$j$'s copy in $s$. On $R$ every copy is the header, so each node reads either fact off its copy.
Node 1 acts only where its copy, and so the header, says finalized, and acts at the finalized
header with no gas used; that state shows gas used fails node 1's reliance. Any event relied on by
node 1 holds wherever node 1 acts, which on $R$ is wherever the header is finalized, so
``finalized'' is the strongest.
\end{proof}

It's a sanity check with maps I wrote, and it shows only that the tightened definition can tell the two apart where plain copying can't. Which of the two it picks, the actions pick: let every node act when its copy says gas was used, and gas used is the pointer. When what the other parties act on is copied, that is the pointer, so here the argument lives in the actions, and I wrote those too.

\begin{thesis}[The pointer thesis]\label{conj:u14-pointer}
Let $C$ be the class of ecosystems with reliance that faithfully model deployed record-keeping
disciplines, each with its reachable states, its observers reading independent carriers in the
sense of Definition~\ref{def:u14-reliance}, its certification event, and the records its
discipline prices. Then for every member of $C$: (1) the certification event is the pointer on
the reachable states, so it is copied and relied on by parties who didn't produce it, and every
event copied and relied on in that sense holds
wherever certification does; and (2) every record the discipline prices is copied and relied on
by parties who didn't produce it.
\end{thesis}

The thesis leans on two notions with no precise mathematical definition: what it is to
``faithfully model'' a system, and which systems count as ``deployed.'' Those two tie the
definitions to the world, the way ``computable in the plain-English sense'' does in the
Church-Turing thesis, and no definition can do that job, so the claim is a thesis. The other
term it needs, independent carriers, is defined in
Definition~\ref{def:u14-reliance}. The schema takes the class, the reachable states, the certification event and the priced
records as inputs; it proves nothing about which real systems satisfy them.

The toy has three observers on a replicated ledger, where certification proliferates and ``work
done'' doesn't. It's an illustration, and that's all it is; it isn't evidence.

\begin{theorem}[The toy]\label{thm:u14-toy}
Let the toy have states (a certified bit, a work count), three observers, and every fragment
equal to the certified bit. Then ``certified'' is the unique pointer among the one rival
``work at least 1''.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Every fragment is the certified bit, so every observer records ``certified'' by definition.
For the rival, take the state with the bit false and work 1: the event holds and observer 0's
fragment is false, so observer 0 does not record it.
\end{proof}

The survey covers twelve events in one theorem: for each of the five systems in Section~\ref{sec:models}, the
designated event (finalized, committed, attested, logged, checked) proliferates in the
observer map I wrote for that system, and a rival (proposer work, a scratch counter,
measurement noise, submission latency, prover steps) doesn't. The five together are one
statement, an instance of the schema above.
The survey adds a symmetric message-authentication code, which does \emph{not} proliferate, and a digital
signature, which does, for twelve rows in all. The five maps all use the same construction: a state has a designated
Boolean event and a separate nonnegative rival count, three observers each return
the event bit, and the rival asks whether its count is at least one. The bit and
count can vary independently. The signature map likewise gives all three observers
the authentic-signature bit. In the MAC map, observers 0 and 1 receive the authentic-tag
bit and observer 2 always returns false. These maps, not a protocol running
on a network, are the entire tests here. And there's a thirteenth, which I think is the most important one: swap which bit
every observer copies, and the criterion picks the \emph{other} event. The criterion selects
whatever the observer map copies. The map is where the argument lives, and I wrote the maps.
So the five ``confirmations'' are five instances of one construction with the fields renamed.
I'm saying that twice on
purpose, so it can't slip past once.

\begin{theorem}[The survey, and the swap]\label{thm:u14-survey}
(1) In each of the five observer models (proof-of-stake, gas, attestation, transparency,
proof-carrying), the designated event proliferates and the designated rival does not; in the
symmetric-MAC model the authentic-tag event does not proliferate; in the signature model the
authentic-signature event does. (2) Let the states be pairs of bits (first, second), with
three observers whose fragments all equal the second bit. Then ``second is true'' is the
unique pointer among the one rival ``first is true''.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Each confirmation holds by definition: each observer's fragment is true exactly when the
event holds.
Each refutation exhibits one state where the event holds and some observer's bit is down.
In (2) that state is (true, false).
\end{proof}

Two stronger claims are both refuted, and I'd ask you not to run them together, because they fail for
different reasons.

The first stronger claim is that \emph{every forgery-resistant commitment proliferates}. If that were
true, certification would be the pointer because it's the commitment. It's refuted in three
observer models (deniable authentication, where only the designated verifier's bit tracks the
event; a symmetric MAC, where the key holders share a secret and nobody else can check; an
object capability, an unforgeable token that grants access to whoever holds it) and
confirmed in two (a public log; a digital signature). Build the first
with three observers: give one a copy of the event's bit and the other two a constant false.
The one records it; it doesn't proliferate. The proved half is the map computation. Whether
my maps are \emph{fair} to the real designs is argued in prose, and you should argue back.

\begin{theorem}[One blind observer is enough]\label{thm:u14-blind}
(1) In any ecosystem, if some observer $i < N$ has $F_i(s_0)$ false at a state $s_0$ where
$E$ holds, then $E$ does not proliferate. (2) Let the deniable model have states (authentic,
verifier-accepts), three observers, observer 0's fragment the authentic bit and observers 1
and 2 constantly false. Then observer 0 records ``authentic'', and ``authentic'' does not
proliferate. The symmetric-MAC and object-capability models also fail to proliferate their
events; the public-log and signature models proliferate theirs.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Recording would require $E(s_0) \iff F_i(s_0)$, and the left side is true while the right
is false. (2) Observer 0's fragment is true exactly when the event holds. Apply (1) with observer 1 and
the state (true, true). The other two refutations apply (1) to a blind observer of their own model (the symmetric-MAC map gives observer 2 a constant false; the object-capability map gives the token holder the bit and the other two constant false). The two confirmations hold by definition: the public-log map gives all three observers the logged bit, and the signature map gives all three the authentic-signature bit.
\end{proof}

The theorem is about the observer maps, and only them. That a third
party in deniable authentication really cannot be convinced is the modelling claim, and the
model has no transcript, key or verifier in it to check that against.

The second stronger claim is that \emph{agreement plus accuracy plus locality imply permanence}. That is,
if all observers agree, each sees the event exactly, and each updates by the same local rule
with no coordinator, then the recorded event can't be undone. The smallest thing
imaginable refutes it: one bit, two observers who both see it, and the rule ``flip.'' All three conditions
hold and true becomes false in one step. Do
it on paper; it takes a minute and it's humbling. What \emph{does} give permanence is durability,
``an observer's true view stays true,'' added as a premise, and then it follows in a few lines. So durability is the premise doing the work, and
durability is Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s permanence wearing a different coat. Agreement doesn't buy it. Do the
paper version again with one change, the rule ``stay true once true'' in place of ``flip,'' and
the bit can't fall, because the rule won't let it. The observers agreeing has nothing to do with it. (The
small machine of Section~\ref{sec:smallest} has a reading that's durable in exactly this sense: its flag never comes
down, by its step rule (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll}).) None of this rules out a narrower theorem with real assumptions about the network,
the adversary or durability; it rules out these two strong forms.

\begin{definition}[Observation game]\label{def:u14-game}
A \emph{game} has states, a number $N$ of observers, a Boolean event $e$, a Boolean view $V_i$ for
each observer, and a step map. For $i, j < N$ it has \emph{consensus} when $V_i = V_j$ on every
state; \emph{authenticity} when $V_i(s) = e(s)$ for every state and every $i < N$;
\emph{coordinator-free update} when one function $\ell$ on Booleans has
$V_i(\mathrm{step}(s)) = \ell(V_i(s))$ for every state and every $i < N$; \emph{durable views} when
$V_i(s)$ true gives $V_i(\mathrm{step}(s))$ true for every $i < N$; and a \emph{permanent event}
when $e(s)$ true gives $e(\mathrm{step}(s))$ true.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[What buys permanence]\label{thm:u14-toggle}
(1) It is false that every game with $N > 0$, consensus, authenticity and coordinator-free
update has a permanent event. (2) Every game with $N > 0$, authenticity and durable views has
a permanent event.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) The toggle game: states are Booleans, two observers, event and both views the identity,
step ``flip''. Consensus and authenticity hold trivially, the local rule is ``flip'', and the
state true steps to false. (2) If $e(s)$ is true, observer 0's view is true by authenticity,
stays true by durability, and authenticity turns it back into $e(\mathrm{step}(s))$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{What isn't proved, and must stay that way on the page}

What isn't proved is that certification \emph{in deployed systems} is singled out by being copied and relied on across
\emph{independent} carriers. The criterion defines independence; it has no precise definition of ``deployed'' or ``faithfully model,''
and no cost law connecting being copied and relied on to price. Every correspondence between a mathematical observer
map and a real system is a sentence I wrote. The thesis is a thesis, and anyone who
says the formal object proves it is reading more than is there.

\subsection{What the thesis asks of the examples}

There are three concrete comparisons to make. First, look at the record a deployed
discipline prices. Do parties who did not produce it copy and rely on it? A priced record
that nobody else relies on would contradict the thesis's second half.

Second, compare certification with rival events. If an event not implied by certification
is copied and relied on to the same standard, certification is not the unique pointer.
Multiplication counts or head-turn counts would qualify if they met that same test in the
system being described.

Third, apply the independence condition of Definition~\ref{def:u14-reliance} to a faithful
model of the ecosystem and ask whether certification itself meets the test. The symmetric-MAC
example shows why the carriers and their access matter. The two stronger forms already
refuted above help locate the distinction this thesis needs.

These comparisons supply the evidence the worldly claim asks for. The mathematical
criterion supplies a definite question once the model and its observer maps are chosen.

\subsection{The end of the logic}

The logic that started in Part I ends here. Part I found what keeping takes: anything kept is paid in a merge or in fresh states, alongside the model-dependent thermal bounds (Section~\ref{sec:what-a-chair-is}), and a toll on raising a flag is forced by three premises
(Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}). Learning doesn't have to merge anything, so it owes no floor; it
borrows a blank page, which is a supply of fresh states, and can hand it back. Committing on a finite supply of fresh states has to merge
(Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}). Part II earned the rest. The counter is arithmetic once the schedule is
fixed (Section~\ref{sec:counter}). A window with a colliding pair in it can't price the flag exactly (Section~\ref{sec:windows}). Entitlement is an object,
a check, and a paid event, and, given lists, a tree and a covering that someone supplies, and a run that
paid for the tree's depth, it
costs at least the index bits it commits to (Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}). Insight is a distinction made to stay, and a committed relation is that at its best (Section~\ref{sec:insight}).
A feeling doesn't qualify.
Over any base a record that is driven by the computation and never comes
down is a latch, with two unforced choices, the price list and the event
(Section~\ref{sec:latch}). With more than two places, a record that is driven by the computation
and climbs a partial order is a
row of cups, each one a latch; the toll over the whole row charges at least one on any step that
turns up some cup, and a
straight line of stages needs exactly one cup fewer than it has stages, cups that only turn up (Section~\ref{sec:direction}). When the
machine has finitely many states, its record only grows, and the
ordinary machine forgets nothing, the toll prices crushing two states of one fibre, and a window
can price exactly by seeing the cups move (Section~\ref{sec:shadow-exact}). No inside procedure whose flip a substrate can represent decides a shortcut property,
given a recursion theorem, which the nat family has by construction. L
is handled on its own terms rather than as a substrate, and
on L the same diagonal is proved again
from a recursion theorem it has by proof. What a
record can do is carry the commitment (Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}). This part made ``established''
a record that a check of the claim passed (Section~\ref{sec:established}), and the small machine earns
one by a check, a commitment and a certificate, one unit each (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}). Of
five specifications, read through my transcriptions, one charges a fee at the write (Section~\ref{sec:models}).
For the choice of event, the pointer thesis proposes certification and lists how
that proposal could fail (Section~\ref{sec:pointer}).

One question about the price itself is still open: do the requirements I've put on a price
pick out the toll and nothing else? If a short list of them left only one price standing,
that would settle it. The lists I tried don't, and
the no is small enough to check on three states. Call them blank, once and twice, with once and
twice reading yes. The flip takes blank to once and leaves the other two where they are. The
smooth takes both once and twice to twice and leaves blank alone. The smooth forgets something, so
the price on merging from Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} charges it one unit. (The flip forgets too, blank and once both land on once, so the price on merging charges it as well, as the list requires.) It raises nothing, so the toll
charges it nothing. Now try requirements that name no reading: no charge on a move that changes
nothing, none on a move that forgets nothing, the same cost when you rename the states, a total
that adds up along a run, a cost that looks only at the step, and a cost of one on the flip from blank. The toll, read as
the price that charges the flip from blank and nothing else, meets every one of them on this machine.
So does the price on merging. They disagree on the
smooth, so that list doesn't pick between them. What picks the toll is a requirement that names
the record: over any run the total is never more than the number of times the reading went up.
With the floor, that leaves exactly one price, one unit per raise and nothing else
(Section~\ref{sec:windows}), and it rules the price on merging out, because the smooth costs that price one
unit and raises nothing. The only renaming
of the three states that respects the moves is the identity,
so the renaming requirement asks nothing there. So the uniqueness is real and it's small. It holds once you've said which
reading you're charging for, and which reading deserves the charge is the pointer thesis,
which is still a thesis.

The uniqueness theorems that do exist are about pricing information loss, and they're worth
a look because they say what kind of charge the price on merging is. John Baez, Tobias Fritz
and Tom Leinster (2011), mathematicians who work in category theory, the mathematics Lawvere's
diagonal theorem came from, asked what a measure of information loss has to look like. As I read
their paper, they proved that, for maps that preserve a probability measure,
Shannon entropy is up to a constant factor the only
measure of information loss that is functorial, convex-linear and continuous. J\'anos Acz\'el and Bruno Forte, mathematicians at the University
of Waterloo who worked on functional equations, and C.\
T.\ Ng, who had taken his doctorate there under Acz\'el in 1971, asked in a paper of 1974 which entropies deserve to be called
natural, and proved, by their account, that the entropies with
a short list of natural properties are exactly the linear combinations of Shannon's and Hartley's, where
Hartley's is the log of the count, so even for merges the choice between the average and the
worst case is a real choice. Both price merges. Neither prices raises, so neither picks out the toll, and
that's the three-state example again, at a larger size. On the other side of the fence, Luciano
Pomatto, Philipp Strack and Omer Tamuz (2023), economists at Caltech and Yale who asked what
learning something should cost, proved, by their account, a uniqueness result for what it costs to
\emph{acquire} information, with constant marginal costs. That result prices producing a
signal, which is a different matter from what Section~\ref{sec:narrowing} reads off a copy onto a blank page;
the copy owes no floor and borrows fresh states.

Most of that isn't a machine. The theorems of Parts I and II quantify over ``any states, any
steps,'' and the five models are small copies of somebody else's systems. The example machine is the
small one of Section~\ref{sec:smallest}, the least I could make that still shows the whole model,
with every part named and every price written down, and the program that runs every program of it
and, with one paid move added, every Thiele machine whose workings a program can compute, is
in Appendix~\ref{sec:universal-machines}. That's where everything above has something to bump into. If a
statement up there doesn't mean what I think it means, that's where it shows, and Part IV is how
you'd go looking.

%===========================================================================
\section{The counter against physics}
\label{sec:landauer}
%===========================================================================

Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} did the physics argument once: on a finite machine a permanent flag merges states,
a price list that charges merges (a named premise, with Landauer's principle, another named premise, as the physics behind it) charges the flag, and the toll follows. I'm not going
to do it again. This section is about what a machine's counter, the small machine's $\mu$
included, has to do with any of that, and the answer is: less than naming Landauer suggests, and I want you to hear the exact amount from me.

\subsection{The calibration is a unit conversion}

Multiply the counter by an energy per unit of cost that you choose,
and you get a theorem: a state with one unit, at the scale kT ln 2 per unit, carries kT ln 2 of
energy, for every k and T. Read that for exactly what it is: a unit conversion, true by definition,
with the scale as an unforced input. Nothing in it picks the scale. The theorem would be just as
true with the scale set to a dollar a unit. What \emph{would} connect units of cost to joules is the premise in Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary},
Landauer's principle, which is a physical premise. And even
as a scale, $k_B T \ln 2$ a unit is the floor for one particular squeeze, a halving.
Corollary~\ref{cor:heat-floor}'s floor for a flip that brings $k$ states in beside $m$ already
reading yes, starting
from the even spread on those $m+k$ states, is the larger of $k_B T \ln \frac{m+k}{m}$ and $\frac{2k}{m+k}\,k_B T\ln 2$, and for one newcomer among many yes-states that's far below a halving, about $1.4\,k_B T / m$. Price every unit at $k_B T \ln 2$ and you can overstate the floor
of a single narrow flip by a factor that grows with $m$.

Remember the constant from Boltzmann's grave in Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}, the exchange rate between a count and
heat? It has a newer chapter, and it makes the point sharper than I can. The $k_B$ in
$k_B T \ln 2$ turns a temperature into an energy, and for most of its
history it was a measured number, with error bars, pinned down by careful experiments. Since
20 May 2019 it isn't. That day the international system of units was redefined so that
Boltzmann's constant is exactly $1.380649 \times 10^{-23}$ joules per kelvin, by definition, and
the kelvin is whatever makes that true. So the conversion from temperature to energy has been a
convention since then, in the strictest sense: its numerical value in those units is fixed. Realising the kelvin in a laboratory still
requires measurements, with uncertainty. What's still
physics is everything around it, whether wiping a bit at a temperature really sheds that much
heat, which is what the Lyon bead was measuring. The calibration theorem is the same kind of move
as that redefinition. It fixes a conversion, and the physics, if there is any, is somewhere else.

\begin{definition}[Energy at a scale]\label{def:u24-scale}
For a real number $c$ (joules per unit) and a state $s$, the energy of $s$ at scale $c$ is
$\mu(s) \cdot c$. The \emph{Landauer calibration} at $k_B$ and $T$ is the statement that every
state with $\mu(s) = 1$ has energy $k_B T \ln 2$ at scale $k_B T \ln 2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The calibration is a unit conversion]\label{thm:u24-calibration}
(1) For all real $k_B$ and $T$, the Landauer calibration at $k_B$ and $T$ holds. (2) For any counter, there are two real-valued functions of
the state that give 1 and 2 on every state with
one unit, so the counter alone fixes no energy value.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) The scale says what one ledger unit is worth. At a ledger reading of
one, multiplying by that scale returns the scale itself:
$1\cdot k_B T\ln2=k_B T\ln2$. No condition on the signs of $k_B$ or $T$
is needed for that multiplication.

(2) Choose a scale of one and a scale of two. The same ledger reading of
one is assigned energy one by the first choice and energy two by the
second. The ledger has not changed; only the conversion I supplied has.
Thus that conversion was not determined by the counter.
\end{proof}

The physics is the premise of
Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}, restated here once in the form the next theorems test. In words first: a \emph{dissipation}
hands each instruction a whole number of heat units, each unit worth kT ln 2. The floor premise
says an instruction that takes at least one state where some yes-or-no
property is false to a state where it's true, never sends a true one back to false, and sends
two different states to one, dissipates at least one unit. That's a different statement from Landauer's principle as
Premise~\ref{prem:landauer} has it. That one depends on the spread over states,
$Q \ge k_B T \ln 2 \cdot \Delta H$, and gives no floor for a known state (there the distinction was
absent from the chosen point distribution; that alone says nothing
about a prior preparation bill). This one gives every such
instruction a floor of one whole unit, whatever the spread. To get the second from the first
you'd need more, at the least a spread with a full bit of uncertainty removed at every such
step, and the known-state theorem and the narrow squeeze of Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}
