show that isn't automatic. So I give it its own name, \emph{structural dissipation pricing}. The calibration says no instruction dissipates more units than the counter charges
it. One word about that word: ``dissipation'' here means heat handed to the surroundings, the
quantity Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} read off Sagawa as owed even when no entropy is
produced, the heat that pays for where the forgotten bit goes. It is not what Section~\ref{sec:what-a-chair-is}
calls dissipating, which is entropy produced, and it has nothing to do with waste, or with doing
the job badly. There are two premises here, nothing is proved about either,
and the only question is whether they can hold together:

\begin{premise}[Structural dissipation pricing]\label{prem:u24-landauer-pair}
A \emph{dissipation} is a function $\delta$ from instructions to naturals, counted in units of
$k_B T \ln 2$. The \emph{floor}, a hypothesis separate from Premise~\ref{prem:landauer} of
Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}:
every instruction that collapses a yes-or-no property has $\delta(i) \ge 1$, where $i$
\emph{collapses} $P$ when some state with $P$ false is sent to a state with $P$ true, every
state with $P$ true is sent to one with $P$ true, and some two different states are sent to the
same state. The \emph{calibration}: $\delta(i) \le
\mathrm{cost}(i)$ for every instruction. Neither is proved anywhere; the theorems below ask
whether they can hold together.
\end{premise}

The last clause of the floor is there because the first two don't make a step forget anything
on a machine with infinitely many states. INC $A$ sends a state with $A = 0$ to one with $A = 1$
and keeps every positive $A$ positive, so it raises ``$A \ge 1$'' one way, and it is
one-to-one. Any one-to-one map that misses some state does the same to the property ``is in my
image''. Its input can be read back off its output, so it loses no entropy, and Landauer's premise as
this book takes it then puts no heat floor under it at all. It pays in fresh states instead: INC moves
every value of $A$ up one, Hilbert's front desk, and only a counter with no top can keep doing
it. A thermal implementation can dissipate under the model-specific conditions above; the premise only sets no floor under it. A floor read without the last clause would charge a whole unit. On a finite machine the clause asks
nothing extra. A step that sends one false state into the true ones and keeps every true state true
puts one more state into the true set than the set holds, so two of them land on the same state. And on any machine the property comes along for the ride: an instruction that sends two different states $a$ and $b$ to one collapses the property ``is reached from $a$ in one or more steps'', since one of $a$ and $b$ lies outside it and lands in it. So the floor is a price on merging, one unit for every instruction that merges, read as heat.

\subsection{The premises have to be able to hold together}

The one piece of this section that I think is good physics discipline is a
consistency test. Suppose you want to claim the counter tracks dissipation. You need two
premises: that every step you've chosen to count dissipates at least one unit, and an upper
calibration that bounds dissipation by the charge. Can those two hold at once? There's a
theorem saying exactly when: a model
satisfying both exists precisely when every operation you've chosen to count (the statement
below calls those \emph{eligible}) costs at least one. I should say how little that shows. The model the proof builds takes the dissipation to be
the cost itself, so the theorem shows the two premises don't contradict each other. It
doesn't show that the counter tracks any dissipation. Still, it does bite on a schedule: if you count a
zero-cost step, no such model can exist. One example where the premises hold is a
one-bit restore, where restoring the bit to one costs one and idling costs
nothing; the small machine's flag-raising steps, below, are another.

Now point the test at the small machine of Section~\ref{sec:smallest}, counting every step
that collapses some yes-or-no property, and it fails. Read without the last clause of the
floor, it would fail at a step that forgets nothing: INC $A$ raises ``$A \ge 1$'' one way, is
one-to-one, and costs zero. With
the clause in place the failure sits at a merge. Its unpriced instructions merge states (the
last item of the list at the end of that chapter has the pair: two cores that one DEC sends to
the same core, at zero cost), so DEC A 2, which collapses the property ``$A$ is zero or the line
number is 2'' by sending a state where it's false and a state where it's true to the same
state, costs zero there, and (1) below says no dissipation can charge it one and stay under its cost.
The machine prices the
certifying chain and leaves its other merges unpriced, so the premise pair holds for the steps
the toll is about and fails for the whole instruction set. That follows from computing at no cost on a base that keeps no history, and the base is the part that's by design. The hardware
pays for those unpriced merges in heat, off the ledger. The ledger counts the record only. A unit of cost is
not a joule.

\begin{theorem}[When the premises can hold together]\label{thm:u24-consistency}
(1) For any set of operations, any predicate ``eligible'' on them, and any cost, a dissipation
with $\delta(i) \ge 1$ on every eligible $i$ and $\delta(i) \le \mathrm{cost}(i)$ on every
$i$ exists if and only if every eligible operation costs at least one. (2) On a one-bit
machine with a reset of cost 1 and an idle of cost 0, taking ``eligible'' to mean ``sends two
different states to one'', such a dissipation exists.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) If such a $\delta$ exists, $1 \le \delta(i) \le \mathrm{cost}(i)$. Conversely, take
$\delta = \mathrm{cost}$. (2) The reset is the only operation that sends two states to one,
and it costs 1; apply (1).
\end{proof}

Three statements are in play, and each points its own way. Energy at a scale, $\mu \cdot c$, is a
conversion and points nowhere. The calibration, $\delta(i) \le \mathrm{cost}(i)$, puts the charge
above the dissipation: an upper bound. Landauer's principle puts the heat above an entropy loss: a
lower bound. The theorem above says the assumptions can hold together, which is compatibility,
and it isn't evidence. It doesn't make the ledger the least energy anything needs, and it doesn't
make it the heat anything gives off.

Now point the first way out of Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}, keep everything and pay by taking fresh states,
at a machine. Keep the previous state in a
history list (push it onto the front each step; below, $s:: h$ is the list $h$ with $s$ put
on the front) and every fixed-instruction step becomes injective, while the step you can see
stays the same; the line number can collapse to one place while the bigger state keeps
its past. The unpriced merge, lifted to a machine with
history, isn't a merge. It still pays, though: the list gets one state longer every step, so
the run never comes back to a state it has been in, and that's the fresh-state column of what keeping takes. On
any memory you can build the list fills it, and then the merge is back. So ``this step merged, so it dissipated'' can't be said of the
visible step alone. It's a sentence about the whole state including whatever
history is retained, and a physical model has to say what's retained. The
permanent-certificate theorem in Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} supplies that for the certifying step on finite memory.
For the rest of a machine's steps it's unsaid.

\begin{theorem}[Keeping history makes every step injective]\label{thm:u24-history}
Let the history step send a pair $(s, h)$, a state and a list of past states, to
$(\mathrm{apply}(s, i), s:: h)$. For any step function, the history step with a fixed
instruction is injective, and its first component is the original step. Each step makes the
list one longer, so a run of history steps never visits the same pair twice.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Undoing the history step, by popping the list, returns the old pair, so two pairs with the same
image are equal. The list after $n$ steps has $n$ more entries than at the start, so two pairs
at different times of one run differ in the length of their lists.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The calorimeter protocol, as a specification}

What follows is how one \emph{would} measure this, and it's here because it makes the boundary exact. Take a two-state
register with energies zero and a gap, a population p in the excited state, and the simplest
possible rate equation for how p changes in one time step (a rate for climbing into the
excited state, a rate for falling out of it, and the length of the step). For the canonical reset
(population one half to zero, with the rates chosen so the equation closes), the heat
delivered to the bath is exactly half the gap. Choose the gap
to be twice kT ln 2 and that heat is exactly kT ln 2.

Read that twice, because the temptation is to read it as a derivation of Landauer's number
and it's the opposite. The gap was \emph{chosen} to make the heat come out as Landauer's number.
The same populations and rates with half that gap give half the Landauer value, and there's
a theorem exhibiting identical population dynamics with different heat. The rate equation fixes the \emph{shape}; the energy
scale is a selected Hamiltonian (the physicist's name for the rule that says what energy each
state has), and selecting it is not deriving it.

The canonical reset is a bookkeeping toy, and its rates show it. A register that trades heat
with a bath at temperature $T$ has rates in \emph{detailed balance}: the rate up over the rate
down is $e^{-\Delta/k_B T}$, which at the gap $2 k_B T \ln 2$ is $1/4$. The canonical rates are
0 and 1, and the factor $e^{-\Delta/k_B T}$ is never 0, so no gap and no temperature put them in
that ratio. With rates that are in it, a
relaxation at a fixed gap moves toward the equilibrium population $1/(1 + e^{\Delta/k_B T})$ and,
with steps short enough not to overshoot, never goes below it. At the
gap $2 k_B T \ln 2$ that population is $1/5$. The
toy has no work term either; nothing in it pays for the squeeze. Part (4) of the theorem below
says what follows from that: at the gap $k_B T \ln 2$ the toy books less heat than Landauer's bound
asks for the same squeeze from one half to zero, so the toy has no second law.

\begin{definition}[The two-state protocol]\label{def:u24-calorimeter}
For a gap $\Delta$, the register's mean energy at excited population $p$ is $\Delta \cdot p$.
One step of the rate equation is
\[
p' = p + \delta t \, \big(k_{01} (1 - p) - k_{10} \, p\big),
\]
and the heat to the bath over a step from $p$ to $p'$ is defined as $\Delta p - \Delta p'$. The
canonical reset takes $p = \tfrac12$, $\delta t = 1$, $k_{01} = 0$, $k_{10} = 1$, ending at
$p' = 0$, and counts one logical event.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The heat is fixed by the chosen gap]\label{thm:u24-calorimeter}
(1) The canonical numbers satisfy the rate equation. (2) For every $\Delta$, the canonical
reset's heat is $\Delta / 2$. (3) For all $k_B$, $T$, the gap $\Delta = 2 k_B T \ln 2$ gives
heat $k_B T \ln 2$. (4) If $k_B > 0$ and $T > 0$, the heat is below $k_B T \ln 2$ exactly when the gap is below $2 k_B T \ln 2$; at the gap $k_B T \ln 2$ it is half of $k_B T \ln 2$. (5) There are two different gaps for which the same canonical populations
satisfy the rate equation and the heats differ.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Half the population starts excited. The upward rate is zero, so none
enters the excited state; the downward rate is one for a step of length
one, so the entire excited half leaves. Substitution gives
$\tfrac12+1\cdot(0-\tfrac12)=0$.

(2) The register began with mean energy $\Delta/2$ and ended with zero.
The defined heat is their difference, $\Delta/2$.

(3) Choose $\Delta=2k_B T\ln2$. Half of that gap is $k_B T\ln2$.

(4) Asking whether $\Delta/2<k_B T\ln2$ is the same as multiplying both
sides by two and asking whether $\Delta<2k_B T\ln2$. At the particular
gap $k_B T\ln2$, part (2) gives half that value. With positive $k_B,T$
it is strictly smaller because $\ln2$ is positive.

(5) Take gaps one and two. The population equation in part (1) contains
neither gap, so the same populations solve it in both cases. Their heats
are one half and one respectively. The rate equation alone did not select
between them.
\end{proof}

A reset that pays its way is driven. Raise the gap a little, let the register settle with
rates in detailed balance, raise it again, and so on, starting from a gap of zero, where the
two states are alike and the population is one half. Raising the gap while the population
holds is work done on the register; settling at the new gap is heat to the bath. That's the textbook way to wipe a bit slowly, and here it is with its numbers worked out.

\begin{definition}[The driven reset]\label{def:u24-driven}
Write $kT$ for $k_B T$. At gap $\Delta$ the equilibrium excited population is
$\pi(\Delta) = 1/(1 + e^{\Delta/kT})$ and the register's free energy is
$F(\Delta) = -kT \ln(1 + e^{-\Delta/kT})$. Rates satisfy \emph{detailed balance} at gap $\Delta$
when $k_{01} = k_{10} \, e^{-\Delta/kT}$. A \emph{driven reset} along a schedule of gaps
$g_0, g_1, \dots, g_n$ takes, at step $m$, the gap from $g_m$ to $g_{m+1}$ with the population
held at $\pi(g_m)$, which is work $\pi(g_m)(g_{m+1} - g_m)$, and then lets the register settle to
$\pi(g_{m+1})$, which is heat $g_{m+1}\big(\pi(g_m) - \pi(g_{m+1})\big)$ to the bath. The reset's
work and heat are the sums over its steps. The uniform schedule from 0 to $D$ in $N$ steps has
$g_m = D m / N$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[A driven reset pays $kT \ln 2$ in work]\label{thm:u24-driven}
(1) With rates in detailed balance at gap $\Delta$, one step of the rate equation takes $p$ to
$\pi(\Delta) + \big(1 - \delta t\,(k_{01} + k_{10})\big)\big(p - \pi(\Delta)\big)$; when
$\delta t\,(k_{01} + k_{10}) = 1$ this discrete update lands on $\pi(\Delta)$ from any $p$. (2) For any schedule, work
minus heat is $g_n \pi(g_n) - g_0 \pi(g_0)$, the change in the register's mean energy. (3) If
$kT > 0$ and the schedule never falls, the work is at least $F(g_n) - F(g_0)$; if also every
step raises the gap by at most $h$, the work is at most $F(g_n) - F(g_0) + h\big(\pi(g_0) -
\pi(g_n)\big)$. (4) If $kT > 0$, $D \ge 0$ and $N \ge 1$, the uniform reset from 0 to $D$ in $N$
steps does work between $kT \ln 2 - kT e^{-D/kT}$ and $kT \ln 2 + D/(2N)$, and leaves an excited
population of at most $e^{-D/kT}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Detailed balance gives
$k_{01}=(k_{01}+k_{10})\pi(\Delta)$. In the rate equation, the upward
contribution minus the downward one is
$k_{01}-(k_{01}+k_{10})p$. Substitute the balance equation and this becomes
$-(k_{01}+k_{10})(p-\pi(\Delta))$. The update therefore subtracts the
fraction $\delta t(k_{01}+k_{10})$ of the distance from equilibrium. What
remains is exactly
\[
 p'=\pi(\Delta)+\bigl(1-\delta t(k_{01}+k_{10})\bigr)
                   \bigl(p-\pi(\Delta)\bigr).
\]
When that fraction is one, none of the distance remains: $p'=\pi(\Delta)$.

(2) Follow one raise from gap $a$ to gap $b$. Its work is
$\pi(a)(b-a)$ and its heat is $b(\pi(a)-\pi(b))$. Subtract the heat from
the work. The two occurrences of $b\pi(a)$ cancel, leaving
$b\pi(b)-a\pi(a)$, the final mean energy minus the initial mean energy.
At the next raise, that final energy becomes the next initial energy.
Adding over the schedule cancels every intermediate energy and leaves
only $g_n\pi(g_n)-g_0\pi(g_0)$.

(3) Differentiating the displayed free energy gives slope $F'(\Delta)=\pi(\Delta)$.
With $kT>0$, this slope decreases as the gap rises. Over $a\le b$, the
increase of $F$ therefore lies between the widths times the two endpoint
slopes:
\[
 \pi(b)(b-a)\le F(b)-F(a)\le\pi(a)(b-a).
\]
The work uses the right-hand quantity, the slope before the raise. It is
at least the free-energy increase. Its excess is at most
$(b-a)(\pi(a)-\pi(b))$. If the raise is at most $h$, that excess is at
most $h(\pi(a)-\pi(b))$.

Add those bounds over the schedule. Intermediate free energies cancel,
and intermediate populations cancel in the excess bound. I obtain work
between $F(g_n)-F(g_0)$ and that amount plus
$h(\pi(g_0)-\pi(g_n))$.

(4) For the uniform schedule, $h=D/N$, $\pi(0)=1/2$, and
\[
 F(D)-F(0)=kT\ln2-kT\ln(1+e^{-D/kT}).
\]
For $x\ge0$, $0\le\ln(1+x)\le x$: it starts at zero and its slope
$1/(1+x)$ is between zero and one. The free-energy difference is thus
at least $kT\ln2-kT e^{-D/kT}$ and at most $kT\ln2$.
The excess from (3) is at most $(D/N)(1/2)$, giving the work bounds.
Finally the denominator of $\pi(D)=1/(1+e^{D/kT})$ is at least
$e^{D/kT}$, so the remaining excited share is at most $e^{-D/kT}$.
\end{proof}

Try one finite step in units where $kT=1$: start with gap zero and half the
registers excited, then raise the gap to $\ln2$. The work is $\tfrac12\ln2$.
After settling, the excited share is $1/3$, so the bath receives
$(\tfrac12-\tfrac13)\ln2=\tfrac16\ln2$ and the registers retain
$\tfrac13\ln2$ more energy. Work equals those two amounts added together.
A third are still excited: one such step has not wiped the bit.

The word ``step'' matters here. Part (1) is a discrete update of the population.
Its multiplier can be zero. Continuous relaxation at fixed positive rates
instead multiplies the distance from equilibrium by
$e^{-(k_{01}+k_{10})t}$, which is positive at every finite time.
Exact settling in the schedule is an idealisation; the algebra does not prove
that a continuous bath completes it in one finite waiting period.

Here nobody picked the gap to make the number come out. Take $D$ large and $N$ much larger
than $D$: the work closes in on $kT \ln 2$ from both sides, and the population left in the
excited state goes to zero. Perfect erasure is the limit, not the result at any finite gap. To reuse the
original symmetric memory, the gap must also return to zero while transitions
are suppressed. Lowering it at the final fixed population recovers
$D\pi(D)$ of work and leaves that population unchanged. This term tends to
zero in the same limit. The reset of the population, restoration of the trap
and time needed for settling are separate parts of the physical protocol.
Detailed balance supplies the thermal premise; the displayed sums supply the
work and heat accounting for the idealised schedule.

What ties it to a machine is that the protocol counts one logical event, by definition, and one is what the small machine's CERTIFY charges, the last of
the three paid acts behind a raised flag (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}). The tie is two numbers that happen to match, the protocol's one by definition and the machine's the least the record-layer premise lets CERTIFY cost, and nothing more. No theorem maps the
protocol's two register states onto any state of the machine. And ``heat to the bath'' here
means the register's mean energy before minus after, which quietly assumes the bath gets
exactly what the register loses; nothing here establishes that. So a device test would have to measure the gap, the
populations, the rates, and the bath heat independently; separately establish
that the device's rates are in detailed balance (that the up and down rates stand in the ratio the
temperature dictates), which the driven reset assumes and the canonical one breaks; and separately establish that the device's
physical reset \emph{is} the machine's certify event. The driven reset is an executable experimental
specification. The canonical reset is a bookkeeping toy. Neither is a measured device, and neither is an unconditional conversion of
units of cost to joules, and anyone who tells you otherwise has skipped the conditions.

\subsection{Permanence and the heat premise}

Is there a heat prediction the permanent-certificate theorems make that Landauer's principle
alone doesn't? No, and the reason is short. The smallest case, one certified state and one
flipping in, is ``set a bit to one whatever it held,'' which is the reset Landauer described
and Bérut measured; Landauer's own name for it is ``restore to one,'' and
Section~\ref{sec:toll} put it beside the toll. The general bound, the larger of kT ln((m plus k) over m) and 2k over (m plus k) times kT ln 2, for squeezing m plus k
equally likely states into m, is what Landauer's principle gives for that squeeze, at kT ln 2 for
each bit removed. What the permanence theorems add is the structural half: finiteness and a
permanent reading force any flag-raising instruction to merge some full states.
They don't say the newly certified state is one of the states that collide, and they
don't supply the spread over inputs or the physical conditions a heat bound needs. Supply
those and Landauer's premise prices the uncertainty that was actually removed. The
machine result and the physical premise do different jobs, and neither does the other's.

\subsection{What this section is}

This section holds a calibration that's a unit conversion; a pair of premises, consistent on
the steps the toll is about and inconsistent on the whole instruction set; a history that makes any step injective by paying with a fresh state at every step; and a
measurement protocol that's a specification with a selected scale. The physics in this book is
in Part~I: Landauer's principle as a named premise with its critics named (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}), and conditional finite-time dissipation bounds, cited, and proved for one model (Section~\ref{sec:what-a-chair-is}). Here there's
accounting, and I've tried to call every line by its right name. That's the end of the example machine.
What's left, after one suspicion I can't prove, is how you'd break any of this, and where it stops.

\subsection{At the bottom: what I suspect and can't prove}

This is underneath the proofs, so read it with the lights on. None of it is a theorem, and I'm not
going to dress it up as one. It's why I care, and I'm putting it here, after
the main text's proofs and apart from them, so you can check that none of it got into them.

Physics has a word for the moment a question closes: \emph{measurement}. And the people who thought
hardest about it keep describing it in this book's shape. They ran together for me until I put
them on one picture. Flip a coin in a crowded room. Before it lands, it could go either way. After,
it's settled, somebody chalks it on a board, and the result gets copied out into the world, the
light and the air, so many times that it can't be taken back and everybody who looks agrees. There are five
pieces: the question, the landing, the chalk mark, the copies, the agreeing. Each person leans on a
different one. Zurek, in Section~\ref{sec:pointer}, leans on the copies. Rovelli's coin has to hit
the ground, so his piece is the landing.

Niels Bohr, the Danish physicist whose institute in Copenhagen was where quantum mechanics got
argued into shape, leans on the mark. In a 1954 talk he said seeing anything at that scale depends
on an apparatus that works irreversibly, like permanent marks on a photographic plate: a door that
swings one way. I found that line quoted in a recent paper and haven't seen the page in Bohr's book
myself. John Wheeler, the Princeton physicist who made the name ``black hole'' stick, went further in a 1989 talk
in Tokyo and leaned on the question: every physical thing gets its existence from yes-or-no
questions answered and registered, boiled down to ``it from bit.'' As I read him, the coin has no
face until something asks and something writes the answer down. How literally he meant that, I can't
tell. And Peirce, way before any of them, leans on the agreeing: the kind of settling worth trusting
is the kind that has to answer to everybody. Laid out like that, they pair up. Bohr and Rovelli lean
on a step that only goes one way, in the plate and in the coin. Zurek and Peirce lean on many
onlookers who agree, one with light and one with people.

Lay that next to everything in this book and the parts line up: a check that could have come out either
way, a result that's now settled, a price paid in forgetting or in fresh states, a record that stays. I suspect that
isn't a coincidence. I suspect the event this book prices on a machine is the same kind of event
physics calls a measurement, showing up in a different place. The forgetting is my step. Bohr only
says irreversible, and getting from a record that stays to a merge or to fresh states is Part~I's counting of states. Push
on it and it gives at Zurek, for the reason Section~\ref{sec:pointer} gave: copying onto fresh light
merges nothing and uses up fresh states, which is Bennett's measurement that owes no floor. So physics' own word lands on both sides of the line between Bennett and
Rovelli: the chalk on the paying side, the copies on the borrowing side. The landing I'd put
with the chalk, and when Section~\ref{sec:narrowing} pushes on Rovelli's paper it slides toward the
borrowing side, the side of finding out. So two pieces already stick out, and I'll leave them
sticking out. Which picture a settling on a
machine matches is part of the suspicion, and the suspicion doesn't settle it. That's as far as I'll
take it here: a suspicion.

John Bell asks for precision in those words. He was the Northern Irish physicist at CERN whose 1964 theorem is behind
the CHSH check of Appendix~\ref{sec:chsh}. In 1990 Bell wrote a short,
furious essay against the word ``measurement,'' with a list of words he said have no place in a
physics that wants to be precise. On the list: system, apparatus, environment, irreversible,
information, and measurement, which he called the worst of all. I used half of them in the last few
paragraphs. To turn that suspicion into a physical claim, each of those words would need a
specified meaning and a connection to the device. The proofs here work with the models and
machines I have defined; the physical applications state the further premises they use.

\part[The results together]{Results\\together}
\clearpage

Part~III followed one example machine from its first step to the host running a guest. Bring those
pieces back to the bench. The holding count says what the arrows must do. The price
rule says what goes on the ledger. The window says which of those distinctions a
reader receives. The earned chain says how the flag got there.

%===========================================================================
\section{The claims and their conditions}
\label{sec:falsification}
%===========================================================================

Start with a box holding an answer. I need to know which full states count as holding it,
which moves keep it there, and whether the box has finitely many such states. Those choices
make the counting argument possible. Add a price on merging and the same count gives a
charge. Give a reader only the tabletop picture and there is another question: how much of
that event reaches the reader?

Here I put the connections in one place. The statements and their proofs stay in the
chapters where I built them; this is a way to follow what each piece contributes to the next.

\subsection{Keeping a distinction}

\emph{One next state.} Follow one deterministic rule from a start. Until the first repeated
state, every visit is new. At the first repeat, either you have returned to the start, or two
different predecessors have reached the same state. From then on the rule repeats the same
successors. Those are the three columns of the step law
(Section~\ref{sec:what-a-chair-is}). A choice between several successors would change the
argument at precisely the point where you follow the next arrow.

\emph{A finite place to hold the answer.} Suppose a move keeps every YES state at YES and
brings a NO state in. With $K$ YES states, those states and the entrant give $K+1$ sources
landing in $K$ places. Two arrows meet. The entering arrow need not be one of them: a chain
can run through the held states before meeting a fixed endpoint.
Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} gives the general count and its attaining constructions.

Each part of that picture matters. An endless strip can keep moving to a different YES
state forever. A two-state toggle keeps the arrows one-to-one by turning YES back to NO.
A finite permanent holder has neither route available. For a single rule, if its entered
holding run were to repeat while remaining one-to-one, cancelling the equal successors
backwards would identify the unfinished entrant with a held state. That is why the
one-to-one alternative needs a fresh configuration at every later tick.

Section~\ref{sec:what-a-chair-is} also follows finite noisy and unitary systems using their
own preservation conditions. For a table of chances, both row and column sums enter the
count. For a unitary map, preservation of inner products supplies it. For the zoom argument,
keep track of the full states behind the coarse picture. The finite collection being
counted must remain closed under the step; otherwise the next tick can move into a state
the count left out.

\subsection{Putting a price beside the arrows}

A graph tells you which states meet. A price schedule tells you what a move costs. The finite
holding count and a rule charging merging moves together force a charge on a permanent
raise. Once the one-step toll is part of the machine, every run from NO to YES includes a
charged crossing; adding nonnegative costs gives the universal floor
(Section~\ref{sec:toll}).

There are two useful schedules to keep separate. Charge by instruction name and repeating
that instruction has the same price even after the flag is up. Charge by the source state
and the schedule can ask whether this particular step raises the flag. The floor together
with a ceiling of one unit per raise selects the latter charge, one for a raise and zero
otherwise. When the same instruction performs the raise and the later idle, this
state-sensitive policy lets the raise pay once and the idle stay free.
The first is the cost signature in the basic definition; the second is the
broader interface used in the source-charge and exact-pricing comparisons.

The three-card example makes the choice visible. Call the states blank, once and twice;
once and twice read YES. A move sending once to twice and fixing blank and twice merges two states
without raising the reading. A merge price charges it. A raise price leaves it free. The
chosen reading and the chosen schedule specify which question the ledger answers.

With a halving allowance on each move, the list of possible starts can shrink only as far
as the accumulated allowance permits. The entropy form additionally counts a supplied
probability distribution. A physical heat reading uses Landauer's premise for the device
and process being described. These are the successive inputs to the arguments in
Sections~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} and~\ref{sec:narrowing}.

The four-state demon shows the distinction between learning and wiping. MEASURE copies
onto a blank page reversibly; applied again it can return that page. WIPE sends different
page contents to the same blank state. The first operation uses the prepared page; the
second merges the alternatives. The price rule can therefore charge them differently.

\subsection{What reaches the reader}

Put a raising step and a quiet step behind a window that shows the same before-and-after
pictures for both. Any price computed only from those pictures gives the same answer for
both. It cannot both charge the raise and leave the quiet step free. Let the window show
the raise and that ambiguity disappears (Section~\ref{sec:windows}).

The same argument applies to a question about an earlier value. If a good and a bad value
leave the same complete retained observation, a reader of that observation has one input
for two required answers. Inspect the value while it is live and retain an adequate answer,
or retain the distinctions the later questions will need. Which questions are allowed
determines how much must survive.

A permanent base-driven record has the latch form: it switches on at the first occurrence
of an event and stays on (Section~\ref{sec:latch}). A toggle changes that task by allowing
the record to fall; a hidden clock changes what drives it. For an ordered growing record,
threshold readings give the row of cups in Section~\ref{sec:direction}. A chain with $k$
cups can have at most $k+1$ different arrangements if cups only turn up.

Entitlement adds a particular claim and the evidence permitting a later step to use it.
Its index count uses a covering tree whose depth the paid steps cover. The uncovered
narrowing example in Section~\ref{sec:entitlement} shows why that connection belongs in
the statement: narrowing a candidate list alone supplies no such bound on the ledger.

\subsection{The concrete machine and its guests}

From a clean start, only CERTIFY raises the flag, only a successful COMMIT supplies its
channel, and only a successful CHECK supplies the matching fact. The counter's edition
must still match at commitment. Following those entry points backwards gives the earned
chain and its minimum charge of three (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}). A claim such as
``this counter is at least zero'' passes everywhere and still uses the same three acts.
The flag records their occurrence; the claim says what they established.

The ledger starts at zero and each step adds its scheduled price. Induction on the run
then gives both its total and its uniqueness: two ledgers following that same start and
schedule agree before the first step and still agree after each addition
(Section~\ref{sec:counter}).

The universal program follows a guest through matching points, preserving its halting,
flag and ledger guarantees (Appendix~\ref{sec:universal-host}). The presented-machine
interpreter extends this to guests with computable transitions, prices and readings, with
the surcharge stated in Appendix~\ref{sec:presented-universal}. Each interpreter earns its
own flag through the host's instructions.

\emph{The computational slice.} The lift in Appendix~\ref{sec:every-model} gives a universal
base a check language, room for a fact, a channel and the earned operations. While the lift
is live, base moves follow the base and the panel leaves its working value alone. A failed
check can trap the lift. Later free moves then freeze, so keeping that failure globally
invisible would also hide the change in subsequent computation. The live-state clause is
what connects this lift to its stated slice.

The Thiele-complete interfaces specify free base moves and a record that separates runs
with the same working observation. The clock and silent-machine examples show what each
requirement contributes; the four independence witnesses separate the clauses. Interface
and instruction choice also explain why the one-rule presentation and its macro version
have different coverage.

Independent components compose by interleaving their moves. Each move changes its own
component, so the pair's cost is the sum of the two component costs. Keep each component's
own move order fixed and every interleaving has the same final state. Nesting instead follows a guest through a host map;
the record-order condition carries the guest's crossings into the host's accounting
(Appendix~\ref{sec:parts}).

\subsection{The diagonal and the worked models}

The diagonal argument supplies the contradiction inside a substrate that can represent
the candidate's flip and has the stated recursion property. Its fixed point makes the
proposed decision disagree with itself. An outside calculation of the natural-number
example does not supply an inside program for that substrate. Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}
and the appendices state the input conventions separately for the natural-number family,
L, the counter programs and the host.

The protocol examples in Section~\ref{sec:models} isolate particular mechanisms: finality,
a charge on commitment, an attestation window, an inclusion proof and a bounds check. Their
statements follow the operations in those fragments. The pointer thesis then asks why
certification is the event to choose. It proposes a connection to records copied and relied
on by independent parties. The counting and window arguments apply to any record meeting
their premises; the thesis supplies the proposed reason for this choice.

The game checks in Appendix~\ref{sec:chsh} give another worked construction. Four fixed
bits yield the classical bound by the displayed sign calculation. The matrix arguments
relate contraction, positive semidefiniteness and the score bound. The integer checker
implements its specified test on tallies with every pair sampled. Its earned chain connects
a raised flag to that test. The pinned-matrix test and the completion test ask different
questions: the appendix's all-ones and PR-box examples make the difference visible.

Those connections are what the book has built: a count, a schedule, an observation and an
earned record, with instructions carrying them through actual runs.

\subsection{Sources and contributions}

Appendix~\ref{sec:whats-mine} sets out the sources and contributions item by item. Here is
the short form: the earlier results I use, the statements proved here, and the constructions
that put them to work.

\emph{Borrowed, with names.} As \hyperref[sec:point]{The point} warned, I usually had the hunch first and
found these names after, and that order doesn't make any of it mine. Everything in
Section~\ref{sec:structure} and the Afterword (every
source is cited where it's used), the category theory (Eilenberg, Mac Lane) included. Minsky's
two-counter machines and the constructions that prove their halting undecidable and compile
computable functions into them (Forster, Larchey-Wendling and coauthors). Turing, Church, Kleene, Rice, Cantor, Gödel, the
diagonal pattern, Lawvere's unification, and later detailed developments:
Michael Norrish's, Mario Carneiro's, and Yannick Forster, Fabian Kunze and Gert Smolka's. Bell, CHSH, Tsirelson, Stephanie Wehner's semidefinite proof of Tsirelson's bound (2006), NPA, Landau,
Masanes, Fine, the elliptope, and Echenim and Mhalla's detailed treatment of Tsirelson's bound. Landauer, Bennett, Szilard,
Maxwell, and their critics. The potential method (Tarjan) and later treatments (Nipkow, Charguéraud and Pottier), Lamport's clocks, Floyd and Hoare. Gettier, Necula, Cook, Hartley,
Shannon, Rissanen, Zurek. The guarantee about every program: the reference monitor (Anderson),
execution monitors (Schneider), and monitors checked at every instruction and proved correct
(Azevedo de Amorim and coauthors). The counting under the permanence results: Poincaré's
recurrence, as Zermelo used it. The seL4 and CompCert discipline. The facts under the permanence results are Landauer's own example and Shannon's
bounds, and ``set a bit to one whatever it held'' is my way of saying his RESTORE TO ONE.

\emph{What I proved, each inside its stated interfaces,} is listed in the claims section (Section~\ref{sec:ledger}) with what each stands on.

\emph{Interpretation, which is mine and not proved.} That structure is what a computation
establishes and the toll is the right thing to price. That certification is the pointer
event. That the record axis ``belongs in the step.'' Those are proposals, with the arguments
I've given, and the proposals are where I'd aim first if I were you.

\section{The claim ledger}
\label{sec:ledger}
%===========================================================================

The full ledger, in the companion volume, lists everything this book claims, one line each, with what kind of claim it is and
where it lives; this section places the headline results. ``Proved'' means proved under the premises printed in that section, and nothing more.
If a line here ever says more than its section does, the section is right and the line is
wrong. ``Directly from the rules'' means the claim can be read off the stated
operations by checking their cases. ``Directly from the interface'' means its
requirements already include the claimed behavior. These claims are true, but
carry almost nothing beyond what those definitions already say. If you're counting results, count those
differently. I mark them so they don't pad the list, and where they're stated in the book they
carry the label \emph{observation}, with three exceptions: Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll}, part (3)
of Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-presented-surcharge}, and the parts of Theorem~\ref{thm:slice} its line names.

Ledger is a good word for it, and it's older than bookkeeping. Around 1400 a \emph{ledger} was a
book that lay permanently in one place, a big church breviary, say, from the old verb
\emph{leggen}, to lay; the account-book sense turns up in the 1500s. Staying put is
the job here too. The home sections are long and they wander, and this is the one place where
every claim lies still, so you can come back and find it where you left it.
\label{sec:assumptions}

The claims below are placed by where they sit in the model, with the status each carries and the premise it stands on. (S) is a structural theorem about the model or a stated machine, (C) a conditional result under a named premise no machine fact discharges, (R) a refutation by a named construction; the pointer criterion is a thesis. A2 is the toll's name in the mathematical specification; \texttt{neutral\_complete}, \texttt{thiele\_complete} and \texttt{landauer\_heat} are the Coq names of the two completeness definitions and the heat premise.

\section{Scope}
\label{sec:scope}
%===========================================================================

The definition asks for states, moves, readings and charges.
To use a result elsewhere, put that other system beside the drawing and match
the pieces. Which states carry the record? Which operation establishes it? What does the
reader see, and what does the price count?

The following comparisons work through those questions for heat, computation and the
choice of record. They show which further connections an application needs.

\emph{Physical interpretation of the counter.} Choose a start and a price schedule and the
ledger is determined on reachable states. To read it as a physical quantity, specify which
states carry information and how the scheduled charge relates to dissipation, under
physical premises that hold together. The permanent-certificate theorems
supply the first for an abstract finite machine with a permanent reading. The two premises
are shown able to hold together whenever every counted step costs at least one, and for a
one-bit reset. The small machine's unpriced steps merge states and are charged nothing, so its ledger is not a heat
meter for computing: whatever those merges cost the hardware is off the ledger, and the two
premises hold together for the record steps only (Section~\ref{sec:landauer}); and the calorimeter protocol shows that population
dynamics don't fix the energy scale. No joule value attaches to one unit of cost without thermal and
device premises (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}, Section~\ref{sec:landauer}).
Once you pick the start and the price list, the number is forced by arithmetic, and
it isn't energy. What I'd need before it could be is the list at the top of this paragraph.

\emph{Class separation.} The witnesses show specific windows losing specific fields. They don't
stop a conventional simulator from keeping those fields in its encoding. No separation of
standard complexity classes follows from the collisions (Section~\ref{sec:windows},
Section~\ref{sec:smallest}).
I'll be blunt about why I'm careful here. Whether P equals NP is one of the seven problems the
Clay Mathematics Institute put a million dollars on, at a meeting in Paris in May 2000. One of
the seven has been solved since, the Poincaré conjecture, by the mathematician Grigori Perelman, who posted the proof as preprints in 2002 and 2003. P versus NP
hasn't. If a two-state collision on my machine settled it, I'd be owed a million
dollars. Nobody owes me anything. A window that loses a field is a fact about that window. A
complexity class is a fact about what every possible program can do within a budget, and
nothing in these collisions reaches that far.

\emph{Trace initiality, and what it doesn't settle.} The universal property of the trace fold is
about evaluating lists of instructions: pick where a target starts, and there's exactly one
way to fold a list into it (Section~\ref{sec:counter}). The counter's uniqueness
assumes a schedule. Rise-only pricing assumes an event, and a reference count that says what
charging too much means (Section~\ref{sec:windows}). Those results make the construction precise. None of them
shows that the schedule I chose, or the event I chose, is physically necessary.

\emph{Other observables.} Certification is one worked example. A family of other observations
could turn up other structural laws, but each would need its own events, its own evidence,
and its own cost rules, justified on their own terms. The window and oracle
results are about
what specific maps
keep, and nothing more.

\emph{Program predicates versus state observations.} The state-level collision (Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s wall) and
the program-level diagonal (Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}'s wall) live in different domains. Linking them would take a
theorem of its own. The nat family and L (Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}) keep their explicit
quantifiers and representability premises.

\emph{Entitlement bounds.} The count is handed its tree and its covering, along with the
payment condition. It doesn't dig the tree out of an arbitrary run, and it isn't a Shannon bound
on every trace (Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}). On every certified Thiele-complete machine the payment is
the record moves, each costing exactly one, and a floor that takes no tree exists when the questions
are the run's own CHECKs; but its answers are taken at the rivals as they start, a branch that costs nothing can
still narrow, the lists, tree and fibres are supplied except in the worked members,
and the covering can't be dropped. The search through $n$ bits is capped at 16 questions by the
machine's fact table, and the time tax is a lower bound for programs of INC and DEC only. Nothing here
extends it to every certified Thiele-complete machine (Section~\ref{sec:part3-on-machine}).

\emph{Quantum behaviour.} The fixed-matrix equivalence is about one completion with zero
marginals and zero within-party moments. The elliptope lets the within-party moments move,
at the level of correlators. A completion of the correlators is realised by actual measurements, by the construction in
Appendix~\ref{sec:chsh-derivation}. A full behaviour, with each room's own odds prescribed as
well, asks for more, and the construction doesn't deliver those extra probabilities. A sound
check isn't complete for those bigger sets, and the elliptope decider is mathematics on the
page, not a part of the small machine (Appendix~\ref{sec:chsh}).

\emph{The record axis.} The proved structural result is: a permanent record driven by a base
computation is a latch on an event; on a finite machine its write merges states; and the named
windows don't recover it. Certification is one instance. No theorem
selects it as the unique event every system must record (Section~\ref{sec:latch}, Section~\ref{sec:pointer}). A finite monotone
multi-valued record decomposes into threshold latches. One Boolean latch can't hold it.
Revocation, including revocation priced from the other side as in Casper, lies outside the
permanent-record axis; a price on revocation doesn't transfer to a price on the write (Section~\ref{sec:models}).
Probabilistic records don't inherit the uniqueness result either. Two honest random records
can have the same branches and the same charges and still give those branches different
weights, one choosing evenly and one two to one, so the schedule doesn't fix the
probabilities. And no single deterministic
latch explains a record that can branch both ways from the same observation.
Weak base equivalence is defined and is an equivalence; no two of the three bases of
Definition~\ref{def:u11-concrete-bases}, and none of them and the small machine, are related by it in
this book, and the latch form holds on each separately, so it doesn't tell
them apart (Section~\ref{sec:latch}).
Records that can come back down lie outside all of this: they're limit computability's, and
Section~\ref{sec:latch} points at Ershov's ladder.

\emph{Who it's safe against.} Every guarantee about the record is about programs: any list of
instructions, run from a clean start on a step that does what its definition says, one writer
stepping at a time. That covers the buggy program and the hostile one. It doesn't cover whoever
sets the start (a snapshot put back, a table loaded with facts nobody checked), a reset or a
power cycle, the wire that carries the report, someone who
flips the flag with a probe, the tools that built the step, or a second writer that changes a
counter without bumping its edition. Those are the operator, the device and the tool chain,
and they're outside this fence. A record read by someone who didn't watch it being made is only
as good as their reason to believe the box that shows it. The ways across that I know of, a quote
over measured state and a proof that travels on its own, are in Section~\ref{sec:windows} and
Section~\ref{sec:models}, and this book builds neither.
What the guarantee gives inside the fence is safety: no program forges the chain. Availability is
a different promise, and it isn't given. A hostile program can put the trap up or fill the table,
and after that nothing useful gets done. The mathematical machine uses whole numbers, which never
overflow, so versions and the ledger grow without bound. A build with fixed-width counters,
versions or ledger has to stop before any of them wraps, failing safe with the trap up, because a
wrapped version could make an old fact look live again and a wrapped ledger would fall.
Starting, restoring, resetting and that overflow stop belong to the implementation, and none of
them is proved here.

\emph{The diagonal on the machine.} What's proved for the small machine's programs is that
halting is undecidable in the reduction sense of Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-undecidable}, for them and for the universal program
(Section~\ref{sec:smallest}; for the universal program, Appendix~\ref{sec:universal-host}). L has its recursion theorem, Rice and halting by proof
(Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}). On the host machine, the one with a counter for every number, Rice's
theorem holds for properties that depend on everything a program ends with (every register, the
table, the channel, the trap, the ledger and the flag; the line number and the versions are left out), for
programs run on an input in register 1; s-m-n holds with no premise on register 2; and Kleene's recursion theorem
holds for the transformations a host program carries out on numbers, with a fixed point that agrees with
its image on stopping, register 0, the trap latch, the ledger, the flag, the number of facts and whether
the channel is empty; for some of these transformations no fixed point agrees on every register. On the
two-counter machine itself Rice's theorem is proved on every input, with facts compared by what they're
about, their versions left out of the comparison; Kleene's is proved with inputs written as powers of two and refuted
with plain inputs (Appendix~\ref{sec:small-diagonal}).

\emph{The five models.} Each is a fragment transcribed from a specification, with a named
theorem and a named limit: the Casper transcription has no deposits or fork choice; the gas
fragment omits the refund cap; the attestation fragment has no signatures; the transparency
verifier covers control flow and leaves collision resistance out; the proof-carrying checker is
a
three-instruction memory-bounds language. None is a claim about the real system beyond its fragment
(Section~\ref{sec:models}).

\emph{The machine.} Part III has one small machine, with the hosts that run it in an appendix,
and this paragraph is its fence. The small machine of
Section~\ref{sec:smallest} (two counters, six instruction kinds) is where commitments are
earned: from a clean start, a raised flag went through a passing check, a commitment and a certification of the
same claim, nothing is forged, and the cheapest such run adds exactly three to the ledger, a price reached
by a check that could have failed (the step doesn't police trivial checks: a check that can't
fail certifies for three too). It's also
where universality is proved, by matching Minsky's two-counter machines step for step and
using the halting reduction of Forster, Larchey-Wendling and coauthors. It's certified Thiele-complete under a
definition every clock-style machine fails, and every machine meeting that definition hides its
record and ledger from its own window. The universal Thiele machine for the small machine's
programs (Definition~\ref{def:universal-thiele}) is a host with the small machine's instruction
kinds and more counters, running one fixed program, $U$, with no guest step built
in: it runs every program of the small machine from every clean start $\mathrm{start}(x, y)$, halts when the guest halts, raises
its own flag by its own check, commit and certificate if and only if the guest's flag rises somewhere in the guest's run,
and keeps a ledger equal to the guest's at every matching point. With one paid move added, one
fixed program, $U_P$, runs every computably presented Thiele machine: its step, prices and
reading computed by programs, the reading decided on every state, the run fixed by a driver. The
host halts when the guest stops, its flag is the latch of the guest's reading, raised on its own
earned chain whose claim is that reading, and its ledger is the guest's plus a surcharge of at
most two when the reading starts at no, a surcharge no program on that host, run from a clean start, can avoid when the guest certifies
with its whole ledger below three. A machine whose reading no program decides is outside. A simpler
host with a guest step built in runs guests by construction and keeps a mirror of the guest's
flag; its ledger only covers the guest's. The small machine's check price is flat, its fact table holds sixteen,
and its certificate is historical (Section~\ref{sec:smallest} lists the rest).

\emph{The comparison machines.} The bases I put the latch on are fragments too. The register
machine of Section~\ref{sec:latch} is the one with indirect addressing in
Definition~\ref{def:u11-concrete-bases}, and Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-four-bases} is about it. The reversible result
(Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-reversible}) covers any base whose step is injective, and on a finite
state space says only that no injective step raises a permanent reading.
None is a theorem about real memories or full reversible languages. The cost-semantics
results are local correspondences, short of full cost-framework embeddings: the trace's cost is a
writer cost and a grade, and the toll is the potential method with one potential (Section~\ref{sec:counter}).
Nobody's whole type system gets embedded either.

\emph{Outward consequences.} I looked for results about real systems that would need the record
axis. What's proved are the five fragments of Section~\ref{sec:models}, each a transcription
with its own named limit, and none is a theorem about the deployed system. Stronger candidates
would need protocol or hardware semantics I haven't formalised, and I've proved nothing about
them. So none of this yields a new outside result that both needs the record axis and is ready
to use.

\emph{Where each result lives} is the premise column of the claims section (Section~\ref{sec:ledger}).

\emph{Models and processes.} For a model of computation written down as states, a step and a reading
that stays, what keeping takes is a theorem about the model, not a thesis. The thesis in the
Conclusion is only the tie from a physical process to such a description. Here's how far the
theorems reach, and where they stop. A step that gives every state one next state, on any number of
states: a run that raises a reading and keeps it up merges two of its own states or never visits a
state twice (Proposition~\ref{prop:heat-or-room}), and with finitely many states reading yes the
move that raises it merges (Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges},
Proposition~\ref{prop:raise-needs-room}). That takes in a Turing machine or a counter machine stepping
by its program, and a cellular automaton stepping its whole grid at once. A model that halts has no
next state at its halt, and slips past with no merge; give the halt a next state and the run is one
rule again, so keeping the answer merges or takes fresh states, and with the halted state stepping to
itself the step onto it is a merge (Theorem~\ref{thm:halting-hole}). Steps by chance on finitely many
states: one whose chances into each state add to one, which is what keeping the even spread takes,
never enters a finite set nothing leaves from a state outside it (Theorem~\ref{thm:noisy-chairs}). A
unitary step that keeps a finite-dimensional part of the space keeps the part at right angles to it,
so a state at right angles to the kept part stays at right angles (Theorem~\ref{thm:quantum-chairs}).

A model whose step may offer several next states, or none, comes in too: a nondeterministic machine,
a lambda term reduced at whichever redex you like, a rewriting system, a proof system read as
derivations made one rule at a time. Nothing earlier in the book is stated for such steps, so here are the
two arguments. The first is the pigeonhole of Proposition~\ref{prop:raise-needs-room} on one choice
of next state, and the second is the walk back of Proposition~\ref{prop:heat-or-room}, stopped at
the raise. First, suppose only finitely many states read yes, none of them can step to a state
reading no, each has at least one next state, and some state reading no can step to one of them.
Pick one next state for each yes-state, and the outside state's step into the yes-states: that's one
more step than there are yes-states, each leaving a different state and landing on a yes-state, so
two land on the same one, and two different states share a next state. That needs the yes-states
finite; Hilbert's hotel, everybody moving up one, keeps a reading with no two states sharing a next
state. Second, along any one run, however its choices fall, take the step where a reading goes up,
and suppose it stays up for the rest of that run. If the run is in one state at two times after the
raise, step both times back together. They can't stay equal past the raise, because the state at the
raise reads no and every later one reads yes, so at the first pair that differs, two different
states of that very run step onto one. So after the raise the run merges or never repeats a state,
on any number of states. Before the raise it can come back to a state and then leave it for good
with no merge, which one rule can't do. A normal form, with no next state, is the halt again: a reading
kept by stopping is kept with no merge, as Theorem~\ref{thm:halting-hole} says. For such steps
the first argument says little by itself: in the lambda calculus every term $N$ is one step from two
different terms, $(\lambda x.x)N$ and $(\lambda z.N)M$ with $z$ not free in $N$, so two states
sharing a next state is no news there, and the second argument is the one that carries weight. And
when a step can branch, a shared next state doesn't by itself bunch the crowd up, since a branch
spreads it out again; with chances on the steps and finitely many states, the count that does is
Theorem~\ref{thm:noisy-chairs}.

Where they stop. Steps in continuous time have no next state to count, and nothing here covers them.
Steps by chance where endlessly many states read yes, and unitary steps whose kept part has endlessly
many dimensions, get none of the finite results above, and the bilateral shift keeps a reading with
no merge, a fresh state every step. What still reaches them is the run: a unitary step is one rule,
so its runs are Proposition~\ref{prop:heat-or-room}'s, and one run of steps by chance is a run the
second argument covers. And a truth isn't a process at all: that a statement is provable is a fact
with no step in it, and the theorems are about a run that derives it. What they give is the merge or
the fresh states. The heat stays Landauer's premise.

\emph{What I'm proposing beyond that.} A way of describing computation in which the
relations a computation carries live in the state, what each move does to them lives in the
step, and a price list is one part of the description, not an afterthought. The permanent
record is the one case I took apart all the way. The pointer thesis asks whether certifying
is the thing that deserves that record in the systems it talks about, and it can be wrong
without touching the latch or the window arguments, which never use it.

Underneath that is a question about which distinctions a description of a computation
ought to keep. The constructions show particular ways of keeping some, and what follows once
you do, under premises I've printed. What that's worth depends on what you need the
description to answer. A program log with a proof about its updates may recover the
required distinctions. A host can instead enforce those updates through every guest
program. A system may prevent an act with a wall, penalise it afterwards, or charge it at
the step. Comparing those choices means following what each one guarantees for the task.

%===========================================================================

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
%===========================================================================

Put the blank cell, the triangle, the cups and the two computers back on the table. The cell
went from a specified blank state to a 0 and stayed under its write-once rule.
The rule merges blank and zero; a heat floor still needs the input preparation
and the thermal premises. Turning the
triangle preserves relations you can check with your fingers. Turning a cup records
an act; a row of cups can distinguish stages that one cup cannot. The two computers
can leave the same answer while differing in what they did to reach it. In each
case I had to say what the things were, which moves were allowed, which relations
survived, and what my way of looking could tell apart.

Part I started at the bottom, with the cell. On any machine run by one rule, every step lands on a
fresh state, merges two into one, or goes round a loop, and a run that raises a reading that stays
either merges somewhere or never repeats a state, so it's paid in a merge or in fresh states, alongside the model-dependent thermal bounds, more the faster it goes. The counting needs nothing but one rule and a reading that stays. A single 0 written on a blank cell is already a merge, and every
zoom pays the same way. Then the model got an exact form: five parts, one rule, one theorem you proved at the
table, what keeping takes written into a step. Then the rule stopped being only my preference.
With finitely many yes-states and a flag that stays up, the fresh states run out, every move that raises the flag merges, and under the merge-pricing rule the toll follows. The
collision belongs to the instruction, over the states it's allowed to act on; the state that just
came in needn't be one of the two that collide. Turning that into heat takes a spread over inputs
and Landauer's premise on top, its critics named; from a start somebody already knows, the premise
puts no floor under it, because that prepared distribution has no entropy to remove; the step
can dissipate under the stated thermal-model assumptions. The toll is a
derivation under three premises you can refuse one at a time, each with the machine that walks
past it built; what keeping takes, underneath it, isn't. Learning borrows: copying onto a blank page merges
nothing, the copy can be handed back, and the page is paid for when it's wiped. Committing makes a
record that can't be handed back, so it pays. That's as far as physics goes in this book, and I've tried to keep it exactly
that far.

Part II gave the triangle and the cups their words: structure is relations among things, kept under
the changes you choose, carried by whatever stuff happens to be there, relative to a
frame. A partition turned out to be the smallest sorting by the ruler I picked, and a cell that goes from blank to 0 and stays is that smallest sorting, one yes-or-no question, kept. And making
a grouping, keeping it, checking it and standing behind it came apart into four different
acts. So the question became how an account of
computation could carry what keeping the cell's 0 takes, and the difference between those acts, in its step.

The rest of Part II was the logic, and what it earned comes next, in the order it was earned. The counter
is arithmetic once the schedule is chosen. A window in which a raising step and a quiet one
look the same can't price the raise exactly, by a fact about functions far older than the
machine. Entitlement is defined as an object, a checked relation, and a paid event; given
lists, a tree and a covering somebody supplies, a run that paid a charged step for every level
of the tree has paid for the index bits it commits to (that count doesn't show a run has to pay them, the run doesn't recover the tree, the lists count repeats, and the index bits aren't the questions anybody asked); when the run makes the narrowing itself, every candidate dropped was dropped by a test the run paid for, and the index bits are at most $k$ times the cost when each test keeps a $2^{-k}$ share; on
every certified Thiele-complete machine the same count, for a run from a clean start, is a theorem about its record moves, with the earned
chain inside the run, and the count can't do without the covering; and it
is a license to lean on a claim. It doesn't prove the claim true.
Insight, in the sense the toll prices, is a distinction made to stay. A feeling doesn't count. Its floor
is flat: at least one, however deep. The claim behind the flag is something a check could
have refused, and in the bare model nothing makes the commit wait for the check. Over any base,
a base-driven record is a latch, with two unforced choices, the event and the price list; ``only one
substrate'' is false and ``one structure, many price lists'' is true once the event is fixed. No procedure whose flip the substrate itself can represent decides the shortcut predicate, given a
recursion theorem, by the same diagonal that broke Frege's floor, and the machine's answer is
to record the commitment. It leaves the judgement unautomated.

Part III built an example that meets the definition. The small machine's state ties a checked claim to an edition of a
counter, and its step uses the tie: change the counter and the old check no longer lets
you commit. So from a clean start a raised flag needs a passing check, a commitment about
the same edition and a certificate, in that order. A cost of three is enough, and no such run
pays less. Those are facts about the example, the check that can't fail included,
and its two-counter base is universal under Minsky's packing.

The universal programs ask whether those relations survive somebody else's machine doing
the work. On the host with more counters, $U$ runs the small machine's programs from clean
starts, halts when they halt with their answers, earns its own flag exactly when the guest
raises one, and matches the ledger wherever the two line up. With PAY added, $U_P$ runs
every computably presented Thiele machine, latches the guest's reading through its own
earned chain, and carries the guest's ledger to within the stated surcharge: at most two at
the raise when the reading starts at no. The theorems say which states match; the companion
volume, in its section on running it, says how long this particular build takes to get there, which is a long time.

Then I changed the base and joined machines up, to see what carried over. The panel bolts onto any box with a universal base, with the boxes it won't fit named
(Appendix~\ref{sec:every-model}). Two machines side by side need both records kept; one
total loses which side did the work. Hand-offs and nested runs each come with conditions
of their own (Appendix~\ref{sec:parts}). Every one of those constructions makes you say
which relation survives the change and which is lost, and that saying is the work.

Then came a check worth earning, the two-player game with an integer test whose
pass forces Tsirelson's bound for the tally it's handed. Of five record disciplines I
modelled in fragments, one charges a fee at the write, and which event to record is a thesis, with
its refutations listed. And then came what the counter has to do with physics, which is less than
the name Landauer might suggest. Two facts about the machine sit where they belong. Its unpriced
steps merge states, because that's what forgetting scratch work is; whatever those merges cost the
hardware is off the ledger, so the toll on this machine comes from the record layer's
merge premise, with no finiteness premise on the whole machine; the only finiteness in it is the
flag's two readings. And a check that cannot fail still certifies for three,
because the step charges for the act, and the entitlement count says what the claim bought.

Part~IV brings those pieces together (Section~\ref{sec:falsification}). A finite permanent
holder has to merge; the named price rule puts that merger on a ledger; a window determines
which part of it a reader can recover. The example machine then supplies the earned path
from a passing check to commitment and certification. Each argument has its place in that
chain, and the constructions show how to carry it out.

Four contributions bring that chain into focus, each alongside the earlier work it builds on. First, the toll isn't only my
preference: on a finite machine a reading nothing turns off can only be turned on by a step that
merges states, so if merges are priced, raising it costs (Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges},
Observation~\ref{thm:toll-derived}); and on any machine a raise that merges nothing needs
endlessly many yes-states, so it pays in fresh states instead (Proposition~\ref{prop:raise-needs-room}). The counting under it is the finite cousin of the recurrence
argument Zermelo threw at Boltzmann in 1896, and the abstract merge price is motivated by Landauer's reset example. Identifying that
price with heat needs the further premises stated in Part I. Ouldridge and Wolpert (2023) had already put a physical price on that merge for finite
automata, and Li and Vitányi (1996) had already assumed a unit price on each irreversibly erased
bit in a model of computation, and Demaine and his coauthors (2016) a price on instructions that
destroy bits, so what's here is the toll such a price forces on a reading that stays. Second, a window that shows a raising step and a quiet one the same can't price the
raise exactly (Observation~\ref{thm:shadow-price}); that a price computed from what a window shows
can't tell apart two steps the window shows the same is elementary, and what's here is the
pricing form. Third, a record driven by the
computation that never switches off is a latch on one event, over any base
(Observation~\ref{thm:u11-latch}); latches and history variables are old, and the theorem covers
only records that never come down. Beside it, built rather than new, sit the definition of Thiele-complete, which any universal base
meets once marks are added (Section~\ref{sec:complete}), and the slice under it: a computer with a
move for each two-counter instruction is what's left of a certified Thiele-complete machine with
its record layer forgotten, blind to the record and the ledger, and every Thiele-complete machine
leaves one through its window (Theorem~\ref{thm:slice}). That forgetting a layer gives the runs back,
where the step doesn't read it, is the ghost-code erasure of Section~\ref{sec:counter}; what's here is
that the forgotten layer still earns its record, and that what's left can't see it. It's a theorem
about boxes with a universal base, and it uses no equivalence between models; the one that carries a
box to the other models is imported (Theorem~\ref{thm:lift-models}). Fourth, a record that's priced, and on the small machine
earned (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-cert-earned}), under the move of guaranteeing something about
every program. That move isn't mine at all. It's the reference monitor's (Anderson, 1972),
made precise for monitors that watch a run (Schneider, 2000), and proved for monitors
checked at every instruction (Azevedo de Amorim and coauthors, 2015). What I put together under
it is built, and its idea isn't new: the check bound to the edition it looked
at, the toll charged on top, and universal programs that carry both to every program of the small
machine and to every computably presented Thiele machine, earning their own flag as they go.
Appendix~\ref{sec:whats-mine} sorts all four with sources.

And there are two things I'd point at if you asked how far the proofs reach. Neither is a fifth new
thing.

In the game: an integer check on eight counts forces a five-by-five matrix to be positive
semidefinite, and from there the Tsirelson bound follows, and the chain never once reaches for
physics. There's no Hilbert space in it, no operators, no observables. The route through the matrix is the
first rung of a ladder Navascués, Pironio and Acín built in 2007. None of that route is mine, and
the semidefinite road to Tsirelson's bound is older than that. What's here is the check that runs in
whole numbers, and the proved link from ``the check passed'' to the bound. It's algebra you can
follow line by line. It's algebra and nothing more, because nothing in the definitions or
the argument ties the counts or the matrix to any physical device. And on the small machine's host a raised flag can stand on that
check: from a clean start a raised flag contains a passing CHECK of the packed counts, a COMMIT and
a CERTIFY, and the check passes exactly when every pair was sampled and the five-by-five is
positive semidefinite (Appendix~\ref{sec:chsh}).

In the model: the diagonal rules out a correct decider whenever its flip can be expressed
inside the substrate and the substrate supplies the fixed point; in L the fixed point is
proved from the reduction rules and the diagonal is Rice's theorem. On the small machine's host,
Kleene's recursion theorem and Rice's theorem are proved for its own programs, so the wall stands
there by proof, with its premise a theorem: no host program decides a property of what a program
computes that some program has and some lacks; such a property is undecidable in the reduction sense of Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-undecidable} (Appendix~\ref{sec:small-diagonal}).

There are things this book doesn't settle, by my count. It doesn't settle whether the toll is the \emph{right} thing to price; the
five real systems mostly built a
wall or a penalty for contradiction.
It doesn't settle whether certification is the pointer event. And it doesn't settle whether Landauer's critics
are right, which would leave every theorem standing and one premise unowned by the world.
And the question I'd most like someone to take from me: is there a smaller start than a
partition, by a ruler they can state? I said in Section~\ref{sec:structure} it would change this book, and it would.

One more claim ties the counting to the world, the way Church and Turing's ties computing to it,
and I'll state it as what it is, a thesis, the \emph{Thiele thesis}: every physical process that
computes with final answers has an exact description as a machine run by one rule, with a next
state for every state, computably presented (its states written as whole numbers, and its step,
its reading and its start for each input computed by programs that halt on every input), on
which the answer is a reading that no run from any input ever turns off, on inputs accepted and
rejected alike. No proof settles it, because ``a physical process that computes'' isn't a
mathematical object. A model of computation is one, and for a model written down as states, a step
and a reading that stays, what keeping takes needs no thesis: it's a theorem, and
Section~\ref{sec:scope} says how far it reaches. The thesis is about what a physical computation pays for what it keeps, which is Part~I, and not a
claim that its description run by one rule, with its program loaded, is a Thiele machine: by
Theorem~\ref{thm:slice}(4) that one-rule description is one only as a clock or with a reading that
never rises. Whether the computer underneath is a Thiele machine depends on the moves it offers
before a program is chosen, and with the program in the state a reading is a record, not a
simulated bit, exactly when it never comes down from any state
(Observation~\ref{obs:program-in-state}).
So the thesis is about physical processes and the one-rule descriptions of them. The Thiele Machine is the model that prices what such a description keeps; the thesis does not say a physical process is one.
There is an established route to a conditional physical description.
Gandy's work on mechanisms, restated by Arrighi and Dowek, starts with
homogeneity in space and time, finite local state sets, bounded propagation
and an initially finite departure from a preserved quiescent background.
Their classical theorem makes the resulting evolution computable. In the
construction, a cell consults finitely many neighbours through one finite
table; a finite active region can therefore be advanced by a program.
These are substantive modeling premises. They do not select a certification
event or a price in joules, and they are not asserted of every physical
system here. The quantum extension uses different premises.
See Arrighi and Dowek, \emph{The physical Church--Turing thesis and the
principles of quantum theory}, Section~2,
\url{https://arxiv.org/abs/1102.1612}.

What is proved sits on either side of the thesis. On one side, Part~I applies to
every such description on the states its inputs reach, where the answer never comes down: a run
that raises it merges two of its own states or never visits a state twice
(Proposition~\ref{prop:heat-or-room}). On the other, seen only through which inputs it accepts,
the thesis implies that every set a physical process accepts with final answers is one a
Turing machine can list. At that extensional level it has the physical
Church-Turing thesis's conclusion. Run the description from every input, a step at a time across all of them, and list an
input the first time its reading says yes; no run turns its answer off, so a yes seen once is
the answer. The other way, a set a Turing machine lists is accepted by the machine that searches
the list for its input and then steps from its halted configuration to itself, with the reading
``halted,'' which nothing turns off. This converse constructs a machine with
the same accepted set; it does not prove an exact state-by-state description
of the original physical process. Nothing about how the keeping is paid survives that view: the
same search held at its halt by a step to itself, which merges, or by a counter that goes on
ticking, which takes fresh states, accepts the same inputs. And ``final'' has to cover the
rejected inputs too. A machine that starts at no, reads yes while program $n$ is still running
